en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.
1. Saṃyutta Nikāya: Connected Discourses on the Path 1.
The Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga) 1–2.
Explanations of the Discourse on Ignorance and Others (Avijjāsuttādivaṇṇanā)
1–2. In the first [chapter] of the *Mahāvagga*, "preceding" (*pubbaṅgama*) means that it precedes in two ways: by way of co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*).
"For attainment" (*samāpattiya*) means for the entering into, for the acquisition of its own nature; the meaning is "for arising.

"Immediately following" (*anvadeva*) refers to shamelessness (*ahirika*) and lack of moral dread (*anottappa*); for this [shamelessness] is that which is established in the mode of non-shame, and that which is established in the mode of fearlessness.
Lack of moral dread (*anottappa*) arises simultaneously with that, together with it, and not without it; this is the meaning.

"Of one immersed in ignorance" (*avijjāgatassa*) means of one who has approached or is possessed of ignorance. "Wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhi*) is a view that is not according to reality, a view that does not lead to liberation.

"Occurs" (*pahoti*) means it exists or arises. In the case of wrong intention (*micchāsaṅkappa*) and the others as well, their state of being "wrong" is likewise by way of their not being according to reality and not leading to liberation.
It should be understood thus: these eight factors are called the "factors of wrongness" in the attainment of unwholesome states.
However, they are not all obtained simultaneously; rather, they are obtained at different moments.
How so? For when a consciousness associated with wrong view arises producing a bodily intimation, at that time—
There are six factors: wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, wrong concentration, and wrong action.
When it is dissociated from view, there are then five, excluding wrong view.
When those same two [factors] produce vocal intimation, then, in place of wrong action, those same [factors] are included together with wrong speech.
Six or five. This so-called livelihood (ājīva), when it becomes corrupted, is corrupted only in one or another of the doors of body and speech, not in the mind-door.
Therefore, when those very same thoughts, under the heading of livelihood, give rise to bodily and verbal intimation (viññatti), then bodily action is called wrong livelihood (micchājīva);
likewise, verbal action [is so called] by way of wrong livelihood. Thus, those very [thoughts]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*

Either six or five. However, when those consciousnesses arise without having produced a communicative intimation (viññatti), then there are either five—by way of wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, wrong mindfulness, and wrong concentration—or four, by way of wrong intention and so forth.
Thus, they are not all obtained at one moment; they are obtained at different moments.

In the bright fortnight, "true knowledge" (*vijjā*) refers to the knowledge that one is the owner of one's own kamma. Here too, its role as a precursor should be understood in two ways: by way of co-nascence and by way of decisive support.

"Moral shame" (*hirī-ottappa*) refers to both shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*). Among these, shame is established in the mode of modesty, while dread of blame is established in the mode of fear.
This is the summary here; for the detailed exposition, however, see the *Visuddhimagga*.
It has already been stated. "Of one who has reached true knowledge" (*vijjāgata*) means of one who has approached or is endowed with true knowledge (*vijjā*).
"The wise one" (*vidvasu*) means the learned, the sage. "Right view" (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is the view according to reality, the liberating view.

The same method applies to right action and the others as well. Thus, these eight factors constitute the attainment of wholesome states; however, at the moment of the mundane path (*lokiya-magga*), they do not all exist simultaneously.
They are obtained; however, they are obtained at the moment of the supramundane path (*lokuttara-magga*).
Moreover, these exist in the path of the first jhāna, whereas in the paths of the second jhāna and so forth, there are only seven factors, excluding right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*).
In this regard, one might say: "Because in the Mahā-Ṣaḷāyataniya Sutta of the Majjhima Nikāya, it is said of one who has become thus..."
The view he possesses is right view. The intention of one who has become such is right intention.
The effort of one who has become such is right effort. The mindfulness of one who has become such is right mindfulness.
The concentration of one who has become such is right concentration. Furthermore, previously for him...
“Bodily action, verbal action, and livelihood are perfectly pure. Therefore, it must be said that even the supramundane path consists of five factors.

Regarding this, one should ask: why do you not see this statement in that very same sutta: “In this way, this noble eightfold path reaches fulfillment through development”? As for what was stated there as “But previously for him,” that—
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the state of complete purity from the very day of going forth.
For it is shown that the bodily actions and so forth, which are pure from the day of going forth, become exceedingly pure at the moment of the supramundane path.
As for what is stated in the Abhidhamma, "At that time, however, there is a five-factored path," that refers to one [moment].
This was said in order to show another function. For at the time when one abandons wrong action and fulfills right action, at that time there is neither wrong speech nor wrong livelihood;
rather, right action is fulfilled within these very five factors of the path—right view, intention, effort, mindfulness, and concentration. Indeed, right action is established by way of abstinence.
It is called "fulfilling. The same principle applies to right speech and right livelihood as well. Thus, this was said in order to show this distinct function.
Furthermore, at the moment of the mundane path, there are only five factors; however, the abstinences (virati) are not fixed.
Therefore, instead of saying "sixfold," it is specifically stated as "fivefold": "And that, monks, which belongs to the noble mind, the taintless mind..."
“Bhikkhus, for one who possesses the noble path and is cultivating the noble path, the abstaining, desisting, refraining, abstinence, non-doing,
and non-performing of the three types of bodily misconduct— this, bhikkhus, is right action that is noble, taintless, and supramundane. Thus,
in many suttas such as the Mahācattālīsakasutta, [the Buddha describes] right action and the other factors of the supramundane path.
It should be understood that because its constituent factors are established, the supramundane path consists of exactly eight factors.
In this sutta, this eightfold path is described as a mixture of both mundane and supramundane. The second [sutta] is already stated in the *Kosalasaṃyutta*.
3. Commentary on the Sāriputta Sutta.

3. Regarding the third [verse], "O Bhante, all this... the Elder Ānanda, because he had not yet reached the pinnacle of the disciple’s knowledge of perfections (sāvakapāramīñāṇa), did not understand that even the entire holy life of the path (maggabrahmacariya) is obtained by relying upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta).
However, the Dhammasenāpati, standing at the pinnacle of the disciple’s knowledge of perfections, understood it; therefore, he spoke thus. For that very reason, the Blessed One [said to him]:
"Excellent, excellent! he said, giving his approval. 4.
Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Brāhmaṇa Sutta. 4.
Regarding the fourth [sutta]: "With a completely white chariot drawn by four mares" means with a chariot that is entirely white and yoked to four mares.
It is said that the entire chariot, including its wheels, felloes, and hubs, was encased in silver. This chariot is of two kinds:

the warrior-chariot and the ornamental chariot. Of these, the warrior-chariot is square in shape, not very large, and capable of carrying two or three persons. The ornamental chariot is large, long in length and broad in width.

And there, eight or ten people—such as the umbrella-bearer, the chowrie-waver, and the palm-leaf fan-bearer—are able to stand, sit, or lie down with ease upon its broad surface. This too is indeed a decorated chariot.
"The horses were white" means that those mares were naturally white in color. "White ornaments" refers to their adornments.

It was made of silver. As for the "white chariot," because it was encircled with silver and inlaid here and there with ivory work, the chariot itself was white according to the method already described. Regarding the "white covering":
while other chariots may have covers of lion skin, tiger skin, or yellow woolen blankets, this one did not; rather, it was as follows.
He was enveloped in thick, fine cotton cloth. "White rays" means that even the reins were encased in silver tubes.
"The white goad-stick" means that even the goad-stick was encased in silver.
"The white parasol" means that the parasol raised in the middle of the chariot was also white. "The white turban" refers to one eight finger-breadths in width.
The turban-band was made of silver and white. "White garments" means that the robes were also white, the color of a mass of foam.
Among them, the lower garment was worth five hundred [pieces], and the upper robe was worth a thousand.
"White sandals" refers to sandals worn by one who has set out on a road or is entering a forest; however, this person had mounted a chariot, therefore his—
It should be understood that this very ornament for the feet, called *pādālaṅkāra*, which was used by Rajata and is appropriate for him, was spoken of in this way.
"With a white yak-tail fan" means with a yak-tail fan made of white yak-tail hair and having a handle made of crystal.
Not only was his [appearance] white in this way, but that brahmin also smeared himself with white ointment, wore a white garland, and on his ten fingers...
His finger-rings, earrings, and other such ornaments were likewise made of silver.
His retinue of brahmins, numbering about ten thousand, was similarly dressed in white garments, with white unguents, garlands, and ornaments.
As for what was said regarding his departure from Sāvatthī, the following is the account of that departure: it is said that he...
Every month, once a month, he circumambulates the city, and a proclamation is made beforehand: "In this many days from now, he will circumambulate the city.
Hearing this, those who had not yet departed from the city do not depart;
and even those who have already departed, thinking, "We shall behold the splendor and majesty of one possessed of merit," [return].
They come. On the day the brahmin wanders through the city, they sweep the city streets early in the morning,
scatter sand, strew flowers with parched grain as the fifth ingredient,
set out full water-jars, raise plantain trees and banners, and perfume the entire city with incense.

The brahmin, having bathed his head early in the morning and eaten before the midday meal, adorned himself with white garments and other ornaments in the manner previously described. Descending from the palace, he mounted his chariot.

Then those brahmins, all dressed in white garments, anointed with white unguents, and adorned with white garlands and ornaments, surrounded him holding white parasols. Thereafter, for the purpose of assembling the great multitude, [he first sent] young children...
They scattered various fruits, and immediately after that, silver coins and the like; then they scattered kahāpaṇas.
A great crowd of people gathered, and shouts and the waving of garments went on.
Then the brahmin, while auspicious reciters and those chanting protective verses performed blessings and protective rites, wandered through the city with great prosperity. Those possessed of merit...
People, having ascended palaces of one story and more, opened the window shutters—which were like parrot feathers—and looked out.
The brahmin, too, was facing the southern gate as if overwhelming the city with the excellence of his own glory and splendor;
it is with reference to him that this was said.
"Seeing him, the people"—that is, the great multitude seeing that chariot. "Brahma" is a designation for what is best (*seṭṭha*).
"O, what a Brahma-like vehicle!"—the meaning here is: "O, what a vehicle indeed, which is like the most excellent vehicle!
"And this very thing belongs to him," Ānanda, means that humans, having given wealth to those who recite praises, [cause] songs of praise to be sung for their own daughters.
People sing its praises, saying, "It is handsome, beautiful to behold, wealthy, and opulent," yet it does not become handsome or wealthy merely by such praise.
In the same way, when the great multitude sees the brahmin’s chariot and exclaims, "Oh, what a divine vehicle this is!
they may speak such praise, but this vehicle does not become [divine] by mere praise alone.
It is called the "Brahma-vehicle. For this is indeed a wretched corpse.
But in the ultimate sense, Ānanda, this is a designation for this very Noble Eightfold Path.

Because it is supreme through the departure from all faults, and because by means of it the noble ones go to Nibbāna, it is called the "Brahma-vehicle"; and because it is the Dhamma and because it is a vehicle, it is the "Dhamma-vehicle."
Thus, because it is unsurpassed and because it has conquered the battle of the defilements, it is appropriate to say that it is "the unsurpassed victory in battle.
Now, demonstrating both its faultless nature and its status as a victory in battle, he said: "having the subduing of lust as its consummation," and so forth.

In this context, it is "having the subduing of lust as its consummation" because, while subduing lust, it brings it to a conclusion, reaches its end, and results in its accomplishment. This same method applies everywhere.

"Whose faith and wisdom": for that vehicle of the Noble Path, faith exists by way of being a follower of faith (*saddhānusārī*), and wisdom exists by way of being a follower of the Dhamma (*dhammānusārī*).
The meaning is that these two factors are always yoked to the yoke; they are yoked to the pair consisting of equanimity (*tatramajjhattatā*).
"Modesty is the pole": together with the outwardly-arising sense of shame (*ottappa*) which is designated along with oneself, [modesty] is that which arises inwardly.

Moral shame (*hirī*) is the pole of that chariot of the Path. The mind is the yoke-tie; both the consciousness of insight (*vipassanā-citta*) and the consciousness of the Path (*magga-citta*) are the yoke-tie.

For just as the yoke-tie of a chariot made of leather and so forth binds the oxen together and keeps them unified, even so the mundane consciousness of insight—fifty-one types—and the supramundane consciousness of insight—sixty-two types—bind the wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) of the Path-chariot together.
He makes them a single bond and a single unification; therefore it is said, "the mind is the yoke.
Mindfulness as the protective charioteer means that mindfulness associated with the Path is the protective charioteer.

For just as the protector of a chariot is called the charioteer—he who urges on the draft animals, harnesses them, greases the axle, drives the chariot, and renders those yoked to the chariot free from toil—so too, for the chariot of the Path...
Mindfulness (*sati*). For this is said to be both manifested as protection and to investigate the courses of wholesome and unwholesome phenomena.
The chariot is the chariot of the Noble Eightfold Path. The equipment of virtue is the ornament of the fourfold purification of virtue.
The axle made of jhāna is the axle consisting of jhāna by way of the five jhāna-factors associated with insight. The wheels of energy...
The "wheel of energy" (*vīriyacakka*) means that the two types of energy—consisting of the bodily and the mental—are its wheels.

"Equanimity as the concentration of the burden" (*upekkhā dhurasamādhi*) means the concentration of the burden; the meaning is the evenness of both poles simultaneously due to the absence of the states of being too high or too low.
For this equanimity of balance (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*), having removed the states of lethargy and agitation from the arising of consciousness...
He establishes the mind in the middle of the application; therefore, for this chariot of the Path, "steadfast concentration" (dhura-samādhi) is spoken of.

"Non-desire as the covering" means that just as external chariots have coverings such as lion skins and so forth, so too for this Noble Path-chariot, non-desire—characterized by non-greed—is called the covering.
Non-ill will (*abyāpāda*) is loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the preliminary stage of loving-kindness. Non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*) is compassion (*karuṇā*) and the preliminary stage of compassion.
Seclusion (*viveka*) is the threefold seclusion, beginning with physical seclusion.

"For whom this is the weapon" means that for the clansman established on the chariot of the Noble Path, this fivefold [set] is the weapon. For just as one standing on a chariot [overcomes] enemies with five weapons...
Just as one pierces with a spear, so too the practitioner of yoga (yogāvacara), standing upon this mundane and supramundane chariot of the Path,
pierces hatred with loving-kindness, cruelty with compassion, attachment to social circles with physical seclusion, attachment to defilements with mental seclusion,
and all unwholesome states with seclusion from acquisitions (upadhiviveka). Therefore, these five are called his "weapons."
"Endurance" (*titikkhā*) is the patience of acceptance toward paths of speech that are ill-spoken and ill-directed. "Armored with hide" (*cammasannāha*) means one whose armor is made of hide.

For just as a charioteer standing in a chariot, equipped with his armor, endures arrows as they come and go, and they do not pierce him, so too a bhikkhu endowed with the patience of acceptance endures paths of speech as they come and go.
They endure it; they do not pierce it. Therefore, it is called "patience, the armor of the hide.
"He conducts himself for the sake of security from bondage" means that he conducts himself for the sake of Nibbāna, which is secure from the four bondages; he goes directly toward Nibbāna;
the meaning is that he neither stands still nor turns back.
"Arising within oneself": because this vehicle of the path is obtained by relying on one's own personal effort (*purisakāra*), it is said to have "arisen within oneself.
"The unsurpassed Brahma-vehicle": it is the peerless, supreme vehicle. "The wise depart from the world":
those who possess this vehicle—those wise and learned persons—depart and go forth from the world.
*Aññadatthu* means "absolutely. They conquer victory by repeatedly conquering their adversaries, such as lust and the rest.
5–6. Commentary on the *Kimatthiya-sutta* and others:

In the fifth [sutta], the word *eva* (only) has the sense of restriction; by it, he excludes any other path. In this sutta, both the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) and the mixed path are discussed. The sixth is self-evident.
7. Commentary on the Second Discourse to a Certain Bhikkhu Regarding the seventh [discourse]:
"This, bhikkhu, is a designation for the element of Nibbāna" means that this is a designation for the unconditioned, deathless element of Nibbāna.
Furthermore, "the destruction of the taints is thereby spoken of" means that by means of that very same discipline of passion and so forth, there is the destruction of the taints (*āsava*).

It is also called *khaya* (destruction). "The destruction of the taints" (*āsava-kkhaya*) refers to Arahantship; this indicates that for Arahantship as well, this is merely a name such as "the removal of lust" (*rāga-vinaya*) and so forth. He said this:
thinking, "While the Teacher spoke of Nibbāna as the 'element' (*dhātu*), he described it as the Deathless (*amata*), but did not speak of the Path to it.
I shall cause that to be spoken," he asked this out of skill in connecting the discourse (*anusandhi*).
8. Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta.

In the eighth [sutta], having analyzed the Eightfold Path by way of one method with the words, "And what, bhikkhus, is right view?", the Blessed One began this teaching wishing to analyze it again by another method. Therein, "knowledge regarding suffering" means:
Knowledge that has arisen in four ways by way of contemplation, comprehension, penetration, and review;
the same method applies to the origin as well. In the remaining two truths, however, because there is no comprehension, only three ways are applicable.
Thus, this meditation subject on the Four Noble Truths has been shown by means of the passage beginning with "knowledge regarding suffering."

Therein, the first two truths are the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*), and the latter two are the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭa*). Among these, a bhikkhu has a focused application of his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-abhinivesa*) toward the round, but there is no such application toward the cessation of the round.

For the first two truths are taught both in brief—as "the five aggregates are suffering, craving is its origin"—and in detail, as "Which are the five aggregates? The aggregate of form... and so forth.
Having learned [the Dhamma] in detail from a teacher according to the method, the practitioner performs the task by repeatedly turning it over in his mind through speech.
Regarding the other two truths, however—the truth of cessation and the truth of the path—he performs the task merely by hearing that "the truth of cessation is desirable, lovely, and pleasing;
the truth of the path is desirable, lovely, and pleasing. Performing in this way, he...
One penetrates the four truths by a single penetration; one realizes them through a single realization. One penetrates suffering through the penetration of full understanding;
the origin through the penetration of abandoning; cessation through the penetration of realization; and the path through the penetration of cultivation.
One realizes suffering through the realization of full understanding... [and so on] ...one realizes the path through the realization of cultivation.
Thus, in the prior stage, there is for him penetration through learning, interrogation, hearing, retention, reflection, and realization regarding two truths;

regarding the other two, there is only penetration through hearing. In the subsequent stage, there is penetration by way of function regarding three truths, and penetration as an object regarding cessation.
However, review occurs once the truths have been attained. For this bhikkhu, previously...

As for "by way of comprehension": there is no application of attention, coordination, mental advertence, or reviewing such as, "I fully understand suffering, I abandon its origin, I realize its cessation, I develop the path";
rather, these arise starting from the moment of comprehension itself.
At a later time, however, suffering has indeed been fully understood... [and so on] ...the path has indeed been developed.
In this context, two truths are profound because they are difficult to see, and two are difficult to see because they are profound.
For the truth of suffering is evident in its arising; even when one encounters stumps, thorns, blows, and the like, one exclaims, "Oh, what suffering!

The origin [of suffering] is also evident in its arising through such things as the desire to eat and the desire to consume. [The others are profound] from the penetration of their specific characteristics.
But both [of these] are profound. Thus, they are profound because they are difficult to see.

The application for the sake of seeing the other two is like stretching out one's hand to grasp the peak of the world-system (bhavagga), like stretching out one's foot to touch the Avīci hell, and like joining the tip to the tip of a hair split a hundredfold. Thus, because they are profound...

They are difficult to see. Thus, because they are difficult to see and because they are profound among the four truths which are difficult to master, this is stated as "knowledge regarding suffering" and so forth by way of apprehension and the rest.
However, at the moment of penetration (*paṭivedha*), that knowledge is one and the same.

Regarding the intention of renunciation (*nekkhammasaṅkappa*) and the others, it is so called either by virtue of being the opposite of sensual desire or by virtue of having emerged from sensual desire for one who is comprehending sensual desire.
Or it is called "arisen" because it arises while striking down the basis for sensual desire and bringing about the subsiding of sensual desire;
or it is called "arisen" because it arises in the seclusion from sensual desire. The same method applies to the other two phrases as well.

And all these—renunciation-intention and the rest—are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of abstaining from sensuality, ill-will, and cruelty; however, at the moment of the Path, among these...

By means of cutting off unwholesome thoughts that have arisen in three instances and accomplishing their non-arising, a single wholesome thought arises, thereby fulfilling the factor of the path. This is called right intention (*sammā-saṅkappa*).

Although the abstinences from false speech and so forth are diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of abstaining from false speech and so on, at the moment of the path—

However, in these four instances, there arises only a single wholesome abstention (*kusalaveramaṇī*) which fulfills the factor of the Path by means of preventing, through the cutting off [of the course], the unwholesome and immoral volition that has arisen. This is what is called Right Speech (*sammāvācā*).
Even the abstentions from killing living beings and so forth are diverse in their preliminary stages due to the diversity of the perceptions of abstaining from killing living beings and so on.

At the moment of the Path (maggakkhaṇa), however, a single wholesome abstention arises which fulfills the path-factor by way of non-doing, cutting off, and establishing non-occurrence of the unwholesome, immoral volition that has arisen in these three instances. This is called right action (sammākammanta).
"Wrong livelihood" (micchāājīva) refers to bodily and verbal misconduct engaged in for the sake of food, drink, and so forth. "Having abandoned" (pahāya)—
"Having avoided. "By right livelihood" means by a livelihood praised by the Buddha. "He makes his living" means he maintains the course of life.
Right livelihood is also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the perceptions of abstaining from hypocrisy and so forth;
however, at the moment of the Path, it is the cutting off of the unwholesome volition of wrong livelihood that has arisen in these very seven instances.
By way of accomplishing non-arising, a single wholesome abstinence arises, fulfilling the factor of the path; this is called right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*).

Regarding the phrase "of those not yet arisen": it refers to those [unwholesome states] that have not arisen for oneself within a single existence or toward such an object, but having seen them arising in another, one thinks:
"Oh, may such evil states never arise in me! Thus...
For the non-arising of unarisen evil, unwholesome states:
"Desire" means he generates the desire for energy that accomplishes the practice leading to the non-arising of those unwholesome states. "Exerts himself" means he makes an effort.
"Arouses energy" means he sets energy in motion. "Upholds the mind" means he makes the mind upheld by means of energy.

"Strikes" means that he exerts effort [with the resolve]: "Let there remain only skin, sinew, and bone. Regarding "those that have arisen": this refers to those that have previously arisen within himself by way of active manifestation.
He generates desire for their abandonment with the thought: "Now, I shall not allow such things to arise again. Regarding "wholesome states that have not yet arisen":
this refers to the first jhāna and so forth, which have not yet been attained. Regarding "those that have arisen": this refers to those very same states.
Of those already acquired. "For stability" means for the purpose of persistence by way of a continuous succession of repeated arisings.

"For non-confusion" means for the purpose of non-destruction. "For increase" means for further development. "For abundance" means for a state of vastness. "For fulfillment" means for the purpose of completing the cultivation.
This right effort as well [is included] because of the diversity of mind, such as the non-arising of unwholesome states that have not yet arisen, and so forth.

In the preliminary stage, they are diverse. However, at the moment of the path, a single wholesome energy (*kusala-vīriya*) arises, fulfilling the factors of the path by way of accomplishing its respective functions within these same four bases.
This is called right effort (*sammā-vāyāma*).
Right mindfulness (*sammā-sati*) is also diverse in the preliminary stage due to the diversity of the minds that grasp the body and so forth; however, at the moment of the path, within these—
A single mindfulness arises fulfilling the path factor by way of accomplishing its function in four stations; this is called right mindfulness (*sammāsati*).

While the jhānas and so forth differ both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path—in the preliminary stage they differ by way of attainment, whereas at the moment of the path they differ by way of the various paths—for one person, the first path is accompanied by the first jhāna, and the second path and those following it may also be accompanied by the first jhāna.
Or they may consist of any one of the second jhānas and so forth. For one person, the first path consists of any one of the second jhānas and so forth;
for others, the second and subsequent paths may consist of any one of the second jhānas and so forth, or they may consist of the first jhāna.
Thus, all four paths are either similar, dissimilar, or partially similar by way of the jhānas.
However, its distinction lies in the restriction regarding the foundational jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*).

For, by the restriction of the foundational jhāna, when one who has attained the first jhāna emerges from the first jhāna and practices insight (*vipassanā*), the path that arises is of the first jhāna;

yet, in this case, the path-factors (*maggaṅga*) and enlightenment factors (*bojjhaṅga*) are indeed complete. When one emerges from the second jhāna and practices insight, the path that arises is of the second jhāna.
However, there are seven path factors here. For one who has emerged from the third jhāna and is practicing insight, the [path] arises with the factors of the third jhāna;
here there are seven path factors and six enlightenment factors. This same method applies from the fourth jhāna up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
It is stated that in the formless realm (ārūpa), the fourfold and fivefold jhānas arise, and those are supramundane (lokuttara), not mundane (lokiya). How is this so?

Here too, having emerged from the first jhāna and so forth, and having attained the path of stream-entry (sotāpattimagga), one develops the formless attainments (arūpasamāpatti) and is thus reborn in the formless realm;
there, for one who possesses those jhānas, the three paths arise. Thus, it is precisely the foundational jhāna (pādakajjhāna) [that serves as the basis].
It determines. Some elders, however, say: "The aggregates that serve as the object for insight determine it.
Others say: "The inclination of the individual determines it. Still others say: "Insight leading to emergence determines it.
The adjudication of these views is according to the method already stated in the *Visuddhimagga* in the section on insight leading to emergence.
This should be understood. "This, monks, is called right concentration"—this is called mundane right concentration in its prior stage, and supramundane right concentration in its subsequent stage.
9. Commentary on the Sūka Sutta.
9. In the ninth [case], "wrongly directed" (*micchāpaṇihita*) means that one pierces the hand or foot by placing a needle with its point facing upwards;

however, when it is not placed in such a way, it is called "wrongly directed. "By a wrongly directed view" (*micchāpaṇihitāya diṭṭhiyā*) means by a wisdom regarding the ownership of one's actions (*kammassakatapaññā*) that has been wrongly established.
"He will pierce ignorance" (*avijjaṃ bhindissati*) means he will pierce that which conceals the Four Noble Truths.
"He will break through ignorance; he will arouse true knowledge"—this means he will arouse the true knowledge of the path to Arahatship.

"Because his view is wrongly directed, monks"—the meaning is that it is because it has been wrongly established, not set forth, by both the wisdom of the ownership of kamma and the cultivation of the path.
In this sutta, having made the knowledge of the ownership of kamma dependent upon the path, the mixed path is taught.
10. Commentary on the Nandiyasutta:
In the tenth [discourse], "paribbājaka" refers to the wandering ascetic Channa. The rest here is self-evident.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on Ignorance (Avijjāvagga).
2. The Chapter on Dwellings (Vihāravagga) 1. Commentary on the First Discourse on Dwellings (Paṭhamavihārasuttavaṇṇanā) 11.
In the first [discourse] of the second chapter: "Bhikkhus, I desire to dwell in seclusion for half a month. Thus [he said].
"Monks, for one half-month I wish to dwell in seclusion, to remain hidden, and to live all alone"—
this is the meaning. "I am not to be approached by anyone except a single alms-food carrier"— that is, one who, without being commissioned by me,
brings forth prepared alms-food from faithful families for my sake.
"Except for one bhikkhu who brings almsfood, no other bhikkhu or householder should approach me. But why did he speak thus?
It is said that during those half-months there was no being to be converted. Then the Teacher—
“I shall spend this half-month in the bliss of the attainment of fruition;
thus there will be a dwelling in happiness for myself, and in the future, later generations will follow my example, thinking: ‘Even the Teacher dwelt alone, having left his company;
how much more so should we? This will lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.”
For this reason he spoke thus. The community of monks, having accepted the Teacher’s word, assigned one monk.

That monk, having performed all his duties at that very moment—such as sweeping the courtyard of the Perfumed Chamber, providing water for rinsing the mouth and tooth-sticks—he would depart before dawn.
"By which [I said] 'Svāhā'—by that am I. "The first after attaining full enlightenment" means: having become fully enlightened, during the very first period within forty-nine days.
"I dwell" (*viharāmi*) is a present tense verb used in the sense of the past.

"By a portion of that" (*tassa padesena*) means by a portion of that dwelling of the first attainment of full enlightenment. In this context, a "portion" (*padesa*) refers to a portion of the aggregates (*khandhapadesa*).

The "Dhamma-topic" (*dhammapadesa*) is manifold, consisting of the bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), truths (*sacca*), faculties (*indriya*), modes of conditionality (*paccayākāra*), foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), and the categories of mind-and-matter (*nāmarūpa*).
With reference to all of these, he said: "He dwelt by means of a portion of that.

For during the forty-nine days following his first enlightenment, the Blessed One—just as a king who has newly ascended the throne might do in order to demonstrate his mastery over his own power—did so.

Just as one might dwell opening up various cavities and contemplating the treasures within, such as gold, silver, pearls, and gems, even so he dwelt contemplating and scrutinizing the five aggregates by breaking them down into their constituent parts.
During this half-month, however, he dwelt specifically contemplating the feeling-aggregate (vedanā-khandha) as a part of those aggregates. For him—
As he surveyed them, thinking, "These beings experience such happiness,
such suffering," all pleasant feelings occurring as far as the peak of existence (bhavagga) and all painful feelings occurring as far as the Avīci hell appeared to him in every aspect.
Then, he dwelt examining them according to the method beginning with, "Feeling also has wrong view as its condition."
Likewise, during the first enlightenment, he dwelt having treated the twelve bases (āyatana) as being without exception;

but during this half-month, he dwelt [contemplating] a portion of those bases by way of feeling—as a portion of the base of mental phenomena (dhammāyatana); a portion of the elements (dhātu) by way of feeling—as a portion of the element of mental phenomena (dhammadhātu);
and a portion of the truths (sacca) by way of the aggregate of feeling alone—as a portion of the truth of suffering (dukkhasacca).
He dwelt contemplating a portion of the conditions by way of feeling as the condition for contact; a portion of the jhānas by way of feeling as a single factor of jhāna;
and a portion of name-and-form by way of feeling as a single aspect of name.
For within forty-nine days of his first enlightenment, he had established the infinite methods [of analysis] by treating wholesome and other phenomena without exception.
He dwelt reviewing the seven treatises. During this half-month, however, he dwelt reviewing only the triad of feelings as the representative portion of all phenomena.
In each respective instance, that particular meditative attainment was produced through the power of feeling.
Now, showing the manner in which he dwelt, he said: “Conditioned by wrong view,” and so forth.

Herein, “conditioned by wrong view” includes feeling associated with that view; it also includes wholesome and unwholesome feeling arisen by relying on (upanissaya) the view, as well as resultant feeling.
Among these, that associated with wrong view is exclusively unwholesome, whereas [the other types]—relying on the view—...
Depending upon [wrong view], both wholesome and unwholesome states arise. For those with wrong view, depending upon their view, give rice gruel, meals, and so forth on the observance days;
they establish rest-houses for travelers and others; they build halls at the four great crossroads; they have lotus ponds excavated;
they plant flowering shrubs in temples and other sacred places; and they construct bridges over rivers, difficult passes, and the like.
They level what is uneven and thus experience wholesome feeling.

But relying on wrong view, they revile and abuse those with right view, subject them to killing, imprisonment, and the like, and having slaughtered living beings, they offer them as sacrifices to the deities;
thus, unwholesome feeling arises for them. This is resultant feeling (*vipākavedanā*).
However, it occurs only for those who have passed into another existence.

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by right view" (*sammādiṭṭhipaccayā*), here too feeling associated with right view is included, as well as wholesome and unwholesome feelings—and even resultant feelings—that arise having used right view as a decisive support (*upanissaya*). Among these, that which is associated with right view...

They become exclusively wholesome; yet, relying upon right view, they perform meritorious deeds such as making offerings to the Buddha, lighting lamps and garlands, attending great Dharma assemblies, and establishing shrines in regions where none exist—thus, wholesome feelings arise in them.
However, relying on that very same right view, they revile and abuse those with wrong views.
They exalt themselves and disparage others; thus, unwholesome feeling arises in them.
However, resultant feeling occurs only for those who have passed into another existence. The same method applies to the phrases beginning with "conditioned by wrong intention" and so forth.

In the phrases beginning with "conditioned by desire," however, feeling associated with the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed should be understood as being conditioned by desire; [likewise] conditioned by applied thought...
The feeling of the first jhāna itself. With perception as a condition—excluding the first jhāna—the feelings associated with the remaining six attainments of perception arise.
In the cases of "desire not being stilled" and so forth, when three factors are not stilled, there is a feeling associated with the eight types of greed-accompanied consciousness;
when only desire is stilled, there is the feeling of the first jhāna itself. When both desire and applied thought are stilled, there is the feeling of the second jhāna and those that follow.
What is intended is the feeling of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) in the subsiding of all three [feelings].
"For the attainment of what has not yet been attained" means for the sake of attaining the fruit of arhatship (*arahattaphala*). "There is energy" means there is vigor.

"When the cause for that has arrived" means when the condition for that fruit of arhatship has come about by means of the exertion of that vigor. "Feeling conditioned by that" refers to the feeling of arhatship.
Feeling has its basis as a condition (*ṭhānapaccayā vedayitaṃ*). By this, only the supramundane feeling produced together with the four paths is included.
2. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Abiding (Dutiyavihārasutta). 12.

In the second [discourse], the reason for seclusion (*paṭisallāna*) should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. [It is] "by way of the condition for the subsiding of wrong view" (*micchādiṭṭhivūpasamapaccayā*).

The pacification of wrong view is called right view. Therefore, whatever feeling is said to arise with right view as its condition should be understood to arise precisely with the pacification of wrong view as its condition.
However, it is stated that in this sutta, some do not include resultant feeling, thinking it to be too remote.
In this manner, the meaning is to be understood in all cases. Of whichever...

For it is said that [feeling] has "the condition of subsiding" (*vūpasama-paccaya*); yet, in each case, what is intended is that specific feeling which arises precisely from the condition of its respective opposing state (*paṭipakkha-dhamma*).

Among the phrases beginning with "from the condition of the subsiding of desire" (*chanda-vūpasama-paccaya*), the feeling of the first jhāna should be understood as arising from the condition of the subsiding of desire;
the feeling of the second jhāna from the condition of the subsiding of applied thought (*vitakka*); and the feelings of the six attainments from the condition of perception (*saññā*).

Feeling pertaining to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises conditioned by the subsiding of perception. "Desire has subsided," and so forth, have meanings already explained in the aforementioned passages.
3–7. Commentary on the *Sekkhāsutta* and others. 13–17.

In the third [sutta], "one in training" (*sekkha*) means one whose nature is to train. What does he train in? In the three trainings. "By means of training" (*sekkhāya*) means by means of the three [trainings].

[It is] arisen together with the four fruits and the paths. For that [wisdom] is also called "of one in training" (*sekkhā*) because it is still training in its own task since its function is not yet completed.
The fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh [terms] have their meanings already explained.
8–10. Commentary on the First Kukkuṭārāma Sutta, etc.

18–20. In the eighth [sutta], "a riddle" (*ummaṅga*) means a riddle of wisdom; its meaning is the investigation of wisdom, the seeking of wisdom. "In this way, friend," he said this for the purpose of establishing his question. The ninth and tenth [suttas] have their meanings plain.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Chapter on Monasteries (*Vihāravagga*). 3. Commentary on the Chapter on Wrongness (*Micchattavagga*)
21–30. In the first [sutta] of the third chapter: *micchatta* means a false nature; *sammatta* means a right nature.
*Micchāpaṭipattādhikaraṇahetu* means the cause for performing wrong practice; the meaning is: because one performs wrong practice, therefore [it is so].
*Anārādhako* means one who does not accomplish. *Ñāyaṃ dhammaṃ* means the Dhamma of the Noble Path.
"One of wrong knowledge" means one of wrong consciousness and wrong reflection. "One of wrong liberation" means liberation that is not according to reality, liberation that does not lead to escape.
In these four suttas beginning with the third, the cycle of existence and its reversal are explained;
however, in the last two here, the person is questioned and the Dhamma is analyzed—thus the person is shown by means of the Dhamma.
"Suppavattiyo" means "those that turn well. The meaning is that they can be made to turn in whatever direction one desires, just as a wheel runs turning toward whichever direction it is wished.
"With its proximate cause and its equipment" means together with its conditions and its accessories.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The third chapter: The Chapter on Wrongness.
4. Explanation of the Chapter on Practice (Paṭipattivagga), 31–40.
In the fourth [section], "wrong practice" means practice that is not according to reality; "one who has practiced wrongly" means one who has practiced in a manner that is not according to reality.
Thus, one discourse is spoken by way of the Dhamma, and one by way of the person. "From the hither shore to the further shore" refers to Nibbāna as opposed to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

Regarding the term "those going to the further shore," it should be understood that all those who have gone to the further shore, those who are going, and those who will go, are indeed "goers to the further shore."
"He runs along the very shore" means he runs along the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*), he wanders within the cycle.
"Black" refers to unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*). "White" refers to wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*). "From home to homelessness" refers to Nibbāna as opposed to the cycle of existence.

"Having come to" means having undertaken, having aimed at, having intended, or having depended upon. "He would cleanse" means he would make completely pure. "By mental defilements" means by those things that cause the mind to become defiled.
Regarding the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Regarding the factors of enlightenment (*sambodhiyaṅga*):

this refers to the seven factors of awakening (*bojjhaṅga*). The goal of recluseship (*sāmaññattha*) is Nibbāna; for it is called the "goal of recluseship" because it is to be approached by means of recluseship.
The state of brahminhood (*brahmañña*) is the state of excellence. The goal of brahminhood (*brahmaññattha*) is Nibbāna, because it is to be approached by means of brahminhood. Wherever...
Furthermore, in these three suttas below, the term "destruction of lust" (*rāgakkhaya*) appears; they say that in each instance, this also applies to Arahantship.
The fourth chapter, the Section on Practice (*Paṭipattivagga*).
5. Commentary on the Aññatitthiyapeyyālavagga (41–48).

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the full understanding of the course" (*addhānapariññattha*) in the *Aññatitthiyapeyyāla*: the course of saṃsāra is said to be "fully understood" upon reaching nibbāna.

Therefore, nibbāna is called "the full understanding of the course"; this is the meaning of "for the sake of that. Regarding "for the sake of final nibbāna through non-clinging" (*anupādāparinibbānattha*).
"For the sake of final Nibbāna without remainder. Thus, in this series (peyyāla), Arahantship is described by means of the fruit of true knowledge and liberation (vijjāvimutti).
By means of "knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassana) there is reviewing; by the remaining terms, Nibbāna.
This concludes the Chapter on the Series of Other Sectarians.
6. Commentary on the Sūriyapeyyāla-vagga (49–62).

In the Sūriyapeyyāla, the meaning is to be understood in every instance as follows: just as the dawn, so too is the quality of having a virtuous friend; and just as the appearance of the sun, so too is the Noble Path together with insight that is produced by standing upon the quality of having a virtuous friend. Regarding "perfection of virtue" (*sīlasampadā*): [text continues].

The fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). Perfection of aspiration (*chandasampadā*) is the desire to perform wholesome deeds. Perfection of self (*attasampadā*) is the perfection of the mind.

Perfection of view (*diṭṭhisampadā*) is the attainment of knowledge (*ñāṇa*). Perfection of diligence (*appamādasampadā*) is the attainment of diligence that brings about [the goal]. Perfection of wise attention (*yonisomanasikārasampadā*) is the attainment of skillful attention.
Furthermore, "good friendship" (*kalyāṇamittatā*) and so forth are another way of describing right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*) and the other factors.
These have been spoken for the purpose of demonstrating existence. And all these suttas were spoken individually according to the inclinations of individuals.
Thus ends the Section on the Summary of the Sun (Sūriyapeyyālavagga). 7. Commentary on the Section on the Summary of Single Qualities (Ekadhammapeyyālavagga), etc.

63–138. Both the *Ekadhamma-peyyāla* (The Series on a Single Dhamma) and the *Gaṅgā-peyyāla* (The Series on the Ganges) were taught according to the inclinations of those who would understand them when they were spoken in various ways, solely by way of the individual dispositions of persons.
8. The Chapter on the Series on Heedfulness (*Appamāda-peyyāla-vagga*) 1. Commentary on the *Tathāgata-sutta* (The Discourse on the Tathāgata)

139. Regarding the section on diligence (*appamāda-peyyāla*), the phrase "even so" (*evameva kho*) should be understood as follows: just as the Fully Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) is the foremost among all beings, so too is diligence the foremost among all wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) because it is that which causes them to be performed.

But is this not merely mundane (*lokiya*), whereas wholesome states can also be supramundane (*lokuttara*)? Furthermore, this [diligence] belongs only to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), whereas wholesome states belong to all four planes of existence.
In what sense is this their "foremost"? In the sense of being acquired. For they are acquired through diligence;
therefore, that is their foremost [condition]. Hence it was said: "All these have diligence as their root," and so forth.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on Words (Padasutta)
140. "Of those that dwell in the jungle" means of those dwelling on the surface of the earth. "Of living beings" means of living beings with feet. "Footprints" means tracks.
"They come together" means they come to a convergence or a collection. "It is declared the foremost" means it is declared the best.
"By way of its greatness" means it is declared the foremost by virtue of its magnitude, not by virtue of its qualities; this is the meaning.
3–10. Commentary on the Kūṭasutta, etc., 141–148.

*Vassika* means the jasmine flower (*sumana*). It is said that after hearing this sutta, King Bhātika, desiring to test it, had a chamber decorated with the four kinds of fragrant substances and had fragrant flowers brought there.
Having placed a handful of *sumana* flowers in the middle of one casket and arranged the remaining caskets around it, he closed the door and went outside.
After a short while had passed, as he opened the door and was entering, the fragrance of the *sumana* flowers first struck his nose. He [stood] right there on the great floor.

Having prostrated himself facing the Great Shrine (Mahācetiya), he paid homage to the shrine, saying: "The Perfectly Enlightened One has spoken well when he declared that 'the Vassika flower is their foremost'.
"Kuṭṭarājāno" means minor kings; there is also a reading as "khuddarājāno.
"Tantāvutānaṃ" means those woven on a loom; the meaning is "those woven after the warp has been set up. And this is a genitive used in the sense of the nominative. Those which...

"Some cloths woven on a loom"—this is the meaning here. Alternatively, the meaning should be understood according to a method of recitation that leaves something remaining: "whatever cloths among those cloths woven on a loom. Everywhere else, the rest is self-evident.
The eighth chapter, the Chapter on Heedfulness, is concluded.
9. Balakaraṇīya-vagga 1.
Balasutta-vaṇṇanā 149.

In the Balakaraṇīya-vagga, "tasks requiring strength" (*balakaraṇīya*) refers to such activities as running, leaping, heating oneself, and carrying loads, which are to be performed by means of the strength of the thighs and the strength of the arms.

"Occupations. "Established in virtue" means being established in the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*). "The eightfold path" refers to the Noble Path together with insight (*vipassanā*).

2. Commentary on the Seed Sutta (Bījasutta): 150. Regarding the phrase "seed-creatures and plant-creatures": here, all five kinds of seeds are called "seed-creatures" (*bījagāma*). That same [seed] from the time it possesses foliage and begins its state of greenness should be understood as "plant-creatures" (*bhūtagāma*).
3. Nāgasutta Commentary 151.
"They take strength" means they acquire strength; having acquired strength, they become firm-bodied. Regarding the passage beginning "They descend into the pools," this is the sequential account:
it is said that when the female nāgas have conceived during the season, they think: "If we..."
"Here we shall give birth; thus our children will not be able to withstand the force of the ocean waves or the force of the Supaṇṇas as they swoop down.

Having said this, they dive into the great ocean, reach the opening of the Sambhacca cave, enter the five great rivers, and proceed to the Himavat. There, in golden, silver, and gem-studded caves inaccessible to Supaṇṇas, they dwell.
Once they have lived there and given birth, they lower the young nāgas into water as deep as their ankles and so forth, and teach them how to cross the water.

Then, when those nāgas gradually become capable of crossing from the near shore to the far shore of rivers such as the Ganges, and from the far shore back to the near shore—crossing and re-crossing—the [elephants] say:
"Now our children can withstand the force of the waves and the force of Garuḷas."
Knowing that they would be able to endure it, he manifested a great cloud through his own supernatural power;
making the entire Himavat mountain range appear as if filled with a single body of water, he caused the rain to fall.

He fashioned ships made of gold, silver, and other precious materials, and above them he fastened a canopy of cloth variegated with golden stars and draped with garlands of fragrant flowers. [He then provided] fragrant sandalwood, incense, flowers, and so forth.
Having taken those boats and entered the five great rivers, they gradually reach the great ocean.
Dwelling there, they attain vastness and abundance, reaching dimensions of ten fathoms, a hundred fathoms, a thousand fathoms, and even a hundred thousand fathoms.
"Even so," it is said here: the mountain Himavat should be seen as the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*);
the young nāgas as the practitioners (*yogāvacara*); the small pools and so forth as the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*); and the great ocean as Nibbāna.
Just as the young nāgas, having established themselves on Himavat and reached the great ocean via the small pools and so forth, attain a vastness of body, even so—
Relying upon virtue and being firmly established in virtue, the yogis reach Nibbāna by means of the Noble Path;
and through the very path of Arahatship, they attain greatness of body in terms of qualities regarding the six supernormal powers (abhiññā) that have been acquired.
5. Commentary on the Kumbha Sutta.
153. *Kumbho* means a water-jar. *No paccāvamati* means it does not pour back; the meaning is that it does not let [the water] enter inside.
7. Commentary on the Ākāsa Sutta 155.
*Puratthimā* refers to winds coming from the eastern direction. The same principle applies to the western direction and so forth. All four [directions] are treated in this way.

Regarding "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*): just as the convergence of these winds, distinguished by their directions such as the east and so forth, occurs in space, so too here the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*)—spoken of in the manner beginning with "the four foundations of mindfulness"—succeed through the cultivation of the Noble Path accompanied by insight (*vipassanā*). Therefore, this has been said.
8–9. Commentary on the First Meghasutta, etc.
(156–157). “In the last month of summer” means in the month of Āsāḷha.

“It was stirred up” means that by the trampling of the feet of bipeds and quadrupeds, it rose from the surface of the earth and, forming into circles, ascended into the sky. “Dust and dirt” means the dust and dirt of the soil.
10. Commentary on the Nāvāsutta (The Ship Discourse) 158.
"On a sea-going ship," and so forth, has already been explained in detail below in the Simile of the Merchant.
11–12. Commentary on the Āgantukasutta (The Guest Discourse), etc.

159–160. "Guest-house" (*āgantukāgāra*) refers to a guest-house established in the center of a city by those seeking merit, where even kings, royal ministers, and high officials are able to take up residence.
Regarding the phrase "the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) are to be fully understood":
just as the lodging of the kṣatriyas and others who have arrived from the eastern direction and so forth is successfully provided in a guest-house, so too...

These phenomena, such as "to be fully understood through direct knowledge" (*abhiññā-pariññeyya*) and so forth, succeed through the cultivation of the Noble Path together with insight (*vipassanā*), by means of direct knowledge, full understanding, and the rest; therefore, this has been said. The *Nadīsutta* follows the same method as explained above.
The ninth chapter, the *Balakaraṇīyavagga*.
10. The Chapter on Searches (Esanāvagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Searches (Esanāsuttavaṇṇanā) 161.

In the Chapter on Searches: "Search for sensual pleasures" (kāmesanā) means the seeking, searching, hunting, and longing for sensual pleasures. "Search for existence" (bhavesanā) means the seeking for states of existence. "Search for the holy life" (brahmacariyesanā) means the seeking for the holy life that is characterized by wrong view.
2–11. Commentary on the *Vidhā-sutta*, etc. (162–171).
*Vidhā* means divisions of conceit (*māna*) or the establishing of conceit. "I am superior" (*seyyohamasmi*) is a division of conceit or the establishing of conceit, meaning "I am superior.
*Nīghā* means suffering (*dukkha*). As for the etymological meaning here, it refers to that in which they arise.
They drive away that person, thus they are *nīghā*. The rest here is self-evident.
This is the tenth chapter, the Chapter on Searches (*esanāvagga*). 11. The Chapter on Floods (*oghavagga*).
1–2. Commentary on the *Ogha-sutta* and others (172–173).

In the *Oghavagga*, "the flood of sensual desire" (*kāmogha*) is lustful craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure. "The flood of existence" (*bhavogha*) is lustful craving for existence in the realms of form and formlessness.

"The flood of views" (*diṭṭhogha*) refers to the sixty-two types of views. "The flood of ignorance" (*avijjogha*) is lack of knowledge regarding the Four Noble Truths. The same principle applies to the "yokes of sensual desire" (*kāmayoga*) and the others as well.
3–4. Commentary on the *Upādāna-sutta* and others (174–175).
*Sensual clinging* (*kāmupādāna*) means the grasping after sensual pleasures. The same method applies to *clinging to views* (*diṭṭhupādāna*) and the others as well.

*Ties* (*gantha*) means binding, lacing together, or constriction. A *bodily tie* (*kāyagantha*) is a defilement that binds and constricts the mental body (*nāmakāya*). *Insistence on "this alone is the truth"* (*idaṃsaccābhiniveso*).
The adherence that arises by way of extreme views, thinking "this alone is the truth," is thus called *abhinivesa*.
5–10. Commentary on the *Anusaya-sutta* and others (176–181).
*Kāmarāgānusaya*: in the sense of being firmly established, sensual lust itself is the underlying tendency; thus it is *kāmarāgānusaya*. The same applies to the remaining [tendencies].
The method is the same. "Lower-fettering" means those belonging to the lower section. "Fetters" means bonds.
"Higher-fettering" means those belonging to the upper section. Everywhere else, the meaning is already clear.
The eleventh chapter, the Chapter on Floods, is concluded.
The commentary on the Saṃyutta on the Path is finished.
2. The Saṃyutta on the Factors of Enlightenment.
1. The Chapter on Mountains.
1. Commentary on the Himavanta Sutta 182.

In the first sutta of the Saṃyutta on the Factors of Enlightenment, the phrase "these nāgas" refers to those who dwell within the waves upon the surface of the great ocean, not to the nāgas who reside in palaces.
Their entire development of the body and so forth, based upon the Himalayas, is exactly as described in the method set forth below.
It should be understood. Regarding the term *bojjhaṅga*: here, they are called *bojjhaṅgas* because they are limbs (*aṅga*) of enlightenment (*bodhi*), or limbs for the sake of enlightenment.

What is meant? It is this collection of states (*dhammasāmaggī*) which, when arising at the moment of the mundane or supramundane path, serves as the antidote to numerous calamities—namely, the foundations of sloth and agitation, the accumulation [of defilements], and the adherence to indulgence in sensual pleasure, self-mortification, annihilationism, eternalism, and so forth.

Because the noble disciple awakens by means of this harmony of qualities—consisting of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity—he is called "Bodhi" (Awakening).

"He awakens" means that he rises from the sleep of the continuity of defilements, or that he penetrates the Four Noble Truths, or that he realizes Nibbāna itself; so it has been said. As it was stated:
“Having developed the seven factors of enlightenment, he has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.

They are called *bojjhaṅgas* because they are the factors (*aṅga*) of that enlightenment (*bodhi*) which is defined as the harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggī*), just as there are factors of meditation (*jhānaṅga*) and factors of the path (*maggaṅga*).
Furthermore, since the noble disciple is called “enlightenment” (*bodhi*) by virtue of awakening through this aforementioned harmony of states, these are also the factors of that enlightenment.

The enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) are like the parts of an army or the parts of a chariot. Therefore, the teachers of the commentaries said: "They are called enlightenment factors because they are the factors of a person who is awakening.
Furthermore: "In what sense are they 'enlightenment factors'? They are enlightenment factors because they lead to awakening; they are enlightenment factors because they awaken."

The meaning of "factor of enlightenment" (*bojjhaṅga*) should also be understood according to the method of the *Paṭisambhidā*: "They awaken, thus they are factors of enlightenment; they awaken thoroughly, thus they are factors of enlightenment; they awaken fully, thus they are factors of enlightenment.

Furthermore, in expressions such as "the mindfulness factor of enlightenment," it is called a "factor of enlightenment" (*sambojjhaṅga*) because it is a praiseworthy and beautiful factor of enlightenment. It is simply mindfulness.
“Factor of enlightenment” (*sambojjhaṅga*) means the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*satisambojjhaṅga*); in all instances, the meaning should be understood in this way.
“He develops” (*bhāveti*) means he increases it; he generates it repeatedly within the continuum of his own mind; the meaning is that he brings it forth.
Regarding the phrases beginning with “dependent on seclusion” (*vivekanissita*), these are explained in the *Kosalasaṃyutta* in the passage: “He develops right view dependent on seclusion.”
These should be understood in the same manner already described.

However, this is the distinction: there, only the threefold seclusion—namely, seclusion by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-viveka*), seclusion by eradication (*samuccheda-viveka*), and seclusion by escape (*nissaraṇa-viveka*)—was mentioned;
but according to some, when one reaches the development of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga-bhāvanā*), it is also based on five kinds of seclusion.

They explain [this]. For they extract the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) not only at the moments of powerful insight, the path, and the fruit, but also in the jhānas based on insight—namely, the kasiṇa-jhānas, the ānāpāna-jhānas, the asubha-jhānas, and the brahmavihāra-jhānas—and this has not been prohibited by the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathās.
Therefore, according to their opinion, at the moment these jhānas occur, [the factors of enlightenment exist] by way of their function (kicca).

Thus it is based on seclusion by suppression. And just as it was stated regarding the moment of insight that it is "based on seclusion by escape according to one's inclination," so too it is appropriate to say that one develops it as being based on seclusion by subsiding. The rest here is exactly according to the method explained below.
2. Commentary on the Kāya Sutta.
183. In the second [section], "subsistence through nutriment" means subsistence through conditions (*paccaya*). "Dependent on nutriment" means dependent on a condition.
"The sign of the beautiful" (*subhanimitta*): the beautiful itself is the sign of the beautiful, and the object of the beautiful is also the sign of the beautiful.
"Improper attention" (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) means unskillful attention, off-track attention—such as regarding the impermanent as "permanent," the painful as "pleasant," or the non-self as "self."
Or, there is the mental attention [directed] toward the unattractive as "attractive. As one frequently engages that [attention] with respect to that attractive object, sensual desire arises.
Therefore it was said: "There is, monks, the sign of the beautiful," and so forth. In this way, the application [of the formula] should be understood for all the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, in the phrases "the sign of aversion" and so on, both aversion itself is the "sign of aversion," and the object of aversion is also [the sign of aversion]. "Discontent" (*arati*)...
Dissatisfaction. With reference to this it was said: "In this context, what is discontent (arati)? Discontent with regard to remote lodgings or with regard to various other wholesome states;
discontent, the state of being discontented, lack of delight, lack of enjoyment, dissatisfaction, agitation—this is called discontent."

*Tandi* is adventitious physical languor arising from conditions such as extreme cold and so forth. When this has arisen, one says, "It is too cold," "It is too hot," "I am too hungry," "I am too thirsty," or "I have traveled too far.
With reference to this, it is said: "In this context, what is *tandi*?
That which is *tandi*, the state of being *tandi*, the act of becoming *tandi*; laziness, the state of laziness, the quality of being lazy."
This is called *tandī* (drowsiness).
*Vijambhitā* (stretching) is the bending of the body due to the influence of the defilements. With reference to this, it is said: "In this context, what is *vijambhitā*?
It is the stretching, the yawning, the bending forward, the bending backward, the stooping, the bowing, and the bodily ailment of the body; this is [called *vijambhitā*]."
"It is called yawning.
"Drowsiness after eating" (*bhattasammada*) is the feverish distress caused by food. With reference to this it was said: "In this context, what is drowsiness after eating?
That which, for one who has eaten, is the stupor of food, the fatigue of food, the feverish distress of food, and the heaviness of the body—this is called drowsiness after eating."
"And mental sluggishness" (*cetaso līnatta*) refers to the mode of the mind’s sluggishness, with reference to which it is said:

"In this context, what is mental sluggishness? Whatever unfitness, unwieldiness, sinking, deep sinking, sluggishness, state of sluggishness, sluggishness itself, torpor, state of torpor, torpor itself of the mind—this is called mental sluggishness."
"Non-quiescence of the mind" means that just as a charcoal that has been extinguished does not yet settle down but continues to emit heat,
and just as in a place where rice is being cooked it does not yet settle down but continues to emit heat, so too is the unquiet state of the mind;
in its actual meaning, however, this is simply restlessness and remorse (*uddhacca-kukkucca*).
"States conducive to doubt" refers to those states that serve as the objects of doubt. "Improper attention" is to be understood according to the method already explained in all instances.
Thus, in this context, these two factors—sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*)—are described by way of their object;

ill-will (*byāpāda*) is described by way of both its object and its decisive support (*upanissaya*); and the remaining factors are described by way of both their co-nascence (*sahajāta*) and their decisive support.

“Phenomena that are the basis for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness” refers to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment and the nine supramundane phenomena which serve as the objects of mindfulness.
In this context, “frequent application of wise attention” means the repeated practice of skillful attention toward those [objects].

Regarding the passage beginning with “wholesome and unwholesome phenomena,” “wholesome” (*kusala*) means arisen from skill (*kosalla*), having blameless and pleasant results. “Unwholesome” (*akusala*)...
"Born of unskillfulness, they have a blameable and painful result. "Blameable" means unwholesome (*akusala*); "blameless" means wholesome (*kusala*).

The same method applies to the inferior and superior, and to the dark and bright. "With counterparts" refers to the dark and bright themselves. For the dark are called "with counterparts" because they give a dark result, and the bright because they give a bright result;
the meaning is that they are portions consisting of similar results. Alternatively, it is because there exists a counterpart portion.
They have counterparts (*sappaṭibhāga*). For the white [states] are the counterparts of the black, and the black are the counterparts of the white;
thus they have counterparts. Alternatively, they have counterparts in the sense of being opposed:
for the unwholesome gives its own result by opposing the wholesome, and the wholesome does so by opposing the unwholesome; thus the black and white states have counterparts.
The "element of initiative" (*ārambha-dhātu*) is the energy of the first undertaking. The "element of exertion" (*nikkhama-dhātu*) is stronger than that because it has emerged from indolence.
The "element of perseverance" (*parakkama-dhātu*) is even stronger than that because it advances toward ever-higher stages;
thus, by all three terms, energy itself is described.
“Conducive to the enlightenment factor of rapture” means phenomena that serve as the objects of rapture. “Tranquillity of body” is the tranquillity of the distress of the three aggregates.
“Tranquillity of mind” is the tranquillity of the distress of the consciousness aggregate. “The sign of serenity” refers to both serenity itself and its object;
it is also a synonym for that very thing. “The sign of non-distraction” is another term for the same.

"Conducive to the enlightenment factor of equanimity" means the phenomena that serve as the object for equanimity; however, in terms of its actual meaning, it should be understood as those phenomena whose mode is neutrality (*majjhattākāra*) that are conducive to equanimity.
Thus, in this context, the enlightenment factors of mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, and equanimity are described by way of their object;
the remaining ones are described by way of both their object and their decisive support (*upanissaya*).
3. Commentary on the *Sīlasutta* 184.
Regarding the third [verse], "endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampanna*): here, both mundane and supramundane virtue of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) is spoken of;

the meaning is "endowed with that. The same method applies to concentration and wisdom as well. As for liberation (*vimutti*), it is specifically the liberation of the fruit (*phalavimutti*). Knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*)...
The knowledge of reviewing. Thus, herein, the three beginning with virtue are both mundane and supramundane; liberation is exclusively supramundane;
and the knowledge and vision of liberation is exclusively mundane.
"Vision," I say, refers to vision. And that vision is twofold: vision by the eye and vision by knowledge.
It is twofold. Therein, "vision with the eyes" (cakkhudassana) refers to the seeing or looking upon the Noble Ones with clear eyes.

However, "knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassana) refers to the seeing of the characteristics perceived by the Noble Ones, and the penetration of what has been penetrated—whether by means of jhāna, insight (vipassanā), or the paths and fruits. In this context, it is "vision with the eyes" that is intended.
This is what is intended. For even the mere looking with eyes full of faith upon the Noble Ones is of great benefit. As for "hearing":
it is hearing with the ear those who say, "A certain one whose taints are destroyed dwells in such-and-such a kingdom, province, village, town, monastery, or cave";
this too is of great benefit. As for "approaching": [the thought], "I shall give a gift..."

Approaching the Noble Ones with such a mind as: "I will give [an offering], or I will ask a question, or I will listen to the Dhamma, or I will pay them honor"—this is approaching. "Attending upon" means attending upon through questions.
Having heard of the virtues of the Noble Ones, one approaches them, invites them, gives a gift, and [inquires] by way of such phrases as, "Venerable sir, what is wholesome? and so forth.
The meaning is "asking questions.
"Recollection" (anussati) refers to the recollection of those noble ones while sitting in night-quarters or day-quarters, thinking:

"Now the noble ones are spending their time in the bliss of jhāna, insight, the path, and the fruit within rock shelters, caves, pavilions, and so forth"; or it is the reviewing of the exhortation received from them.
“Virtue was taught in this place, concentration in this, insight in this, the path in this, and the fruit in this”—such is the recollection.

“Going forth after” means having inspired confidence in the minds of the Noble Ones, one leaves the household life and goes forth in their presence. For, having inspired confidence in the minds of the Noble Ones, it is in their very presence that...

For one who, having gone forth in the presence [of the Teacher], practices while awaiting instruction and advice from those very same ones, that going forth is called "following-going-forth" (*anupabbajjā*).

Likewise, for one who, out of confidence in the Noble Ones, goes forth elsewhere and practices while awaiting instruction and advice from the Noble Ones, that going forth is also called "following-going-forth.
However, for one who, out of confidence in others, goes forth in the presence of those very others...
For one who wanders while looking forward to receiving instruction and guidance from others alone, there is no such thing as "following in the footsteps" (anupabbajjā) of the renunciation.

However, among those who followed in the footsteps of the renunciation of those who had thus gone forth, there were approximately one hundred thousand who followed in the footsteps of the Elder Mahākassapa;

likewise, there were those who followed in the footsteps of the Elder Candagutta, who was the Elder Mahākassapa’s own pupil (saddhivihārika), and also those who followed in the footsteps of his pupil.
There was the Elder Sūriyagutta; his co-resident (saddhivihārika) was the Elder Assagutta; his co-resident was the Elder Yonaka Dhammarakkhita;
and the co-resident of that latter was the Elder named Tissa, who was the younger brother of King Asoka.
Following him into the religious life, two and a half koṭis of people went forth.
There is no limit to the number of those who followed Mahinda Thera into the homeless life.
To this day, those in the island of Laṅkā who go forth out of faith in the Teacher are said to follow the very ordination of Mahinda Thera.
"That Dhamma" means that Dhamma of his exhortation and instruction. "Recalls" means remembers. "Reflects upon" means...
He strikes it with thought. "Exerted" means it is fulfilled. "Investigates," and so forth—all this is stated by way of the movement of knowledge therein.
Alternatively, "investigates" means he investigates the specific characteristics (lakkhaṇa) of those various phenomena.
"Examines" means he causes knowledge to move through them. "Enters upon scrutiny" means he enters upon investigation, observation, and searching.

"Seven fruits and seven benefits"—both of these are identical in meaning. "He attains final knowledge early in this very life" means that while striving for arahantship, he attains it in this very existence;
and "early" means before the time of death has arrived. "Then at the time of death" means at the time close to death.
"One who attains final nibbāna in the interval" (antarā-parinibbāyī) is one who attains final nibbāna without having exceeded the midpoint of his lifespan; he is of three types.
First, among those with a lifespan of a thousand kappas, having been reborn in the Aviha heaven, one attains Arahantship on the very day of rebirth.
If he does not attain it on the day of rebirth, he attains it at the end of the first hundred kappas. This is the first type.
The one who attains parinibbāna in the interval (*antarāparinibbāyī*). Another, being unable to do so, reaches the end of two hundred kappas;
this is the second. Another, being unable even to that, reaches the end of four hundred kappas; this is the third *antarāparinibbāyī*.
However, having passed beyond five hundred kappas and attained *arahatta*, he is called one who attains parinibbāna upon reaching [the next life] (*upahaccaparinibbāyī*).
