The same method applies to the Atappa and other realms as well. However, one who attains Arahantship with effort and exertion, having arisen anywhere [in the form realm], is called "one who attains Parinibbāna with exertion" (sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī);
one who attains it without effort or exertion is called "one who attains Parinibbāna without exertion" (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī).
Furthermore, one reborn in the Aviha and other such realms remains there for the full duration of their lifespan, and by being reborn successively higher, reaches the Akaniṭṭha realm.
The one who has reached the upward stream, going to the Akaniṭṭha realm, is so named.
However, at this point, forty-eight non-returners (anāgāmin) must be explained.

For among those in the Aviha heaven, there are three who attain parinibbāna in the interval, one who attains parinibbāna upon arrival, and one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm—thus making five. These [five] are those who attain parinibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyin).
There are five who attain final nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāra-parinibbāyino*) and five who do not; thus there are ten. It is the same for the Atappa and other heavens.

However, among the Akaniṭṭha devas, there is no one who goes upstream (*uddhaṃsota*); therefore, there are eight there—four who attain final nibbāna with exertion and four who attain final nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyī*).
Thus, there are forty-eight in total. Among them, the one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha heaven is the most senior of all.
And he was the youngest of all. How so? Because his lifespan was sixteen thousand eons, he was the eldest of all in terms of age;
yet because he attained Arahantship last of all, he was the youngest of all.

In this sutta, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are described as the insight into the preliminary stages of the path to Arahantship, which possesses various characteristics within a single moment of consciousness, neither before nor after.
4. Commentary on the Vatthasutta 185.
In the fourth [sutta], "If it occurs to me: 'This is the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness'": thus it occurs to me that "this is the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness.
"It is immeasurable to me": thus it occurs to me that "it is immeasurable. "Well undertaken" means well fulfilled. "It abides": [it remains].
Herein, the mindfulness enlightenment factor abides in eight ways: the mindfulness enlightenment factor abides because of not attending to arising and attending to non-arising;

because of not attending to occurrence, non-occurrence, signs, and the signless, and because of attending to the signless and to the cessation of formations (*visaṅkhāra*). It abides by these eight modes.
The Elder knows; he understands that one who passes away does so by means of the eight modes that are the opposite of those already mentioned.
This same method applies to the remaining factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) as well. Thus, in this sutta, the fruit-factors of enlightenment are explained.

For when the Elder enters the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) with the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*satisambojjhaṅga*) as the head, the other six follow accordingly. When [the mindfulness factor] is among the investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicaya*) and the rest...
At that time as well, the others followed suit; thus, demonstrating his mastery over the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), the Elder spoke this sutta.
5. Commentary on the Bhikkhu Sutta.
186. "They conduce to enlightenment" means they conduce to the purpose of awakening. For the purpose of awakening to what?
It is said that they conduce to the awakening to the unconditioned Nibbāna by means of the Path; to the state of having accomplished the task through review;
or to awakening from the sleep of defilements by means of the Path, and to the state of being awakened by means of the Fruit. Therefore, the realization of Nibbāna occurs herein.
The "reviewing of the abandoning of defilements" has thus been shown in its entirety.
6–7. Commentary on the *Kuṇḍaliya-sutta* and others, §§187–188.
In the sixth [sutta], "one who dwells in dependence on a monastery" (*ārāmanissayī*) means one who dwells by depending upon a monastery. "One who frequents assemblies" (*parisāvacaro*)—
"One who moves within the assembly. As for "the assembly," both fools and the wise approach it;
however, one who is able to crush the doctrines of others and illuminate his own doctrine is called "one who moves within the assembly.
"From monastery to monastery" means that he walks from monastery to monastery by way of the monasteries themselves, not by the outside. The same method applies to the phrase "from park to park."
The meaning here is: having entered by one monastery, [one goes] to another monastery; by one park, to another park.

Regarding "the benefit of the release from such talk": according to this method—"such is the question, such is the answer, such is the grasping, such is the unraveling"—there is the talk, and there is the release from that talk; this is the benefit.
"Having the advantage of censure" means having the advantage of finding fault with speech, thinking, "This is a fault in the question; this is a fault in the answer.

And how is it developed? O Kuṇḍaliya, the Teacher, knowing that "this much has been asked by the wanderer, and now he is unable to ask further," [thought], "This teaching is not yet according to the proper sequence..."
“It has been explained. Now I shall lead it to its logical conclusion,” he said, and beginning this teaching, he asked the question himself.
In that context, “he does not covet what is pleasing” means he does not covet a desirable object.
“He does not exult” means he does not exult in worldly satisfaction. “His body is steady and his mind is steady within” refers to his mental body (nāmakāya).
And the mind remains established in its proper range. "Well-established" means well-settled by way of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
"Well-liberated" means well-liberated by way of liberation from the meditation subject.

"Unpleasant" means an undesirable object. "He does not become dejected" means he does not become dejected regarding that. "One whose mind is unestablished" means one whose mind is not fixed due to the defilements (*kilesa*). "Undepressed in mind" means...
"With a mind undepressed by way of dejection" means with a mind not putrid through hatred. "With a mind free from ill will" means with a mind not corrupted by way of hatred.
Thus, Kuṇḍaliya, when the restraint of the sense faculties is developed and frequently practiced in this way, it fulfills the three types of good conduct.
Herein, the fulfillment of good conduct should be understood as follows: first, regarding these six doors, there are eighteen types of misconduct.

...they exist. How so? First, regarding the eye-door: when a desirable object has come into range, for one who arouses greed toward that object without moving the limbs of the body or the members of speech, there is mental misconduct (*manoduccarita*).
For one who speaks with a mind accompanied by greed, saying, "Oh, how desirable, lovely, and pleasing this is!", there is verbal misconduct (*vacīduccarita*); likewise, [if one acts] with the hand...
...the bodily misconduct of one who touches [what should not be touched]. The same method applies to the other doors as well.

However, this is the distinction: in the case of the ear-door, for one who touches what is untouchable—the musical instruments such as conchs, drums, and wind-instruments which serve as the physical basis for the sound-object;
in the nose-door, [for one who touches] the perfumes, garlands, and so forth, which serve as the physical basis for the odor-object; in the tongue-door, [for one who touches]...
Bodily misconduct should be understood as touching, by way of the body-door, fish, meat, and so forth—which serve as the physical basis for the object of taste;

or clothing, cotton wool, curtains, and so forth—which serve as the physical basis for the object of touch at the body-door; or ghee, oil, honey, molasses, and so forth—which, by way of designation, serve as the object of mental phenomena (dhamma) at the mind-door.
In brief, however, bodily transgression here refers to misconduct through the six doors.
There are three kinds of misconduct: misconduct of body, transgression of speech as misconduct of speech, and transgression of mind as misconduct of mind.
This bhikkhu, established in the reflective contemplation of his own development, transforms these forms of misconduct into good conduct.
How so? First, when a desirable object comes into the range of the eye-door, he does not move his limbs of body or speech.
For one who establishes insight (vipassanā) with visible form as its object, there is good mental conduct;

for one who speaks of that which is subject to destruction and subject to vanishing with a mind accompanied by insight, there is good verbal conduct; and for one who does not touch it, thinking, "This is an untouchable object," there is good bodily conduct.
This same method applies to the other sense doors as well. Thus, these are the eighteen types of good conduct in detail.
In brief, here too, within the six doors, there are only three types of good conduct:
bodily restraint as bodily good conduct, verbal restraint as verbal good conduct, and mental restraint as mental good conduct.
Thus, it should be understood that sense-restraint fulfills the three kinds of good conduct. Up to this point, the virtue of sense-restraint protected by virtue has been explained.
Regarding the phrases "having abandoned bodily misconduct," and so forth: there are three kinds of bodily misconduct, four kinds of verbal misconduct, and three kinds of mental misconduct.
Their opposites should be understood as good bodily conduct and so on.
To this extent, through bodily restraint and verbal restraint, one has the Pātimokkha virtue; through mental restraint, one has the three virtues—thus, the virtue of the fourfold purification.
This has been explained. However, it should be understood that in this entire sutta, the foundations of mindfulness rooted in good conduct are mixed with the supramundane;
the foundations of mindfulness that serve as the root for the seven factors of enlightenment belong to the preliminary stage;

and those factors of enlightenment rooted in the foundations of mindfulness likewise belong only to the preliminary stage. But those rooted in clear knowledge and liberation are exclusively supramundane.
The seventh [sutta] is self-evident.
8. Commentary on the Upavāna Sutta: 189.

In the eighth [sutta], "by oneself" (*paccattaṃ*) means by one’s own self. "By wise attention" (*yonisomanasikāra*) means by means of wise attention (*yoniso manasikārena*). "Exerting himself" (*ārabbhamāno*)...
"Even while practicing. "Well-liberated" means well liberated by liberation through the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). "Making it one's bone" means making it one's purpose;
what is meant is that one becomes one who has need of it.
9. Commentary on the First Uppannasutta (Discourse on What Has Arisen)
190. Regarding the ninth [point], "not otherwise than through the manifestation of a Tathāgata": the meaning is that they do not arise at any other time except for the manifestation of a Tathāgata.
10. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Arising (Dutiya-uppanna-sutta-vaṇṇanā) 191.
Regarding the tenth [point], "not otherwise than through the discipline of the Sugata": the meaning is that they do not arise except through the instruction of the Sugata.
The Chapter on Mountains. 2.
The Chapter on the Sick. 1–3.
Commentary on the *Pāṇasutta* and following.
192–194. Regarding the first [sutta] of the second chapter: "They maintain the four postures" means this is said with reference to those very persons who possess the four postures.
"Depending on virtue" means making the virtue of the fourfold purification the basis.
"The seven factors of enlightenment" refers to the path-factors of enlightenment accompanied by insight. The second and third [suttas] have meanings that are self-evident.
4–10. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Sick, etc., 195–201.
Regarding the fourth [sutta]: "In that way, that illness of the Venerable Mahākassapa was abandoned.
It is said that as the Elder was listening intently to this cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), it occurred to him: "From the day I went forth..."
“On the seventh day, as he was penetrating the Truths, these factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) became manifest.

Then, as he thought, “How truly leading to liberation is the Teacher’s instruction!”, his blood cleared, his derived form (upādārūpa) became purified, and the disease departed from his body, turning back like a drop of water fallen upon a lotus leaf. Therefore it is said: “Thus abandoned...”
"And that same affliction befell the Venerable Mahākassapa. The same method applies to the fifth and sixth cases as well.

It should be understood, however, that the affliction arising for these three individuals was a mild fever of cold caused by contact with the wind from trees in full bloom at the foot of the mountain. The rest is clear throughout.
The Chapter on the Sick.
3. The Chapter on Udāyin. 1–2.
Commentary on the Bodhāya Sutta and others.
202–203. In the first [sutta] of the third section, he asks: “To what extent, venerable sir, are they called ‘factors of enlightenment’?
That is to say, to what extent are they called the factors for awakening? He asks this because they lead to enlightenment; that is, they conduce to the purpose of awakening.
In this sutta, the mixed factors of enlightenment are discussed. In the second, the classification of phenomena (*dhammapariccheda*) is discussed.
3–5. Commentary on the *Ṭhāniyasutta*, etc. (204–206).
In the third [sutta], “of things that are the basis for sensual lust” (*kāmarāgaṭṭhāniyānaṃ*) means of those objective phenomena (*ārammaṇadhammā*) which have become the cause for sensual lust.

The same method applies to “things that are the basis for ill will” (*byāpādaṭṭhāniyādi*) and so forth. For this entire sutta is spoken solely in terms of the object (*ārammaṇa*). [End of] the First Chapter.
The specific delimitations stated in the second sutta are indeed applicable here as well. In the fourth [sutta], the mixed factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are explained.
In the fifth, "states conducive to non-decline" refers to those phenomena by their very nature that cause one not to decline.
6–7. Commentary on the *Taṇhakkhayasutta* and others.

207–208. Regarding the sixth [question], "He said this": knowing that the Blessed One had concluded his teaching with the thought, "There is a monk named the Elder Udāyin sitting in this assembly who is skilled in connecting the discourse;

he will question me," and thinking, "I shall link the connection of the teaching," he asked this while questioning. The entire passage beginning with "Vipula" (vast) was spoken with reference to the state of being well-developed (*subhāvitatā*).
For when the mindfulness enlightenment factor is well-developed, it is called "vast," "lofty," "immeasurable," and "free from affliction.
It is "vast" because of its pervasiveness; "lofty" because it has attained greatness; "immeasurable" because its growth is beyond measure;
and it is "free from affliction" because it is devoid of distress due to the removal of the hindrances. [This applies] to craving.
"By the abandoning [of craving], karma is abandoned": whatever karma might arise rooted in craving is abandoned by the abandoning of that craving.
"From the abandoning of karma, suffering": whatever suffering of the cycle of existence (vaṭṭadukkha) might arise rooted in karma is abandoned by the abandoning of that karma.
The terms "the destruction of craving," and so forth, refer to the very destruction of craving and the rest; however, in actual meaning, Nibbāna is what is described by these.
This should be understood. The seventh [sutta] is self-evident. 8.
Commentary on the Nibbedhabhāgiya Sutta: 209.

In the eighth, "pertaining to penetration" (*nibbedhabhāgiya*) means belonging to the category of that which penetrates. "By developing the mindfulness factor of enlightenment" (*satisambojjhaṅgaṃ bhāvitenā*)...
When the enlightenment factor of mindfulness has been developed, or when the mind stands having developed the enlightenment factor of mindfulness—in this way, the path factors here are mixed.
The consciousness developed by them, or that which stands having developed them, is indeed supramundane once it has arisen.
Nevertheless, it is appropriate to describe even that as "mixed" by making it dependent upon the path.
9. Commentary on the Ekadhamma Sutta (210).
In the ninth [sutta], "fetters and bonds" (*saṃyojana-vinibandhā*) refers to the fetters known as bonds. "Clinging" (*ajjhosāna*) refers to grasping after having reached a final conclusion.
10. Commentary on the Udāyi Sutta.
211. "In the tenth [verse], 'one who has not much respect' means one who has not developed great esteem. Regarding the phrase 'turning up and turning down':
here, 'turning up' refers to arising (*udaya*), and 'turning down' refers to passing away (*vaya*); thus it indicates that one is comprehending by way of reflecting upon arising and passing away.

'And the Dhamma has been realized by me, Bhante' means that the Dhamma of insight (*vipassanā*) has been fully understood. 'The Path' refers specifically to the path of insight (*vipassanā-magga*). If..."

For at that time the Elder was a stream-enterer; this insight should be understood as being for the sake of the three higher paths, or, if he were a non-returner, for the sake of the path to arahatship.
"Dwelling in such and such a way" means dwelling in various modes. "For the sake of suchness" (*tathattāya*) means for the state of being thus.
By the words "birth is exhausted," etc., the intended "state of being thus" (*tathābhāva*) is indicated.
He shows this. For the intended meaning here is that [the mind] is brought forward for the purpose of reflection; demonstrating this, he spoke thus.
The remainder is clear throughout.
This concludes the Udāyi-vagga.
4. Nīvaraṇavagga 3–4.
Commentary on the Upakkilesasutta and others, 214–215.
In the third sutta of the fourth chapter: "And it does not shine" means it does not possess radiance; it is subject to decay.
"And" (ca) refers to that which has the nature of melting. "Iron" (ayo) is black iron. With the exception of the four types of metal mentioned here, the remainder is called "metal" (loha).
"Silver" (sajju) is silver. "Of the mind" (cittassa) means of the mind belonging to the four planes. [Objection: Let it be an affliction for the mundane mind;
how can it be so for the supramundane? [Response: By way of not allowing it to arise. For to the extent that it does not allow [the supramundane] to arise—
They do not give [obstruction]; by that very quality, they are called "worldly" (*lokiya*) and "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) defilements (*upakkilesa*).
"Frail" (*pabhaṅgu*) means having a nature of breaking apart through the process of being reduced to powder and dust upon the object. "Unobstructing" (*anāvaraṇa*) and "unhindered" (*anīvaraṇa*):
they do not obstruct wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), thus they are "unobstructing"; they do not hinder or conceal, thus they are "unhindered."
"Defilements of the mind" means defilements of the consciousness belonging to the four planes.
8. Commentary on the Discourse on Obstructions and Hindrances (Āvaraṇanīvaraṇasutta):
219. "Those which weaken wisdom" means those that cause wisdom to become dull. For when there is the frequent arising of hindrances, wisdom—arising only at intervals—is weak, dull, and unclear.
At that time, the five hindrances do not exist. At that time, the seven factors of enlightenment reach the fulfillment of their development.
For when a noble disciple hears the Dhamma that is conducive [to progress], the five hindrances remain far away.
If he is able to produce a distinction right there and then, in this way his seven factors of enlightenment [reach fulfillment].

They reach the fulfillment of their development. If he is unable to do so, then having emerged from that state and gone to his night-quarters or day-quarters, by not abandoning that same joy, he will suppress the five hindrances and produce a distinction.
Even if he is unsuccessful there, as long as within seven days he does not abandon that same joy, he will suppress the hindrances and [achieve his goal].
This was said with reference to the fact that one will produce a specific distinction (*visesa*).

For the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) belonging to the side of rapture and gladness, which were once obtained by means of hearing the Dhamma, may perish due to delighting in work and so forth;
yet, when they arise again after obtaining such favorable conditions as a suitable climate, it is said that at that time they reach the fulfillment of their development (*bhāvanāpāripūri*).
9. Commentary on the Rukkha Sutta (The Tree) 220.

Regarding the ninth [verse]: *ajjhāruhā* means those that climb up. *Kacchaka* refers to the *aṭṭhikacchaka* (the thorny shrub). *Kapitthana* refers to the *vijāta-pilakkha* (the wild wood-apple tree), which bears fruit resembling the breast of a monkey (*makkaṭathana*).
10. Commentary on the Nīvaraṇa Sutta (The Hindrances)
221. "Causing blindness" means causing the state of being blind. "Causing lack of vision" means the non-arising of the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakkhu*).
"Obstructing wisdom" means the cessation of wisdom. "Belonging to the side of affliction" means belonging to the side of suffering.
"Not conducive to Nibbāna" means not tending toward the goal of Nibbāna. The rest is clear in meaning throughout. In this entire section as well...
The mixed factors of enlightenment have been explained.
The Chapter on the Hindrances. 5.
The Chapter on the Wheel-turning Monarch.
1. Commentary on the *Vidhā-sutta* (222).

In the first [sutta] of the fifth chapter, "three *vidhās*" refers to three divisions of conceit (*māna*), or conceit itself. For it is conceit that is called "*vidhā*" because it burns (*vidahati*) in such and such ways.
2. Commentary on the *Cakkavatti-sutta* (223).
223. Regarding the phrase, "Bhikkhus, of the second [type], the Wheel-turning Monarch (rājā cakkavattī)":
here, he is a king (*rājā*) because he shines (*rājati*) by means of his own glorious attainment, or because he gladdens (*rañjeti*) the world through the four bases of sympathy. Of that king.

He is a Wheel-turner (*cakkavattī*) because he sets the wheel in motion (*vatteti*), prompted by the words that have emerged through the power of his merit, saying, "May your lordship turn the precious wheel. Of that Wheel-turner.
“Pātubhāvā” means by way of manifestation. “Sattannaṃ” is a delimitation by number. “Ratanānaṃ” shows the meaning of what has been delimited.
As for the etymological meaning here: it is a “ratana” (jewel) in the sense of producing delight (*rati*). Furthermore:
“It is honored and of great value, incomparable, and difficult to behold;”
“Because it is enjoyed by beings who are peerless, it is therefore called a ‘jewel’ (ratana).
From the moment the Wheel-Jewel (cakkaratana) comes into being, there is no other place for the gods;
all of them offer worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and perform salutations and other honors toward it alone. Thus, in the sense of being highly esteemed, it is a jewel.
Furthermore, there is no measure for the value of the Wheel-treasure such that one could say, "It is worth this much wealth"; thus it is a *ratana* in the sense of being of great value.
And because the Wheel-treasure has no equal among the other treasures existing in the world, it is a *ratana* in the sense of being incomparable.
Moreover, since the Universal Monarchs arise in the very same eon in which the Buddhas arise, and [the Buddhas] sometimes...
They arise only occasionally; therefore, they are a treasure in the sense that their appearance is difficult to encounter.

Furthermore, this [wheel-treasure] arises only for a sublime being who is peerless in terms of birth, beauty, lineage, sovereignty, and so forth, and not for anyone else; thus it is a treasure also in the sense of being the possession of a peerless being.
And just as it is with the wheel-treasure, so it is with the remaining ones as well. Therefore it was said:
“Wrought by mind, of great value, incomparable, rare to behold, and the enjoyment of extraordinary beings—therefore it is called a ‘jewel.

As for the phrase “its manifestation occurs,” this means its arising occurs. Herein, the construction is as follows: through the manifestation of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*), there is the manifestation of seven [jewels].

"It is improper to say that the appearance of the jewels [occurs] when he has turned the wheel. For it is not improper to say that one becomes a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti) after having turned the wheel once it has arisen.
Why? Because of the dependence on the fixed law of the Wheel-turner.

For whoever shall turn the wheel by necessity, from the moment of rebirth-linking onwards, comes to be designated as "the Wheel-turner has appeared. This applies to one who has already acquired that name.

And this is indeed appropriate even from the perspective of it being a statement regarding the origin of the person. For the meaning here is this: the manifestation of that particular being who has acquired the name "Wheel-turning Monarch" (cakkavatti)—which is termed "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi)—is what occurs.
Through his manifestation, the jewels appear. And when those [jewels] have appeared, he becomes conjoined with them once the equipment of merit (puññasambhāra) has reached maturity.
At that time, a thought regarding their manifestation arises in the world. Furthermore, this is logical due to the frequent usage [of the plural].
For when a perception of their manifestation arises in the world, then one appears first and subsequently the other six appear;
thus, it is logical on account of frequent usage as well. Moreover, this is indeed logical because of the diversity of the meanings of "manifestation."
For "manifestation" (pātubhāva) does not mean only that which has already become manifest; it also means "that which makes manifest. This is the analysis of the meaning of manifestation.

Because that equipment of merit (puññasambhāra) manifests the Wheel-turning Monarch (cakkavatti) by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it is therefore called "the manifestation of the Wheel-turning Monarch.
For it is not only the Wheel-turning Monarch [who is manifested]; rather, these seven...

"The appearance of the treasures" is the meaning here. For just as that accumulation of merit is the cause for the birth of the king, so too, in a figurative sense, it is the decisive support (upanissaya-hetu) for the treasures;
thus it is entirely appropriate [to say]: "Bhikkhus, with the appearance of a Wheel-turning Monarch, there is the appearance of the seven treasures."
Now, in order to show the nature of those treasures, he said: "Of which seven? Of the wheel-treasure," and so forth.

Regarding the phrases "of the wheel-treasure" and so on, this is the summary of the intended meaning: the manifestation of the wheel-treasure occurs when it is capable of taking up and bestowing the glory and wealth of the four great continents, each surrounded by two thousand islands.
Likewise, there is the elephant-treasure, capable of traveling through the air and traversing the earth bounded by the ocean even before breakfast;

the horse-treasure, of a similar nature; and the jewel-treasure, which, even in darkness possessing fourfold density, is able to dispel a surrounding gloom of a league’s extent and provide the sight of light—provided that one avoids the six kinds of defects.
The appearance of the Woman-treasure who conducts herself agreeably; the appearance of the Householder-treasure capable of perceiving treasures hidden within the earth at a distance of one *yojana*;
and the appearance of the Counsellor-treasure, known as the eldest son, capable of governing the entire kingdom, having been conceived in the womb of the Chief Queen—this is the summary here.
In detail, however, the manner in which those treasures, beginning with the Wheel-treasure (cakkaratana), appear is already set forth in such suttas as the Mahāsudassana.
Their meaning has also been fully explained in the commentary on them.
Regarding the phrases "of the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor treasure" and so forth, their similarity is to be understood thus: just as for a wheel-turning monarch...

Just as the wheel-treasure (cakkaratana) precedes all other treasures, so too does the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor-treasure (satisambojjhaṅgaratana) precede all phenomena belonging to the four planes;
in the sense of being a precursor, it is like the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch (cakkavatti-rāja).

And among the treasures of a universal monarch, there is the elephant-treasure (hatthiratana), which possesses a massive body, is towering, vast, and great; this enlightenment-factor-treasure of the investigation of phenomena (dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgaratana) is likewise.
"Endowed with a great body of Dhamma, lofty, vast, and immense"—this is like the elephant-treasure.
"The horse-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch is swift, light, and fleet"—this treasure of the energy factor of enlightenment (*vīriya-sambojjhaṅga*) is likewise swift, light, and fleet;
by virtue of this swiftness, lightness, and fleetness, it is like the horse-treasure. The jewel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch...

It dispels darkness and shows light. This jewel of the joy factor of enlightenment (*pītisambojjhaṅga-ratana*), because it is exclusively wholesome, dispels the darkness of the defilements and, by way of being a co-nascent condition and so forth, shows the light of knowledge; thus, by this quality of dispelling darkness and showing light, it is similar to a precious gem.
The woman-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch allays the distress of body and mind and pacifies the fever of passion.
This treasure of the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility likewise allays the distress of body and mind and pacifies the fever of passion;
thus, it is similar to the woman-treasure. The householder-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch, at whatever moment it is desired...
By cutting off distraction through the giving of wealth, one makes the mind one-pointed;

this jewel of the concentration enlightenment factor (samādhi-sambojjhaṅga) likewise brings about absorption by means of fulfilling whatever is desired, and because it cuts off distraction and makes the mind one-pointed, it is similar to the householder-jewel.
And the counselor-jewel of a wheel-turning monarch [is so called] because of his accomplishment of all duties everywhere.

It brings about a state of non-exertion. This jewel of the equanimity enlightenment factor (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga), having freed the arising of consciousness from lethargy and agitation, establishes the application in a state of neutrality and thus brings about non-exertion; therefore, it is like a counselor-jewel.
Thus, it should be understood that in this discourse, the section on the all-inclusive states belonging to the four planes has been explained.
4–10. Commentary on the *Duppañña-sutta* and others, 225–231.

In the fourth [sutta], "one who is like a he-goat" (*eḷamūga*) refers to one who, although capable of uttering speech with the mouth, is mute due to faults—that is, one whose speech is not perfected. The rest is entirely clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the Chapter on the Wheel-turning Monarch (*Cakkavattivagga*).
6. Sākacchavagga 1.
Āhārasuttavaṇṇanā 232.
Regarding the first sutta of the sixth chapter, in the passages beginning with "This nutriment leads to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor that has not yet arisen," and so forth:

This is the distinction from the previous method. For it is not only these aforementioned factors that serve as conditions for the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor and the others, or for the cultivation and fulfillment of those already arisen; other factors should also be understood in this way.
Indeed, there are four other things that lead to the arising of the mindfulness enlightenment factor: mindfulness and clear comprehension, and the avoidance of persons who are forgetful.
"Attending to mindfulness, associating with persons who possess it, and being intent upon that.

For, in the seven instances beginning with "when walking," etc., one should practice by means of mindfulness and clear comprehension; by avoiding persons of muddled mindfulness who are like crows dropped upon food; by associating with persons of established mindfulness such as the Elder Tissadatta, the Elder Abhaya, and others;
and by having a mind that is inclined, bent, and directed toward the arousal of mindfulness during standing, sitting, and other postures.
And the enlightenment factor of mindfulness arises. Thus, for that which has arisen through these four causes, there is the fulfillment of its development by means of the path of arahantship.
Seven things lead to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor: being a questioner, making the basis pure, ... [and so forth].
These are: the balancing of the faculties, avoiding persons of poor wisdom, associating with persons possessed of wisdom, reflecting on the practice of profound knowledge, and devotion thereto.

In this context, "being one who asks many questions" means having an abundance of inquiries concerning the meaning of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, path factors, jhāna factors, serenity, and insight.
“Making the basis clean” means making the internal and external bases clear.
For when one’s hair of the head, nails, and body hair are long, or when the body is full of humors and smeared with sweat and dirt, then the internal basis is unclear and impure.
But when the robe is worn out, soiled, and foul-smelling...
When there is a foul-smelling body or a dirty lodging, then the external object is unclear and impure.
Therefore, the internal object must be made clear by cutting off hair and so forth, by making the body light through emetics and purgatives, and by anointing and bathing.
The external object [must be made clear] by needlework, washing, dyeing, and repairing, and so forth.

It must be made clear. For when this internal and external basis is not clear, the knowledge regarding the consciousness and mental factors that have arisen is also unclear and unpurified, like the radiance of a lamp flame produced by depending on unpurified oil in a lamp-stand.
But when the internal and external basis is clear, those [consciousness and mental factors] that have arisen...
Knowledge regarding the mind and mental factors also becomes clear and purified, like the radiance produced by the flame of a lamp when it relies on a clean lamp-stand, a pure bowl, and refined oil.
Therefore it is said: "The act of making the basis pure conduces to the arising of the investigation-of-phenomena factor of enlightenment."
The "balancing of the faculties" means making the faculties, beginning with faith, equal in strength.
For if his faculty of faith is strong while the others are weak, then the faculty of energy cannot perform its function of exertion,
the faculty of mindfulness its function of establishing, the faculty of concentration its function of non-distraction, and the faculty of wisdom its function of seeing.

He is unable to do so. Therefore, that [restlessness] should be diminished either by reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), or by not attending to them in such a way as to cause [the mind] to become strong when one is attending to them. The story of the Elder Vakkali is an illustration of this.
However, if the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) is too strong, then the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*) is unable to perform its function of resolution.
The others do not [perform] the specific functions of the others. Therefore, that [hindrance] must be abandoned through the cultivation of serenity and the rest.

In this regard, the story of the Elder Soṇa should be cited. Likewise, when one among the remaining [hindrances] is predominant, it should be understood that the others are incapable of performing their own respective functions.
In particular, however, they praise here the balance between faith and wisdom, as well as concentration and energy.

For one who has strong faith but weak wisdom has blind confidence; he places his trust in what is not a proper basis. On the other hand, one who has strong wisdom but weak faith sides with the cynical;
like a disease arising from medicine, he becomes incurable. [This occurs] by the mere arising of a thought...
"It is wholesome" means that by over-exerting oneself and failing to perform acts such as giving, one is reborn in hell.

Through the balancing of both, one gains confidence in the object itself. Furthermore, when strong concentration is coupled with weak energy, because concentration belongs to the side of indolence, it is overcome by indolence.
When strong energy is coupled with weak concentration, because energy belongs to the side of restlessness, [it is overcome by restlessness].

It overcomes [the opposite]. However, concentration joined with energy does not allow one to fall into indolence, and energy joined with concentration does not allow one to fall into agitation. Therefore, both of these must be made equal.
For it is through the equality of both that absorption (appanā) occurs.
Moreover, for one whose task is concentration, even strong faith is required. One who thus has faith and resolves will reach absorption (*appanā*).
For one whose task is concentration and wisdom, however, a strong state of one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*) is required;
for it is in this way that he reaches absorption. For one whose task is insight (*vipassanā*), strong wisdom is required; for it is in this way that he penetrates the characteristics [of phenomena].
[The mind] attains [absorption]. Furthermore, absorption certainly occurs even through the balancing of both [factors]. However, mindfulness must be strong in all instances.

For mindfulness protects the mind from falling into agitation through the influence of faith, energy, and wisdom—which belong to the side of agitation—and from falling into indolence through concentration, which belongs to the side of indolence. Therefore, it is like a seasoning of salt.
Among all [mental] factors, mindfulness is to be desired everywhere, like a minister who oversees all affairs for a king in every royal matter.
Therefore he said: "And mindfulness has been called 'all-beneficial' by the Blessed One. For what reason?
Because the mind has mindfulness as its refuge, and mindfulness is manifested as protection; without mindfulness, there is no exertion or restraint of the mind."
"Keeping company with those of poor wisdom" means staying far away from foolish persons who lack deep insight into the analysis of the aggregates and so forth.

"Associating with wise persons" means associating with individuals endowed with the wisdom of arising and passing away (*udayabbaya-paññā*), which discerns the fifty characteristics of conditioned phenomena.
"Reflecting on the conduct of profound knowledge" means...
The analysis and reflection on the distinctions [of phenomena] occurs through profound wisdom as it proceeds toward the deep aggregates and so forth.

"Inclination toward that" means a state of mind that is slanted, leaning, and disposed toward the arousing of the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor while standing, sitting, and so forth.
When this has thus arisen, its fulfillment of development occurs through the path of arahantship.
Eleven things lead to the arising of the energy enlightenment factor: reflecting on the fear of the states of deprivation,
seeing the benefits [of energy], reflecting on the path of travel, honoring the alms-food received, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance,
reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of one’s birth, and reflecting on the greatness of one’s fellow practitioners of the holy life.
Avoiding indolent persons, associating with persons who have aroused energy, and being intent upon that.
Therein, [this applies] even at the time of experiencing great suffering in the hells, starting from the time of being subjected to the fivefold torture;
or when caught by nets, fish-traps, and so forth in the animal realm; or when pierced by the stroke of a whip, a thorn, and so on.

Furthermore, even at times such as when carrying a cart, or during the realm of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya) for many thousands of years or even an entire interval between Buddhas while suffering from hunger and thirst,
or among the Kālakañjika asuras while experiencing the pains of wind, heat, and so forth with a physical frame measuring sixty or eighty cubits consisting of nothing but bone and skin—
it is impossible [to lose] the energy factor of enlightenment (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga).
“...to arouse [it]. This very moment is yours, O bhikkhu. Thus, for one who reflects upon the fear of the states of misery (apāya), the energy factor of enlightenment (vīriya-sambojjhaṅga) arises.
It also arises for one who sees the benefit, thinking: “It is not possible for one who is lazy to attain the nine supramundane states;

it is only for one who has initiated energy that this is possible—this is the benefit of energy. Furthermore, [it arises] through [the example of] all the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and Great Disciples.
"The path you have already traveled must be traveled again; and that cannot be done by one who is indolent. Thus it arises even for one reflecting on the route of travel.

"Those people who attend upon you with alms-food and so forth are neither your relatives, nor your slaves or laborers, nor do they give you excellent alms-food and such thinking, 'We shall live depending on you. Rather, it is because of their own deeds..."

They give things while hoping for great fruit. The requisites were not permitted to you by the Teacher with the thought, "Having used these requisites, he will dwell in comfort, possessing physical strength";
rather, those requisites were permitted with the thought, "While using these very things, he will perform the duty of a recluse (samaṇadhamma) and be liberated from the suffering of saṃsāra."

"If you now dwell indolent, you will not honor that alms-food; for it is only for one who has aroused energy that there is what is called 'honoring alms-food,'" thus it arises even for one reflecting on the honoring of alms-food, as it did for the Elder Mahā Mitta.
It is said that the elder resided at a place called Kassaka-leṇa. In the village where he went for alms, there was a certain great female lay devotee who [honored] the elder...
Having adopted him, she looked after him. One day, while going to the forest, she said to her daughter:
"My dear, in such-and-such a place there are old rice, in such-and-such a place milk, in such-and-such a place ghee, and in such-and-such a place molasses.
When your brother, Master Mitta, arrives, cook a meal and give it to him together with the milk, ghee, and molasses."
“You may eat [today], but yesterday I ate the leftover cooked food with sour gruel.
“What will you eat during the day, mother? “Put some leaf vegetables in it, cook a sour rice-gruel with broken grains, and set it aside, mother.”
The Elder, having put on his robe and while taking out his bowl, heard that sound and admonished himself:
"It seems the Great Laywoman, after eating discarded rice with sour gruel, will even during the day eat only thin, sour rice-gruel with broken leaves;
yet she is mentioning old rice and such for your sake. Relying on her, however, he [the donor] will not even [prepare] a field..."
"She does not expect a dwelling, nor food, nor clothing; rather, she gives while aspiring for the three kinds of excellence.
Will you be able to grant her those excellences, or will you not?
Furthermore, this alms-food cannot be accepted by you as long as you are possessed of lust, hatred, and delusion. Having said this, he placed the bowl into its bag.
Releasing the knot, he turned back and went to Kassakalena itself.
Placing his bowl beneath the bed and his robe on the robe-stand, he sat down, resolving with renewed energy: "I shall not leave until I have attained Arahatship.
Having lived there for a long time with diligence, that bhikkhu increased his insight and, before the meal itself—
Having attained arahantship, like a blooming lotus, he emerged with a smile, his great taints being exhausted.
At the entrance of the cave, the deity dwelling in the tree said:
“Homage to you, O noble steed among men! Homage to you, O supreme among men!”
“Since your taints are exhausted, you are worthy of offerings, O venerable one.
Having uttered this inspired utterance, she said, “Venerable sir, by giving almsfood to Arahants like yourself who have entered for alms, elderly women will be freed from suffering.
The Elder rose, opened the door, and [waited] for the time.
Looking out, he realized it was already dawn; taking his bowl and robe, he entered the village.
The girl, having prepared the meal, sat watching at the door, thinking, "Now my brother will arrive; now he will arrive.
When the Elder reached the door of the house, she took his bowl and [filled it] with food mixed with ghee and molasses.
Having filled a bowl of milk-rice, she placed it in his hand. The Elder, having offered the blessing of "May there be happiness," departed.

She, however, remained standing, gazing after him. For at that time, the Elder’s complexion was exceedingly pure, his faculties were serene, and his face shone with great brilliance like a palmyra fruit released from its bond.
The Great Laywoman, having returned from the forest, asked, "What is it, mother? Has your brother come? She related the entire account of what had occurred.
The laywoman, realizing that today her son’s task of going forth had reached its culmination, said, "Is your brother, mother, finding joy in the Buddha's teaching? Is he not weary of it?"
“Now, this inheritance from the Teacher is indeed great— namely, what are called the seven treasures of the noble ones—
and it cannot be acquired by one who is indolent. For just as parents cast out a son who has gone astray, saying,
‘He is no son of ours,’ and he does not receive their inheritance after their passing, even so, the indolent person does not receive this inheritance of the noble treasures.”
"One does not obtain it; only one who has aroused energy obtains it"—this arises even when reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance:

"Moreover, your Teacher was great. For at the time of your Teacher’s conception in the mother’s womb, at his Great Departure, at his full enlightenment, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, at the Twin Miracle, at the descent from the deva-world, and also at the relinquishing of the life-force..."
Even at the time of his final *parinibbāna*, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.
"Is it fitting for you, having gone forth in the teaching of such a Teacher, to be lazy?"—thus it arises even when reflecting upon the greatness of the Teacher.
"By birth as well, you are not of lowly origin; you have come from the royal lineage of King Okkāka, descending through the unbroken succession of the Great Elect (*Mahāsaṃmata*)."
"You are born as the grandson of the Great King Suddhodana and Queen Mahāmāyā, and as the younger brother of the auspicious Rāhula;
it is not fitting for one such as you, a son of the Conqueror, to dwell in indolence"— thus it arises even for one who reflects upon the greatness of his birth.
“Both Sāriputta and Moggallāna, as well as the eighty great disciples, penetrated the supramundane Dhamma through energy alone.

Yet you, among these fellow practitioners of the holy life, are you following their path or not? Thus it arises even for one who reflects upon the greatness of his fellow practitioners of the holy life.
It arises for one who avoids persons who are lazy, resembling pythons that remain with their bellies full, having abandoned both physical and mental energy;

for one who associates with persons who have aroused energy and are resolute; and for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward the arousal of energy during standing, sitting, and other postures.
Once it has thus arisen, its cultivation reaches completion through the path of Arahantship.
Eleven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of rapture: recollection of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue,
generosity, recollection of the deities, recollection of peace, avoidance of persons who are harsh, association with persons who are gentle,
reflection on discourses that inspire confidence, and devotion to that [rapture].

For when one recollects the qualities of the Buddha, the enlightenment factor of rapture arises, pervading the entire body as far as the skin’s surface; likewise when one recollects the qualities of the Dhamma and the Saṅgha,
or when one reviews the fourfold purification of virtue (catupārisuddhisīla) that has been guarded unbroken for a long time,
or when a layperson reviews the ten precepts or the five precepts.
It occurs for one who, during times of famine, fear, and so forth, gives excellent food to his fellow celibates and reflects on that generosity, saying, "Thus indeed have we given";
for a householder as well, when reflecting on the gift given to the virtuous at such a time;
and for one who reflects on the presence within himself of those very qualities endowed with which others attained the state of the gods.
For one who reflects that even for sixty or seventy years the defilements suppressed by meditative attainment do not manifest;

and for one who avoids coarse persons—who are like the dust on a donkey’s back due to the absence of serene confidence and affection toward the Buddha and others, as indicated by their lack of reverence when visiting shrines, seeing the Bodhi tree, or meeting elder monks; and [for one who dwells] upon the Buddha and others...
It arises for one who associates with people who abound in confidence and have gentle minds; for one who reviews those inspiring discourses that illuminate the virtues of the Triple Gem;
and for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward the production of rapture during standing, sitting, and other postures.
Once it has arisen in this way, its cultivation reaches completion through the path of Arahantship.
Seven things lead to the arising of the enlightenment factor of tranquility:
using refined food, dwelling in a pleasant climate, maintaining a comfortable posture, practicing equanimity, avoiding persons with agitated bodies,
associating with persons whose bodies are tranquil, and being intent upon that.

Tranquility arises even for one who eats refined and succulent food, and even for one who resorts to a suitable climate and posture during cold and hot seasons or while engaged in the various postures.
However, this was not said with reference to one who is of the nature of a Great Man (mahāpurisa), for such a person is capable of enduring all climates and postures.
This applies to one for whom there is similarity or dissimilarity [of conditions].
It exists; it arises for one who avoids dissimilar postures and resorts to those that are similar.
"The practice of equanimity" refers to reflecting on the fact that both oneself and others are the owners of their own karma. It arises through this practice of equanimity.
It also arises for one who avoids a person whose body is agitated, such as one who wanders about actually harassing others with clods of earth, sticks, and so forth.

It arises even for one who associates with a person whose hands and feet are well-restrained and whose body is tranquil, and it arises for one whose mind is inclined, directed, and bent toward the production of tranquility during standing, sitting, and so forth.
When it has arisen in this way, its fulfillment through development occurs by means of the path of Arahantship.
Ten things conduce to the arising of the concentration enlightenment factor: making the basis pure, balancing the faculties, and so forth.
Skill in signs; uplifting the mind at the proper time; restraining the mind at the proper time; gladdening the mind at the proper time;
maintaining equanimity toward the mind at the proper time; avoiding persons who are unconcentrated; associating with persons who are concentrated; and being intent upon that.
In this context, the purification of the basis and the balancing of the faculties are to be understood in the manner already described.
Skill in the sign means skill in grasping the kasiṇa-sign.

"Exerting the mind at the right time" means that at whatever time the mind becomes sluggish due to excessive laxity of energy and so forth, at that time one exerts it by arousing the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, and rapture.
"Restraining the mind at the right time" means at whatever time [the mind becomes agitated] due to over-exertion of energy and so forth...
When the mind is agitated, at that time its suppression is achieved by arousing the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

"Encouragement at the proper time" means: when the mind becomes disenchanted due to a deficiency in the application of wisdom or due to the absence of the bliss of peace, at that time [it should be encouraged] by reflecting upon the eight grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
It causes spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). The eight bases for spiritual urgency are: birth, aging, sickness, and death—these four; the suffering of the states of deprivation as the fifth;
the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*) in the past; the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence in the future; and the suffering rooted in the search for food in the present.
Furthermore, one generates serene confidence (*pasāda*) by recollecting the qualities of the Triple Gem. This is called "encouragement at the proper time."
“Equanimity at the proper time” means that when, by means of right practice, the mind has become neither sluggish nor agitated, neither dissatisfied nor overly excited,
but is proceeding evenly toward the object and has entered the path of serenity (samatha), then it does not engage in the functions of exertion, restraint, or encouragement,
just as a charioteer does not intervene when his horses are proceeding evenly. This is called “equanimity at the proper time.”
Avoidance of persons who are unconcentrated means keeping far away from those whose minds are distracted and who have not attained either access concentration or absorption.
Cultivation of persons who are concentrated means associating with, frequenting, and attending upon those whose minds are concentrated by way of either access or absorption.
Devotion to that [practice] means, in standing, sitting, and so forth—
It is the state of the mind being inclined, leaning, and tending toward the very production of concentration. For one who practices in this way, this [concentration] arises.
Furthermore, for that which has thus arisen, there is the fulfillment of its development through the path of arahantship.
Five things lead to the arising of the equanimity enlightenment factor: neutrality toward beings, neutrality toward formations, and so forth.
Avoiding persons who dally with the formations of beings, associating with persons who are neutral toward the formations of beings, and being intent upon that [neutrality].
Therein, one arouses neutrality toward beings by way of two aspects:
"You have come by your own kamma and you will go by your own kamma; this person too has come by his own kamma..."
“By means of karma one will go; whom do you cherish?”—thus by reflecting on the ownership of one’s own karma; and “In the ultimate sense, there is no self at all;
whom do you cherish?”—thus by reflecting on the absence of a sentient being. In these two ways, he arouses equanimity toward conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra-majjhattatā*):
“This robe will gradually undergo changes in its color and reach a state of decay.”
"Having approached and used this foot-wiping cloth, it will be discarded at the end of the staff;
moreover, if it had an owner, he would not have allowed it to be thus destroyed.
Thus, by reflecting on its ownerless state, and by reflecting on its temporary nature, thinking, "This is not for long; it is merely for the time being. Just as...
And as it is with robes, so should the application [of the rule] be understood regarding bowls and other such items.
Regarding the phrase "avoiding persons who cherish the seven types of conditioned things":

here, a person—whether a layperson who cherishes their own sons, daughters, and so forth, or a renunciant who cherishes their own pupils, co-residents, preceptors, and so forth—performs for them with their own hands tasks such as cutting hair, sewing with a needle, washing robes, dyeing them, or boiling bowls.
Even when not seeing him for a moment, he looks here and there like a bewildered deer, wondering, "Where is that novice? Where is that young man?

And even when requested by another for the sake of tasks such as cutting hair, saying, "Please send so-and-so for a moment," he replies, "We ourselves do not perform that work; you will only weary yourselves by taking him along."
He does not give; this is called "one who hoards living beings" (*sattakelāyana*).

But he who treats robes, alms-bowls, water-pots, walking-sticks, and so forth as his own property, and does not allow even another’s hand to touch them, and who, even when asked for them temporarily, says, "We too do not use these because we regard them as our wealth;
what shall we give to you?", this is called "one who hoards conditioned things" (*saṅkhārakelāyana*). But he who...
In both of these two cases, one who is neutral and indifferent is said to be "neutral toward beings and formations. Thus,

this factor of enlightenment of equanimity arises for one who avoids from afar a person who dotes on beings and formations, for one who associates with a person who is neutral toward beings and formations,
and for one whose mind— in standing, sitting, and so forth— is inclined, directed, and bent toward the production of that [equanimity].
It arises. For that which has thus arisen, there is the fulfillment of its development through the path of Arahatship.
"The sign of foulness" refers to the ten objects of meditation on foulness, consisting of the various stages beginning with the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*).

"Frequenting of wise attention" (*yonisomanasikāra-bahulīkāra*): here, "wise attention" means attention as a skillful means, attention as the primary path, and attention that brings about [the state].

Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire: apprehending the sign of the foul, devotion to the development of the foul, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, having virtuous friends, and appropriate talk.
For sensual desire is abandoned both by one who apprehends the tenfold sign of the foul and by one who develops it.

This refers both to one who guards the doors of the sense faculties and to one who knows the proper measure in eating, having the habit of drinking water after allowing space for four or five mouthfuls. Therefore it was said:
“Without having eaten four or five mouthfuls, one should drink water;”
“It is sufficient for the comfortable dwelling of a bhikkhu who is resolute.
Thus, for one who serves virtuous friends like the Elder Tissa the practitioner of foulness—those who delight in the meditation on foulness—even sensual desire is abandoned;
it is also abandoned through talk appropriate to the ten signs of foulness during standing, sitting, and other postures. Therefore it was said:
“Six things lead to the abandoning of sensual desire. Furthermore, for sensual desire abandoned by these six things, there is no further arising in the future through the path of Arahantship.

Regarding the phrase “the liberation of mind through loving-kindness” (*mettā cetovimutti*): when “loving-kindness” (*mettā*) is mentioned here, both absorption (*appanā*) and access concentration (*upacāra*) are applicable; as for “liberation of mind” (*cetovimutti*), [it refers to the state of being liberated from the hindrance of ill will].
It is absorption itself. Wise attention has the characteristic already stated. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of ill will:

apprehending the sign of loving-kindness, devotion to the development of loving-kindness, reviewing one’s own ownership of kamma, frequent reflection, having virtuous friends, and talk that is suitable.

For even in one who learns loving-kindness (*mettā*) by means of any one of the methods—whether directed toward specific persons, non-specific persons, or the pervasion of directions—as well as in one who develops loving-kindness by way of the directional pervasions with or without specific limits, ill-will (*byāpāda*) is abandoned. [The Teacher says:
"What will you do by being angry with this person? Will you be able to destroy his virtue (*sīla*) and so forth? Is it not rather by your own karma..."

Having come here, will you depart by the very power of your own karma? To become angry with another is like desiring to strike someone while holding a glowing charcoal, a red-hot iron spike, or excrement; it is similar to that. What will this person, who is angry with you, do?
Will he be able to destroy your virtue (*sīla*) and other qualities? He too has come by the power of his own karma and will depart by the very power of his own karma.
"Like a gift that has not been accepted, or like a handful of dust thrown against the wind, this anger will fall back upon his own head"— thus,
for one who reflects on the ownership of kamma by oneself and by another, and for one who stands in reflective discernment after having reflected on the ownership of kamma by both,
there are virtuous friends such as the Elder Assagutta, who delight in the cultivation of loving-kindness.
Ill will is abandoned even while one is practicing [the meditation]; it is also abandoned through talk based on loving-kindness and conducive to its development while standing, sitting, and so forth.

Therefore it is said: “Six things lead to the abandoning of ill will. Furthermore, for one who has abandoned ill will by means of these six things, there is its non-arising in the future through the path of the Non-returner.
"Monks, there is discontent," and so forth; the meaning of this has already been explained. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor:

taking note of the sign [of satiety] regarding overeating, changing one's posture, attending to the perception of light, living in the open air, having virtuous friends, and engaging in appropriate talk.
For one who has eaten a handful of food, or until full, or until turning over on the spot, or until satisfied, or having consumed food like crows' mouthfuls,
and then sits in a night-station or day-station practicing the duty of a recluse, sloth and torpor come upon him like a great elephant charging;
but for one whose habit is to subsist by leaving space for four or five morsels and drinking water, [sloth and torpor do not arise].
"That does not happen to the bhikkhu"—thus, even for one who takes this as the sign regarding over-eating, sloth and torpor are abandoned.

Even for one who changes from whatever posture sloth and torpor have overcome him; or for one who attends to the light of the moon, the light of a lamp, or the light of a torch at night, and to the light of the sun by day;
or for one living in the open air; or for one such as the Elder Mahākassapa—[sloth and torpor are abandoned].

For one who has abandoned sloth and torpor, sloth and torpor are abandoned even by associating with virtuous friends; they are also abandoned by talk concerning the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) that are conducive [to their removal] while standing, sitting, and so forth.
Therefore it was said: "Six things lead to the abandoning of sloth and torpor.
Furthermore, for sloth and torpor abandoned by these six things, [it is abandoned] by the path of Arahantship.
There is non-arising in the future.
Monks, there is the calming of the mind; these and other such points have already been explained. Furthermore, six things lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse:
being well-learned, asking questions, knowing the Vinaya thoroughly, attending upon the elders, [and so forth].
Having virtuous friends and appropriate conversation.

For even in one who possesses great learning—having mastered one, two, three, four, or five Nikāyas by way of the text and by way of the meaning—even for such a person, restlessness and remorse are abandoned;
as is [restlessness and remorse] for one who frequently inquires into what is allowable and what is not allowable.
Restlessness and worry are abandoned by one who has mastered the formulation of the Vinaya, even if they are already knowledgeable; by approaching elder and senior theras;
by attending upon spiritual friends such as the thera Upāli, who are experts in the Vinaya;
and also by appropriate talk concerning what is allowable and what is unallowable regarding standing, sitting, and so forth. Therefore it was said: "Six..."

“...these states lead to the abandoning of restlessness and remorse. Furthermore, when restlessness and remorse have been abandoned by these six states, there is no further arising of restlessness through the path of Arahantship, and no further arising of remorse through the path of Non-returning.
The phrases “wholesome and unwholesome states,” and so forth, have already had their meaning explained. Moreover, there are six states for the abandoning of doubt.
They lead to [success]: being learned, being inquisitive, understanding what has been formulated in the Vinaya, abundance of resolve, having good friends, and appropriate talk.
For even by means of great learning, for one who masters one or... up to five Nikāyas according to both the text and the meaning—
Doubt is abandoned by one who frequently inquires about the Three Jewels; by one who has attained mastery over the Vinaya;
by one who possesses abundant resolve known as unwavering faith in the Three Jewels; and by one who serves a virtuous friend such as the Elder Vakkali, who is resolved through faith.
Furthermore, doubt is abandoned while standing, sitting, or otherwise engaged, through [reflection upon] the Three Jewels.
It is also abandoned through talk that is dependent on the virtues [of the Triple Gem] and is conducive to progress. Therefore it was said:
“Six things lead to the abandoning of doubt. When doubt has been abandoned by means of these six things, its non-arising in the future occurs through the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*).
Thus, in this sutta, the Blessed One brought his teaching to a conclusion with the state of Arahantship, having turned away from the three realms of existence.
He took the false measure. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship.
2. Commentary on the Pariyāya Sutta: 233.
Regarding the second [sutta], "a large number" (*sambahula*): according to the Vinaya method, three persons are called "a large number," and beyond that, it is even more so.
The Saṅgha. According to the method of the Suttantas, there are three or three [monks], and beyond that, many.
Here, according to the method of the Suttantas, they should be understood as "many. "They entered for alms" means they had entered for alms. However, they had not yet actually entered;
nevertheless, because they had set out with the intention, "We shall enter," it is said that "they entered. How so? Just as when one says, "I will go to the village."
Just as a man who has departed is said to have "gone to the village" even before he has reached it when asked, "Where is so-and-so?", so it is here.
"The park of the wanderers" refers to a park belonging to wanderers of other sects located not far from Jetavana;
it is with reference to that that this was said. "The ascetic, friends," means: "Friends, your teacher, the ascetic Gotama."
"Friends, we too teach the Dhamma to our disciples in this way. However, in the systems of the sectarians, there is no such thing as "the five hindrances are to be abandoned;

the seven factors of enlightenment are to be developed. Yet, having gone to the monastery and standing at the edge of the assembly, they listen to the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma as if looking elsewhere, as if their minds were preoccupied with something else.
Then, observing that "the ascetic Gotama says, 'Abandon this;

cultivate this,'" he went to his own monastery. In the middle of the monastery, having prepared a seat and surrounded by male and female attendants, he raised his head and straightened his body, demonstrating the manner in which he had realized [truth] through his own self-born knowledge (sayambhūñāṇa), saying: "Five..."
"The hindrances are called those that must be abandoned; the seven factors of enlightenment are called those that must be developed"—thus they speak.
Regarding the phrase "here, friends": here means in this presentation. What is the distinction (*visesa*)? What is the excess?
What is the special application (*adhippayāsa*)? What is the difference (*nānākaraṇa*)? Or rather, it refers to the teaching of the Dhamma as the teaching of the Dhamma.

They say: "What indeed would be called the distinction concerning our teaching of the Dhamma compared with the teaching of the Dhamma by the ascetic Gotama, or the teaching of the Dhamma by the ascetic Gotama compared with ours?
The same method applies to the second phrase as well.
“They did not rejoice” means they did not accept it by saying, “It is exactly so.
“They did not reject” means they did not oppose it by saying, “This is not so. But were they capable [of speaking] and yet acted thus, or were they incapable?
They were capable. For it was not that they were unable to speak such words as, “Friend, in your system the five hindrances are to be abandoned.”
“...there is nothing called ‘the four foundations of mindfulness,’ nor is there anything called ‘the seven factors of enlightenment that are to be developed. But they thought:
“We have this topic for discussion; we shall report it to the Teacher, and then the Teacher will give us a sweet discourse on the Dhamma.
*Pariyāya* means a reason or method. “They will not be able to master it” means they will not be able to explain it having mastered it themselves.
"And further frustration" means that they will encounter even greater suffering because they are unable to fulfill [the expectation].
For suffering arises for those who, having undertaken [the task], are unable to explain it. In the phrase "as if, monks, in an improper domain," *tanti* is merely a particle;
*yathā* is a word expressing reason, meaning "because the question was asked in an improper domain. "Together with the devas":
"Together with the devas, including the world of devas. The same method applies to the worlds of Māra and so forth. Thus, having included three bases in the world, he says "two generations";

by including even these five, he demonstrates that within this world—divided into the categories of "together with the devas" and so on—he does not perceive any deva or human [who has attained such a state]. Or, "having heard from here," means from me.
"Having heard from the teaching. For by hearing this, both a Tathāgata and a disciple of the Tathāgata would be pleased and satisfied;
he shows that there is no other way to please them.
Now, demonstrating the pleasing of their minds by answering those questions himself, he says: "And who, monks..."
He says, "The method," and so forth. Therein, "internal sensual desire" (*ajjhattaṃ kāmacchando*) is the desire and lust that has arisen with reference to one's own five aggregates.

"External sensual desire" (*bahiddhā kāmacchando*) is the desire and lust that has arisen with reference to the five aggregates of others. "Enters into the enumeration" (*uddesaṃ gacchati*) means it enters into the count.
"Internal ill will" (*ajjhattaṃ byāpādo*) is the aversion that has arisen toward one's own hands, feet, and so forth. "External..."

Ill will (*vyāpāda*) is the aversion that has arisen toward others with respect to them. Doubt regarding internal phenomena (*ajjhattaṃ dhammesu vicikicchā*) is uncertainty regarding one's own aggregates (*khandha*).
Doubt regarding external phenomena (*bahiddhā dhammesu vicikicchā*) is great doubt regarding the eight external points.

Mindfulness regarding internal phenomena (*ajjhattaṃ dhammesu sati*) is the mindfulness that arises in one who is attending to internal formations (*saṅkhāra*). [Mindfulness] regarding external phenomena...

“Mindfulness” (*sati*) is the mindfulness that arises in one who is comprehending external formations (*saṅkhāra*). The same method applies to the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dhammavicayasambojjhaṅga*).
“Bodily” (*kāyika*) refers to the energy (*vīriya*) that arises in one who is intent upon walking meditation (*caṅkama*).
“Mental” (*cetasika*) refers to the bodily application [of energy] expressed thus: “I shall not break this cross-legged posture until my mind is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.”
[This occurs] without the arising of energy. Tranquillity of body (*kāyappassaddhi*) is the tranquillity of the distress of the three aggregates.

Tranquillity of mind (*cittappassaddhi*) is the tranquillity of the distress of the consciousness aggregate. The exposition for the enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekkhāsambojjhaṅga*) is the same as that for the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (*satisambojjhaṅga*).
In this sutta, the mixed enlightenment factors are taught. For when there is mindfulness regarding these internal phenomena, there is investigation [of states].
Equanimity (*upekkhā*) and physical energy (*kāyikavīriya*) that has not yet reached the path are purely mundane (*lokiya*), because they have one's own aggregates as their object.

However, although joy (*pīti*) and concentration (*samādhi*) without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitakka-avicārā*) belong to the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), they are nonetheless supramundane (*lokuttara*), for the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are not found in the fine-material sphere.
And as for those elders who [teach] regarding the jhānas that serve as the basis for the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) and insight (*vipassanā*), etc.
According to those who extract [the factors] as awakening-factors (*bojjhaṅga*), they belong to both the form realm (*rūpāvacara*) and the formless realm (*arūpāvacara*).
For among the awakening-factors, only joy (*pīti*) is exclusively absent from the formless realm; the remaining six are indeed mixed [with respect to their presence there].
At the conclusion of the teaching, some monks became stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), some once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*), some non-returners (*anāgāmī*), and some attained arahantship.
3. Commentary on the Fire Sutta (Agni-sutta) 234.
Regarding the third [sutta]: "And mindfulness, monks, I declare to be beneficial in all respects" (*satiñca khvāhaṃ, bhikkhave, sabbatthikaṃ vadāmi*).
The meaning is that I declare it to be desirable in every situation, like salt seasoning or like a prime minister who oversees all affairs. For just as salt seasoning is required in all sauces...

It settles down. And just as a minister who performs all duties accomplishes every task—whether it be military service, counsel, or diplomatic missions—so too, the restraining of an excited mind and the uplifting of a sluggish mind are all accomplished through mindfulness;
this cannot be achieved without mindfulness. Therefore, he spoke thus. In this...
In the Sutta, only the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) pertaining to preliminary insight are mentioned.
4. Commentary on the *Mettāsahagata-sutta* 235.
In the fourth [sutta], the entire passage beginning with "with a mind imbued with loving-kindness" has already been explained in detail in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"We too, friends, teach the Dhamma to our disciples in this way"—this they say because, having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, they speak according to the same method as before.

For in the systems of the sectarians (titthiya), there is neither the abandoning of the five hindrances nor the cultivation of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) such as loving-kindness. "What is its destination? means what is its result. "What is its supreme? means what is its highest. "What is its fruit? means...
What is the benefit? What is the culmination? What is the final goal? "Accompanied by loving-kindness" means accompanied by, conjoined with, and associated with loving-kindness.
This same method applies everywhere. "Dependent on seclusion," and so forth, have already been explained. "Non-repulsive":
there are two kinds of non-repulsiveness—the non-repulsiveness of beings and the non-repulsiveness of formations. In that regard...
The meaning is: "in a desirable object that is not repulsive. "Perceiving it as repulsive" means perceiving it as undesirable. But how does one dwell in this way?
By either performing the pervasion of foulness (*asubha*) or by attending to [the object] as impermanent. For this has been stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*:
"How does one dwell perceiving what is not repulsive as repulsive? One performs the pervasion of foulness toward a desirable object..."

"Or he brings it to mind as impermanent. However, when one performs the pervasion of loving-kindness (*mettā*) or attends to the elements (*dhātu-manasikāra*) toward an unattractive or undesirable object, one is said to "dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive.
As it is said: "How does one dwell perceiving the unrepulsive in the repulsive?
One pervades an undesirable object with loving-kindness, or one brings it to mind in terms of its elements."
The same method applies to the passages concerning both mixed together.
For when one attends to the same pervasion of the foul or to the attention to impermanence regarding both the repulsive and the non-repulsive, one is said to dwell perceiving the repulsive.

And when one attends to the same pervasion of loving-kindness or to the attention to the elements regarding both the repulsive and the non-repulsive, one is said to dwell perceiving the non-repulsive.
Furthermore, one who exercises the sixfold equanimity as described in the passage beginning, “Having seen a form with the eye, he is neither glad,” should be understood thus:
“Whether there is the unrepulsive or the repulsive, having avoided both, he dwells therein equanimous,
mindful, and clearly comprehending.”
Up to this point, the teaching might have been concluded, since for this bhikkhu— who, having produced the third and fourth jhānas of loving-kindness (*mettā*),
made that very state the basis, and having developed insight (*vipassanā*), attained Arahantship—
