the factors of enlightenment of the Path (*maggasambojjhaṅga*) and noble psychic power (*ariyiddhi*) were shown together with that insight. However, this [present] jhāna of loving-kindness is the basis.
Even one who, having performed formative activities (*saṅkhāra*), reflects upon them, may not be able to reach Arahantship;
for his loving-kindness does not have Arahantship as its limit. However, that which has it as its limit must be shown. Therefore, this teaching was commenced in order to show that.
Furthermore, in the subsequent passages beginning with "or by completely surmounting perceptions of form," it should be understood according to this same method.
Furthermore, the purpose for undertaking the teaching should be understood.
"Ending in beauty" (*subhaparama*) means having beauty as its culmination, having beauty as its limit, and having beauty as its perfection.
"One who has wisdom here" (*idhapañña*) means one whose wisdom exists right here; because he does not transcend this world, he is "one who has wisdom here," that is, one with mundane wisdom.
The meaning is as follows: "One who does not penetrate further liberation" means one who does not penetrate supramundane states (*lokuttara-dhamma*).
However, for one who is able to penetrate them, loving-kindness (*mettā*) culminates in Arahantship; this is the meaning. The same method applies to compassion (*karuṇā*) and the others as well.
But why did the Blessed One state that these—loving-kindness and the rest—culminate in the beautiful (*subha*) and so forth? It was because of their commonality (*sabhāga-vasena*).
Because it is its decisive support (*upanissaya*). For beings are not repulsive to one who dwells in loving-kindness (*mettāvihārin*);
thus, when he applies his mind to pure colors such as blue and so forth—which are not repulsive due to his familiarity with the non-repulsive—his mind enters into them with ease.
Thus, loving-kindness is the decisive support for the beautiful liberation (*subhavimokkha*), but nothing beyond that; therefore...
They are called "having beauty as their ultimate.

For one who dwells in compassion, because compassion arises when he perceives the suffering of beings—such as the physical signs of being struck by heat and so forth—the disadvantage in form is thoroughly understood.
Then, because the disadvantage of form has been thoroughly understood by him, [he applies it] to the earth-kasiṇa and the rest.
Having opened one [door] and directing the mind toward space as the escape from form, the mind enters into that state with ease.
Thus, compassion is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the base of infinite space, but not for what follows it;
therefore, it is said to be "culminating in the base of infinite space."

Furthermore, for one dwelling in sympathetic joy (*muditā-vihārin*), as they contemplate the consciousness of beings who have arisen in joy through various causes of gladness, sympathetic joy comes to occur; thus, their mind becomes familiar with the apprehension of consciousness.

Then, having successively transcended the base of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) and directing the mind toward the consciousness that has the sign of space as its object, it [the mind] enters with ease.
Therein, the mind leaps forward. Thus, sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the base of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatana*), but not beyond that;
therefore, it is said to have the base of infinite consciousness as its limit.
For one who dwells in equanimity (*upekkhā*), however, [the thought arises]: "May beings be happy, or may they be freed from suffering, or may they possess happiness..."

Because there is an absence of mental application (ābhoga) such as "let them not depart," and because there arises a state of mind that is turned away from grasping at ultimate realities such as pleasure and pain, there is a painful state of mind that grasps what does not exist.

Then, for one whose mind is habituated to being turned away from grasping at ultimate realities and possesses a painful state of mind that grasps what is non-existent in the ultimate sense, the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana) occurs through the transcendence [of the base of nothingness]; thus, regarding that which is non-existent, [there is the perception] of that which is ultimately real.
When one applies the mind to the absence of consciousness, the mind enters into that state with ease.

Thus, equanimity is the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*), but not for what follows it; therefore, it is said to have the base of nothingness as its limit.
At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred bhikkhus attained arahantship.
5. Commentary on the Saṅgāravasutta 236.
In the fifth [verse], *pageva* means "first and foremost. *Kāmarāgapariyuṭṭhitena* means "one who is overwhelmed by sensual lust. *Kāmarāgaparetena* means "one who is pursued by sensual lust.
*Nissaraṇaṃ* refers to the threefold escape from sensual lust: the escape consisting in suppression (*vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa*), and so forth.

"Escape by way of its factors" (*tadaṅga-nissaraṇa*) means escape by way of eradication (*samuccheda-nissaraṇa*). In this context, regarding the foul (*asubha*), the first jhāna is called "escape by suppression" (*vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa*);
insight (*vipassanā*) is called "escape by way of its factors"; and the path of Arahantship is called "escape by eradication.
The meaning is that he does not understand these three kinds [of escape]. Regarding the phrase "his own welfare too," etc., "his own welfare" refers to the state of Arahantship.
One's own welfare is called *attattha*; the welfare of those who provide the requisites is called *parattha*; and that same twofold welfare is called *ubhayattha*.
In this manner, the meaning should be understood in all sections.

However, there is this distinction: in such passages as "the escape from ill-will," there are indeed two kinds of escape—the escape by suppression (*vikkhambhana-nissaraṇa*) and [the escape by eradication].
And there is escape through eradication. In this regard, for ill-will (*byāpāda*), the first jhāna through loving-kindness (*mettā*) is the escape by suppression;
the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*) is the escape by eradication. For sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*), the perception of light (*ālokasaññā*) is the escape by suppression;
the path of Arahantship is the escape by eradication. For restlessness and remorse (*uddhaccakukkucca*), any form of serenity (*samatha*) is the escape by suppression.
Herein, the path of Arahantship is the escape by way of eradication for restlessness; the path of Non-returning is the escape by way of eradication for remorse.
For doubt, the defining of phenomena is the escape by way of suppression, while the first path is the escape by way of eradication.
As for the similes spoken here, such as "just as, O Brahmin, a bowl of water mixed with lac... and so forth, [they illustrate this].
"Born in them" means a bowl filled with water. "Mixed together" means mixed by way of breaking down the distinction between colors.
"Boiled up" means heated. "Becoming warm water" means becoming steaming.

"Covered with moss and water-moss" means covered by moss such as *tilabījaka* and so forth, or by water-moss (*paṇaka*) produced by covering the surface of the water, which is blue in color like the back of a frog.
"Stirred by the wind" means shaken or agitated by the wind. "Turbid" means lacking clarity. "Agitated" means unsettled. "Become a mire" means become like mud.
"Placed in darkness" means set in a place devoid of light, such as the interior of a storehouse and so forth.
In this sutta, the Blessed One concluded his teaching by way of the three existences and brought the discourse to its conclusion with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
But the brahmin was established in mere refuge.
6. Commentary on the Abhaya Sutta: 237.
Regarding "for the sake of ignorance and non-seeing": this means for the purpose of ignorance and for the purpose of non-seeing. "Surely, Blessed One, these are hindrances..."
The Blessed One stated categorically that these are hindrances. "Bodily fatigue" means bodily distress; "mental fatigue" means mental distress.

"That too has been stilled by me": it is said that as he sat having entered a cool, climate-conducive place in the presence of the Teacher, his bodily distress was stilled, and when that was stilled, his mental distress was likewise stilled in its wake.
Furthermore, it should be understood that both of these have become tranquil for him by means of the path itself.
7. Ānāpānavagga 1.
Commentary on the Aṭṭhikamahapphalasutta and others.
238. Regarding "the perception of bones" among the seven [perceptions] and so forth: it is the perception that arises for one who develops the thought, "a bone, a bone.
While one is developing this, however, until the sign (*nimitta*) arises, even the skin and the hide appear.
But once the sign has arisen, the skin and hide no longer appear at all; there is only a pure collection of bones, the color of a conch shell.

It manifests like that of the novice monk who looked at King Dhammika Tissa as he sat upon the back of an elephant, or like that of the Elder Tissa, a resident of Cetiyapabbata, who looked at a laughing woman on the opposite path.
These accounts are detailed in the *Visuddhimagga*. Or, when there is a remainder of the substrate (*upādisesa*), meaning when a residue of clinging (*upādāna*) still exists.
2–10. Commentary on the *Puḷavaka-sutta* and others (239–247).

"Perception of the worm-infested" (*puḷavaka-saññā*) is the perception that arises in one who develops [the meditation] as "worm-infested," "worm-infested. The same method applies to the "perception of the livid" (*vinīlaka-saññā*) and the others.
However, the analytical discussion regarding these, together with the method of development, is set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*. [The following applies to] loving-kindness (*mettā*) and the others.
They should be understood by way of the threefold and fourfold jhānas; equanimity, however, is by way of the fourth jhāna alone.
8. Nirodhavagga: Commentary on the *Asubha-sutta* and others (1–10).
248–257. *Asubhasaññā* (perception of foulness) is the perception of the first jhāna regarding what is foul.
*Maraṇasaññā* (perception of death) is the perception that arises in one who frequently reflects: "One must certainly die; my life is bound up with death.

*Āhāre paṭikūlasaññā* (perception of the repulsiveness of food) is the perception of repulsiveness toward edible things such as boiled rice and sour gruel. *Sabbaloke anabhiratisaññā* (perception of non-delight in the entire world) is [the perception] regarding the whole world...

The perception of loathsomeness arises in one who is producing disenchantment. The perception of abandoning and the perception of dispassion are two preliminary stages. The perception of cessation is mixed.
Thus these twenty meditation subjects, beginning with the perception of the skeleton, have been explained.

Of these, nine lead to absorption (appanā), while eleven consist of access concentration (upacāra-jhāna). Furthermore, the detailed exposition regarding the remainder here is found in the *Visuddhimagga*.
[The two] have arrived. The sections beginning with the Gaṅgā-peyyāla are to be understood according to the method already explained in the Saṃyutta on the Path (Maggasaṃyutta).
The commentary on the Saṃyutta on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta) is finished.
3. The Saṃyutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness (Satipaṭṭhānasaṃyutta).
1. The Ambapālī Chapter. 1.
Commentary on the Ambapālī Sutta. 367.

Regarding "in the Ambapālī grove" in the first sutta of the Saṃyutta on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*Satipaṭṭhāna*): it refers to the grove belonging to Ambapālī, who was a woman living by her beauty.

When the mango grove had been planted—this, it is said, was her park. Having heard the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, she, with a mind full of faith, had a monastery built there and dedicated it to the Tathāgata; it is with reference to this that it was said.
"Leading to the one goal" means this is the one-way path. In this context, "one-way path" means a single path. For regarding the path:
“‘Path, road, way, track, direct route, course, journey;
boat, ford, bridge, raft, mat, and crossing’—these are its many names.
Here, however, it is called by the name ‘course. Therefore, monks, this is the one-way course.”
In this context, there is only one path. "This, monks, is the path; it is not a forked road"—this is how the meaning should be understood.
In what sense is it called a "path"? It is in the sense of leading to Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought after by those who desire Nibbāna.
"For the purification of beings" refers to those whose minds are defiled by stains such as lust and by secondary corruptions such as covetousness and improper greed.
For the sake of the purification of beings. "For the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation" means for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, that is to say, for their abandonment.
"For the passing away of pain and dejection" means for the passing away of these two—bodily pain and mental dejection—that is to say, for their cessation. Of the True Way...
“Attainment of the way” (ñāyassa adhigamāya) refers to the Noble Eightfold Path; what is meant is: for the attainment, for the reaching, of that.
For this mundane path of the foundations of mindfulness, when cultivated in the preliminary stage, leads to the attainment of the supramundane path.
Therefore he said: “for the attainment of the way. “For the realization of Nibbāna”: because it is free from the obstruction of craving.
"For the realization of Nibbāna"—that is, for the direct personal experience of the Deathless which has received the name "Nibbāna.
For this path, when developed, gradually accomplishes the realization of Nibbāna; therefore he said, "for the realization of Nibbāna.
Thus the Blessed One has spoken the praise of the "path leading to the one goal" by means of seven phrases. Why is that? [It is] for the sake of the bhikkhus...
For the purpose of generating enthusiasm. Indeed, having heard this praise, those bhikkhus thought: "This path, it is said, removes the four calamities—sorrow, which consists of heart-burning;
lamentation, which consists of verbal prolixity; pain, which consists of bodily unpleasantness;
and grief, which consists of mental unpleasantness—and it brings about the three excellences: purification, the method, and Nibbāna."
"Filled with enthusiasm, they will think: 'This teaching should be learned, mastered, and remembered;

and this path should be developed. Thus, for the sake of generating enthusiasm in those bhikkhus, he spoke in praise of them, just as a blanket merchant and others speak in praise of their blankets and so forth."
*Yadidam* is a particle; its meaning is "those who are these. *Cattāro* (four) is a numerical delimitation.
By this, it indicates the delimitation of the foundations of mindfulness as being neither less than nor more than that. *Satipaṭṭhānā* (foundations of mindfulness) refers to three things:
the objective range of mindfulness, the Teacher’s transcendence of aversion and attachment toward disciples who have practiced in the three ways, and mindfulness itself.
“Monks, I will teach you the arising and the passing away of the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna).
Listen to that. And what, monks, is the arising of the body? With the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of the body.

In such passages as these, the object of mindfulness is called the foundation of mindfulness. Likewise: “The body is the foundation, not the mindfulness; mindfulness is both the foundation and the mindfulness.”

And so it is in such passages as these. Its meaning is as follows: that in which something is established (*patiṭṭhāti*) is a "foundation" (*paṭṭhāna*). What is it that is established? Mindfulness (*sati*).

The foundation of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*. Alternatively, a foundation (*paṭṭhāna*) is a primary station (*padhāna-ṭhāna*); the foundation of mindfulness is *satipaṭṭhāna*, just like the term "elephant-station" (*hatthi-ṭhāna*), "horse-station" (*assa-ṭhāna*), and so forth.
Regarding the statement, “Three foundations of mindfulness, which the Noble One cultivates, by cultivating which the Teacher is worthy to instruct a following”:
here, the Teacher’s state of having transcended aversion and attachment toward disciples who have practiced in three ways is called a “foundation of mindfulness.
Its meaning is as follows: it is a “foundation” (*paṭṭhāna*) because it is to be established; that is to say, it is to be set forth. By whom is it to be established?
“By means of mindfulness. In the expression “the foundation of mindfulness” (*satipaṭṭhāna*), it is the establishing (*paṭṭhāna*) by means of mindfulness that is meant.

However, in such passages as “The four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment,” it is mindfulness itself that is called the foundation of mindfulness.
Its meaning is as follows: it is called a “foundation” (*paṭṭhāna*) because it establishes (*patiṭṭhāti*); it stands firm, having plunged in.
The meaning is that it proceeds after having leaped forward. Mindfulness itself is the foundation (*paṭṭhāna*); thus, it is "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

Alternatively, it is mindfulness in the sense of remembering (*saraṇa*), and a foundation in the sense of being established (*upaṭṭhāna*); thus, it is "mindfulness which is a foundation," and so it is also called *satipaṭṭhāna*. This is what is intended here.
If this is so, why is the plural form "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhānā*) used? Because of the multiplicity of the types of mindfulness, due to the diversity of their objects.
For there are indeed many kinds of mindfulness. Now, why is the word "path" (*magga*) used in the singular? Because of its unity in the sense of "seeking.
For all four of these types of mindfulness attain unity in the sense of seeking. For this has been said: "In what sense is it a 'path'?
In the sense of seeking Nibbāna, and in the sense of being sought by those who desire Nibbāna. And later on, all four of these...

Because they accomplish their task regarding objects such as the body and so forth and proceed toward Nibbāna, and because they are sought from the very beginning by those seeking Nibbāna, all four are called "one path.
This being the case, the teaching possesses a logical sequence through the connection of the words. "Which four? is a question arising from a desire to explain.
"Body" (kāya) refers to the material body (rūpakāya). "Contemplating the body" (kāyānupassī) means one whose nature is to contemplate the body.
Or, contemplating the body: for this bhikkhu contemplates this body by way of the seven contemplations, beginning with the contemplation of impermanence;
he contemplates it as impermanent, not as permanent; he contemplates it as suffering, not as pleasure;
he contemplates it as non-self, not as self; he becomes disenchanted, not delighted; he becomes dispassionate, not passionate; he causes cessation.
It does not arise; he relinquishes it and does not grasp at it. Contemplating that as impermanent, he abandons the perception of permanence;
contemplating it as suffering, he abandons the perception of pleasure; contemplating it as non-self, he abandons the perception of self.
Becoming disenchanted, he abandons delight; becoming dispassionate, he abandons lust; bringing about cessation, he [abandons] the origin.
One who abandons and relinquishes should be understood as abandoning grasping.
"Dwells" means he conducts himself. "Ardent": one who scorches away (*ātapati*) defilements within the three realms of existence is "ardent" (*ātāpa*);
this is a name for energy (*vīriya*). One who possesses such ardor is "ardent. "Clearly comprehending" means endowed with knowledge known as clear comprehension (*sampajañña*). "Mindful" means...

He is endowed with mindfulness that encompasses the body. Now, because he contemplates by means of wisdom after having encompassed the object by means of mindfulness—since there is no such thing as contemplation for one devoid of mindfulness—it was said:
"Bhikkhus, mindfulness, indeed, I declare to be all-beneficial. Therefore, in this context, it says: "He dwells contemplating the body in the body."

Thus far, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body has been explained. Alternatively, because one who lacks ardor experiences internal contraction which acts as an obstacle;
because one who lacks clear comprehension is confused regarding the adoption of skillful means and the avoidance of unskillful means;
and because one who lacks mindfulness is incapable of relinquishing what is unskillful and adopting what is skillful, his meditation subject does not succeed.
Therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful" was stated for the purpose of showing those qualities by whose power that [practice] succeeds.
Thus, having shown the factor of association for the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body, he now shows the factor of abandonment:

It is said: "Having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. In this context, "having removed" means having removed it either by way of removal through substitution (*tadaṅgavinaya*) or by way of removal through suppression (*vikkhambhanavinaya*).
"Regarding the world" (*loke*) refers to that very body; for here, the body is intended as "the world" in the sense of breaking up and falling apart.
However, since covetousness and dejection are not abandoned in the body alone, they must also be abandoned in regard to feeling and so forth.
It is indeed abandoned. Therefore, it is stated in the *Vibhaṅga*: “The five aggregates of clinging are the world.
Alternatively, this was said by way of enumerating those phenomena because they are reckoned as the world. As for what he said: “In that context, what is the world?
That very body is the world,” this is precisely the meaning here. The connection should be understood thus: “having removed covetousness and dejection regarding that world.”
Regarding "the arising of feelings" (*vedanāsūti*): here there are three kinds of feeling, and these are exclusively mundane (*lokiya*). The mind is also mundane, as are mental states (*dhammā*).
One who contemplates in such a way that feelings are to be contemplated is to be understood as "one who contemplates feelings.
This same method applies to the mind and mental states. And how are feelings to be contemplated? First, pleasant feeling is to be contemplated as suffering.
The painful [feeling] as an arrow, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling] as impermanent. As it is said:
“He who saw pleasure as suffering, Who saw suffering as an arrow, And who saw the peaceful neither-painful-nor-pleasant As impermanent;”
“Indeed, that bhikkhu who sees rightly will live in peace.
Furthermore, all these [feelings] should be contemplated as suffering. For it has been said:
“Whatever is felt, all that is included in suffering; so I say. And they should also be contemplated according to pleasure and pain, as it was said: “Pleasant feeling, indeed...”
"Friend Visākha, feeling is pleasant in its persistence and painful in its change"—all this should be expanded in detail.
Furthermore, it should be contemplated by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence (*anicca*).
As for mental states (*cittadhamma*), first, regarding consciousness (*citta*), there are various distinctions such as object, predominance, conascence, plane, kamma, result, and functional.
It should be contemplated by way of the contemplations on impermanence and so forth, and by way of the distinctions such as those with lust and so forth.

Phenomena (*dhammā*) should be contemplated by way of their specific characteristics and general characteristics, by way of the phenomenon of emptiness, by way of the seven contemplations beginning with impermanence, and by way of the distinctions such as "internally there exists sensual desire" and so forth.
The rest is exactly as previously stated. This is the summary here; the detailed exposition [is as follows].
However, it should be understood according to the method stated in the commentary on the *Satipaṭṭhāna* in the *Dīgha Nikāya*, *Majjhima Nikāya*, and *Aṭṭhakathā*.
2. Commentary on the *Satisutta* 368.

In the second [verse], "mindful" (*sato*) means endowed with mindfulness that contemplates the body and so forth. "Clearly comprehending" (*sampajāno*) means endowed with the wisdom of the four kinds of clear comprehension.
Endowed [with this]. Regarding the phrase "in going forward and in returning": here, "going forward" (*abhikkanta*) refers to advancing, and "returning" (*paṭikkanta*) refers to turning back;
both of these are found within the four postures (*iriyāpatha*). First, in the case of walking:
one who moves the body forward is said to be "going forward," and one who turns back is said to be "returning. Even in the posture of standing, while still standing, moving the body forward...
Bowing forward is called "approaching"; turning back from behind is called "receding.
Even while seated, one who remains sitting but shifts toward the front part of the seat is said to be "approaching," and one who shifts back toward the rear part of the seat is said to be "receding.
The same principle applies when lying down.

“He acts with full awareness” means he performs all his duties with full awareness (*sampajañña*), or he acts only with full awareness. For he indeed exercises full awareness regarding going forward and so forth; he is never devoid of full awareness in any situation. In this context, there are four kinds of full awareness:

full awareness of purpose (*sātthaka-sampajañña*), full awareness of suitability (*sappāya-sampajañña*), full awareness of the range of activity (*gocara-sampajañña*), and full awareness of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*). In that regard, when the thought to go forward arises, instead of going merely by the power of the thought, [one reflects]: “What...?”

"Is there any purpose for me in going here, or is there not?"—having thus discerned what is beneficial and what is not, the discernment of what is beneficial is *sātthaka-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of the purpose).

In this context, "purpose" (*attha*) refers to spiritual progress (*dhammato vaḍḍhi*) by way of visiting a shrine (*cetiya*), seeing the Bodhi tree, seeing the Saṅgha, seeing senior elders (*thera*), or observing the foul (*asubha*).
For even by seeing a shrine, one gains a mental object consisting of the Buddha; by seeing the Saṅgha, one gains a mental object consisting of the Saṅgha.
Having generated rapture, one who contemplates that very same [rapture] as subject to destruction attains Arahantship.

Indeed, at the Mahāvihāra, thirty thousand bhikkhus attained Arahantship while standing at the southern gate gazing at the Mahācetiya; likewise at the western gate, the northern gate, and the eastern gate;
and likewise at the site of the Pañhamaṇḍapa, along the embankment of the Abhayavāpi, and at the gate of the Thūpārāma.
At the southern gate of the city, on the embankment of the Anurādhavāpi.
However, the Elder Mahāariyavaṃsabhāṇaka said: "What do you say?
From the lower part of the inner railing surrounding the Mahācetiya, starting from wherever it is visible—at whichever place two feet can stand level—[that is where it was]."
"It is possible to say that thirty thousand bhikkhus reached Arahantship at each single step along the way.
But another great elder said, "On the surface of the Great Cetiya, amidst the thick sand, even more bhikkhus attained Arahantship.
Having seen those elders and established himself in their instruction, he beheld the foulness [of the body].
Therein, having first produced the first jhāna and then contemplating that very state as subject to destruction, one attains Arahantship.

Therefore, seeing these [four requisites] is purposeful. Some, however, say: "Even material growth is indeed purposeful, because by depending upon it, one has set out for the support of the holy life."
In that journey, however, having discerned what is suitable and what is unsuitable, the discernment of the suitable is "clear comprehension of the suitable.
For example: visiting a shrine (cetiya) is indeed purposeful.

But if, during a great festival for the shrine, crowds gather within a radius of ten or twelve leagues, and men and women, according to their means, are adorned and prepared like figures in a painting—
They wander about as it were. Therein, greed arises toward a desirable object, aversion toward an undesirable one, and delusion toward indifference;
he incurs an offense through physical contact, or there is an obstacle to his life or the holy life.
Thus that place is unsuitable; it is suitable only when the aforementioned obstacles are absent.

Even visiting the Saṅgha is purposeful. However, if while people are having a Dhamma discourse held all night after having a great pavilion built inside a village, there is a gathering of people and obstacles in the manner already described, then such a place is unsuitable;
it is suitable only when there are no obstacles. The same principle applies to visiting elders who have large retinues.
The contemplation of the foul is also purposeful. To illustrate its meaning, here is this account: It is said that a certain young bhikkhu went with a novice to fetch tooth-sticks.
The novice, having stepped off the path and walking ahead, saw a foul object;
he attained the first jhāna, and making that very attainment his basis, he contemplated conditioned phenomena.
Having realized the three fruits and having taken up a meditation subject for the sake of the higher paths, he stood there.

Not seeing him, the youth called out, “Novices! He thought: “From the day I went forth, I have never before engaged in two conversations at once with a bhikkhu; on this other day as well, I shall achieve a further distinction.”

Having reflected, he gave the reply, "What is it, venerable sir? When told, "Come," he came with that very singular command and said, "Venerable sir, first go by this path and, at the place where I am standing, look for a moment facing the east.
He did so and attained the very same distinction as the other. Thus, one [type of] foulness [leads to] two.
It was born for the welfare of people. Furthermore, although it is thus purposeful, the unattractiveness of women is unsuitable for a man, and the unattractiveness of men is unsuitable for a woman;
rather, what is of a similar kind is suitable. Thus, the discernment of suitability (*sappāya-sampajañña*) consists in grasping what is suitable.
Then, among the thirty-eight meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), one should choose that which is pleasing to one's own mind.
Having mastered the range known as the meditation subject, the act of going to the range for alms-round while still carrying that very subject with one is called "clear comprehension of the range.
To explain this in detail, the following tetrad should be understood: here, a certain bhikkhu goes out but does not return;
another returns but does not go out; yet another neither goes out nor returns; and another both goes out and returns.
In this regard, a bhikkhu who has purified his mind of obstructive states through walking and sitting during the day,
and likewise during the first watch of the night, having lain down to rest during the middle watch, and having spent the last watch of the night in sitting and walking,
and who— far earlier than that— has performed the duties at the shrine grounds and the Bodhi-tree grounds and has sprinkled water at the Bodhi-tree;
Having set out drinking water and water for washing, he conducts himself by undertaking the duties toward his teacher and preceptor and so forth.
Having performed the bodily grooming and entered his lodging, he applies himself to his meditation subject while generating heat through two or three cross-legged postures.
Then, rising at the time for the alms-round, he takes his bowl and robe with the meditation subject as his primary focus.
Having emerged from his lodging and attending to his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), he goes to the shrine terrace (*cetiyangaṇa*).
If his meditation subject is the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), he enters the shrine terrace without relinquishing it.

If it is another meditation subject, he stands at the foot of the steps, sets it aside like a commodity held in the hand, and taking up the joy (*pīti*) directed toward the Buddha, he enters the shrine terrace.
If it is a large cetiya, one should ascend it, circumambulate it three times, and pay homage at four places;
if it is a small one, having likewise circumambulated it, one should pay homage at eight places.

Having paid homage to the cetiya, even when reaching the precincts of the Bodhi tree, one should display an attitude of profound reverence as if in the very presence of the Blessed Buddha, and [pay homage] to the Bodhi...
They should be paid homage. Having thus paid homage to the shrine and the Bodhi tree, he goes to the place where his requisites were kept;
and as if taking up the goods that had been stored there, he takes up the meditation subject he had set aside.
Near the village, having put on his robe with the meditation subject foremost in mind, he enters the village for alms.
Then, when people see him, they think, "Our venerable one has arrived," and they go out to meet him.
Taking his bowl, they seat him in a rest-house or in their own home. After giving him rice-gruel, they wash and anoint his feet while the meal is still unfinished.
Then, sitting before him, they either ask questions or wish to hear the Dhamma. Even if he does not engage them in conversation, [they remain there].
The commentators say that a discourse on the Dhamma must indeed be delivered for the purpose of winning over people.

For there is no discourse on the Dhamma that is divorced from a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, having preached the Dhamma with a meditation subject as its core, and having partaken of food with a meditation subject as its core, one should return from the village followed even by those people who have come to offer a blessing of thanks (*anumodana*).
Having departed, he turns back there and sets out upon the path.

Then, having departed earlier and already finished their meal outside the village, the novice monks and young bhikkhus see him, go out to meet him, and take his bowl and robe. It is said that the elder bhikkhus do not think, "Our preceptor..."
They perform their duties by looking at the face [of the teacher], saying, "The teacher," and they do so according to the limits of their acquaintance.
They ask him: "Venerable sir, who are these people to you? Are they relatives from your mother’s side or your father’s side? "What have you seen that you ask this? [He replies:
"It is because of their love and great respect for you. "Friends, even more than for one's own mother and father..."
“They do this for us which is even more difficult; even our bowl and robe belong to them alone.
By their power, we know neither fear in times of danger nor hunger in times of famine. There are no benefactors like these for us!
Thus he goes along, speaking of their virtues. This is called “he takes away but does not bring back.”
However, for one who performs the aforementioned duties and observances from early on, the fire born of karma blazes up;
having released the non-clung-to [heat], it seizes the clung-to [heat]. Sweat breaks out from the body, and the meditation subject does not enter its proper course.
Such a person, having taken his bowl and robe early, should quickly pay homage at the shrine and depart at the very time when the cattle are coming out.
Having entered the village for alms of rice-gruel and obtained some, he goes to a rest-house and drinks it.
Then, with only two or three mouthfuls swallowed, his kamma-born heat (tejo) releases the clung-to (upādiṇṇaka) elements and takes up the unclung-to (anupādiṇṇaka).
Like one bathed with a hundred jars of water, having attained the cooling of the fever of the fire-element, he consumes the gruel while keeping the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) foremost.
Having washed his bowl and face, and having attended to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) during the interval between meals, he wanders for alms in the remaining places.
Having consumed his food under the heading of the meditation subject, he returns from there taking up the meditation subject that presents itself to him in continuous succession.
This is called "he brings back [the object] but does not carry it. And such as this...
The number of monks who, having drunk rice-gruel and applied insight (vipassanā), attained Arahantship in the Buddha’s dispensation,
is beyond calculation. Even in the island of Sri Lanka alone, in various villages,
there is no rest-house where there are not monks who have attained Arahantship after drinking rice-gruel.
But he who dwells in negligence, having cast off his burden and broken all his observances, remains with his mind bound by the fivefold mental shackles;

and entering a village for alms, not even forming the perception that "there is such a thing as a meditation subject," he goes about and eats in association with householders in an unbecoming manner, and then departs empty-handed. This person is called...
"Neither takes away nor brings back.
However, that which is described as both taking away and bringing back should be understood by way of the practice of going and returning.
For sons of good family who desire their own welfare, having gone forth in the Dispensation, [practice this] for ten, twenty, thirty, forty, or even fifty [days].
Even when living together as a group, they dwell having made a formal agreement: "Friends, you have not gone forth out of debt, nor out of fear, nor because of a livelihood;
rather, you have gone forth here desiring to be liberated from suffering. Therefore, whatever defilement arises while walking, subdue it right there while walking;
whatever defilement arises while standing, sitting, or lying down, subdue it right there while lying down."

Having made this agreement, when they go on their almsround, there are stones at intervals of half an usabha, one usabha, half a gavuta, or one gavuta; they proceed while attending to the meditation subject with that as their signpost.
If defilement arises in anyone while walking, he restrains it right there. If he is unable to do so, he stops. Then, from behind him—
Even when it arises, it remains; then, having reproached himself, thinking, "This monk knows the thought that has arisen in you;
this is not suitable for you," he develops insight and right there enters the plane of the Noble Ones (ariyabhūmi).
If he is unable to do so, he sits down—the same method applies. Even if he is unable to enter the plane of the Noble Ones, regarding that defilement...
He goes along attending only to the meditation subject after having suppressed [distractions]; he does not lift his foot with a mind dissociated from the meditation subject.
If he should so lift it, he must turn back and go to the very same previous spot, as was the case with the Elder Mahā Phussadeva, who dwelt in the Ālindaka.
It is said that for nineteen years he lived fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning;
and indeed, people along the road—while plowing, sowing, threshing, or performing their labors—saw the Elder traveling in such a manner and thought:
"This Elder goes back again and again; is he perhaps lost, or..."

"Have you forgotten something? they conversed. But he, disregarding them, performed the duties of a recluse with a mind intent solely on his meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and within twenty years he attained *arahantship*.
On the day he attained *arahantship*, a deity dwelling at the end of his walking path stood there having lit a lamp with her fingers. The Four Great Kings and Sakka [also appeared].
Sakka, lord of the devas, and Brahmā Sahampati came to attend upon him. On the following day, having seen that radiance, the elder Mahātissa the Forest-Dweller asked:
"Venerable sir, there was a radiance in your presence during the night; what was that radiance?
The elder, seeking to divert the question, replied: "What is called radiance includes the radiance of a lamp, the radiance of a gem," and so forth.
Then, being instructed with the words, "You must conceal [this]," he acknowledged it, saying "Yes," and reported it,
just like the Elder Mahānāga who resided in the Kāḷavalli bower. It is said that he, while fulfilling the duties of one who has gone forth and returned,
first spent seven years solely in standing and walking meditation, thinking, "I shall honor the Great Struggle (Mahāpadhāna) of the Blessed One."
He made a resolution. Then, after fulfilling the practice of going forth and returning for sixteen years, he attained Arahatship.
With a mind intent upon his meditation subject, he lifted his foot; when it was set down, he turned back.
Having reached the vicinity of the village, he stood in a place that might arouse suspicion—wondering, "Is this a cow or a renunciant?"—and put on his robe.
Having washed his bowl with water from a water-pot, he takes a mouthful of water. For what reason? Thinking:
"Lest there be a distraction of the meditation subject for me by even the mere words 'May you be long-lived' when people come to give alms or pay homage," or when asked:
"Venerable sir, what is today's date? or "What day of the fortnight is it? or "How many monks are there? or "What is the question [of the day]?"...

However, he swallows the water and then informs [the others]. If there is no inquiry regarding the day and so forth, he goes out at the time of departure after spitting it out at the village gate, like the fifty bhikkhus who entered the rains residence at Kalambatittha Vihāra.
It is said that on the full moon of Āsāḷha they made a formal agreement: "We shall not speak to one another until we have attained Arahantship. And as for the village, for alms—
As they entered, they made a mouthful of water and went inside. When questioned regarding the day and other such matters, they acted in the manner already described.
There, the people, seeing the spitting, realized: "One has come today; two have come today. And they thought:
"Why is it that these do not converse with us? Or perhaps they do not even speak among themselves? If they do not speak to one another..."
“They do not speak to one another; surely they must have fallen into a dispute. Come, let us go and reconcile them with each other.
Having gone to the monastery, he did not see even two monks in a single place among those fifty monks.
Then, the man among them who possessed sight said: “Friends, such a space does not belong to those who create quarrels; it has been well-swept.”
“The courtyard of the shrine and the courtyard of the Bodhi tree have been well-swept; the drinking water and the water for washing are well-provided.
Having said this, they turned back from that very spot. Those monks, within that very month, attained Arahantship and, at the Great Invitation ceremony, performed the invitation of purity.
Thus, just like the Elder Mahānāga who dwelt in the Kāḷavallimaṇḍapa, the monks who entered the rains retreat at the Kalambatittha monastery [attained their goal].
And as if lifting his foot with a mind intent solely on the meditation subject, he goes near the village;
having rinsed his mouth with water and observed the streets, he enters that path where there are no drunkards, gamblers, or other quarrelsome people, nor fierce elephants, horses, and so forth.
And while wandering for alms there, he does not act as if in great haste.
He goes with speed. Indeed, there is no such thing as a "speedy alms-collecting ascetic practice" (*piṇḍapātika-dhutanga*).
Rather, like a water-cart that has reached uneven ground, he proceeds while remaining motionless.
Having entered house by house, observing whether the donor is willing or unwilling to give, and taking alms after waiting for the appropriate time accordingly, [he remains] within the village...
Having come either outside the village or to the monastery itself, and having sat down in a suitable and comfortable place, he attends to his meditation subject.
Establishing the perception of repulsiveness toward food, and reflecting upon it by way of the similes of the axle-oil,
the wound-ointment, and the son’s flesh, he consumes food endowed with the eight factors— neither for sport, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment.

It is not for the sake of adornment... [and so on]... Having eaten and performed the water-rite, and having rested for a moment to allay the fatigue from the meal, he attends to the meditation subject after the meal just as he did before the meal, during both the first watch and the last watch of the night.
This is called "carrying it away and bringing it back."

Furthermore, while fulfilling this practice of going and returning—consisting of taking and bringing back—if one is endowed with the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*), one attains *arahantship* in the very first stage of life.
If one does not attain it in the first stage, then one attains it in the middle stage.
If one does not attain it in the middle stage, then one attains it in the final stage; if not even in the final stage...
He attains it; or else at the time of death. If he does not attain it at the time of death, then having become a son of the gods, he attains it.
If he does not attain it even as a son of the gods, then being reborn when no Buddha has appeared, he realizes pratyekabodhi.
If he does not realize pratyekabodhi, then in the presence of Buddhas, he becomes one of swift direct knowledge.
Just as the elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya was of great wisdom; just as the elder Sāriputta was of great psychic power;
just as the elder Mahāmoggallāna was a proponent of the ascetic practices (dhuta); just as the elder Mahākassapa possessed the divine eye;
just as the elder Anuruddha was a master of the Vinaya; and just as the elder Upāli was a bearer of the Vinaya.
Or he may be a preacher of the Dhamma, such as the Elder Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇī; or a forest-dweller, such as the Elder Revata;
or one of great learning, such as the Elder Ānanda; or one who desires training, such as the Elder Rāhula, the Son of the Buddha.
Thus, in this fourfold set, for him who both carries out and brings back [the task], his clear comprehension of the domain reaches its pinnacle.
Furthermore, non-delusion regarding advancing and so forth is non-delusive clear comprehension (*asammoha-sampajañña*). This should be understood as follows:
here, when a bhikkhu is advancing or retreating, he does not—as do blind worldlings—think regarding advancing and so forth, "The self advances;
advancing is produced by the self," or "I am advancing; advancing is produced by me."

Or they are deluded; but when the thought "I am stepping forward" arises in one who is thus undeluded, the wind-element originating from consciousness (cittasamuṭṭhāna-vāyodhātu) arises together with that very consciousness, generating intimation (viññatti).
Thus, by way of the expansion of the wind-element of mental activity, this collection of bones known as the body steps forward. As he thus steps forward, at the lifting of each individual foot—
In the two elements—the earth element and the water element—they are deficient and weak; the other two are excessive and powerful.

Likewise, in the acts of lifting up and moving away, the fire element and the air element are deficient and weak, while the other two are excessive and powerful. Likewise, in the acts of setting down and pressing together.
In that regard, the material and immaterial phenomena occurring in lifting do not reach the stage of carrying; likewise, those occurring in carrying do not reach the stage of shifting;
those occurring in shifting do not reach the stage of letting go; those occurring in letting go do not reach the stage of placing down;
and those occurring in placing down do not reach the stage of pressing down. At each respective stage, they remain joint by joint and joint by joint.
Becoming as if flattened like sesame seeds placed in a hot pan, they break apart with a crackling sound.
In that regard, who is it that goes forward alone, or whose is this going forward?

For in the ultimate sense, there is only the going of the elements, the standing of the elements, the sitting of the elements, and the lying down of the elements. Indeed, in each respective part, together with material form—
“Another consciousness arises, another consciousness ceases;
there is a continuous succession like the flow of a river.
Thus, non-delusion regarding such actions as stepping forward and so forth is called clear comprehension of non-delusion (*asammoha-sampajañña*).
The meaning of the phrase "acting with clear comprehension when going forward and returning" is thus concluded.

Regarding the terms "looking ahead" (*ālokita*) and "looking aside" (*vilokita*): here, "looking ahead" means gazing straight forward, while "looking aside" means glancing toward the intermediate directions.
Furthermore, by way of looking downward, upward, and backward, there are also what are known as "looking down," "looking up," and "looking behind."
Those [other instances] are not included here; rather, only these two are taken because they are appropriate. Or, by way of this example, all of them are indeed included.

In that regard, when the thought "I shall look" has arisen, grasping the meaning without looking merely according to the impulse of the mind is *sātthaka-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of purposefulness). This is to be understood by taking the Venerable Nanda as an eyewitness. For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, if Nanda needs to look toward the eastern direction, he looks toward the eastern direction having first applied his whole mind, thinking:
‘May no covetousness, grief, or evil unwholesome states overwhelm me as I look toward the eastern direction. In this way, he is clearly comprehending in that regard. If, bhikkhus, …”
“The western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, above, below, and the intermediate directions must be looked at by Nanda.
Having applied his whole mind, Nanda looks toward the intermediate directions, [thinking]: ‘As I look toward the intermediate directions in this way…’ …he is clearly comprehending.
Furthermore, here too, the purposefulness and suitability should be understood in the same way as previously stated regarding the visiting of shrines and so forth.

Furthermore, *gocara-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of the domain) is simply the non-abandonment of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*). Therefore, those whose meditation subjects are the aggregates, elements, and bases should look forward and around precisely according to their own meditation subject;
or rather, those whose meditation subjects are the kasiṇas and so forth should do so by means of the meditation subject as their primary focus. [One should reflect:
"Inwardly, there is no such thing as a 'self' that looks forward or looks around; rather, when the thought 'I shall look forward' arises in the mind..."
Along with that very consciousness, the consciousness-originated air element arises, producing intimation.
Thus, by the expansion of the air element produced by mental activity, the lower eyelid sinks down and the upper one leaps upward;
there is no one at all opening them by means of a machine. From that, the eye-consciousness performs its function of seeing.
In this context, the knowledge that understands, "It arises for one who is accomplishing [the object]," is called non-delusive clear comprehension (*asammoha-sampajañña*).

Furthermore, non-delusive clear comprehension should be understood here by way of the thorough understanding of the root (*mūla-pariññā*), adventitiousness, and the temporary nature [of the process]. First, by way of the thorough understanding of the root:
"The life-continuum, adverting, seeing, receiving," and so forth.
“Investigation, determining, and the impulsion becomes the seventh.
Therein, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) proceeds performing the function of a factor for the state of rebirth;
having turned it back, the functional mind-element performs the function of adverting; and with its cessation, eye-consciousness performs the function of seeing.
While that [sensual-sphere consciousness] is performing its function, the resultant mind-element (*vipākamanodhātu*) performs its function of receiving (*sampaṭicchana*);

following its cessation, the resultant mind-consciousness-element (*vipākamanoviññāṇadhātu*) performs its function of investigating (*santīraṇa*); following its cessation, the functional mind-consciousness-element (*kiriyamanoviññāṇadhātu*) performs its function of determining (*voṭṭhabbana*);
following its cessation, the impulsion (*javana*) proceeds for seven moments. Therein, even in the first impulsion—
“‘This is a woman,’ ‘this is a man’— such looking and gazing does not occur through the influence of lust,
hatred, or delusion, neither in the second impulsion nor even up to the seventh. However, when these [impulsions] fall away, broken down in successive order like warriors on a battlefield,
there occurs looking and gazing through lust and so forth, thinking, ‘This is a woman,’ ‘this is a man.’”
Thus, in this context, clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood by way of the full understanding of the root.

However, when a visible form enters the range of the eye-door, after the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and after the adverting consciousness and the others have arisen and ceased in the performance of their respective functions, finally the impulsion (javana) arises; that [impulsion] arises subsequent to those that arose previously.
In the eye-door, which is like a house belonging to the adverting consciousness and the rest, it is like a guest.
Just as it is not fitting for a guest who has entered another’s house to request something while the owners of the house remain silent,
so too, in the eye-door belonging to the adverting consciousness and the rest, it is not fitting [for the mind] to act while the adverting consciousness and the rest are neither attached nor averse.
And since it is improper for lust, hatred, and delusion to arise in those who are not deluded, thus should clear comprehension of non-delusion be understood by way of its adventitious nature.

Furthermore, those consciousnesses that arise at the eye-door, ending with the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), perish right there along with their associated mental factors; they do not see one another, being momentary and temporary.

They exist. In this regard, just as when all the human inhabitants of a house have died, it is not fitting for the one survivor—who is himself subject to death at that very moment—to take delight in dancing, singing, and so forth;

even so, when the advertence and other mental factors associated with them have perished right there at each respective stage within the single door, it is likewise not fitting for the remaining javana, which is itself subject to death at that very moment.
Delight, by way of lust, hatred, and delusion, is not appropriate; thus should non-delusive clear comprehension be understood in terms of its temporary nature.
Furthermore, it should also be understood by way of reflecting upon the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions.
For herein, the eye and visible forms constitute the aggregate of form; the act of seeing is the aggregate of consciousness; and the feeling associated with that is the aggregate of feeling.
Perception is the perception aggregate; volitional formations beginning with contact are the formations aggregate.
Thus, it is in the combination of these five aggregates that looking forward and looking around are discerned. In that regard, who is it that looks forward alone, and who looks around?
Likewise, the eye is the eye-base, visible form is the visible-form-base, seeing is the mind-base, and feeling and so forth are the associated mental states.
and the sense-base of mental phenomena (*dhammāyatana*). Thus, it is through the coming together of these four bases that looking forward and looking around are discerned.

In this regard, who is it that looks forward? Who is it that looks around? Likewise, there is the eye and the eye-element; the visible form and the form-element; the seeing, which is the eye-consciousness-element;
and the mental states associated with that, such as feeling and so forth, which constitute the mental-phenomena-element (*dhammadhātu*). Thus, of these four...
In the coming together of the elements (dhātu), looking forward and looking around are perceived. In that regard, who is it that alone looks forward, and who looks around?

Thus, the eye is the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya); visible form is the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya); adverting consciousness is the proximity, contiguity, decisive-support, presence, and absence-conditions;

light is the decisive-support-condition (upanissaya-paccaya); and feeling and the other mental factors are the co-nascent conditions (sahajāta-paccaya). In this way, through the coming together of these conditions—

Looking ahead and looking around are discerned. In that regard, one should understand non-delusive clear comprehension by way of reflecting upon the aggregates, bases, elements, and conditions, asking: "Who is it that looks ahead? Who is it that looks around?
Regarding "in the bending and the stretching," this refers to the bending and stretching of the limbs. Therein, the bending and stretching occurs solely through the power of the mind.
Situational awareness of purposefulness is the grasping of what is beneficial after considering what is beneficial and what is not beneficial,
rather than moving the hands and feet without such consideration. In this regard, for one who stands with the hands and feet bent or extended for too long,
painful sensations arise from moment to moment, the mind fails to attain one-pointedness, and the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) falls away.
One does not attain distinction. However, when one bends at the proper time and extends at the proper time, those painful feelings do not arise;

the mind becomes one-pointed, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) reaches full development, and one attains distinction. Thus should the discernment of what is beneficial and what is harmful be understood.

Furthermore, even when there is something beneficial, having discerned what is suitable and what is unsuitable, the discernment of suitability consists in grasping what is suitable. This is called "clear comprehension of suitability" (sappāya-sampajañña).
In this regard, the method is as follows: It is said that in the courtyard of the Great Cetiya, young bhikkhus were engaged in recitation.
Behind them, young bhikkhunīs were listening to the Dhamma. There, one young man, while extending his hand, came into physical contact with a bhikkhunī;
for that very reason, he was reborn as a householder. Another bhikkhu, while extending his foot, extended it toward a fire.
One monk sat in meditation with his foot pressed against a bone. Another stretched out his foot toward an anthill and was bitten by a venomous snake.

Another stretched it out toward the pole of his robe-shed and was bitten by a jewel-serpent. Therefore, one should not stretch out the foot toward such unsuitable objects, but should stretch it out toward what is suitable.
This is "clear comprehension of suitability" in this context.
Clear comprehension of the range of activity (*gocara-sampajañña*), however, should be illustrated by the story of the Great Elder (*Mahāthera*).

It is said that while the Great Elder was sitting in his daytime quarters conversing with his pupils, he suddenly bent his hand, then placed it back in its original position, and finally bent it slowly.
The pupils asked him: "Venerable sir, why did you bend your hand so suddenly?"

“Then, having placed it back in its original position, he slowly bent his arm. “Friend, ever since I began to attend to my meditation subject, I have never before bent my arm while letting go of that meditation subject;
but now, while conversing with you, I let go of the meditation subject and bent it, which is why I am placing it back in its original position.”
"Excluding the act of bending. "It is well, Bhante; a bhikkhu indeed ought to be such as this.
Thus, even here, it should be understood that *gocara-sampajañña* (clear comprehension of the range) consists precisely in not abandoning the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that bends or stretches; rather, [the movement occurs] through the expansion of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*) and the mental activity (*cittakiriyā*) of the aforementioned kind.

Furthermore, it should be understood that "clear comprehension of non-delusion" here refers to the thorough understanding that the bending and stretching [of the limbs] occurs like the moving of the hands and feet of a wooden puppet by means of pulling the strings.
Regarding "wearing the outer robe, the bowl, and the inner robe": here, [it refers to] the wearing of the outer and inner robes by way of undergarment and upper garment, and of the bowl...
"Use" refers to wearing [the robes] by way of receiving almsfood and so forth; "wearing" means this. In that regard, first, concerning the wearing of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭicīvara*):

while walking for alms after having dressed and put on the robe, there is the acquisition of material food, and there is also the purpose described by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with, "for the warding off of cold.
It is by virtue of these that "clear comprehension of purposefulness" (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) is to be understood.
For one who has a hot temperament and is weak, a fine robe is suitable; for one who is sensitive to cold, a thick double-layered robe is suitable.
The opposite is unsuitable. For anyone, a worn-out robe is simply unsuitable, for by providing it with a latch and so forth, it becomes an impediment.
Likewise, robes made of wool, silk, and the like that are alluring are unsuitable; for such [robes]...
It creates an obstacle to living alone in the forest and also becomes an obstacle to life itself.

In the direct sense, however, that which arises through wrong livelihood such as fortune-telling and the like, and that by the practice of which unwholesome states increase and wholesome states decline, is unsuitable. The opposite of that is suitable. Of this—
Herein, clear comprehension of suitability should be understood by way of the suitability of the robe, and clear comprehension of the domain by way of not abandoning the meditation subject.

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that puts on the robe; rather, the putting on of the robe occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element and the activity of consciousness of the kind already described.
In this regard, the robe is insentient and the body is also insentient. The robe...
One knows, "I have clothed my body. The body, however, does not know, "I am clothed with a robe.
It is simply the elements that conceal the collection of elements, just as a ragged scrap of cloth conceals a form made of rags.
Therefore, one should feel no joy upon obtaining a beautiful robe, nor any dejection upon obtaining an unattractive one.

For instance, regarding the Nāgavammika tree and other such shrines, some people offer honor with garlands, perfumes, incense, clothing, and so forth, while others offer dishonor by striking them with excrement, urine, mud, sticks, or weapons.
Yet those trees, such as the Nāgavammika, feel neither joy nor dejection because of these acts.
In the same way, one should not feel joy upon receiving a beautiful robe.

"Having received what is unattractive, there is no mental distress"—it is by way of such reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) that non-delusive clear comprehension (*asammoha-sampajañña*) should be understood here.

Furthermore, when holding the bowl, one should not seize it hastily; rather, with the thought, "By taking this and wandering for alms, I shall obtain food," one should exercise purposeful clear comprehension (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) regarding the benefit to be gained from the act of taking up the bowl.
It should be understood that for one with a thin and weak body, a heavy bowl is unsuitable.

For anyone whose bowl has five or six dents, it is difficult to clean and is therefore unsuitable; for a bowl that is hard to wash is not permitted, and it becomes a hindrance to the very person washing it.
Furthermore, a jewel-colored bowl is attractive and, by the same principle stated regarding the robe, is unsuitable. This applies also by way of making marks and so forth.
However, that which, when practiced by him, causes unwholesome states to increase and wholesome states to diminish, is exclusively unsuitable;

the opposite is suitable. In this context, clear comprehension of the suitable should be understood through its influence, and clear comprehension of the domain through the non-abandonment of the meditation subject.

Within, there is no so-called "self" that grasps the bowl; rather, what is called "grasping the bowl" occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element and the activity of consciousness of the kind already described.
In this regard, the bowl is insentient, and the hands are also insentient.
The bowl does not know, "I am being held by the hands," nor do the hands know, "The bowl is being held by us. It is merely the elements [that act].

They seize the collection of elements, like grasping a glowing iron pan with tongs; it is by way of such reflective contemplation that non-deluded clear comprehension (*asammoha-sampajañña*) should be understood here.
Furthermore, just as when one has had a hand or foot cut off, and there is a wound from which pus and blood are trickling, swarming with families of maggots and surrounded by blue flies...
Seeing destitute people at the almshouse, compassionate men provide them with bandages and rags for their wounds, as well as medicinal substances in bowls.
Among these, some receive soft rags while others receive coarse ones;
likewise, some receive bowls of good shape while others receive ill-shaped ones. They do not [discriminate] therein.
They may be happy or they may be unhappy. For their need is met merely by a rag to cover a wound and a bowl to receive medicine.

In the same way, the bhikkhu who regards his robe as a bandage for a wound, his alms-bowl as a vessel for medicine, and the alms-food received in the bowl as the medicine itself—this is [the proper attitude] in wearing the outer cloak, the bowl, and the robes.
By means of non-delusive clear comprehension (*asammoha-sampajañña*), one should be understood as acting with supreme clear comprehension.

Regarding "eating" and so forth: "eating" refers to the consumption of alms-food; "drinking" refers to the drinking of rice-gruel and the like; "chewing" refers to the chewing of flour-based snacks and the like; "tasting" refers to the tasting of honey, molasses, and the like.
In this context, even the eightfold manner described by the method beginning with "not for sport" and so forth—
"Meaning" (attha) means purpose; by way of that, clear comprehension of what is beneficial (sātthaka-sampajañña) should be understood.
Furthermore, among coarse, refined, bitter, sweet, and so forth, whatever food causes discomfort for someone is unsuitable for them.
However, that which is obtained through divination and the like, or that which causes unwholesome states to increase while one is eating it, [is also unsuitable].
When wholesome states decline, that is entirely unsuitable; the opposite is suitable.

By way of this, one should understand here "clear comprehension of the suitable" (sappāya-sampajañña), and "clear comprehension of the domain" (gocara-sampajañña) by way of not abandoning the meditation subject.
Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that eats; it is solely through the expansion of the air-element consisting of mental activity of the kind already described.
There is what is called "taking up the bowl"; there is what is called "lowering the hand into the bowl" by means of the expansion of the air-element produced by mental activity;
and there is the making of a mouthful, the lifting of the morsel, and the opening of the mouth by means of the expansion of the air-element produced by mental activity.
No one opens the jawbones with a key or a mechanical device; it is solely by means of the expansion of the air-element produced by mental activity.
The placing of the morsel in the mouth serves as a pestle for the upper teeth, a mortar for the lower teeth, and a hand for the tongue.
Thus, the tip of the tongue is smeared with thin saliva and the base of the tongue with thick saliva.
That morsel, turned by the hand of the tongue in the mortar of the lower teeth and moistened by the water of saliva—
Once it has been crushed by the pestle of the upper teeth, there is no one who inserts it inside with a spoon or a ladle;
rather, it enters by means of the air-element (*vāyodhātu*) alone. Once it has entered, there is no one who holds it by spreading out a layer of straw;
rather, it remains by means of the air-element alone. Once it has remained, there is no one who builds a hearth and kindles a fire...
There is no such thing as "cooking"; it is cooked by the fire element alone.
There is no one who, once it is cooked, extracts it outwards with a stick or a rod; it is the air element alone that extracts it.
Thus, the air element brings it in and carries it away, supports it and turns it over, crushes it, dries it up, and extracts it; while the earth element...
The earth element holds it together, transforms it, grinds it down, and dries it up; the water element moistens it and maintains its cohesion;
the fire element cooks what has entered within; the space element provides a channel for it; and the consciousness element, through appropriate application in each respective instance, directs it.
It is by way of such reflective contemplation on these processes that clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña) is to be understood here.

Furthermore, non-deluded clear comprehension should be understood here through the contemplation of the tenfold repulsiveness: by way of going, seeking, enjoyment, abode, storage, the unripened, the ripened, the fruit, the outflow, and smearing.
A detailed exposition on this point, however, should be taken from the "Description of the Perception of Repulsiveness in Nutriment" in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Regarding the work of defecation and urination": this refers to the performing of both defecation and urination.

In that regard, for one who does not attend to defecation and urination at the proper time, sweat breaks out from the entire body, the eyes roll, the mind becomes distracted, and other diseases arise.
However, for one who does attend to them, none of that occurs; such is the meaning here. Of that...

By way of this, purposeful clear comprehension (*sātthaka-sampajañña*) is to be understood. However, for one who voids excrement or urine in an improper place, there is an offense, his ill-repute increases, and even a danger to life may arise;
whereas for one who does so in a suitable place, none of that occurs—this is what is "suitable" (*sappāya*) here.
By way of this, there is clear comprehension of the suitable (*sappāya-sampajañña*), and by way of not abandoning the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
And the clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña) should be understood as follows:

Internally, there is no such thing as a "self" that performs the act of defecation and urination; rather, the act of defecation and urination occurs solely through the expansion of the air-element (vāyodhātu) arising from mental activity (cittakiriyā).
Just as, when an abscess has ripened, pus and blood issue forth due to the bursting of the abscess, even though one has no desire for it—

It issues forth; and just as water in an overfilled vessel issues forth even against its will, so too the feces and urine accumulated in the receptacle for digested food and the bladder issue forth, even against their will, when pressured by the force of the wind.
Furthermore, this feces and urine thus issuing forth belongs neither to that bhikkhu himself nor to another; it is merely an excretion of the body.
It is so. How so? Just as when one discards old water from a water-pot, it belongs neither to oneself nor to others;
it is merely the act of clearing it away. In the same way, non-deluded clear comprehension should be understood here by way of the reflection occurring in that manner.
Regarding "gone" and so forth: "gone" means in walking; "standing" means in standing; "seated" means in sitting; "asleep" means in lying down;
"awake" means in being awake; "speaking" means in talking; and "silence" means in not talking. And herein, when someone who has walked for a long time or paced about later stands still and reflects:
"The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of pacing..."
"ceased right here"—this is what is called "one who acts with clear comprehension regarding going.
When someone, while reciting, answering questions, or attending to a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), stands for a long time and later, having sat down, reflects thus:
"The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of standing have ceased right here..."
"have ceased"—this one is called "one who acts with clear comprehension while standing.

One who, having sat for a long time by means of recitation and so forth, later reflects while lying down: "The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of sitting have ceased right here"—this one is called "one who acts with clear comprehension while sitting.
But one who, while still lying down, either recites or attends to the meditation subject and then falls asleep—
Later, having arisen, he reflects thus: "The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred at the time of lying down have ceased right here.

This is what is called one who acts with clear comprehension both in sleep and in waking. For the non-occurrence of functional consciousnesses is called "sleep," while their occurrence is called "waking."

But when speaking, he speaks mindfully and with clear comprehension, thinking: "This thing called sound arises dependent on the lips, the teeth, the tongue, and the palate, and dependent on a corresponding mental application.
Or else, having recited for a long time, or having spoken on the Dhamma, or having rehearsed a meditation subject, or [answered] a question...
Or, having spoken and subsequently become silent, he reflects: "The material and immaterial phenomena that arose at the time of speaking have ceased right here.
This is called one who acts with clear comprehension regarding what has been spoken.
But as for one who, having remained silent for a long time after attending to the Dhamma or a meditation subject, subsequently reflects thus:
“The material and immaterial phenomena that occurred during the time one was silent have ceased right here. When there is the occurrence of derived matter, one is said to speak;
when it is absent, one is said to be silent. This is what is meant by being “one who acts with clear comprehension regarding silence.
In this way, the clear comprehension of non-delusion should be understood here, and through its influence, the state of acting with clear comprehension. In this sutta...
The preliminary stage of clear comprehension associated with the foundations of mindfulness has been explained.
3. Commentary on the Bhikkhu Sutta 369.
Regarding the third sutta, "But here too, some...": it is said that this bhikkhu, having had the meditation subject explained, [looked] here and there.
He wanders about and does not apply himself to physical seclusion. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke thus to restrain him.
"Therefore" means because you request a teaching in brief. "Views" refers to views such as the doctrine of the self as the owner of one's actions (*kammassakatā*).
4. Commentary on the Sāla Sutta.
370. In the fourth [case], "Dhamma and Vinaya": both "Dhamma" and "Vinaya" are names for the Teacher’s teaching alone.
"Should be encouraged to adopt" means they should be made to take it up. "Become unified" means having become one-pointed by means of momentary concentration (*khaṇika-samādhi*).
"Concentrated, with one-pointed minds" means having their minds properly established and being one-pointed by way of access (*upacāra*) and absorption (*appanā*). In this sutta...

The foundations of mindfulness were developed in two ways: by the newly ordained monks and by those whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), which constitutes the preliminary stage; they were developed in a mixed manner by the seven types of trainees (*sekha*).
6. Commentary on the *Sakuṇagghi-sutta* (372). Regarding the sixth [sutta]:
"A hawk" (*sakuṇagghi*) means one who kills birds (*sakuṇa*); this is a designation for a falcon (*sena*). Suddenly...
*Ajjhāpattā* means attained through greed and recklessness. *Alakkhikā* means lacking in fortune.
*Appapuññā* means having meager merit. *Sacejja mayaṃ* means "if today we. *Naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇaṃ* means the act of plowing with a plow;
the meaning is that the field-site has now been cleared of brushwood. *Leḍḍuṭṭhānaṃ* means a place for clods of earth. *Saṃvadamānā* means speaking together correctly.

"Speaking" means speaking highly of one's own strength. "Having climbed onto a large clod" means that among three clods standing in the shape of a hearth, having observed, "When the armies come from this side I will exit from this side;
when they come from that side, from that side," he climbed onto one of those clods and stood there without speaking. "Having arrayed" means...
Having girded himself like one fastening on a sword, and having stood firm, he thought:
"He has come very near me; he has reached a place where much [of his path] is behind him and little remains; now he will seize me.
Realizing this, he turned back like a wooden ball and stood right in the path of that clod of earth; thus he was "proceeding" and had "entered."

The meaning is as follows: "He struck his chest" means that because he had lunged forward with the thought, "I shall seize him by cutting off the head of the quail with a single blow," he was unable to restrain his momentum and struck his chest against that clod of earth. At that very moment, the flesh of his heart was torn apart.
Then the quail, thinking, "Ah, I have seen the back of my enemy! became joyful and delighted, and walked back and forth upon his heart.
7. Commentary on the Monkey Sutta (Makkaṭasuttavaṇṇanā) 373.
