In the seventh verse, *duggā* means difficult to traverse. *Cārī* means movement. "Applying a plaster" (*lepaṃ oḍḍenti*) means they prepare a plaster by mixing it with the milky sap of the *vaṭa* tree and other substances;
having observed that this is a place where monkeys constantly frequent, [they apply it] to the branches of trees and so forth.
They place it down. "Set out with five" means it is set out like a carrying-sling for a load, which is to be grasped by inserting a carrying-pole into five places.
"He lies down while snoring" means he sleeps while snoring.
8. Commentary on the Sūda Sutta.

374. In the eighth [case], "cook" (*sūda*) means a food-preparer. "By various accumulations" (*nānaccayehi*) means by various collections; the sense is "of various kinds. Or rather, this is the very reading [itself].
"With sour portions" (*ambilaggehi*) means with sour parts. This same method applies everywhere.

"He brings forward" (*abhiharati*) means he extends his hand for the purpose of taking. "He takes much" (*bahuṃ gaṇhāti*) means that even when taking much in a single grasp, he does so again and again.
Even when taking much, he takes only a great deal. "Of offerings" means of gifts brought forward, having been set aside by the hundreds or thousands.
"Defilements" refers to the five hindrances. "He does not grasp the sign" means he does not know:
"This meditation subject of mine has reached as far as conformity or the state of change-of-lineage (gotrabhu)"; [thus] he fails to grasp the sign of his own mind.
He is not able. In this sutta, only the preliminary stage of insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) as the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) is discussed.
9. Commentary on the Gilāna Sutta: 375.
Regarding the ninth [sutta], "at Beḷuvagāma": there was a village of that name near Vesālī; it was there. Regarding the phrases beginning with "according to friends" (yathāmitta), etc.:
“Friends” means friends indeed. “Seen there” means those merely seen by coming together here and there; they are not very close friends.

“Those with whom one has shared meals” means those who are well-disposed and affectionate; they are close friends. The meaning is: “Wherever such bhikkhus exist, you should enter the rains retreat there. Why did he say this? For the sake of their dwelling in comfort. For them...

It is said that in the village of Beḷuva there was insufficient lodging and alms were scarce; however, around Vesālī there were many lodgings and alms were easily obtained. That is why he spoke thus. But why did he not dismiss them with the words, "Go as you please"? It was out of compassion for them. For it is said that he thought: [The Buddha’s reflection follows: "If these bhikkhus go to Vesālī, they will be honored by the Licchavis. When they are honored, they will become distracted and fail to apply themselves to their meditation. Consequently, they will fall away from the higher Dhamma and the higher Discipline. However, if they remain here, they will live on simple food such as broken rice and sour gruel, and they will sleep on a bed of straw. Thus, through this regimen, they will attain the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saññā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).

Furthermore, when they have attained the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, even if Māra, the Evil One, should approach them with his host of a thousand-fold army, he would not be able to disturb them. Thinking thus, out of compassion for them, he did not dismiss them. And so it is said: [the Buddha’s reflection continues].
He thought: "I shall attain final Nibbāna after remaining for only ten months.
If these people go far away, they will not be able to see me at the time of my final Nibbāna.
Then they might feel regret, thinking: 'The Teacher, while attaining final Nibbāna, did not grant us even so much as a single mindful thought; had he known, we would not have lived so far away.'"
"But those living in the vicinity of Vesālī who dwell there for the rains will come eight times a month to hear the Dhamma and receive the Sugata’s instruction"—thus he did not dismiss them.
*Khara* means harsh. *Ābādha* means a disease of a discordant nature. *Bāḷhā* means powerful. *Māraṇantikā* means ending in death.

"Capable of bringing him to the very brink of death. "He endured with mindfulness and clear comprehension" means that he established mindfulness firmly, delimited [the situation] with wisdom, and then endured it.

"Without being distressed" means that he endured it without following after the sensations by turning this way and that, and without being oppressed or pained. "Without informing" means without making [him] know.
"Without having taken leave" means without having informed [them], that is, without having given advice or instruction.

"By means of energy" refers both to the energy of the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga-vīriya*) and the energy of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti-vīriya*). "Having directed back" means having suppressed.

Regarding "the life-formation" (*jīvitasaṅkhāra*): here, even life itself is the life-formation; it is that by which life is formed—that is, it is joined together and maintained even as it is being severed.
Thus, the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) is also a life-formative force (*jīvitasaṅkhāra*). That is what is intended here.
"Having resolved" means having resolved and having set it in motion; the brief meaning here is that one should enter the attainment of fruition capable of sustaining life.
But did the Blessed One not enter the attainment of fruition prior to this? He did enter it. However, that...
Momentary attainment (*khaṇikasamāpatti*). Momentary attainment suppresses feeling only during the duration of the attainment itself;
as soon as one has emerged from the attainment, feeling again overwhelms the body, just as water overflows when a log or a stone is dropped into it and the moss is torn away.
However, that which consists of the sevenfold materiality and the sevenfold immateriality remains silent.
Having rendered it free from its "roots" (nijaṭa), the attainment entered by way of great insight (mahāvipassanā) thoroughly suppresses [the defilements].
Just as when a man has plunged into a lotus pond and thoroughly churned up the moss with his hands and feet, the water takes a long time to subside;
even so, for one who has emerged from that state, feeling arises only after a long time. Thus, on that day, the Blessed One—
As if establishing fresh insight (vipassanā) upon the Great Bodhi Throne, he rendered the sevenfold set of materiality and the sevenfold set of immateriality free from thicket and tangle;
having integrated them through fourteen modes and suppressed feeling by means of great insight, he entered into meditative attainment (samāpatti), resolving:
"May [feeling] not arise for ten months. Feeling was thus suppressed by that attainment for ten months.
It does not arise at all within a month.
"Recovered from illness" means having been ill, he has risen again.
"As if become sweet" means having acquired a sense of heaviness and stiffness, like a man impaled on a stake. "They do not flutter" means they do not manifest clearly in their various forms.
"They do not appear" means that even the teachings do not occur to him; this indicates that the teachings on the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) were not clear to him.
However, the Thera was well-versed in the "warp-thread" teachings (*tantidhamma*). "He does not utter [them]" means he does not give his final exhortation;
it is with reference to that that he speaks.
"Neither internal nor external" means doing neither with respect to the Dhamma nor with respect to the person.
For one who thinks, "I will not teach this much Dhamma to another," makes the Dhamma internal;
one who thinks, "I will teach this much to another," makes it external. One who thinks, "I will teach this to this person..."
However, one makes a person "internal" by thinking, "I will not teach this to him," and one makes a person "external" by thinking, "I will not teach this to him.
The meaning is that [the teaching] has been taught without doing so.

"The teacher’s fist" (ācariyamuṭṭhi) refers to how there is what is called the "teacher’s fist" among outsiders: having not told anyone during their youth, they [keep it secret] when lying on their deathbed at the end of their lives.

They speak thus to their own pupil who is dear to them; likewise, this shows that for the Tathāgata there is nothing whatsoever that he has kept hidden, having clenched his fist and carried it about with the thought, "I shall speak of this as my final teaching in my old age.
"I, the Bhikkhu-saṅgha" means "I myself shall lead the Bhikkhu-saṅgha," or "I am its presiding authority. "Mamuddesiko" means "I [am the one]."
"Uddeso assa" means "he has an enumeration (uddesa) in the sense of being designated. Thus, "mamuddesiko" means:

"Let the Saṅgha of bhikkhus exist after my passing only by designating me and looking toward me; let it not exist, or let it be whoever it may be"—this is the meaning of "one for whom [there is such a thought].
"It does not happen thus" means that because envy and avarice have been removed right there on the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), it does not happen in this way.
It exists. "What is it? refers to that [person]. "Eighty years old" means one who has reached eighty years;

this is stated for the purpose of indicating that he has attained the final stage of life. "With repairs and bindings" means with repairs consisting of bindings for the arms, bindings for the wheels, and so forth.
"As it were" means he maintains himself with repairs and bindings like an old cart; [it refers to] the maintenance of the four postures through the binding of the fruit of Arhatship.
This shows that it occurs for the Tathāgata.
Now, elucidating that meaning, he said: "At whatever time, Ānanda," and so forth. Therein, "all signs" refers to the signs of form and so on.
"Certain feelings" refers to worldly feelings. Therefore, Ānanda, because... [the text continues].
He shows: "By means of this dwelling in the attainment of fruition, there is well-being; therefore, you too should dwell in this way for that very purpose. "With yourselves as island" means:
dwell having made yourself your island and your refuge, like an island in the great ocean. "With yourselves as refuge" means:
be ones whose destination is only yourselves, not ones whose destination is another. The same applies to the phrases "with the Dhamma as island" and "with the Dhamma as refuge."
This is the method. And here, "Dhamma" should be understood as the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. Regarding the phrase *tamatagge*: it means "at the very limit of darkness" (*tama-ante*);
the syllable *ta-* is used here for metrical reasons (sandhi). This is what is meant: "These are the foremost of all things," thus they are called *tamatagge*.
Thus, Ānanda, having cut through the entire stream of darkness, these bhikkhus of mine stand at the very summit, in the state of supreme excellence.
"They will exist; they will be foremost among them. Whatever monks there may be who desire training, all of them, having the four foundations of mindfulness as their domain, will be foremost.
Thus he took up the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahantship.
10. Commentary on the Bhikkhunupassaya Sutta (The Discourse on the Nuns' Quarters)
376. "He approached him on that tenth day": there were bhikkhunīs in that dwelling-place who were engaged in the practice of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*);

he approached with the thought, "I will encourage them and explain the meditation subject. "A sublime distinction between what preceded and what followed" means a sublime distinction subsequent to the previous one.
In this context, the discernment of the great primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is the previous distinction, while the discernment of derived form (*upādārūpa*) is [the subsequent one].

"Subsequent distinction" (aparaviseso) means this: likewise, the discernment of all material form is the prior distinction, while the discernment of the immaterial is called the subsequent distinction.
The discernment of both material and immaterial form is the prior distinction, while the discernment of conditions is called the subsequent distinction.

The vision of name-and-form together with its conditions is the prior distinction, while the application of the three characteristics is called the subsequent distinction. Thus, the meaning is that one knows the increasingly sublime distinctions from the former to the latter.
"Body as object": the fever of the defilements arises having made that very body which one contemplates the object.
"Or the mind is distracted externally": the arising of consciousness is distracted toward external, manifold objects.
"The mind should be directed toward some pleasing sign": thus, [one should act] regarding both the fever of the defilements and sluggishness.
When external distraction has arisen, one should not proceed with a mind stained by defilements;
rather, one should fix the mind on the meditation subject upon some inspiring or confidence-inspiring object, such as one of the [Three] Jewels beginning with the Buddha.
"The mind is concentrated" means it is correctly fixed (sammā ādhiyati) and well-established upon the object. "I withdraw" means [withdrawing] from that inspiring object.
"I withdraw" means that I direct it back toward the original meditation subject (*mūlakammaṭṭhāna*).

"He both withdraws" means he sends it back toward the original meditation subject. "Neither thinks nor examines" means he does not think thoughts of defilement (*kilesavitakka*) and does not examine examinations of defilement (*kilesavicāra*).
"I am without thought and without examination" [refers] to the thoughts and examinations of defilement.

It is without applied thought and without sustained thought. Being mindful internally, through the mindfulness that operates within the range of his own experience, he understands: "I am mindful and happy.
Thus, Ānanda, there is development by way of aspiration; thus, Ānanda, there is development by way of setting aside. Of this—
For just as when a man, having lifted a great burden of sugarcane and carrying it to a workshop,
becomes utterly exhausted and sets it down on the ground, eats a piece of sugarcane, and then lifts it up again and continues on; even so,
for a bhikkhu who has mastered a meditation subject in order to reach Arahantship, when bodily fever and other such afflictions arise—
Setting aside that meditation subject, he gladdens his mind by recollecting the qualities of the Buddha and so forth;
having made it pliant, the development proceeds. Therefore it is said: "There is development by way of aspiration.
Then, just as that man brings the load of sugarcane to the press-house, presses it, and drinks the juice, so too for this bhikkhu, having brought the meditation subject to its culmination—
The experience of the bliss of the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) by one who has reached Arahantship is to be understood.
"Externally" means outside of the original meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), upon another object. "Without directing" means having set aside.
Regarding the passage, "Then afterwards he understands that which was previously uncontracted as liberated and desireless," here it is by way of the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
The meaning should be understood either by way of the body or by way of the teaching.
In this context, regarding the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), first there is the "prior" application to the meditation subject, and last there is "Arahatta" (Arahantship).
In that regard, a bhikkhu who has taken up the primary meditation subject [is protected] from the fever of the defilements, from lethargy, or from outward distraction.
Not allowing any opportunity for [defilements] to arise— like driving a well-trained ox,
or like inserting a precisely cut square peg into a square hole— he establishes insight and, without lingering or clinging, attains Arahantship;
this is the transition from the previously mentioned application to the meditation subject to the subsequently mentioned state of Arahantship.
And by means of that [method], one understands that what was previously uncollected is later liberated and signless.
Now, regarding the body, the tip-joints of the toes are called "front," and the skull is called "back.
In this regard, a bhikkhu who, having focused on the bone-fragments at the tip-joints of the toes, releases the bundle of barley-grains by means of the *byābhaṅgiyā* [meditative device]—
When one discerns the bones by way of their color, shape, direction, location, and delimitation,
preventing the arising of the fever of defilements and so forth in the interim, one brings the meditation to completion as far as the skull.
By means of the toes of the feet reckoned as "front" and the skull reckoned as "back," one understands that which is not contracted front-to-back as "liberated" and "wishless."

In the teaching of the thirty-two aspects as well, in the teaching beginning with "hair was called 'first' and brain matter was called 'last,'" there is the bhikkhu who, having focused on the hair, examines the hair and so forth by way of color, shape, direction, and location;
and having prevented the arising of the fever of defilements and the like in the interim, he brings his meditation to perfection up to the brain matter. He...
One is said to understand that which is liberated—uncontracted before and after—with respect to the hairs, reckoned as "before," and the brain, reckoned as "after," [knowing it as] signless.
"In this way, Ānanda, there is development without aspiration"; thus, Ānanda, there is development by setting aside.
For just as a man who, having received a load of sugar and carrying it back to his own village,
might set it down midway and eat the sugar-candy and other edible foods placed in his lap,
yet still reaches his village; even so, for one who has begun the meditation to attain Arahantship, there is the subsiding of bodily fever and the like.
Since the development of the meditation subject proceeds by preventing its arising, it is therefore called "development without aspiration.
Just as that man, having brought his load of sugar to his own village, enjoys it together with his relatives, so too for this bhikkhu,
having brought the meditation subject to its ultimate conclusion and attained Arahantship, there is the experience of the bliss of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
This should be understood. In this sutta, preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) is explained. The remainder is clear throughout.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Ambapālī Vagga.
2. The Nālandā Vagga.
2. Commentary on the Nālandasutta 378.
In the second sutta of the second chapter, "at Nālandā" means in the city named Nālandā; having made that city his alms-resort village.
"In the mango grove of the cloth-merchant" means in the mango grove belonging to the merchant who was a cloth-merchant. It is said that it belonged to him.

It became a park. Having heard the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, he gained confidence in the Blessed One and, having constructed a monastery for the Blessed One in that park—adorned with huts, caves, pavilions, and so forth—he dedicated it [to him].
That monastery came to be known as Pāvārika-ambavana, just as Jīvaka’s mango grove is known as Jīvakambavana. The meaning is: "He dwells in that Pāvārika-ambavana."
"Thus convinced" means one who has thus arisen faith; the meaning is, "I believe in this way. "Of even greater direct knowledge" means more widely known, or possessing even more super-knowledge;
the meaning is, "one with superior wisdom. "Regarding full enlightenment" refers to either the knowledge of omniscience or the knowledge of the path of Arahatship;
for it is by the path of Arahatship alone that the qualities of a Buddha are grasped in their entirety. Both... [are included].
The Chief Disciples attain the knowledge of the Perfection of Discipleship by means of the path to Arahatship itself; the Paccekabuddhas attain the knowledge of Paccekabodhi;
and the Buddhas attain both omniscience and all the Buddha-qualities. All of these are accomplished by means of the path to Arahatship alone.
Therefore, the knowledge of the path to Arahatship is called "Sambodhi" (Perfect Enlightenment). And there is nothing superior to that possessed by the Blessed One.
There is none. Therefore he said: “He is more distinguished than the Blessed One, namely, in regard to full enlightenment.

The word *uḷārā* means “excellent. For this term *uḷāra* occurs in the sense of “sweet” in such passages as “they are eating excellent hard foods,” and in the sense of “supreme” in such passages as “Master Vacchāyana indeed praises the ascetic Gotama with a supreme praise.”
In such passages as “immeasurable and sublime radiance,” the word *uḷāra* means "vast. However, here it is used in the sense of "excellent. Therefore it is said: “*Uḷārā* means excellent.

*Āsabhi* means like the speech of a bull—unshakable and unflinching. *Ekaṃso gahito* means grasped through oral tradition, or through the lineage of teachers, or through hearsay, or through the transmission of the Piṭakas, or through reflection on the modes [of reasoning].
The meaning is that it was not taken as a one-sided position, nor was it spoken as a definitive statement based on mere speculative views, reasoning, or logic;
rather, it was grasped as a certainty after having been penetrated through direct knowledge, as if by means of personal realization.
"Lion’s roar" means the best of roars; the meaning is that it was uttered as a supreme cry, like a lion roaring while filling the forest with its sound.
Why did he begin this teaching with the words, "What now, Sāriputta"? It was for the purpose of eliciting a response.
For some, having let out a lion’s roar, are unable to provide a response to their own lion’s roar; they cannot endure being tested and are like a monkey that has fallen into a trap.
Just as impure iron, when smelted, becomes charcoal, [so too does such a person fail].
Thus he was like a glowing ember. When one was exhorted to roar a lion’s roar, he was able to give it;
he endured the friction, and while being tested, he shone even more brightly like flawless gold being smelted. Such was the Elder.
Therefore, the Blessed One, knowing him to be "one who can endure the exhortation," began this teaching for the purpose of having him give a lion’s roar.
In this context, "all those" means "all those by you. "Of such virtue" means they possess such virtue through the virtue of the path, the virtue of the fruit, and mundane or supramundane virtue.
"Of such Dhamma": here, the factors belonging to the side of concentration are intended;

the meaning is that they possess such concentration through the concentration of the path, the concentration of the fruit, and mundane or supramundane concentration. "Of such wisdom" refers likewise to the wisdom of the path and so forth.

"Thus wise. As for the phrase "dwelling thus," one might ask: since the states belonging to the side of concentration were already included below, why is "dwelling" mentioned again when it has already been taken up? This was indeed already taken up by the Elder;
however, this [mention] is stated for the purpose of illustrating the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Therefore, those Blessed Ones are "dwelling thus" in the attainment of cessation.
"‘They were’—thus the meaning should be understood here. Regarding ‘liberated thus’:

herein liberation is fivefold, namely, liberation by suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*), liberation by substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-vimutti*), liberation by eradication (*samuccheda-vimutti*), liberation by tranquillization (*paṭipassaddhi-vimutti*), and liberation by escape (*nissaraṇa-vimutti*).
Among these, the eight attainments [are liberation] by those [defilements] suppressed of their own accord..."
Because they are liberated from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and so forth, they are designated as "liberation by suppression" (*vikkhambhana-vimutti*).

The seven contemplations, beginning with the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), are designated as "liberation by substitution of opposites" (*tadaṅga-vimutti*) because they are liberated from the perceptions of permanence and so forth, which have been relinquished in opposition to their respective counterparts.
The four noble paths (*ariyamagga*) [are so called] because of the defilements (*kilesa*) that have been completely eradicated by them.

Because they are liberated [from defilements], they are designated as "liberation by eradication. Because the four fruits of recluseship arise when defilements have been subsided through the power of the paths, they are designated as "liberation by subsidence.
Because it has escaped from, departed from, and stands far removed from all defilements, Nibbāna is designated as "liberation by escape."
Thus, the meaning here of "liberated in this way" should be understood by way of these five kinds of liberation.
But as for those, Sāriputta, who will come to be—firstly, those of the past have ceased, having reached the state of non-designation (apaṇṇattika), extinguished like the flame of a lamp;
since they have thus ceased and reached the state of non-designation, how will you know them?
But asking, "Have you discerned and known the qualities of future Buddhas by means of your own mind? he spoke thus.
"What then, Sāriputta, do you say of those [Buddhas] now?"—for future Buddhas are yet unborn, unproduced, and unarisen;
how will you know them? For to know them would be like seeing footprints in the trackless sky. Now, by me...
"You dwell with me in the same monastery, you go for alms together, and at the time of teaching the Dhamma, you sit on my right side;
yet, having examined my virtues within your own mind, how is it that they were known by you?"—inquiring thus, he spoke these words.
But whenever the Elder was questioned, he would refuse, saying, "Certainly not, venerable sir."
The Elder had both what was known and what was unknown. Did he offer a refusal regarding a matter he knew, or regarding one he did not know?
He did not refuse regarding what he knew; he refused only regarding what he did not know. It is said that when the questioning began, the Elder realized:
"This inquiry is not concerning the knowledge of a disciple’s perfection; rather, this inquiry concerns omniscience."
Without denying his own knowledge of the perfection of disciples (*sāvakapāramīñāṇa*), he denies his knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) regarding that which is unknown to him.

By this, he demonstrates: "The Blessed One does not possess the omniscient knowledge capable of knowing the causes of the virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation of myself and of the Buddhas of the past, future, and present."
"Ettha" means among these Buddhas distinguished by their past lives and so forth. "Atha kiñcarahi" means:

"Then why?"—that is to say, he asks, "Since such knowledge is absent [in you], why have you spoken thus? "Dhammanvaya" refers to the inferential knowledge that arises following upon the application of direct knowledge of the Dhamma;
it is the grasping of the method (nayaggāha) that is understood. By abiding in this very knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa), [the Buddha]...
"I know him by his manner, Blessed One," he says. For the Elder’s grasp of the underlying method is immeasurable and boundless.
Just as there is no measure or limit to the knowledge of omniscience, so too is the Dhamma-Senāpati’s grasp of the method. Therefore, he [discerns]:
"By this [method] such-and-such [a quality], by this such-and-such; by this [method] the unsurpassed one, by this the unsurpassed Teacher."
He knows. For the Elder’s grasp of the method leads directly to omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
Now, in order to make that grasp of the method clear, he spoke the passage beginning with "Just as, venerable sir.
In that context, because in the Middle Country, whether the city's moats, ramparts, and so forth are strong or weak, in every respect—
Or even if there were no thieves, there would still be apprehension of them; therefore, not taking that [city] as the example, he said "an outlying city.
"Strongly founded" means having firm foundations and ramparts. "With strong walls and gate-towers" means having both firm walls and firm battlemented gateways.
Why did he say "with a single gate"? For in a city with many gates, there must be many wise gatekeepers.

Only one is suitable for a single door. Since there was no one else equal to the Elder in wisdom, he said "a single door" in order to show only one gatekeeper as an illustration of his own state of being wise.
"Wise" means endowed with wisdom (*paṇḍicca*). "Clever" means endowed with proficiency (*veyyattiya*), possessing clear knowledge. "Intelligent" means...
He was endowed with wisdom characterized as "presence-of-mind" (*ṭhānuppattika-paññā*). "The patrol path" (*anupariyāyapatha*) refers to the walkway along the rampart.
"The breach in the rampart" (*pākārasandhi*) refers to a place where two bricks have come apart. "The gap in the rampart" (*pākāravivara*) refers to a broken section of the wall.
"Corruptions of the mind" (*cetaso upakkilesa*) refers to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), which defile the mind.
They defile, afflict, and harass the mind; therefore they are called "defilements of the mind" (*cetaso upakkilesā*).
Regarding "weakening of wisdom": when the hindrances arise, they do not allow unarisen wisdom to arise;
therefore they are called "weakening of wisdom" (*paññāya dubbalīkaraṇā*). "With well-established minds" means [well-established] in the four foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).

"Having established their minds": having developed the seven factors of enlightenment according to reality—that is, by way of their true nature—they "penetrated the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment," which shows that they realized Arahantship and omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa).
Furthermore, in this context, the foundations of mindfulness are insight (vipassanā), the factors of enlightenment are the path (magga), and the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment is Arahantship.

"Or, *satipaṭṭhāna* is insight (*vipassanā*) accompanied by the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*), while *sammāsambodhi* is simply Arahantship. However, the Elder Mahāsīva, a reciter of the *Dīgha Nikāya*, said:

"If one were to take 'insight' as referring to the foundations of mindfulness, and then take 'factors of enlightenment' and 'the path' as referring to omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), this would constitute an excellent question; but it was not taken in that way.
Thus, the Elder [refers] to the abandoning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) by all Buddhas.

It shows that there is no difference between the development of the foundations of mindfulness and enlightenment, just as there is no difference between gold and silver when they have been melted together.

Standing here, the simile should be correlated: the Venerable Sāriputta showed the inner city, he showed the rampart, he showed the circumvallation path, he showed the gate, he showed the wise gatekeeper, and [finally] the city.
He showed him coarse living beings entering and exiting, and he showed the gatekeeper the visibility of those beings.
If one asks, "In what way are these things similar?"—Nibbāna is like the city; virtue (sīla) is like the rampart;
moral shame (hirī) is like the circumvallation path; the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is like the gate; and the General of the Dhamma (Dhammasenāpati) is like the wise gatekeeper.
The Buddhas of the past, future, and present are like the coarse living beings who enter and exit the city;

the Venerable Sāriputta’s clear knowledge of those Buddhas of the past, future, and present by way of their virtue, concentration, and so forth, is like the gatekeeper’s clear perception of those beings.
To this extent, the Elder [demonstrated] to the Blessed One: "In this way, I [possess] the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple..."
"By means of the method of following the Dhamma and by grasping the underlying principle, I know"—thus he gave vent to his own lion's roar.
"Therefore" means: because he says, "Venerable sir, it is not that I possess the knowledge of encompassing the minds of the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, of the past, future, and present;
rather, the method of following the Dhamma is known," therefore [he said this]. "You should speak repeatedly" means...
"You should speak again and again, saying, 'It was told to me in the morning,' lest you fail to speak at midday and so forth;
or, 'It was told to me today,' lest you fail to speak on the following day and so forth"—this is the meaning. "That [doubt] will be abandoned" means:
"Even a disciple like Sāriputta, endowed with the speed of knowledge, is unable to know the mental movements of the Buddhas."
"Thinking thus, 'The Tathāgatas are immeasurable,' whatever doubt or uncertainty they may have regarding the Tathāgata will be abandoned.
3. Commentary on the Cunda Sutta 379.
"In Magadha" means in the country so named. "In the village of Nālaka" refers to a place not far from Rājagaha, which was his own...
In the village of such-and-such name belonging to his own clan. "Cunda the novice" (samaṇuddesa): this elder was the younger brother of the General of the Dhamma;
while he was not yet ordained, the monks addressed him as "Cunda the novice," and even at the time of his seniority, they continued to address him in that same way.
Therefore it is said, "Cunda the novice. "He became an attendant" means by providing water for rinsing the mouth and tooth-sticks.
And he was one who performed service by sweeping the cell, massaging the back, and taking up the bowl and robes.
"He attained final Nibbāna" means he passed away into the element of Nibbāna without residue. At what time?
In the year of the Blessed One’s final Nibbāna.
In this regard, the sequential account is as follows: it is said that after completing the rains retreat, the Blessed One departed from the village of Veḷuva, intending to go to Sāvatthī.
Returning by the same path he had come, he eventually reached Sāvatthī and entered the Jeta Grove.
Having performed his duties toward the Blessed One, the General of the Dhamma went to his daytime resting place; there, among his resident pupils...

After showing the routine duties, when they had departed, he swept the daytime resting place, spread out his leather mat, washed his feet, sat cross-legged, and entered the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).
Then, as he emerged from that state at the predetermined time, this reflection arose in him: "Do Buddhas pass away first?"
"Or are they the chief disciples? Then, knowing that "the chief disciples have passed away first," he surveyed his own life-force (*āyusaṅkhāra*).
Knowing, "Only seven days of my life-force remain," he reflected, "Where shall I attain final nibbāna?
Thereupon, [he recalled]: "Rāhula has attained final nibbāna among the Tāvatiṃsa gods; the elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña at Chaddantadaha; where shall I..."
Thinking again and again, "I shall attain final Nibbāna," he directed his mindfulness toward his mother:
"Although my mother was the mother of seven Arahants, she lacked faith in the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha;
does she possess the necessary potential (upanissaya), or does she not? Seeing that she possessed the potential for the path of stream-entry, [he considered: "To whom..."
Looking [into the future] with the thought, "There will be a realization through this teaching," he saw: "It will be through my own teaching of the Dhamma, and not that of anyone else.
However, if I were to remain indifferent, there would be those who would say of me: 'The Elder Sāriputta is merely a refuge for the rest of the people;
for instance, on the occasion of his teaching the Samacitta Sutta and other discourses, hundreds of thousands of millions of deities...'"
"Those who have attained Arahatship and those deities who have penetrated the three lower paths are beyond counting;
furthermore, in other places, many clear realizations (abhisamaya) are seen. Even eighty thousand families were reborn in heaven simply by gaining confidence in the Elder;
yet now, he was unable to remove even a mere glimpse of wrong view from his own mother. Therefore, [one should protect] one's mother from wrong view.

Having made the resolution, "I shall attain final nibbāna right here in my birth-chamber," and thinking, "Today, having obtained the Blessed One’s permission, I shall depart," he addressed the Elder Cunda:
"Friend Cunda, give notice to our assembly of five hundred bhikkhus: 'Friends, take up your bowls and robes; the Dhammasenāpati is going to Nālakagāma.'"
"I wish to go. The elder did accordingly.
The bhikkhus, having tidied their lodgings and taken their bowls and robes, went into the presence of the elder.
The elder, having tidied his lodging and swept the daytime sitting area, stood at the door of the daytime sitting area and looked toward it.
“This is now my final sight [of you]; there will be no returning again,” he said, surrounded by five hundred bhikkhus.
Approaching the Blessed One and paying homage, he addressed the Blessed One thus: “May the Blessed One grant me leave, venerable sir;
may the Sugata grant me leave. The time for my parinibbāna has come; my life-faculty has been relinquished. For Buddhas, however—

When it is said, “Parinibbāna,” they will think, “They are praising the beauty of death”; when it is said, “Do not parinibbāna,” they will think, “They are speaking of the virtues of the round of existence.
Thus, those with wrong views will attribute fault [to the speaker]. Therefore, he says neither of these two.
For this reason, the Blessed One said to him, “Where, Sāriputta, will you attain parinibbāna? and [Sāriputta replied], “There is, Bhante...”
When he said, "I was born in the village of Nālaka among the Magadhans;
there I shall attain final nibbāna," [the Buddha] replied, "Sāriputta, do now as you deem fit;
however, it will soon be difficult for your elder and younger brothers to see a bhikkhu such as you, so teach them the Dhamma."

The Elder, realizing, “The Teacher expects me to deliver a Dhamma teaching preceded by a display of supernormal power,” paid homage to the Blessed One, ascended into the air to the height of a palm tree, and having descended, bowed at the feet of the One of Ten Powers;
then, ascending again to the height of two palm trees, he descended and bowed at the feet of the One of Ten Powers; by this method, he ascended to the height of seventy palm trees.
Having ascended, displaying many hundreds of miracles, he began a discourse on the Dhamma. He spoke while his body was visible, and also while it was invisible;
he spoke with either the upper or lower half of his body visible, whether visible or invisible;
at times he displayed the color of the moon, at times the color of the sun, and at times...
At times he appeared with the color of a mountain, at times with the color of the ocean;

at times he was a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin-rāja*), at times the great king Vessavaṇa, at times Sakka the king of the gods, and at times Mahābrahmā—thus, displaying hundreds of such miracles, he delivered a discourse on the Dhamma.
The entire city gathered together. The Elder descended, prostrated at the feet of the One Possessed of Ten Powers (*dasabala*), and...
He stood there. Then the Teacher said to him, "Sāriputta, what is the name of this Dhamma exposition?
"It is called 'The Lion’s Play,' Bhante. "Truly, Sāriputta, it is the Lion’s Play; truly, Sāriputta, it is the Lion’s Play!
Then the Elder, stretching out his hands which were the color of lac, placed them upon the Teacher’s feet, which resembled golden tortoises, at the ankles.
Having taken them, he said: "Venerable sir, for more than a hundred thousand aeons plus an incalculable aeon, the perfections were fulfilled for the sake of worshipping these feet;
that wish of mine has now reached its fulfillment.
From this point on, there will never again be a meeting or a gathering in one place by way of rebirth-linking; this bond of trust is severed. By many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas..."
"I shall enter the city of Nibbāna—secure, blissful, cool, fearless, ageless, and deathless.
If there is anything physical or verbal of mine that you do not approve of, forgive that, O Blessed One; it is time for my departure.
"I forgive you, Sāriputta. Indeed, there is nothing physical or verbal of yours that is disagreeable to me."
“There is, Sāriputta; now you may go at whatever time you deem fit.

As soon as the Blessed One had given his permission, the Venerable Sāriputta paid homage at the Teacher’s feet and, the moment he stood up—even while the mountains of Sineru, the Cakkavāḷa, and the Himavanta ranges were supporting him—he thought: “Today I am able to support this mass of virtues...”
As if saying, "I am unable," the great earth shook all at once with a roar as far as the edge of the waters;
celestial drums resounded in the sky, and a great cloud arose and rained down a shower of lotus blossoms.
The Teacher, thinking, "I shall establish him in the position of Dhammasenāpati," rose from his Dhamma-seat and proceeded toward the Gandhakuṭi.
Having gone there, he stood upon a jeweled slab. The Elder circumambulated him three times, paid homage at four places, and said:
"Lord, at the feet of the Perfectly Enlightened One Anomadassi, more than a hundred thousand aeons ago in the past incalculable, you lay prostrate and aspired for the sight of us;
that aspiration of yours has been fulfilled, for we have now been seen."
"This was your first sight of me; this is the last sight. There will be no further sight of you," he said.
Then, raising his hands in salutation, brilliant with the ten nails joined together, and having walked back toward him as far as the range of vision, he paid homage and departed.
Again, the great earth, unable to bear the weight, shook, making the waters its boundary.
The Blessed One said to the monks standing around him, “Follow your eldest brother, monks.
At that moment, all four assemblies left the Jeta Grove one by one with the Perfectly Enlightened One and departed without exception.
Even the inhabitants of the city of Sāvatthī heard: “It is said that the Elder Sāriputta, having taken leave of the Perfectly Enlightened One...”
Thinking, "He has gone forth desiring to attain final Nibbāna; we shall see him," they went out, opening the city gates so they were not obstructed.
With perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands, and with their hair disheveled, they asked, "Where now does the one of great wisdom sit? Where does the General of the Dhamma sit?
And they asked, "To whom shall we go? In whose hands shall we place the Teacher?"
Lamenting and weeping in this manner, beginning with the words, "The Elder has departed," they followed after the Elder.

Because he was established in great wisdom, the Elder exhorted the great multitude, saying, "This path cannot be bypassed by anyone," and he also addressed the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, saying, "Friends, you too must stop;
do not fall into negligence regarding the One of Ten Powers."

Having turned back, he departed together with his own retinue. Those people who had followed him, lamenting, "Previously the noble one went on a tour of returning, but this departure now is not for a return," he dismissed them, saying, "Be heedful, friends;
such indeed is the nature of conditioned phenomena."
Then the Venerable Sāriputta, staying for only one night at every place along the way, spent seven days providing for the needs of people;
having reached Nālakagāma in the evening, he stood at the village gate at the foot of a banyan tree.
Then Uparevata, the nephew of the Elder, while going out of the village, saw the Elder and approached him.
Having paid homage, he stood there. The Elder said to him, "Is your grandmother at home? "Yes, venerable sir," he replied. "Go and inform her of our arrival here.
When she asks, "Why have you come? say, "It is said that today he will stay in the village for one day;
prepare the birth-chamber, and also a place for five hundred monks to dwell."
“Do you know? he asked. He went and said, “Noble ladies, my maternal uncle has arrived. “Where is he now? “At the village gate. “Is he alone?
“There are five hundred bhikkhus as well. “For what reason has he come? He reported the matter to her.
The brahmin woman thought, “Why indeed does he have so many people prepare a dwelling place? When he was young...”

Thinking, "Having gone forth, I wish to become a householder again when I am old," she had the birth-chamber cleaned, had a dwelling place built for five hundred [monks], lit torches, and sent word to the Elder.
The Elder, together with the monks, ascended the palace, entered the birth-chamber, and sat down. Having sat down, he said, "For you..."
“Go to your place of residence,” he dismissed the monks. As soon as they had departed, a severe illness arose in the Elder;
blood-stained dysentery and terminal pains set in. One vessel would enter [his body] and another would exit.
The brahmin woman, thinking, “The condition of my son does not please me,” stood leaning against the door of her own living quarters.

The Four Great Kings, looking about to see where the Dhamma-Senāpati was dwelling, arrived at Nālakagāma and stood after paying homage, thinking, "He is lying upon his deathbed in the Jātovara hut; we shall go to see him for the last time.
"Who are you? [he asked]. "We are the Great Kings, venerable sir. "For what purpose have you come? "To serve as attendants to the sick."
“Let it be; there is an attendant for the sick. You may go,” he dismissed them.
After they had departed, Sakka, lord of the devas, arrived by that same route. When he too had gone, Mahābrahmā arrived. The Elder dismissed them in the very same manner.
Having witnessed the arrival and departure of these deities, the brahmin woman thought, “Who indeed are these who, having paid homage to my son...”

The Blessed One, having thus expanded upon it, delivered a discourse on the Dhamma connected with the qualities of the Buddha.
At the conclusion of the discourse on the Dhamma, the brahmin lady, having established herself in the fruit of stream-entry, said to her son:

The Elder, thinking, “I have now received the maintenance allowance from my mother, the brahmin lady Rūpasārī;

"As we wander about never leaving you, like our own shadows, there is nothing at all that is unpleasant to us;

The female lay devotee, thinking, "Why does my son not say anything? rose up and massaged his back and feet.
Knowing that he had attained final nibbāna, they cried out with a great sound and fell at his feet, saying: "Father, previously we did not know of your virtues;

but now, starting from this very moment, we have not been able to seat and feed hundreds, thousands, or even hundreds of thousands of bhikkhus in this residence, nor have we been able to clothe them in robes."
“We were able [to build], but we were not able to have a hundred monasteries or a thousand monasteries built,” he lamented until the rising of the dawn.
As soon as the dawn had risen, he summoned the goldsmiths, had the golden chamber opened, and after having the golden jars weighed on a great scale, he gave the order:
“Have five hundred gabled chambers and five hundred *agghika* (ornamental finials) made.”
Sakka, the king of the gods, addressed the divine son Vissakamma, saying: "Dear son, the Dhammasenāpati has attained final Nibbāna;
construct five hundred gabled chambers and five hundred offering-stands.

Seeing her own glorious prosperity, she thought, "This prosperity is magnificent; what deed must I have performed? While reflecting thus, she saw:
"At the place where the Elder Sāriputta attained final Nibbāna, I had made an offering with three golden flower-vases, and the great multitude..."
“Having crushed me, he departed; having died there, I have been reborn here.
Now, supported by the Elder, I shall tell people of the ripening of my merit. Saying this, she descended together with her celestial mansion.
Seeing her from afar, the great multitude thought, “What! Have two suns risen? As they looked on, they saw her approaching in the celestial mansion.
"It appears to have the shape of a gabled chamber; this is not the sun, it is a single celestial mansion," he said.
That mansion immediately approached and stood suspended in the air above the Elder’s funeral pyre. The goddess, having left her mansion in mid-air, descended to the earth.
The great multitude asked, "Who are you, noble lady? "You do not know me," she replied.
"I am Revatī; having made an offering to the Elder with three golden flower-pots, I was crushed by people and, upon passing away, was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Having thus praised the performance of wholesome deeds, she circumambulated the Elder’s funeral pyre.
Having paid homage, she departed for her own divine abode.
The great multitude also, having enjoyed seven days of festive celebrations, prepared a funeral pyre with all kinds of fragrant perfumes; the pyre was one hundred cubits minus one.
Having placed the Elder’s body upon the pyre, they set it ablaze with bundles of usīra grass. Throughout the entire night at the cremation site...
The news of the Dhamma was spread. The Elder Anuruddha extinguished the elder’s funeral pyre with all kinds of scented water.
The Elder Cunda placed the relics in a water-strainer and said: “I can no longer remain here;
I must inform the Perfectly Enlightened One of the passing away of my eldest brother, the Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma.”
Thinking, “I shall inform him,” Cunda took the Elder’s water-strainer and his bowl and robes and went to Sāvatthī.
Without staying even one night at any single place, he reached Sāvatthī by staying only one night at each stop.
To show this matter, the passage beginning with “Then the novice Cunda... was spoken.
In that context, "where the Venerable Ānanda was" means he approached the Venerable Ānanda, his own preceptor and the keeper of the Dharma-treasury.
But why did he not go directly into the presence of the Teacher, but instead went to the Elder?
It was out of reverence for both the Teacher and the Elder. It is said that after bathing in the lotus pond at the Great Monastery of Jetavana and coming out, he [approached the Elder].

To him, who was well-clad and well-robed, this thought occurred: "The Buddhas are indeed as venerable as a great stone parasol, and as difficult to approach as a hooded serpent, a lion, a tiger, or a noble elephant in rut.
It is not possible for me to go straight into the presence of the Teacher and speak; to whom, then, should I go? Then he thought: "My preceptor..."

The Dhamma-treasurer, the most excellent companion of the Elder Jeṭṭhabhātuka, approached him out of reverence for both the Teacher and the Elder, thinking, "I will go to him, take him with me, and speak with the Teacher. [He thought:
"This is his bowl and robe," meaning, "This is his alms-bowl for use, and this is his water-strainer for the relics. Thus...
He explained each one individually. In the Pāḷi, however, it is stated only as: "This is his bowl and robe.
*Kathāpābhataṃ* means the source of the story. For the root (*mūla*) is called *pābhata*. As it is said:
"Even with a small amount of merchandise, the wise and discerning man..."
"He raises himself up like a tiny fire burning.
"In order to see the Blessed One" means for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One. But has the Blessed One not been seen by him before?
No, he has not. For this venerable one had gone [to see him] eighteen times in a single day—nine times by day and nine times by night.
He goes only for the purpose of waiting upon [the teacher]. Even though he might wish to go a hundred or a thousand times a day, he does not go without a reason;
rather, he goes only after taking up a single door of inquiry.
On that day, wishing to go with that particular topic of conversation, he said: "This is his bowl and robe. The Elder also said: "This is his..."
Having pointed out the bowl and robe separately, he said, "And this is the water-strainer for the relics.
The Teacher extended his hand, took the water-strainer for the relics, placed it upon the palm of his hand, and addressed the monks:
"Monks, that monk who on the previous day performed hundreds of miracles and attained final Nibbāna—"
He requested permission [to teach], and now these relics of his alone are visible, resembling the color of refined gold.
Monks, this monk has fulfilled the perfections for an incalculable eon plus one hundred thousand kalpas; this monk is one who sets in motion the Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me;
this monk is one who has obtained a second seat; this monk is one who has fulfilled the assembly of disciples.
Except for me, this bhikkhu is peerless in wisdom throughout the ten thousandfold world-system;
this bhikkhu possesses great wisdom, vast wisdom, joyous wisdom, swift wisdom, sharp wisdom, and penetrative wisdom.
This bhikkhu is of few wishes, contented, secluded, aloof, energetic, an exhorter, and a censurer of evil.
This bhikkhu, having renounced the great prosperity he had attained over five hundred births, has gone forth;
this bhikkhu is as patient as the earth in my teaching; this bhikkhu is like a bull with its horns cut off;
this bhikkhu has a mind as humble as that of a caṇḍāla’s son. Behold, bhikkhus, the relics of one possessed of great wisdom!
"Behold, monks, one of wide wisdom, of laughing wisdom, of swift wisdom, of sharp wisdom,
of penetrative wisdom— one who has few desires, who is contented, secluded, unattached,
energetic, and a reprover; behold, monks, the elements of one who censures evil."
“He who has gone forth from five hundred births,
having abandoned delightful sensual pleasures—
that one free from passion, whose faculties are well-composed— ”
Worship Sāriputta, who has attained final Nibbāna.
"Strong in patience, like the earth, he is not disturbed;
nor does he act under the sway of the mind."
Compassionate, merciful, and extinguished—
worship Sāriputta who has attained final Nibbāna.
Just as the son of a caṇḍāla, having entered a city...
He moves with a humble mind, like one holding a basket;
even so does this Sāriputta dwell.
Pay homage to Sāriputta, who has attained final nibbāna.
“Just as a bull with its horns cut off wanders through the village and the forest without causing harm,
so does this Sāriputta dwell.”
"Worship Sāriputta who has attained final Nibbāna.
Thus the Blessed One spoke in praise of the Elder with five hundred verses.
As the Blessed One spoke in praise of the Elder, the Elder Ānanda was unable to sustain himself, like a chicken that has fallen into the mouth of a wildcat.
It trembles as it were. Therefore he said: "Furthermore, venerable sir, my body is as if intoxicated," and so forth; all of this should be expanded in detail.
Herein, the meaning of "as if intoxicated" and so on has already been stated. However, here "teachings" (dhammā) refers to the teachings consisting of summaries and detailed inquiries.
For if the teachings of summary and inquiry are not grasped, or even if they are grasped, [one fails] to recite them.

His mind was not inclined to act. Then the Teacher, opening his eyes which were variegated with the fivefold grace, looked at the Elder and, thinking, "I shall comfort him," spoke these words beginning with, "Ānanda, what has become of Sāriputta?
In this context, "the aggregate of virtue" (sīlakkhandha) refers to mundane and supramundane virtue. The same method applies to concentration and wisdom as well. "Liberation" (vimutti)...

However, they are exclusively supramundane (*lokuttara*). The knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimuttiñāṇadassana*) is the knowledge of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*); that is exclusively mundane (*lokiya*). An "instructor" (*ovādaka*) is one who gives instruction.
One who has "descended" (*otiṇṇa*) is one whose nature it is to descend in various ways into the matters that have been descended into.

An "expositor" (*viññāpaka*) is one who makes known both the meaning and the reason at the time of preaching the Dhamma. An "indicator" (*sandassaka*) is one who [indicates] those various things by way of the aggregates (*khandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).
A teacher of the Dhamma. An "exhorter" (*samādapaka*) is one who causes others to take up [the practice] by saying, "Take this and that.
An "inspirer" (*samuttejaka*) is one who rouses them to effort. An "encourager" (*sampahaṃsaka*) is one who makes them rejoice and shine with the qualities they have attained.
"Without weariness in teaching the Dhamma" means that having begun the teaching of the Dhamma, [he does not think], "My head aches, or my heart..."
Whether it be the belly or the back—thus, free from the manner of retreating, unhesitating and confident, he plunges into one or even two [monks] with the speed of a lion.
The meaning of the phrase "supporting his fellow celibates" has already been explained in detail in the Khandhaka section.

Regarding "the strength of the Dhamma" (*dhammoja*) and "the enjoyment of the Dhamma" (*dhammabhoga*), both terms refer to the enjoyment of the Dhamma. "Support through the Dhamma" (*dhammānuggaha*)...
Supporting through the Dhamma.
The Teacher, thinking, "This bhikkhu is suffering excessively," spoke again to comfort him, saying, "Is it not so, Ānanda, by me... and so forth.
In that context, "by those who are dear and beloved" refers to mother, father, brother, sister, and others; there is separation from them through birth and dissociation from them through death.
"Becoming otherwise" means change. "How could that be obtained here, Ānanda?"—this refers to "therefore.

Because there is separation from all that is dear and beloved, therefore—even after fulfilling the ten perfections, even after attaining full enlightenment, even after setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, even after displaying the Twin Miracle, and even after performing the Descent to the World of the Gods—that which is born and come to be...
"It is impossible that the body of the Tathāgata, which is conditioned and subject to dissolution, should not dissolve;
even by weeping and wailing, it is not possible to prevent that occurrence. 'It would dissolve' means it would break apart.
'In the same way'—here, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus is like a great rose-apple tree a hundred yojanas high, [standing] to its southern direction."
The Dhammasenāpati was like a great tree trunk extending fifty yojanas.
Just as when that great trunk has been cut down, there is no other trunk capable of gradually growing from that point and filling that space with flowers, fruits, and the like;
even so, when the Elders have attained Parinibbāna, there is no other [disciple] who has reached the pinnacle of the sixteen types of wisdom.
There was no monk like Sāriputta capable of sitting on the seat of honor.
It should be understood that because of her disparagement, the Saṅgha of monks became merely a "heap" (khaṇḍha), just like that tree.
Therefore—because it is impossible to obtain [anything] such that "may all that is conditioned not disintegrate," since everything conditioned is subject to dissolution—therefore.

Having walked for alms there, he stayed on the bank of the Ganges upon a sandy beach with sand the color of a silver plate. By him...
It is said: "Not long after Sāriputta and Moggallāna had attained final Nibbāna.
Here too, the Community of Bhikkhus is like a great jambu tree five hundred yojanas in height;
the two Chief Disciples are like two great branches extending fifty yojanas to the south and north of it. The rest is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained.
It should be applied. In the fifth [sutta], "views" refers to the view that one is the owner of one's kamma.

In the sixth [sutta], "the further shore of the realm of death" means Nibbāna, which stands as the far shore of the threefold round of existence.
8. Brahmasutta Commentary 384.

Regarding the eighth [sutta], “or monks in the body”: at that time there were no monks at all; nevertheless, he spoke thus to show that whoever develops the foundations of mindfulness is indeed a monk by virtue of having broken through the defilements. “The one-way path” means the single path.
"One who sees the end of birth": "the destruction" (*khaya*) and the "end" (*anta*) of birth is Nibbāna; the meaning is that he sees it. "He understands the path":

he understands the path known as the "single way," which constitutes the one and only path. The "single-way path" refers to the preliminary path of the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*); the meaning is that he understands that.
9. Commentary on the Sedaka Sutta 385.
Regarding the ninth [sutta]: "In Sumbha" means in a country of that name. "Medakathālikā" is a name given according to the feminine gender.
As for the words "Protect me, and I will protect you," this is his (the teacher's) tenet: the teacher...

If one does not hold the bamboo pole firmly, and does not go in the direction where the pupil goes, and constantly looks toward the tip of the bamboo pole, one is said not to protect the pupil; thus, the unprotected pupil falls and is reduced to powder and dust.
However, by holding the bamboo pole firmly and [following] the direction where he goes...
As he walks, by constantly looking up at the tip of the bamboo pole, he is said to protect it.
However, a pupil who leaps here and there, playing like a deer, is said not to protect his teacher.

For if that were the case, the sharp point of the bamboo pole, having been placed against the teacher’s throat or forehead, would pierce the spot where it stands and pass through. This is because of his perfection in conduct (*ācārasampannatā*).

However, when the bamboo pole bends, one who does not lean toward it—as if pulling it back—keeps it on one side, causes it to take hold of the support of the wind, establishes mindfulness firmly, and sits perfectly still; such a person is said to "protect the teacher.
Regarding the statement, "Teacher, you protect yourself; I shall protect myself," this is the intended meaning: the teacher...
One who holds the bamboo staff well, following the direction in which the pupil has stepped again and again,
and constantly looking at the tip of the staff, protects himself alone, not the pupil. The pupil also,
having made his body one with the staff, having caused it to be supported by the wind, and having established mindfulness firmly, sits motionless, protecting himself alone.
"Protects" means he does not [protect] the teacher.
"That is the method there," as Medakathālikā said; the meaning is that this is the method, this is the means, this is the reason.

"The foundation of mindfulness should be cultivated" means the fourfold foundation of mindfulness should be cultivated. "By way of cultivation" means by way of cultivating the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
“Thus indeed, monks, one who protects oneself protects others.

This refers to a monk who, having abandoned delight in work and the like, cultivates and develops his primary meditation subject while staying in night-quarters or day-quarters, and thereby attains arahantship;
then, seeing him, another thinks: “How excellent is this monk! He is truly practicing rightly,” and fixes his mind upon him.
Having inspired confidence, one becomes destined for heaven. This is what is meant by "protecting oneself while protecting others.
"By patience" means by patience as endurance (*adhivāsana-khanti*). "By non-violence" means by compassion (*karuṇā*) together with its preliminary stage.

"By a mind of loving-kindness" means by loving-kindness (*mettā*) together with its preliminary stage. "By sympathy" means by sympathetic growth; the meaning is by sympathetic joy (*muditā*) together with its preliminary stage.
Regarding the statement, "By protecting another, one protects oneself": here, that bhikkhu who has gone to a night-station or a day-station,
having attained the triple or quadruple jhānas in the three divine abidings (brahmavihāras), takes that jhāna as a basis,
develops insight by contemplating conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra), and reaches Arahantship— this person should be understood as "protecting oneself by protecting another."
10. Commentary on the Janapadakalyāṇīsutta 386.
In the tenth [sutta], "Janapadakalyāṇī" means one who is beautiful and supreme in her country, free from the six defects of the body, and endowed with the five excellences.
For she is neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair; she has transcended [these extremes].
Not having attained the human form, she has attained the divine form; therefore, she is free from the six defects of the body.

Furthermore, because she is endowed with these excellences—the excellence of the skin, the excellence of the flesh, the excellence of the sinews, the excellence of the bones, and the excellence of age—she is said to be "endowed with the five excellences. For her, there is no need for the application of external ointments, as it is by the radiance of her own body alone that she shines.
She creates light in a space of twelve cubits; she is either the color of yellow *piyaṅgu* or the color of gold—this is her excellence of skin.

Furthermore, her four hands and feet, as well as the area ending at her face, are like red coral or red woolen cloth, as if treated with lac-dye—this is her excellence of flesh. Then there are her twenty fingernails.
In the places where it is not separated from the flesh, they are like being filled with lac-dye; in the places where it is separated, they resemble streams of milk.
This is her excellence of sinews. Her thirty-two teeth appear very smooth, like a row of well-polished diamonds;
this is her excellence of bones. Even though she is actually one hundred and twenty years old, she appears as if she were only sixteen years of age.
It becomes hairless; this is its excellence in maturity (*vaya-kalyāṇatā*).
Regarding the term *paramapāsāvinī*: here, *pasava* means "flowing forth," which signifies "occurrence. *Pasāva* itself is *pāsāva*. That which has the highest flow is *paramapāsāva*;
since she possesses that, she is *paramapāsāvinī*. It refers to her supreme occurrence in both dance and song.
It is said that "the best action" means that the most excellent dance is danced, or the song is sung. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
In these two discourses, however, it is only the preliminary insight (pubbabhāga-vipassanā) that is discussed.

394–396. In the eighth [sutta], "possessing great direct knowledge" (*mahābhiññata*) is stated by way of the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). "I directly know a thousand worlds" is stated specifically by way of his constant dwelling (*satatavihāra*).

6. Commentary on the Pātimokkhasaṃvara Sutta.
412. In the sixth [clause], by saying "restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha," he speaks thus while showing that this is the foremost virtue among the four virtues.
However, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga said: "The restraint of the Pātimokkha alone is virtue; there is no scriptural basis for calling the other three 'virtue'.
Having said this, and then conceding his point, he said: "What is called 'restraint of the faculties' is merely the guarding of the six doors."

Purity of livelihood is merely the obtaining of requisites through the Dhamma alone and in a righteous manner, and merely consuming those requisites after reflecting, "These requisites have been obtained for this purpose. In the ultimate sense, virtue is simply restraint according to the Pātimokkha.
One whose [restraint] is broken is like a man with severed head, hands, and feet; how could he protect the rest?

It should not be said [that he is unguarded]. However, for one who is healthy, this person—like a man whose head has been severed—is able to preserve his life by restoring the remaining [faculties] to their natural state.
Therefore, the restraint of the Pātimokkha itself is virtue (*sīla*);
one who is restrained by that restraint of the Pātimokkha is "restrained by the Pātimokkha-restraint" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuta*), meaning he is endowed with it and possessed of it.
"Endowed with proper conduct and resort" means endowed with both conduct (*ācāra*) and resort (*gocara*). "In even the slightest" means in those that are minimal.
"Offenses" (*vajja*) means unwholesome states (*akusaladhamma*). "Seeing danger" means seeing them as fearful. "Having undertaken" means having correctly taken up.
"Train in the rules of training" means, having undertaken each respective rule of training among the rules of training, train in it. Whatever...
Whatever must be trained in among the training rules and sections of training—whether physical or verbal—one should train by correctly undertaking all of that;
this is the summary meaning here. The detailed explanation, however, is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus, in this sutta, only the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is discussed.
7. Commentary on the Duccarita Sutta (413).
In the seventh [sutta], bodily good conduct and verbal good conduct constitute the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha; mental good conduct constitutes the other three virtues.
Thus, the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) has been explained. By this method, [the same applies] to the five, seven, nine, and ten [precepts].
It should be understood that even the final three among the wholesome courses of action constitute virtue (*sīla*). The remainder is self-evident.
The meaning of the sixth and seventh [chapters] is to be understood in the same manner as stated above.
This is the fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Deathless (*Amatavagga*).
The commentary on the Saṃyutta of the Foundations of Mindfulness is finished.
4. The Saṃyutta of the Faculties.
1. The Chapter on the Pure.
1. Commentary on the Suddhika Sutta 471.

In the first [section] of the *Indriyasaṃyutta*, the faculty of faith (*saddhindriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*)—these three—are found in both the wholesome resultant states and the functional states of the four planes. As for the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*) and the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*)...
They are found everywhere—in the wholesome, the unwholesome, the resultant, and the functional of the four planes.
Thus, it should be understood that this sutta is spoken by way of a classification of phenomena that encompasses everything belonging to the four planes.
7. Commentary on the Second Sutta on Ascetics and Brahmins.
477. “They do not understand the faculty of faith” means they do not understand it by way of the truth of suffering.
“They do not understand the arising of the faculty of faith” means they do not understand it by way of the truth of the origin.
Likewise, “cessation” is by way of the truth of cessation, and “the way” is by way of the truth of the path. This same method applies to the remaining [faculties] as well.
In the bright half of the month, however, through the arising of adverting by way of resolution, there is the arising of the faith faculty;

through the arising of adverting by way of exertion, there is the arising of the energy faculty; through the arising of adverting by way of establishment, there is the arising of the mindfulness faculty;
through the arising of adverting by way of non-distraction, there is the arising of the concentration faculty; and through the arising of adverting by way of seeing—
There is the arising of the faculty of wisdom. Likewise, through the arising of adverting by way of desire, there is the arising of the faculty of faith;
through the arising of adverting by way of desire, there is the arising of the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

Through the arising of adverting by way of attention, there is the arising of the faculty of faith; through the arising of adverting by way of attention, there is the arising of the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
The meaning should also be understood as "it exists. In these six suttas in sequence, only the Four Noble Truths have been explained.
8. Commentary on the Daṭṭhabba Sutta (Sutta 478):
"And where, monks, is the faculty of faith to be seen? In the four factors of stream-entry," and so forth.
This was said for the purpose of showing the preeminence of these faculties within their respective domains.

For example, when four sons of wealthy merchants and a king as the fifth among their companions have gone down to the street thinking, "We shall enjoy a festival," at the time when they have entered the house of one of the sons of merchants, the other four sit in silence;
the master of the house alone [provides] for them—“hard food and soft food...”
“Give [us]! Give perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth! he would direct within the house.

When he had gone to the houses of the second, third, and fourth [brothers], the other four sat in silence, while the master of the house alone directed within the house: “Give these [men] hard food and soft food;
give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth. Then, last of all, [he went] to the king’s house.
Just as at other times the king is the master everywhere, but at this time he directs affairs only within his own palace,
saying, "Give these people hard food and soft food; give them perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and so forth," even so, when the faculties—
with faith as the fifth— descend together upon a single object, like friends entering a street together.
Even when these arise, just as in the case of the first man, where the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone deliberates,
so too, having attained the factors of stream-entry, the faculty of faith— characterized by resolution—
is the eldest and the forerunner, while the others follow in its wake. As in the case of the second man, the other four sit in silence...

They sit down, while the master of the house alone deliberates; likewise, having attained the right efforts (*sammappadhāna*), the faculty of energy (*vīriyindriya*)—characterized by exertion—is the chief and the forerunner, while the others follow in its wake.

Just as in the third house the other four sit silently while the master of the house alone deliberates, so too, having attained the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*), that which is characterized by establishing [the mind]...
The faculty of mindfulness alone is the chief and the precursor, while the others follow in its wake.
Just as in the house of the fourth [brother] the other four sit in silence while the master of the house alone deliberates, so too, having attained the jhānas and liberations,
the faculty of concentration— characterized by non-distraction— is the chief and the precursor, while the others follow in its wake.
But when they have all gone last of all to the king’s house, just as the other four sit in silence while the king alone conducts affairs in the house,
even so, having reached the Noble Truths, the faculty of wisdom (paññindriya) alone—
characterized by understanding— is the eldest and the leader, while the remaining faculties follow after it.
9–10. Commentary on the First Vibhaṅga Sutta, etc. (479–480).
Regarding the ninth [sutta], "by mindfulness and circumspection" (*satinepakkena*): here, the state of one who is *nipaka* is *nepakka*;

this is a synonym for wisdom (*paññā*). But why is wisdom mentioned in the context of the vessel of mindfulness? It is for the purpose of showing the strength of mindfulness. It is strong mindfulness...

For it is this [mindfulness] that is intended here. And since that mindfulness is powerful only when associated with wisdom (*paññā*), and not when dissociated from it, he spoke thus while demonstrating mindfulness associated with wisdom.
"Done long ago" refers to a gift, a precept, or an observance of the Uposatha performed at a distant time.
"Spoken long ago" refers to something spoken at a distant time, such as "in such-and-such a place, such-and-such was said. Its object is relinquishment (*vossagga*).
"Having made" means having made it the object of Nibbāna. "Leading to arising and passing away" means going toward both arising and passing away;
the sense is that it is the apprehender of arising and falling away (*udayabbaya*).

In this sutta, the faculties of faith, mindfulness, and wisdom are the preliminary stages; the faculty of energy is mixed; and the faculty of concentration is spoken of as exclusively the supramundane state already produced. In the tenth [sutta] as well...
This is the section on the Dhamma.
The First Chapter: The Pure.
2. The Second Chapter: The Soft-Toned.
1. Commentary on the *Paṭilābha-sutta* 481.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the second chapter, "concerning the right efforts" (*sammappadhāna*) means depending upon the right efforts; the meaning is: "one who is developing the right efforts. The same method applies to the faculty of mindfulness (*satindriya*).
2. Commentary on the First *Saṃkhitta-sutta* (Abbreviated Sutta)
482. In the second [case], "from that" (tato) should be understood as the ablative in the sense of the insight, path, and fruit.
For when the five faculties are fully developed and perfected, they are called the insight-faculties of the path to Arahantship.
"Weaker than those" means that the insight-faculties of the path to Non-returning are weaker than those insight-faculties of the path to Arahantship.
Then there are the faculties of insight for the path of once-returning, which are softer than those; then the faculties of insight for the path of stream-entry, which are softer than those;
then the faculties of insight for the path of the Dhamma-follower, which are softer than those; and then the faculties of insight for the path of the faith-follower, which are softer than those.
Likewise, when the five faculties are fully developed and perfected, they are called the faculties of the path to Arahatship;
those that are weaker than these are called the faculties of the path to Non-returning; those weaker than these are called the faculties of the path to Once-returning;
those weaker than these are called the faculties of the path to Stream-entry; and those weaker than these are the faculties of the path of the Dhamma-follower.
Then, those same faculties become even more subtle and are called the faculties of the path for one who follows by faith (*saddhānusāri-maggindriya*).

When these five faculties are fully developed and perfected, they are called the faculties of the fruit of arhatship (*arahattaphalindriya*). Even more subtle than those are the faculties of the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphalindriya*);

even more subtle than those are the faculties of the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmiphalindriya*); and even more subtle than those are the faculties of the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphalindriya*).
They are so named. However, both the *dhammānusārī* and the *saddhānusārī* are persons standing on the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-maggaṭṭha-puggala*).
