Their distinction arises from the perspective of the person standing on the path; that is, by way of their approach and by way of the path itself.
For the *saddhānusārī* person reaches the path gradually by receiving instruction and asking questions, whereas the *dhammānusārī* does so after one or two hearings.
Thus, first of all, their difference should be understood by way of their arrival.

However, for the follower by dhamma (dhammānusārī), the path is sharp; it carries forth courageous knowledge and cuts away the defilements without volitional effort or much exertion, like a sharp sword-edge cutting through the trunk of a plantain tree. For the follower by faith (saddhānusārī), it is not like that.
The path is sharp, yet it does not carry a keen wisdom; it cuts away the defilements with effort and application, like an extremely sharp sword blade cutting through the trunk of a plantain tree.
However, once the defilements are exhausted, there is no distinction between them, and all remaining defilements are brought to an end.
3. Commentary on the Second Short Discourse (Dutiyasaṃkhittasutta) 483.

In the third [discourse], the ablative case (*tato*) should be understood as expressing the fruit (*phala*). For when the five faculties are fulfilled and complete, they are called the "faculties of the fruit of arahantship" (*arahattaphalindriya*);
and a person endowed with the fruit of arahantship is called an "arahant" (*arahā*).
It exists. The faculties associated with the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) are softer than those of the fruit of arahantship;
the faculties associated with the fruit of once-returning (sakadāgāmiphala) are softer than those; and the faculties associated with the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala) are softer than those.

A person endowed with the fruit of stream-entry is called a "stream-enterer" (sotāpanna). Thus, there is a difference in fruits due to a difference in faculties; that is, by way of the diversity of faculties.
The diversity of fruits; through the diversity of fruits, there is the diversity of persons.
4. Commentary on the Third Abbreviated Discourse (Tatiya-saṃkhitta-sutta). 484.
In the fourth [discourse], "one who fulfills fulfills the full" means one who, by practicing the path to arahantship, brings it to completion.

One attains the fruit of arahantship. "One who practices partially attains a partial [result]" means that one who practices the three remaining partial paths attains only a partial result consisting of the three fruits.
Thus, in these four suttas, the faculties are described as being mixed.
5–7. Commentary on the First Detailed Sutta, etc.
485–487. Regarding the fifth [type of non-returner], the phrase “with faculties weaker than those” should be understood as an ablative of comparison (*nissakka*) in relation to insight (*vipassanā*).

For the five faculties of one on the path to Arahantship are the faculties of insight; the faculties of insight for one who attains Nibbāna in the interval (*antarā-parinibbāyin*) are weaker than those;

the faculties of insight for one who attains Nibbāna upon landing (*upahacca-parinibbāyin*) are weaker than those; and the faculties of insight for one who attains Nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyin*) are weaker than those.

The insight-faculties of one who attains parinibbāna through exertion are more subtle than those, and the insight-faculties of one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm are even more subtle than those.
At this point, however, one should remain precisely on the path to arahantship and extract the five dependencies. Of the path to arahantship...
Indeed, the insight-faculties of one who attains parinibbāna in the interval (antarāparinibbāyin) are the softest;
those of one who attains parinibbāna in the second interval are softer than those; those of one who attains parinibbāna in the third interval are softer than those;

those of one who attains parinibbāna upon landing (upahaccaparinibbāyin) are softer than those; and those of one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha realm (uddhaṃsota-akaniṭṭhagāmī) are softer than those.

The faculties of insight (*vipassanindriyāni*). There are these same five types of persons: those who attain final nibbāna without exertion (*asaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*) and those who attain final nibbāna with exertion (*sasaṅkhāraparinibbāyī*).
Now, there are three degrees of weakness. For the faculties of the stream-entry path (*sotāpattimagga*) are weaker than the faculties of the once-return path (*sakadāgāmimagga*);

the faculties of the follower by Dhamma (*dhammānusāri*) on the stream-entry path itself are weaker than those [of the once-return path]; and those [faculties] are even weaker than those [preceding ones].

The faculties of one who follows by faith and the path-faculty. The sixth and seventh are exactly as described by the method already stated. However, in these three suttas, only the faculties of insight in the preliminary stage are discussed.
8. Commentary on the *Paṭipanna-sutta*.
488. In the eighth [case], "by those even weaker than those" should be understood as an ablative (*nissakka*) in the sense of the path and its fruit. This has already been stated in the text.

"An outsider" (*bāhiro*) means one who stands outside these eight types of persons. "Standing on the side of the worldlings" (*puthujjanapakkhe ṭhito*) means standing within the category of worldlings.
In this sutta, only supramundane faculties (*indriya*) are discussed.
9–10. Commentary on the *Sampanna-sutta* and others (489–490).
In the ninth [sutta], "endowed with the faculties" (*indriya-sampanna*) means having complete faculties. The tenth is self-evident. In these two suttas, mixed faculties are discussed.
This is the second section, the *Mudutara-vagga*.
3. The Chapter on the Six Faculties (Chaḷindriyavagga) 2. Commentary on the Discourse on the Life-faculty (Jīvitindriyasuttavaṇṇanā) 492.

Regarding the second discourse of the third chapter, concerning the terms "female-faculty" (*itthindriya*) and so forth: it is called the female-faculty because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*) over the state of being female (*itthibhāva*).
It exercises lordship over the male state, thus it is the masculinity faculty (*purisindriya*). It exercises lordship over life, thus it is the life faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
This sutta, it is said, arose from a specific occasion. For in the midst of the Saṅgha, a discussion arose: "How many, indeed, are the faculties of the round of existence?
Then the Blessed One, pointing out the faculties of the round of existence, spoke the words beginning with, "Bhikkhus, there are these three... and so forth.
3. Commentary on the Aññindriya Sutta 493.

Regarding the third [sutta], the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) is the faculty that arises at the moment of the stream-entry path for one who has practiced with the resolve: "In this beginningless saṃsāra, I shall know the Dhamma not known before. The faculty of "knowing" (*aññindriya*) refers to those very same [faculties]...

The faculty of one who has known (*aññātāvindriya*) is the faculty arisen in the six states, beginning with the fruit of stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*), by way of the full comprehension of phenomena already known.
It is the faculty arisen in those who have known—the phenomena of the fruit of arhatship (*arahattaphala*).
This is a designation for the very knowledge that has arisen in each respective case by its corresponding mode. This sutta, too, arises from a specific occasion; for, in the midst of the Saṅgha...
The discussion arose: “How many, indeed, are the supramundane faculties? Then the Blessed One, pointing them out, said:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three faculties,” and so forth. 4.
Commentary on the Ekabīji Sutta.

494. Regarding the phrase "weaker than those" in the fourth [case], it should be understood as an ablative of comparison relative to insight (vipassanā). For when the five faculties are fully developed, they are called the "insight-faculties" of the path to Arahantship;
the insight-faculties of one who attains Parinibbāna in the interval (antarā-parinibbāyin) are weaker than those;

the insight-faculties of one who attains Parinibbāna upon landing (upahacca-parinibbāyin) are weaker than those; and the insight-faculties of one who attains Parinibbāna without exertion (asaṅkhāra-parinibbāyin) are weaker than those.
The insight-faculties of one who attains final nibbāna with exertion are more subtle than those, and those of one who goes upstream to the Akaniṭṭha heaven are even more subtle.
Here too, as in the previous method, one should extract five dependent factors while standing on the path to Arahatta.
Just as three dependent factors were extracted while standing on the path to Sakadāgāmi in the previous method, so here five should be extracted.
For the insight-faculties of the once-returner path are weaker than the insight-faculties of the stream-enterer path;
and the insight-faculties of the paths of those such as the "one-seeder" (ekabījī) are weaker than those insight-faculties of the stream-enterer path.
And here, among those such as the "one-seeder," one who has become a stream-enterer and, after producing only one more personal existence, attains arahantship is called a "one-seeder."
This is what is called a "single-seed" person (*ekabījī*). As it is said: "And who is the person who is a single-seed?
Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for enlightenment;
having wandered and transmigrated only once more through a human existence, he makes an end of suffering. This is called a person who is a single-seed."
But he who, having transmigrated through two or three existences, makes an end of suffering, is called a *kolaṅkolo* (one who goes from family to family). As it is said:

"And what kind of person is a *kolaṅkolo*? Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for enlightenment; having wandered through two or three families..."
“Having wandered through existence, he makes an end of suffering. This person is called ‘one who goes from family to family’ (kolaṅkolo).

In this context, “families” (kulāni) should be understood as existences (bhavā). The phrase “two or three” is merely for the sake of the teaching; however, one who wanders through existence up to the sixth birth is indeed a kolaṅkolo.
One for whom there is rebirth at most seven times, and who does not take an eighth existence, is called "one for whom seven births at most remain.
As it is said: "And what kind of person is one for whom seven births at most remain?

Here, a certain person, through the complete destruction of the three fetters, becomes a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and bound for enlightenment; he [will be reborn] seven times..."
“Having wandered and transmigrated among gods and humans, he makes an end of suffering; this person is called ‘one for whom seven births at most remain.
These names were indeed given by the Blessed One according to the status they had attained. For it is said: “One who has reached such a stage is a ‘single-seeder’ (ekabījī).”
The Blessed One has assigned these names, saying: "This one is a kolaṃkola; this one is a sattakkhattuparama.
However, there is no fixed rule such as, "This one is an ekabījī, this one is a kolaṃkola, and this one is a sattakkhattuparama.
But what determines this distinction among them? Some elders say that it is determined by past causes (pubbahetu).
Some say, "the first path," some say, "the three higher paths," and some say, "insight into the three paths.

In that regard, according to the doctrine that "the prior cause determines [the destiny]," it follows that while the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the first path has been established, the three higher paths have arisen without such a decisive support. According to the doctrine that "the first path determines [the destiny],"...
Otherwise, it would follow that the three higher paths are purposeless.
In the assertion that "the three higher paths determine [the result]," one falls into the position that the three higher paths have already arisen even before the first path has arisen.
However, the claim that "insight determines the three paths" is logical; for if the insight regarding the three higher paths is powerful, [it leads to their attainment].

One is called an "ekabījī" (one-seeded); one who is slower than that is a "kolaṃkola" (one who goes from family to family); and one who is slower than that is a "sattakkhattuparama" (one who has seven births at most).

For a certain stream-enterer may have an inclination toward the round of existence, delight in the round, and wander and reappear within the round again and again—such as the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, the female lay follower Visākhā, or the divine sons Cūḷaratha and Mahāratha.

The deva-son Anekavaṇṇa, Sakka the king of the gods, and the deva-son Nāgadatta—these individuals, whose inclinations were toward the round of existence and who delighted in the round, will, after purifying the six heavenly worlds from the beginning and remaining in Akaniṭṭha, attain final nibbāna;
they are not included here. Nor are these alone; even he who, having transmigrated only seven times among human beings, will attain arahantship...
One who attains [Arahantship] after being reborn in the world of the devas and wandering from one state to another among the devas for seven times is not included here either.
However, only one who attains Arahantship after wandering sometimes among devas and sometimes among humans is included here.

Therefore, the term "one for whom there are seven births at most" (sattakkhattuparama) refers here to the dry-insight practitioner (sukkhavipassaka) who is an "eight-times-at-most" person (aṭṭhakavokiṇṇa).
It should be understood that this is the name [of the path].

Regarding the terms "follower by dhamma" (dhammānusārī) and "follower by faith" (saddhānusārī), in this dispensation there are two duties, two heads, and two points of application for one who is producing supramundane dhamma: the duty of faith (saddhādhura) and the duty of wisdom (paññādhura); the head of faith (saddhāsīsa) and...
The fifty heads are: inclination toward faith (*saddhābhinivesa*) and inclination toward wisdom (*paññābhinivesa*).

In this regard, if a bhikkhu, thinking, "If it is possible to realize through faith, I shall realize the supramundane path," makes faith his primary burden and realizes the path of stream-entry (*sotāpattimagga*), he is called a "follower by faith" (*saddhānusārī*) at the moment of the path.
However, at the moment of the fruit, he is one "liberated by faith" (*saddhāvimutta*).

Having become [stream-enterers], they are of three kinds: the single-seed, the clan-to-clan, and the seven-times-at-most. Each of these attains a fourfold state by way of the difficult path and so forth;
thus, there are twelve persons based on those whose dominant faculty is faith (*saddhādhura*).
However, as for one who thinks, "If it is possible to produce [the fruit] through wisdom (*paññā*), I shall produce the supramundane path," [that person is one whose dominant faculty is wisdom].
Making the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga) his burden, he brings it forth; at the moment of the path, he is called a "follower by Dhamma" (dhammānusārī).
At the moment of the fruit (phala), however, having become one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta), he becomes twelvefold through the divisions such as the "one-seeder" (ekabījī) and so forth.
Thus, including the two who stand on the path, there are twenty-four types of stream-enterers at the moment of the fruit.
It is said that the Elder Tipiṭaka Tissa went to the opposite shore, thinking, "I shall purify the Three Piṭakas.
A certain householder attended upon him with the four requisites. When it was time for the elder to depart, he said, "I am going, lay follower.
"Where, venerable sir? "To the presence of our teachers and preceptors. "It is not possible for me to go, venerable sir; [please take me] to the Blessed One."
"But by relying on you, I have come to know the virtues of the Dispensation; in your absence, what kind of bhikkhu should I approach?

Then the Elder said to him: "A bhikkhu who, having pointed out twenty-four stream-enterers, twelve once-returners, forty-eight non-returners, and twelve arahants, is able to deliver a discourse on the Dhamma—such a bhikkhu [should one approach]."
"It is fitting to attend [to him]. In this sutta, insight (vipassanā) is discussed.
5–10. Commentary on the Suddhaka Sutta and others, 495–500.
In the fifth [sutta], "the eye" refers to that which is the dominant influence (ādhipateyya) over the phenomena produced at the eye-door.

It is the "faculty of the eye" (*cakkhundriya*) because it is a faculty in the sense of being a lord (*inda*). The same method applies to the faculty of the ear and the others. The rest is clear everywhere.
In this chapter, six suttas—the first one and the fifth through the ninth—are explained by way of the Four Noble Truths.
This is the third chapter, the Chapter on the Six Faculties.
4. The Chapter on the Faculty of Pleasure (Sukhindriyavagga) 1–5. Commentary on the Pure Discourses, etc. (Suddhikasuttādivaṇṇanā) 501–505.
In the first discourse of the fourth chapter, "pleasure" (sukhaṃ) is [the faculty] by virtue of its sovereignty over its co-nascent states.

It is called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhindriya*) because it exercises lordship (*indaṭṭha*). The same method applies to the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*) and the others. Herein, the faculties of pleasure, pain, and grief belong exclusively to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*);

the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*), excluding that which belongs to the formless sphere (*arūpāvacara*), pertains to the remaining three planes; and the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*) pertains to all four planes.
The second and subsequent [faculties] are explained solely by way of the Four Noble Truths.
6. Commentary on the First Vibhaṅga Sutta 506.
In the sixth [sutta], "bodily" (*kāyika*) means having the physical sensitivity (*kāyapasāda*) as its basis. "Pleasure" (*sukha*) is the description of its essential nature.
"Sweet" (*sāta*) is a synonym for that very same thing; it is what is meant by "pleasant. "Born of body-contact" (*kāyasamphassaja*) means arisen from body-contact.

"Blissful" (*sukha*) and "pleasant" (*sāta*) are to be understood according to the method already stated. "To be felt" (*vedayita*) is a description of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), distinguished from other phenomena and common to all feelings (*vedanā*).
The meaning should be understood in the same way for the remaining [feelings] as well. Regarding the phrase "whether bodily or mental":
here, it is called "bodily" (*kāyika*) by virtue of its arising based upon the four sensitive bodies (*pasādakāya*), such as the eye and so forth, which serve as its physical basis (*vatthu*).
Furthermore, there is no such thing as "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" feeling that has the physical sensitivity (*kāyapasāda*) as its basis.
9. Commentary on the *Kaṭṭhopama-sutta* (The Simile of the Fire-drill), §509:
Regarding the phrase "of two pieces of wood": it refers to two fire-drills (*araṇī*). "By friction and conjunction" means by means of rubbing together.
And by their combination. "Heat" (*usmā*) is the appearance of warmth; "fire" (*tejo*) is the smoke of a flame.

Herein, the base and the object should be regarded as the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇī*), contact as the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇī*), the friction of contact as the rubbing together, and feeling (*vedanā*) as the fire.
Alternatively, the base and the object should be regarded as the upper fire-drill, and contact as the lower fire-drill.
10. Commentary on the Uppaṭipāṭika Sutta (The Out-of-Order Discourse) 510.

The tenth [discourse], although stated in its proper sequence according to the flavor of the Dhamma, should be understood as the "Uppaṭipāṭika Sutta" because, unlike the remaining suttas in this *Indriyavibhaṅga*, it was not taught [in that specific order].
In that context, all the terms beginning with "the sign" (*nimitta*)...
These are indeed synonyms for conditions. "And he understands the faculty of pain" means he understands it precisely by way of the truth of suffering.

"The origin of the faculty of pain": when one is pierced by a thorn, bitten by a snake, or touched by a fold in a rug, a body-consciousness accompanied by pain arises; he understands that this is its origin.
In the passages beginning with "the faculty of mental grief arises from another," the arising of those [faculties] should likewise be understood by way of their respective causes.

For instance, since the faculty of mental grief arises through the destruction of conditioned things such as the bowl and robes, or through the destruction of beings such as co-residents, one understands that their destruction is its arising. Having eaten fine food on an excellent bed...
When one is lying down, the faculty of pleasure arises through contact with the massaging of the hands and feet, the breeze from a fan, and so forth; he understands that contact to be its origin.
Furthermore, the faculty of mental joy arises by way of obtaining the seven kinds of agreeable formations mentioned above; he understands that obtaining to be its origin.
Furthermore, the faculty of equanimity arises in the mode of neutrality; he understands that its origin is the mode of neutrality toward the seven formations.
And where does the arisen faculty of suffering cease without remainder? Here, monks, a monk, quite secluded...
Regarding the passage beginning with "by sensual pleasures" (*kāmehi*), this is the explanation of the analysis taken as a single unit:

the faculty of pain (*dukkhindriya*) ceases and is abandoned precisely at the moment of the access concentration (*upacārakkhaṇa*) of the first jhāna; the [faculties of] grief (*domanassa*) and so forth cease in the second jhāna and those that follow.

Even though this is so, because these [faculties] are suppressed to an extreme degree in those [higher jhānas], their cessation is stated to occur specifically in the jhānas. For it is an extreme suppression [that is meant].
For them, in the first jhāna and so forth, it is not cessation alone; rather, it is cessation alone at the moment of access (upacāra), but not an intense cessation.

For instance, in the access to the first jhāna during the process of diverse attention (nānāvajjana), even though the faculty of pain has ceased, its arising may still occur through contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, and the like, or through the affliction of an uneven seat;
however, this is not the case within absorption (appanā). Or, even if this [faculty] has ceased in access, [it may still arise].

It is not well-ceased because it has not been struck down by its opposite. However, within the access concentration (antopappanā), the entire body becomes suffused with happiness through the pervasion of joy;
and for one whose body is thus suffused with happiness, the faculty of pain is well-ceased because it has been struck down by its opposite.
And even during the various acts of adverting in the access to the second jhāna, the faculty of mental grief—which was already abandoned [in the first jhāna]—[is likewise well-ceased].
Because this arises even when there are conditions for applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), provided that bodily fatigue and mental affliction are present;
yet it does not arise at all in the absence of applied and sustained thought. Furthermore, wherever it does arise, it is only where applied and sustained thought are present.

And since applied and sustained thought have not been abandoned in the access concentration (*upacāra*) of the second jhāna, its arising might occur there; but it certainly does not occur in the second jhāna itself.

Because its condition has been abandoned. Likewise, in the access to the third jhāna, there might arise the arising of the pleasure faculty (*sukhindriya*) even though it has been abandoned, because the body is touched by the refined matter produced by joy (*pīti*);
however, this is not the case in the actual third jhāna itself. For in the third jhāna, the joy that serves as the condition for pleasure has ceased entirely.

Similarly, in the access to the fourth jhāna, although the faculty of mental joy (*somanassindriya*) has been abandoned, because it is still proximate, [the faculty of equanimity] does not reach absorption.
And because it has not correctly transcended [the lower stages] due to the absence of equanimity (*upekkhā*), its arising might occur; however, this is not the case in the fourth jhāna.
Therefore, the phrase "the arisen faculty of pain ceases there without remainder" is employed with the inclusion of the term "without remainder" in various places.
As for what was said here, "he directs his mind toward that end," it refers to one who, being still unattained [to that state], does so for the purpose of producing it.
"He applies his mind" means that, being already a possessor [of the attainment], he does so for the purpose of entering it; this is how the meaning should be understood.
In both of these suttas, only the section on comprehension (sammasanavāra) is discussed.
This concludes the fourth chapter, the Section on the Faculty of Pleasure.
5. The Chapter on Aging (Jarāvagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Nature of Aging (Jarādhammasuttavaṇṇanā) 511.
In the first [discourse] of the fifth chapter, "behind" (*pacchāta*) refers to the eastern direction being shaded by the shadow of the palace.
The meaning is that there was sunlight in the western part of the palace, and he was seated upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in that place.

Regarding the phrase "warming his back": because even for the body of a Perfectly Enlightened One, which is subject to physical conditions, it becomes warm in the heat and cold in the cold—and since this was a season of snowfall and cold—he took off his great outer robe (*mahācīvara*) and [exposed himself].
He sat down, warming his back with the rays of the sun.
But can the rays of the sun enter within after crushing the rays of the Buddha? No, they cannot.
If that is so, what is it that warms him? It is the power of the rays. For just as at midday, when the sun stands overhead, there is a circular shadow—
Although the rays of the sun do not touch the body of one sitting at the foot of a tree,
yet fire radiates in all directions, so that he appears as if surrounded by flames;
even when the rays of the Buddha cannot enter after being crushed by the rays of the sun, it should be understood that the Teacher remains seated, emitting such fiery heat.

“Anomajjanto” means stroking by way of performing a back-massage. “It is wonderful, venerable sir!”—the Elder, having seen a wrinkle-curve the size of a hair-tip like a golden ring between the two shoulder-blades of the Blessed One as he sat with his great robe drawn down from his back, thought:
“Even in such a body as this, old age is made manifest.”
Having become deeply moved and censuring old age, he spoke thus. This is indeed called "the wonder of censure. He spoke thus while demonstrating:
"Venerable Sir, it is not now as the Blessed One’s natural skin-color was once pure;
it is not so at present. For in the Tathāgata’s youth, [his body] was struck by hundreds of spears...
The body becomes like the hide of a bull with its folds worn away; when the hand is placed upon it, it slips away and does not remain steady, as if it were the residue of oil being wiped off.
But in old age, the network of veins withers, the joints and bones become flaccid, and the flesh, detaching from the bone and becoming slack, hangs down here and there.
But for Buddhas, such a thing does not occur. While it is unknown to others, it becomes known specifically to the Elder Ānanda because of his close proximity [to the Buddha];
therefore, he spoke thus.
As for the phrase "the limbs became flaccid": in the case of others, folds of skin form in various places, such as on the face and between the shoulders.
But this does not apply to the Teacher; rather, the Elder, seeing the circle of wrinkles between the two shoulder-blades, spoke thus.
When he said, "All [wrinkles] have arisen as folds," he spoke thus by way of what was evident to himself—for the Teacher has no wrinkles at all, unlike others.
And his body is "arched forward" because the Teacher’s body is straight like that of Brahmā, like a golden archway erected in a city of the gods.
The body of a youth rises perfectly straight. However, in old age, the body becomes bent forward;
this is not apparent to others, but because he was an attendant, it was evident to the Elder alone, and therefore he spoke thus.
And it is said, "the alteration of the faculties is seen," for the so-called "faculties" (indriyāni) are not cognizable by the eye. Since, however, by nature...

"The complexion of the skin was once pure, but now it is no longer so pure; a fold of skin is visible between the shoulders, and the body, which was once straight as a Brahma-staff, is now bent forward.
For this very reason, there must be a transformation in the sense faculties such as the eyes," he said thus by way of inference.
"Fie on that wretched old age! Fie on you, O vile old age! means: "May that [old age] be upon you, O contemptible old age!"
"May reproach touch him. *Bimba* refers to the personal existence (*attabhāva*).
2. Commentary on the Uṇṇābha Brāhmaṇa Sutta, §512.
In the second [verse], "the range of the field of activity" means the object that has become the field of activity. "Of one another" means of the eye and the ear.
Or the ear [does not experience] the eye's [object]; thus, each does not experience the range and domain of the other.
For if one were to collect various forms as objects—such as blue and so forth—and present them to the ear-faculty, saying: "Come now, you must determine and discern this:
what is this object?", even without the eye-consciousness, by its own inherent nature...

One might say this: "Hey, blind fool! Even if you were to run about for a hundred years, a thousand years, or even a hundred thousand years, where else could you find anyone who knows this except me? Bring it here and place it before my sight;
I myself shall know this object—whether it be blue or yellow. For this [eye]..."

"It is the domain of another; this is my domain alone. This same method applies to the other doors as well. Thus, these do not experience one another's range of activity; this is what is meant by "they do not experience.
"What is their resort?"—he asks this question meaning: "What is their resort? To what do they resort? [The answer is] the mind (*mano*).
"Refuge" means that the impulsion-consciousness (javana-manas) is the refuge.
"Mind is their resort" means that the impulsion-consciousness belonging to the mind-door experiences their objective sphere by way of lust and so forth.
For visual consciousness is merely the seeing of forms; herein there is no lust, hatred, or delusion. However, at one door, the impulsion-consciousness does indeed lust.
It becomes defiled or deluded. The same method applies to ear-consciousness and the others as well.

Herein, this is the simile: it is said that five weak tax-collectors, having served the king, obtained a meager income with great difficulty and hardship in a village belonging to a group of five families. There, their share was a portion of fish, a portion of meat, and four kahāpaṇas.
Whether it be a *vāyottaka* coin, a *māsaka* coin, an eight-coin piece, a sixteen-coin piece, or a sixty-four-coin piece,
the punishment reaches only that much; as for the great tribute consisting of a hundred items,
five hundred items, or a thousand items, only the king receives it.

In this context, the fivefold groups of people should be seen as analogous to the five types of serene confidence (pasāda); the five weak governors to the five types of sensory consciousness (viññāṇa);

and the king to the impulsion (javana). Just as the weak governors obtain only a small portion of the body [of revenue], so too the visual consciousness and the others perform merely the seeing of forms and so forth;
however, there is no passion or the like within them. The king’s seizing of the great army is analogous to those [subsequent processes] within them.
At the doors, attachment and so forth are to be understood as belonging to the impulsion consciousness. Thus, here "mind" refers to wholesome and unwholesome impulsion.
"Mindfulness is the resort" means that path-mindfulness is the resort; for the impulsive mind resorts to path-mindfulness. "Liberation" refers to fruition-liberation.
"Resort" means that Nibbāna is the resort of fruition-liberation, for it is to that which she resorts.
"He was unable to grasp the limit of the question" means he was unable to grasp its boundary or measure;
he asked about a state that is "without a refuge" as being "with a refuge. This very *nibbāna* is without a refuge;
it does not resort to anything. "Plunged into *nibbāna*" means immersed within *nibbāna*, having entered into *nibbāna*. "The holy life" (*brahmacariya*)...
The holy life of the path (*maggabrahmacariya*). "Having Nibbāna as its final goal" (*nibbānaparāyaṇa*) means that Nibbāna is its supreme destination (*para ayanam*), its ultimate resort;
the meaning is that it does not go beyond that. "Having Nibbāna as its consummation" (*nibbānapariyosāna*) means that Nibbāna is its conclusion and its end.
"Rooted and established" refers to faith that has arrived by way of the path. "If, monks, on this occasion... (*imamhi ce, bhikkhave, samaye*)... [text continues]
With what intention did he say this? With the intention that he was a non-returner through meditative absorption (*jhāna-anāgāmita*).
For at that time, five unwholesome states of mind had been abandoned by the Brahmin through the first path, and the five hindrances had been abandoned through the first absorption;

thus, he stood in the position of a non-returner by way of absorption. If, without falling away from that absorption, he were to pass away, he would attain final nibbāna right there. However, if while instructing his wife and children...
While one is occupied with worldly affairs, meditative absorption (*jhāna*) is lost; when absorption is lost, one’s destination is unfixed, but when it is not lost, it is fixed.
It was said thus with reference to this non-attainment of absorption.
3. Commentary on the Sāketa Sutta.
513. In the third [verse], "in the Añjana Grove" means in a grove planted with trees whose flowers have the color of añjana.

"That which, monks, is the faculty of faith (saddhindriya), that is the power of faith (saddhābala)": for that is the faculty of faith in the sense of being a lord (*inda*) regarding the characteristic of resolution (*adhimokkha*);

it is the power of faith by virtue of its unshakability by lack of faith (*assaddhiya*). For the others, it is so in the sense of their respective characteristics of exertion (*paggaha*), establishment (*upaṭṭhāna*), non-distraction (*avikkhepa*), and understanding (*pajānana*).

The state of being a faculty (*indriya*) should be understood in the sense of sovereignty (*indaṭṭha*), and the state of being a power (*bala*) in the sense of unshakability regarding sloth, negligence, agitation, and ignorance.

"In this very way" means that just as there is a single stream in that river, so too the lack of difference between these [faculties] should be understood by way of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom;
whereas by way of the faculties and powers, they are like two streams in the senses of sovereignty and unshakability.
The distinction should be understood. 4.
Commentary on the Pubbakoṭṭhaka Sutta. 514.

In the fourth [discourse], "immersed in the Deathless" means within the Deathless; "having the Deathless as its goal" means producing the Deathless; "having the Deathless as its consummation" means culminating in the Deathless. "Excellent, excellent!"—thus he gives his approval, praising the Elder’s exposition.
5. Commentary on the First Pubbarāma Sutta 515.

In the fifth [sutta], *tadanvayā* means following that, or conforming to it. Starting with the Pubbakoṭṭhaka [Sutta] and proceeding in sequence through the six suttas, only the fruits and the faculties are discussed.
10. Commentary on the Āpaṇa Sutta.
520. "These, indeed, are those states": this refers to the three paths together with insight (vipassanā) mentioned above.
"Those which were previously heard by me" refers to those states which were previously heard by me from those who were saying, "There is such a thing as the faculty of the fruit of arahantship.
"And having touched them with the body" means having touched and attained them with the mental body (nāmakāya). And with wisdom...
"I see having pierced through" means that I see by means of the wisdom of reflective review after having pierced through. "That which, venerable sir, is faith"—of what kind is this faith?
The faith associated with the four faculties was already mentioned above;
however, this is the faith of reflective review. For the faith associated [with the faculties] is mixed, whereas the faith of reflective review is purely mundane.
The remainder is clear in all respects.
The fifth chapter, on Aging, is concluded.
6. The Chapter on the Boar’s Cave.
1. Commentary on the Sāla Sutta 521.
In the first [sutta] of the sixth chapter, "by heroism" means by way of heroic nature. "For awakening" means for the purpose of awakening.
2. Commentary on the Mallikā Sutta.

522. "In the second [sutta], 'Among the Mallas' refers to a country of that name. In this discourse, the four faculties (*indriya*) are mixed; the noble knowledge (*ariya-ñāṇa*) is supramundane (*lokuttara*). Nevertheless, it is appropriate to classify it as 'mixed' by considering it to be dependent upon those four faculties.
3. Commentary on the *Sekha-sutta* (523).
"In the third [sutta], 'he does not dwell having touched with the body' means he does not touch or attain it with the mental body (*nāma-kāya*)."

He dwells [therein], yet he is not able to touch or attain it. And when it is said, "he sees by piercing through with wisdom," this means that by means of the wisdom of reflection (*paccavekkhaṇa-paññā*), he understands:
"Above this, there exists what is called the faculty of the fruit of Arahatship.
"Having touched and dwelt in the stage of the Asekhas" means having attained and dwelling therein. "By wisdom" refers to the wisdom of reflection: "the faculty of the fruit of Arahatship..."
He understands: "There is no name. "Nowhere, in anything whatsoever" (*na kuhiñci kismiñci*)—these two terms are indeed synonyms for one another;

the meaning is that they will not arise in any state of existence whatsoever. In this sutta, the five faculties are described as supramundane (*lokuttara*), while the six [faculties] are mundane (*lokiya*) and dependent upon the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭanissita*).
4–5. Commentary on the *Padasutta*, etc. (Suttas 524–525).
In the fourth [sutta], the phrase "whatever words lead to enlightenment" refers to whatever Dharma-verses, whatever constituent parts of the Dharma, lead to the purpose of awakening.
The fifth is self-evident. 6–7. Commentary on the *Paṭiṭṭhitasutta*, etc.
526–527. In the sixth [jhāna], one "guards the mind regarding the taints and the phenomena associated with taints":

this means that by warding off the arising of taints with respect to the phenomena of the three planes, one is said to guard the mind regarding both the taints and the phenomena associated with taints.
The seventh is self-evident.
8. Commentary on the Sūkarakhatasutta 528.
Regarding the eighth [sutta], "at Sūkarakhata": this refers to the Sūkarakhata cave.
It is said that during the time of the Buddha Kassapa, that cave was submerged beneath the earth as the ground rose up during one interval between Buddhas. Then, one day, a certain boar...
He dug up some earth near the edge of the roof-covering. When it rained, the earth was washed away and the edge of the roof became visible.
A forest-dweller, seeing this, thought, "This must have been a place used by those possessed of virtue;
I shall restore it. He cleared the earth from all sides, cleaned out the cave, and constructed a fence around the hut.

Having provided doors and windows, having completed the work of plastering and painting, and having made a courtyard strewn with sand resembling silver plates, he arranged beds and seats and gave them to the Blessed One for his residence;
the cave was deep, such that one had to descend to enter and ascend to leave. It is with reference to this that it was said: "The supreme act of service."
The neuter form *bhāvana* [is used here]; what is meant is that he proceeds by being one who performs the highest act of homage.
"The unsurpassed security from bondage" refers to Arahantship. "Possessing a protector" means having a superior. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
This is the sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Boar’s Cave.
7. The Chapter on the Factors of Enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiyavagga) 531–650.
In the seventh chapter, there are seven fruits; the first two fruits are mixed with the preceding ones. All that follows this is entirely clear.
The commentary on the Connected Discourses on the Faculties (Indriyasaṃyutta) is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Sammappadhāna-saṃyutta* (Connected Discourses on the Right Strivings) 651–704.
In this entire *Sammappadhāna-saṃyutta*, only the preliminary stage of insight (*pubbabhāga-vipassanā*) is discussed.
The commentary on the *Sammappadhāna-saṃyutta* is finished.
6. Commentary on the *Balasaṃyutta* (Connected Discourses on Powers), §§ 705–812.
In the *Balasaṃyutta*, the powers are explained as being mixed together. The rest is entirely clear in every respect.
The commentary on the *Balasaṃyutta* is finished.
7. Saṃyutta Nikāya: The Book of Bases (Iddhipādasaṃyutta) 1.
Chapter on Cāpāla (Cāpālavagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Far Shore (Apārasuttavaṇṇanā)
813. In the first discourse of the *Iddhipādasaṃyutta*, concentration that proceeds by depending on desire is "concentration due to desire" (*chandasamādhi*).
The volitional formations that constitute the exertion are "exertion-formations" (*padhānasaṅkhārā*). "Endowed with" means possessed of those factors.

It is called a "basis of success" (*iddhipāda*) because it is a foot for success, or because it is itself become success and is a foot; the same method applies to the others as well. This is the summary here.
The detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*. Its meaning is elucidated in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Likewise, it constitutes a single chapter in the *Maggasaṃyutta*, the *Bojjhaṅgasaṃyutta*, the *Satipaṭṭhānasaṃyutta*, and here as well.
5. Commentary on the *Iddhipadesasutta*.
817. In the fifth [sutta], "a portion of psychic power" (*iddhipadesa*) refers to the three paths and the three fruits.
6. Commentary on the *Samatta-sutta*: 818.

In the sixth, "complete psychic power" (*samatta-iddhi*) refers specifically to the fruit of arhatship (*arahattaphala*). However, from the beginning throughout all nine suttas, it is the bases of psychic power (*iddhipāda*) that serve as the foundation for turning away (*vivaṭṭapādaka*) which are explained.
10. Commentary on the Cetiya Sutta 822.
In the tenth [sutta], "seating" (nisīdana) refers to a piece of leather. "Udena Shrine" (Udena-cetiyam) refers to the monastery built at the site of the shrine of the yakkha Udena.
The same method applies to the Gotamaka and others as well. "Developed" (bhāvitā) means increased. "Cultivated" (bahulīkatā) means...

"Repeatedly performed" means done again and again. "Made into a vehicle" means made like a vehicle that has been harnessed. "Made into a foundation" means made like a foundation in the sense of being a support.
"Established" means resolved upon. "Cultivated" means heaped up on all sides, well-increased. "Well undertaken" means properly commenced.
Having thus spoken without specific restriction, [the Buddha] spoke the passage beginning with "Of the Tathāgata... in order to show it again by way of restriction. And here—
They endure for a *kappa*; that is, they may remain filling to completion whatever lifespan humans have at any given time.
Or "for the remainder of a *kappa*" means more than the hundred years mentioned as "a little more.
However, the Elder Mahāsīva said: "There is no such thing as thundering in a place where Buddhas do not abide. For just as in the village of Veḷuva..."

He suppressed the death-threshold sensation that had arisen for ten months; likewise, by repeatedly entering that attainment and suppressing it for ten or ten months each time, he could have remained for this very auspicious aeon (*bhaddakappa*). Why, then, did he not remain?
Because a body subject to grasping (*upādiṇṇaka*) is overcome by decrepitude and the like; [but] the Buddhas...
Without having fallen into a state of brokenness and the like, they attain final nibbāna while still in their fifth decade of life, at a time when they are still dear and pleasing to many people.

When the Buddhas, the Buddhas’ followers, and the great disciples have attained final nibbāna, one must remain like a solitary stump or surrounded by young novices; therefore, [one thinks]: "Oh, the assembly of the Buddhas!"
He would incur contempt; therefore, he is not "established. Even though this was said, it is not accepted;
rather, in the Aṭṭhakathā, only this [term] "for the duration of his life" (āyukappo) has been fixed.
Just as in the phrase "whose mind was obsessed by Māra," the word *tanti* is merely a particle (*nipātamattaṃ*). Just as [in the phrase]: "whose mind was obsessed by Māra."
The meaning is that just as no other ordinary person (*puthujjana*) whose mind is overwhelmed could penetrate [the truth], even so he was unable to penetrate it.
For Māra obsesses the mind of one in whom all twelve distortions (*vipallāsa*) have not been entirely abandoned;
and since four distortions had not yet been abandoned by the Elder, Māra therefore [obsessed] his mind.
It obsesses. But what does it do when it causes the mind to be obsessed? It displays a terrifying visible object or makes a terrifying sound audible;
then, upon seeing or hearing it, beings lose their mindfulness and their mouths go agape.
Inserting its hand into their mouths, it crushes their hearts; they become unconscious.
They stood there. But would this [being] be able to thrust his hand into the Elder’s mouth? He displayed a terrifying object;
having seen it, the Elder did not penetrate the radiance of the sign (*nimittobhāsa*). Knowing [the answer] already, for what purpose did the Blessed One address him up to three times?
Later, when [the Elder] requested, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One stay," [the Buddha replied], "This belongs to you alone."
“It is a transgression; this is your own fault,” he said, in order to alleviate his grief by attributing the blame to him.
Regarding the term *Māra pāpimā*: here, he is called *Māra* because he kills (*māreti*) beings by leading them toward what is harmful. *Pāpimā* is a synonym for that same being;
for he is called “Evil One” (*pāpimā*) because he is possessed of evil qualities (*pāpadhamma*). He is also called *Kaṇha*, *Antaka*, *Namuci*, and *Pamattabandhu*.

These are its names. As for the words "But this has been spoken": on the eighth day after the Blessed One’s attainment of enlightenment, he returned to the very seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and said, "Blessed One, that purpose for which you fulfilled the perfections (pāramitā) has now been reached;
omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) has been penetrated; what is the use of wandering through the world?"—just as he did today.
In this very way, he entreated him, saying: "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna; let the Sugata attain final Nibbāna.
The Blessed One rejected it, saying to him, "Not yet," and so forth. Referring to that, he said: "But this was spoken, venerable sir," and so on.
In that context, "learned" (*viyatta*) means proficient through the Path. Likewise "disciplined" (*vinīta*). Likewise "confident" (*visārada*). "Of much learning" (*bahussuta*)—
They are "learned" (*bahussuta*) because they have heard much by way of the Three Piṭakas. They are "bearers of the Dhamma" (*dhammadhara*) because they retain that very same Dhamma.
Alternatively, they are both learned in the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and learned through realization (*paṭivedha*);

they are called "bearers of the Dhamma" because they retain the Dhamma of both the scriptures and realization—thus should the meaning be understood here. They are "practicing in accordance with the Dhamma" (*dhammānudhammapaṭipanna*) [of the noble Dhamma].

They have practiced the Dhamma of insight (vipassanā), which is in accordance with the Dhamma (*anudhamma*). "Practicing in conformity" (*sāmīcippaṭipanna*) means practicing the appropriate way of practice.
"Followers of the Dhamma" (*anudhammacārino*) means those whose nature is to live according to the Dhamma. "Their own teacher’s doctrine" (*sakaṃ ācariyakaṃ*) refers to their own teacher’s teaching.

All the terms beginning with "they will declare" (*ācikkhissanti*) are synonyms for one another. "By means of the Dhamma" (*sahadhammena*) means by means of that which is accompanied by a reason (*sahetuka*).
"With reasoned speech" means with words that possess a logical basis. "With a demonstration of power" means they will teach the Dhamma in such a way that it leads to liberation.
"The holy life" refers to the entire holy life of the Dispensation, comprised within the three trainings.

"Prosperous" means flourishing by way of the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*). "Thriving" means having reached growth by way of the attainment of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), like a tree in full bloom.

"Extensive" (*vitthārika*) means spread out, by way of being established in various directions and regions. "Widely known" (*bāhujañña*) means known or penetrated by many, through the realization of the great masses of people.
"Become widespread" (*puthubhūta*) means having attained a state of broadness in every respect. How so?
Because it has been well-proclaimed as far as the gods and humans; that is, among all those of a discerning nature, whether gods or humans.
It exists; the meaning is that it has been perfectly proclaimed by all.

"Free from concern" means being without attachment. For you, O Evil One, from the eighth week onwards, have wandered about crying out, "Venerable Sir, let the Blessed One now attain final Nibbāna; let the Sugata now attain final Nibbāna," but from this day forward, you are devoid of hope.
"Wait! Do not exert yourself for the sake of my final Nibbāna," he said.

"Mindful and clearly comprehending, he relinquished the life-force (āyusaṅkhāra)" means that, having established mindfulness well and delimited it with wisdom, he released and abandoned the life-force.
In this regard, the Blessed One did not relinquish the life-force as one might throw a clod of earth with his hand.
He relinquished [the attainment]; however, having entered the attainment of fruition for only three months, he gave rise to the thought, "Henceforth, I shall not enter it again.
It is with reference to this that it is said, "he relinquished" (*ossaji*). There is also a reading, "he released" (*ussajī*).
A "great earthquake" (*mahābhūmicālo*) is a massive shaking of the earth. At that time, it is said, the ten-thousandfold world-system trembled. "Terrifying" (*bhiṃsanako*) means producing fear.
"And the divine drums resounded" means the celestial drums resounded; the sky thundered with a dry roar; lightning flashed out of season;
and a momentary rain fell—this is what is meant.
"He uttered an inspired utterance": why did he utter it? Someone might say: "The Blessed One was following closely behind [the monk]..."
“‘Enter final Nibbāna, venerable sir! Enter final Nibbāna, venerable sir!’—thus, tormented by fear, he relinquished the life-formations.

[The Buddha said this] so that there would be no opportunity for him. For one who is terrified, there can be no utterance of an inspired exclamation (*udāna*); rather, he uttered it as it burst forth through the force of rapture.
In this context, *tula* means that which is weighed and delimited because it is directly perceived by all, including even dogs, jackals, and the like.
What is that? It is sense-sphere karma (*kāmāvacara-kamma*). It is "incomparable" (*atula*) because there is no other mundane karma that is its equal or comparable;

thus it is incomparable. What is that? It is sublime karma (*mahaggata-kamma*). Alternatively, sense-sphere and fine-material-sphere karma are comparable, while immaterial-sphere karma is incomparable.
Karma with little ripening is comparable; karma with much ripening is incomparable. It is "origination" (*sambhava*) because it is the cause of origination, the maker of the mass.
"Delighting" means finding pleasure. "Formations of existence" (*bhava-saṅkhāra*) refers to the volitional formations for renewed existence.

"Relinquished" means he let go. "The Sage" (*muni*) refers to the Buddha, the Sage. "Delighting in the internal" means delighting in what is truly one's own internal state. "Concentrated" means concentrated by way of access and absorption concentration.
"He shattered like armor" means he shattered it as if it were armor. "Born of self" refers to the defilements that have arisen within oneself.
This is what is meant: he abandoned both the worldly karma known as "tulā" and "atulā"— which, in the sense of having a ripening result,
is called "sambhava," and in the sense of forming existence, is called "bhavasaṅkhāra"— and he shattered his own origin, which is defilement,
by being inwardly joyful and concentrated, just as a great warrior at the head of battle shatters his armor.

Alternatively, "weighing" means comparing: weighing both the incomparable—namely, Nibbāna and existence—and the formative forces of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*), which is the karma leading to existence.
"The Sage abandoned" means that the Buddha-Sage, by way of such a method as "the five aggregates are impermanent;
the cessation of the five aggregates is Nibbāna, which is permanent," weighed out the danger in existence and the benefit in Nibbāna.

Having seen that formative force of existence (*bhava-saṅkhāra*), which is the root of the aggregates, he abandoned it by means of the Noble Path—the cause of the destruction of karma—as described in the words, "it leads to the destruction of karma.
How so? "Delighting within, composed, he broke through the self-born armor as if it were a coat of mail.
For he was "delighting within" by way of insight (*vipassanā*) and "composed" by way of serenity (*samatha*).

Thus, having stood enveloping his own being like a suit of armor by means of the power of serenity and insight starting from the preliminary stage, he shattered the entire mass of defilements known as "born of self" because they arise within oneself.
And through the absence of defilements, karma becomes "rendered useless" because it lacks the capacity for rebirth-linking; thus, by the abandoning of defilements—
Abandon action! For one who has abandoned the defilements, there is no such thing as fear.

Therefore, it should be understood that he relinquished the life-formations while remaining fearless, and uttered this inspired utterance (udāna) for the purpose of making known his state of fearlessness.
The first chapter, the Cāpāla Chapter, is concluded.
2. The Chapter on the Shaking of the Palace (Pāsādakampanavagga) 1–2. Commentary on the First Sutta, etc. (Pubbasuttādivaṇṇanā) 823–824.

In the first [sutta] of the second chapter, the phrases beginning with "neither too slack" (na ca atilīno) will be explained further below. In this sutta, the bases of psychic power (iddhipādā) that serve as the foundation for the six direct knowledges (cha-abhiññā) are taught; likewise in the second [sutta].
3. Commentary on the Chandasamādhi Sutta 825.

In the third [sutta], "desire" (*chanda*) refers to the desire consisting of the wish to act. "Depending upon" (*nissāya*) means making it a support; the meaning is "making it the dominant influence" (*adhipati*).
"Exertive formations" (*padhāna-saṅkhārā*) are formations that constitute exertion; this is a term for the energy of right effort (*sammappadhāna-vīriya*) which accomplishes the four functions.
This is a designation. Thus, in the phrases "this desire" and so forth, desire is endowed with both concentration through desire and the formations of striving;
concentration through desire is endowed with both desire and the formations of striving; and the formations of striving are also endowed with both desire and concentration through desire.
Therefore, having taken all those factors together as one, this is called [the basis for success].
"Monks, it is said: 'The basis of psychic power endowed with the volitional formations of striving and concentration through desire.

However, in the *Iddhipādavibhaṅga*, by way of the method beginning with 'the aggregate of feeling of one who has become thus,' it is stated that the remaining immaterial phenomena endowed with these factors are the bases of psychic power."
Furthermore, these three factors are both supernormal powers (*iddhi*) and bases for supernormal power (*iddhipāda*). How so?
For one who develops zeal, zeal is called "supernormal power," and the volitional formations of exertion associated with concentration are called the "basis for the supernormal power of zeal.

For one developing concentration, concentration is called "supernormal power," and the volitional formations of exertion associated with zeal are called the "basis for the supernormal power of concentration. Regarding the volitional formations of exertion...
For one who is developing [the path], the volitional formations of striving (*padhāna-saṅkhāra*) are called "success" (*iddhi*).
The concentration of desire (*chanda-samādhi*) is called a "basis of success" (*iddhipāda*), for when one among the associated states succeeds, the rest also succeed.
Furthermore, their status as bases of success should be understood by way of their respective prior stages. For the first jhāna...
As for "supernormal power" (*iddhi*): the factors such as desire (*chanda*) associated with the preliminary practice for the first *jhāna* are called the "basis of supernormal power" (*iddhipāda*).

By this same method, the principle should be applied from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatana*) downwards; from the various types of supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) up to the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-abhiññā*);
and from the path of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-magga*) up to the path of arhatship (*arahatta-magga*). This same method applies to the remaining bases of supernormal power as well.

However, some say, "The basis of psychic power that has not yet been produced is the basis of psychic power. Here, for the purpose of refuting their argument, the following passage known as the *Uttaracūḷavāra* (The Higher Minor Section) appears in the Abhidhamma:

"There are four bases of psychic power: the basis of psychic power consisting of desire, the basis of psychic power consisting of energy, the basis of psychic power consisting of consciousness, and the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation.
Therein, what is the basis of psychic power consisting of desire? Here, monks, at whatever time a monk develops supramundane jhāna..."
Leading to liberation, leading to the diminution [of defilements], for the abandoning of views, and for the attainment of the first stage—secluded from sensual pleasures...
[as before] ...one enters and dwells in the first *jhāna*, which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge.
At that time, whatever desire, state of desiring, wish to act, and wholesome desire for the Dhamma there is, this is called the basis of psychic power consisting of desire (*chandiddhipāda*).
"The remaining factors are associated with the basis of psychic power consisting in zeal.
These, however, are presented specifically by way of the supramundane.
In that regard, the Elder Raṭṭhapāla produced the supramundane state making zeal his primary focus. The Elder Soṇa...
Vīriya made his burden; Sambhūta Thera made citta his burden; and the Venerable Mogharāja made vīmaṃsā his burden.

In this regard, just as among the four sons of ministers who were living in dependence upon the king while aspiring to high office, one was filled with zeal for service and, having understood the king’s inclination and preference, [attended to him] by day and by night...
And by attending upon the king and pleasing him, he attained a high position. Thus should one who produces supramundane states through the predominance of zeal be understood.
But another—thinking, "I am not able to attend every day;

I shall please him through my prowess when a task arises"—was dispatched by the king to a rebellious border region and, having crushed the enemy through his valor, attained success. Just as he did, so too...

One who produces supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) should be understood as one for whom energy (vīriya) is the primary burden. One person thought, "Even attending [the king] day after day, or even receiving spears and arrows upon my chest, is merely a burden; I shall win him over by the power of spells.

Because he had practiced the science of the Khattavas (khattavijjā), he won over the king through the employment of spells and attained his goal. Just as he did, so too [does one succeed] through the primary burden of the mind (citta).
He should be understood as one who produces supramundane states.
Another, however—thinking, "What is the use of these attendants and such? Kings indeed grant positions to those of noble birth;
if he grants them to such a person, he will grant them to me"—attained a position solely by relying on his noble birth. Just as:
Thus, it should be understood that by relying on such perfectly purified investigation, and with investigation as the primary vehicle, one is a producer of supramundane states.
In this sutta, the supernormal power based on turning away (*vivaṭṭapādakā iddhi*) is explained.
4. Commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta.
826. In the fourth [verse], "restless" (*uddhata*) means those whose nature is agitation (*uddhacca*), whose minds are flickering.
For through agitation, the mind flutters over a single object like a banner struck by the wind on a flagpole. "Arrogant" (*unnaḷā*) means with upraised reeds; it is said they have raised empty pride.
"Fickle" (*capalā*) means possessed of fickleness regarding such things as the decoration of one's bowl and robes. "Garrulous" (*mukharā*) means harsh-mouthed.
"Harsh speech" is what is meant. "Scattered in speech" means having unrestrained speech, babbling useless words even throughout the day.

"Muddle-minded" means having lost mindfulness. "Lacking clear comprehension" means devoid of wisdom (*paññā*). "Unconcentrated" means lacking access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*).
"With wandering minds" means with unsettled minds due to restlessness (*uddhacca*) finding its opportunity through the absence of concentration. "With unguarded faculties" means...

"With unrestrained faculties. "A feat of supernormal power" (*iddhābhisaṅkhāra*): having entered the water-kasina attainment and emerged, he resolved that the section of earth where the palace stood was "water";
then, with the palace standing upon the surface of the water, he rose up into the air and struck it with his thumb.
"Deep-rimmed" (*gambhīranemi*): deep moat; it had sunk into a deep portion of the ground.

The meaning is as follows: *Sunikhāto* means well-planted; it has been firmly established after being pounded. Here, the supernormal power (*iddhi*) based on direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is explained.
5. Commentary on the *Uṇṇābha-brāhmaṇa-sutta*: 827.
"For the purpose of abandoning desire" means for the purpose of abandoning the desire of craving (*taṇhā-chanda*). Here too, the supernormal power based on turning away (*vivaṭṭa*) is explained.
9. Commentary on the Sutta on the Teaching of Supernormal Power, etc.
(Iddhādidesanāsutta-vaṇṇanā) 831. In the ninth [sutta], "that which, monks, is the path," the fourth jhāna serving as the basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) is intended.
10. Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta.
832. Regarding the phrase "accompanied by indolence" in the tenth [chapter]: here, a bhikkhu, having aroused desire (*chanda*), sits down while attending to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Then, a state of lethargy (*līnākāra*) descends upon his mind.

Knowing, "A state of lethargy has descended upon me," he shames his mind with the fear of the states of deprivation (*apāya*) and, having again aroused desire, attends to the meditation subject. Then, once more, a state of lethargy...
He falls [into sloth]. Then, having struck his mind with the fear of the states of misery (apāya) and having generated desire, he attends to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna).
Thus, because it is intermingled with sloth, his desire is said to be "accompanied by sloth. "Associated with sloth" is a synonym for that same state.
"Accompanied by restlessness": here, a bhikkhu, having generated desire and attending to the meditation subject, sits down.

Then his mind falls into agitation. Having called to mind the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, he gladdens and satisfies his mind, makes it pliant, and then, having again aroused desire, he attends to the meditation subject.
Then his mind falls into agitation once more. He again calls to mind the virtues of the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, and gladdens his mind...
Having satisfied [the mind], having made it workable, and having aroused desire, he applies his attention to the meditation subject;
thus, because it is mixed with restlessness, his desire is said to be "accompanied by restlessness. Regarding "accompanied by sloth and torpor":
here, a bhikkhu, having aroused desire and applying his attention to the meditation subject, sits down.

Then sloth and torpor arise in him. Knowing, "Sloth and torpor have arisen in me," he wipes his face with water, pulls his ears, recites a familiar passage of the Dhamma, and—having attended to the perception of light previously grasped during the day—he dispels the sloth and torpor.
Then, generating desire once more, he attends to the meditation subject.
Then sloth and torpor arise in him again. Having once more dispelled that sloth and torpor in the manner already described, and having generated desire, he applies his mind to the meditation subject.
Thus, because it is intermingled with sloth and torpor, his desire is said to be "accompanied by sloth and torpor."
"Distraught" means that here a bhikkhu, having aroused desire and sitting down while attending to his meditation subject,
finds his mind distracted by objects of sensual pleasure. Knowing, "My mind is distracted externally," he reflects upon such discourses as the *Anamatagga*,
the *Devadūta*, the *Celopama*, and the *Anāgatabhaya*, and with the "staff of the Suttas," he [restrains] the mind.
Having suppressed that [distraction] and made the mind pliable, he arouses desire again and attends to the meditation subject.
Then his mind becomes distracted once more. He again makes the mind pliable with the "stick of the sutta," arouses desire, and attends to the meditation subject.
Thus, because it is interspersed with thoughts of sensual desire, his desire for the external [objects]—the five [sensual pleasures]—[increases].
He is distracted and obsessed by the strands of sensual pleasure.
"As before, so after"—this anteriority and posteriority should be understood both in terms of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and in terms of the teaching. How so?
First, regarding the meditation subject: fixation upon the meditation subject is called "before," and Arahantship is called "after."
In this regard, the bhikkhu who, having applied himself to the fundamental meditation subject, restrains the mind from falling into the four states such as excessive laxity and so forth—
like one driving a stubborn ox or lowering a square water-clock—
and without being attached even to a single point among those four states, attains Arahantship by comprehending conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
This one, too, is said to "dwell the same way both before and after. This refers to the priority and posteriority in terms of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
However, in terms of the teaching (*desanā*), the head hairs are called "before" and the brain is called "after.

In this regard, the bhikkhu who, having applied his attention to the head hairs, examines the head hairs and so forth by way of their color, shape, and other characteristics, and remains unattached in four respects—
When he brings his meditation to the attainment of even the brain, this too is called "he dwells as he did before, so he does afterwards.
Thus, the priority and posteriority should be understood by way of the teaching. "As afterwards, so before" is a synonym for "before" itself.
"As below, so above" should be understood by way of the body. Therefore he said: "From the soles of the feet upwards..."

"Down to the tips of the hair. In this context, the bhikkhu who brings his meditation to completion by way of the thirty-two aspects from the soles of the feet up to the tips of the hair, or by way of the bones from the tip of a toe-joint up to the skull, and from the skull down to the tip of a toe-joint—remaining unattached at any of the four places or even at a single place—is like this: [the simile follows].
"One dwells such that above is as below, and below is as above" means this.
"By whatever modes" means by whatever constituent parts. "By whatever characteristics" means by whatever shapes. "By whatever signs" means by whatever appearances.
"The perception of light is well apprehended" refers to the monk who, having sat down in an open courtyard, [cultivates] the perception of light.
He attends to it; he closes his eyes at the proper time and opens them at the proper time.

Then, when for him the image appears exactly the same whether he is closing his eyes or opening them to look, it is said that the perception of light has arisen. "The perception of day" is also its name.
Furthermore, when that arises during the night, it is said to be well-grasped. It is also said to be well-attended.
This is a synonym for that very thing. "Well-established" means well-placed; it is called "well-fixed" (*svādhiṭṭhitā*).

In terms of meaning, this is simply the same as "well-grasped. Or, when one dispels sloth and torpor by means of light, arouses desire, and attends to the meditation subject, then even during the day, the perception of light is well-grasped and well-fixed. This remains so whether it be night or day.

Or, by whatever light one dispels sloth and torpor during the day and attends to the meditation subject, the perception that has arisen regarding that light which dispels sloth and torpor is indeed called "well-grasped.
This same method applies to energy and the other factors as well. In this sutta, the supernormal power that serves as the foundation for the six direct knowledges is explained.
The second chapter, "The Shaking of the Palace.
3. The Chapter on the Iron Ball. 2.
Commentary on the Sutta of the Iron Ball.

834. In the second [sutta] of the third chapter, "by this which consists of the four great elements" means by this which is composed of the four great elements, even though it is thus heavy, burdensome, and equal [to the body].
"He bears" means he is able, he is capable; this is an unambiguous term (*asambhinna-pada*) in the Buddha’s word consisting of the Three Baskets (*Tepiṭaka*).
"He absorbs the body into the mind" means that having taken the body, he places it upon the mind; it is dependent upon the mind.
He performs [the action]; he sends it forth by means of the movement of the mind. "Mind" here refers to the exalted mind (*mahaggata-citta*); the movement of the mind is swift.
"The mind also immerses itself in the body" means that, having grasped the mind, he places it upon the body;

he makes it dependent on the body and sends it forth by means of the movement of the body. "Body" refers to the physical body composed of the four great elements (*karaja-kāya*); the movement of the body is slow. And the perception of pleasure...

"And the perception of lightness" refers to the perception co-nascent with the consciousness of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). For that is called the "perception of pleasure" because it is accompanied by peaceful happiness, and it is called the "perception of lightness" because there is an absence of the sluggishness of defilements.
A red-hot iron ball, having been heated all day, becomes even lighter; for when two or three people lift it up...
Even when placed in the smith’s forge and heated all day long, it becomes so light— due to the entry of heat and air,
and by becoming accompanied by air, accompanied by heat, and accompanied by fire—
that the smith can seize it with large tongs, turn it over on one side, lift it up, and take it out. Thus...
Furthermore, it becomes soft and workable. Just as he cuts it into pieces, striking it with a hammer, he fashions it into various shapes such as long or square.
In this sutta, the supernormal power of transformation (*vikubbaniddhi*) is described.
3–10. Commentary on the *Bhikkhu-sutta* and others.
835–842. In the third [chapter], the supernormal power (iddhi) based on turning away (vivaṭṭa) is explained; likewise in the fourth.

Furthermore, beginning with the two fruits, the mixed bases of supernormal power (missaka-iddhipāda) are explained below as belonging to the preliminary stages (pubbhāga) within the seven fruits. The four beginning with the seventh are exactly according to the method already explained below.
11–12. Commentary on the Moggallāna Sutta, etc. (843–844).
In the eleventh and twelfth [suttas], the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) are explained. The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on the Saṃyutta on the Bases of Psychic Power (*Iddhipāda-saṃyutta*) is finished.
8. Anuruddha Saṃyutta 1.
Rahogata Vagga 1–2.
Commentary on the First Discourse on Being Secluded, etc.
899–900. In the first discourse of the *Anuruddha-saṃyutta*, [the practice] is undertaken and brought to completion.
In brief, here insight is explained as leading to Arahantship through thirty-six bases; in the second, insight is explained as leading to Arahantship through twelve bases.
3. Commentary on the *Sutanu-sutta*.

901. In the third [section], "great direct knowledge" (*mahābhiññatā*) refers to the state of possessing the six direct knowledges (*cha-abhiññā*). Regarding the passage beginning with "inferior phenomena" (*hīnaṃ dhammaṃ*), the meaning should be understood according to this scriptural text:
"Which phenomena are inferior? The twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arisings—these phenomena are inferior. Which phenomena are middling?
The wholesome [states] in the three planes, the resultants in the three planes, the functional-indeterminate in the three planes, and all form."
“These states are mediocre. Which states are sublime? The four paths not included [in the mundane], the four fruits of recluseship, and Nibbāna—these states are sublime.
4–7. Commentary on the First Kaṇḍakī Sutta, etc.
902–905. In the fourth [verse], “in the Kaṇḍakī forest,” means in the Mahākaramanda forest.
In the sixth, “a thousand worlds,” by this the Elder’s constant dwelling is shown. For the Elder, having washed his face early in the morning, recollects a thousand eons of the past and the future.
As for the present, however, ten thousand world-systems come within the range of a single act of attention (*ekāvajjana*).
The seventh [sutta] is self-evident.
8. *Salaḷāgāra-sutta-vannaṇā* (Commentary on the Salaḷāgāra Sutta) 906.

Regarding the eighth [sutta], "in the salaḷāgāra": it refers to a leaf-hut made of *salaḷa* wood, or to a dwelling so named because it stood at the entrance of a *salaḷa* tree. In this sutta, the person who practices insight meditation is discussed together with the practice of insight itself.
9. Commentary on the Ambapālīvana Sutta 907.
In the ninth [sutta], "the lion's roar" (*āsabhiṃ vācaṃ*) refers to the supreme speech that demonstrates one's own state of *arahantship*. The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Rahogatavagga.
2. Commentary on the Second Chapter (Dutiyavagga-vaṇṇanā) 909–922.

In the Second Chapter, the Elder [Mahāmoggallāna] proclaims the knowledge of the Ten Powers (*dasabala-ñāṇa*) by means of such phrases as “the possible as possible” (*ṭhānañ ca ṭhānato*). One might ask: "Is this [knowledge] possessed by disciples (*sāvaka*) as well? It exists in them to a certain extent; however, for the omniscient Buddhas, it is complete in every respect and perfected in all its modes.
The commentary on the *Anuruddha-saṃyutta* is finished.
9. Commentary on the Jhāna Saṃyutta 923.
The Jhāna Saṃyutta is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the Jhāna Saṃyutta is finished.
10. Connected Discourses on Mindfulness of Breathing 1.
The Chapter on a Single Dhamma 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on a Single Dhamma

977. In the first discourse of the *Ānāpānasaṃyutta*, "one thing" (*ekadhamma*) means a single phenomenon. Whatever else might need to be said here, all of it has already been stated in every detail in the *Visuddhimagga* in the exposition of the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati-kammaṭṭhāna*).

6. Commentary on the Ariṭṭha Sutta 982. In the sixth discourse, "bhāvetha no" means "should you develop? "Sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda*) is lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. "Internally" (*ajjhattaṃ*)...
"And in external phenomena" means in the twelve internal and external bases (*āyatana*).
"Perceptions of resistance are well removed" means that perceptions associated with resistance are thoroughly removed; the sense is that they have been completely cut off.
By this, he describes his own path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). Now, demonstrating the insight (*vipassanā*) of the path of arahantship, he says: "He, being mindful..."
He said, "I shall breathe in," and so forth. 7. Commentary on the Mahākappina Sutta: 983.
In the seventh [verse], both "the state of wavering" (*iñjitatta*) and "the state of quivering" (*phanditatta*) refer to movement alone.
8. Commentary on the Lamp Simile Sutta 984.
In the eighth [sutta], "neither the body nor the eyes grow weary": for when one performs the practice with other meditation subjects, the body grows weary and the eyes are distressed.
This is because, when one performs the practice with the meditation subject of the elements (*dhātu-kammaṭṭhāna*), [the body does not grow weary].
