The body becomes weary, as if it were being subjected to pressure after being placed in a machine.
When one practices the meditation subject of the *kasiṇa*, the eyes throb and grow tired, as if they were about to pop out and fall.
But for one practicing this meditation subject, neither the body grows weary nor do the eyes suffer. Therefore, he spoke thus.

Why was it said, "With the complete surmounting of perceptions of form," and so forth? Is the emergence from the kasiṇa obtained in the case of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna)? Regarding this, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷābhaya said:
"Because the sign of mindfulness of breathing appears like the form of a star, a pearl necklace, and so on, therefore the emergence from the kasiṇa is obtained therein.
The Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga, however, said: "It is certainly not obtained."
Why is this classification beginning with noble supernormal power (ariya-iddhi) included when it is not being attained? It is for the purpose of showing its benefits.

For a bhikkhu who aspires to noble supernormal power, or to the four fine-material-sphere jhānas, or to the four immaterial attainments, or to the attainment of cessation, this concentration of mindfulness of breathing should be carefully attended to. Just as...

For when a city is captured, whatever goods were produced in the four directions enter that very city through its four gates; thus the countryside is also captured. This is indeed the benefit of the city itself.
In the same way, this distinction beginning with noble supernormal power (*ariyiddhi*) is the benefit of the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatisamādhi*);
for when concentration through mindfulness of breathing has been developed in every aspect, [these benefits follow].
"All this is accomplished by the yogi" is stated for the purpose of showing the benefits. As for the phrase "and happiness," why is "he" (*so*) not mentioned here?
Because the word "bhikkhu" has not appeared in this particular section.
9. Commentary on the Vesālī Sutta.

985. In the ninth [case], at the city named Vesālī—a designation applied to it by way of its feminine gender—that city is called Vesālī because it became vast through three successive enlargements of its surrounding walls.
It should be understood that this city also reached its full perfection in every respect only when the Perfectly Enlightened One had attained omniscience.
Having thus shown the village as his resort, he stated the place of residence: "In the Great Forest, in the Gabled Hall.

Therein, "Great Forest" (*mahāvana*) refers to a large forest that is self-grown, uncultivated, and well-defined. However, the Great Forest in the vicinity of Kapilavatthu is not defined by such boundaries;
it is continuous with the Himalayas and extends until it meets the great ocean. This [forest] is of that latter kind.
That which is not [unbounded], being large and surrounded by a boundary, is called a "great forest" (*mahāvana*). However,

it should be understood that the Fragrant Chamber (*gandhakuṭī*) of the Blessed Buddha— constructed within a monastery built adjacent to a great forest, enclosing a gabled hall (*kūṭāgāra*), and covered with a *haṃsavaṭṭaka* roof— is endowed with every excellence.

"He speaks a discourse on foulness in many ways" means that he speaks a discourse intended to turn the mind away from the body, one which proceeds by demonstrating the various aspects of foulness through numerous reasons.
That is to say: "In this body there are head-hairs, body-hairs, nails, teeth...
[etc. ... urine. What is meant? Monks, in this fathom-long carcass, in every respect...
Searching through it, no one sees even the slightest trace of purity—whether a pearl, a gem, beryl, aloeswood, sandalwood, saffron, camphor, or fragrant powders;
rather, one sees only various kinds of impurity, such as hair and body hair, which are extremely foul-smelling, loathsome, and unsightly to behold. Therefore, there is nothing here [to be found].
One should apply either desire or passion [to this]. Even those things called hairs that grow on the head, the supreme limb, are indeed foul, impure, and repulsive.

And this state of their being foul, impure, and repulsive should be understood by way of five aspects: by color, by shape, by odor, by habitat, and by location. The same applies to the body hairs and so forth; such is the case here.
This is the summary; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.
Thus, the Blessed One teaches the discourse on foulness (*asubha*) by means of many methods, with fivefold divisions for each individual section.

He "speaks in praise of foulness" by first establishing the matrix of foulness through the bloated corpse (*uddhumātaka*) and so forth, and then [explaining it] through the word-commentary (*padabhājanīya*).
Analyzing and praising that, he speaks in praise of foulness (*asubha*). "He speaks in praise of the development of foulness" means:

regarding this development, increase, and mastery of the mind—which proceeds by apprehending the aspect of foulness in internal and external objects, such as the head-hairs and so forth, or the bloated corpse and so forth—he speaks of the benefit (*ānisansa*) of that development of foulness.
He speaks in praise and extols its virtues as follows:

"Monks, a monk devoted to the meditation on the foul, whether upon the parts of the body beginning with head-hair or upon the bloated corpse and so forth, attains the first jhāna—which has abandoned five factors, possesses five factors, is good in three ways, and is endowed with ten characteristics. He [attains] that which is designated as the first jhāna..."
"By relying on the casket of the mind, one increases insight and attains the supreme goal, arahantship.
"Monks, I wish to go into seclusion for half a month"—the meaning is that I, monks, wish to go into seclusion, to remain hidden, and to dwell all alone. "I am not to be approached by anyone."
"Except for one who brings almsfood": setting aside that single monk who, without having spoken words on my behalf,
brings forth prepared almsfood from faithful families for my sake and presents it to me—
I am not to be approached by anyone else, whether a monk or a householder.
But why did he say this? It is said that in the past, five hundred deer-hunters surrounded a forest with large sticks, snares, and other traps;
being joyful and elated, they made their living for as long as they lived solely by the slaughter of deer and birds, and were reborn in hell.
Having been cooked there, through some wholesome deed performed in the past, they [were reborn] among humans.

Through the power of their newly arisen wholesome supporting conditions (*kalyāṇūpanissaya*), they all received the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of the Blessed One.

However, because the ripening of the results of those previous unwholesome kamma had not yet matured, subsequent volitions (*cetanā*) created an opportunity for the termination of their lives—both through self-inflicted means and through the means of others—within that half-month. The Blessed One saw this.

The ripening of kamma cannot be warded off by anyone. Among those monks, there were both worldlings (*puthujjana*) and noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*)—namely, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and those whose taints were destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). Of these, those whose taints were destroyed were not subject to rebirth;
the other noble disciples were of certain destiny, destined for a happy destination; as for the worldlings, their destiny was uncertain.
Then the Blessed One thought: “These beings, terrified by the fear of death due to their desire and lust for this physical existence, will not be able to purify their destiny.
Come now, I shall speak a discourse on the foul (asubha) so that they may abandon desire and lust.
Having heard it, through the removal of desire and lust for the physical existence, they will purify their destiny and take rebirth in heaven.”
"In this way, their going forth in my presence will be meaningful.
Then, out of compassion for them, he spoke on the subject of the foul (*asubha*) under the heading of meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), but not with the intention of praising death.
Having spoken thus, it occurred to him: "If the monks see me during these next half-months, they will say, 'A certain monk died today;'"
“Today two... [and so on] ...today ten,” they will report upon their arrival. And this result of kamma cannot be warded off by me or by anyone else;
even having heard it, what shall I do? What use to me is hearing such useless, harmful, and ruinous news?
Come now, I shall go into seclusion from the bhikkhus. Therefore he said: “I wish...”
“Monks, I shall go into seclusion for half a month; I am not to be approached by anyone except for one who brings me almsfood.
Others, however, say: “Having spoken thus for the purpose of avoiding criticism from others, he entered into seclusion. It is said that others [criticized] the Blessed One...

They will speak in disparagement, saying: “This man, while claiming ‘I am omniscient, I am the supreme wheel-turner of the true Dhamma,’ is unable even to prevent his own disciples from killing one another; what else could he possibly accomplish?
To this, the wise will say: “The Blessed One is devoted to seclusion and does not know of this occurrence; who [else] would [know it] for him?”
“There was no one to inform him either; had he known, he certainly would have prevented it. But this is merely a matter of wishful thinking;

the primary reason lies elsewhere. Regarding the phrase *nāssudha*: here *assudha* is a particle used for the mere purpose of completing the metrical line or for emphasis, meaning “not even anyone approached the Blessed One.”

"Anekākāravokāra" means that which has a variety (*vokāra*) of many aspects (*aneka-ākāra*), such as color, shape, and so forth. What is meant is that it is "interspersed with many aspects" or "mixed in many ways.
What is this? It is the practice of the meditation on the foul (*asubha-bhāvanānuyoga*); that is what is "anekākāravokāra.
"They dwell devoted to the practice of the meditation on the foul" means they dwell engaged and intent upon it. "Being distressed" (*aṭṭīyamānā*) refers to being [distressed] by that.
They are distressed and suffering in body. "Feeling ashamed" means feeling embarrassed. "Feeling loathing" means giving rise to disgust.
"Seeking a weapon-taker" means seeking a weapon that would take away their life.
Not only do they seek out a weapon and deprive themselves of life by their own hand, but they even [employ] Migalaṇḍika, who was merely a sham ascetic.
Having approached, they said, "It would be well for us, friend, if you were to take our lives.
In this matter, the Noble Ones neither committed the destruction of life, nor incited others to do so, nor approved of it; however, the worldlings did all three.
"Emerging from seclusion" means having learned that those five hundred monks had met their end.
Then, having emerged from that state of unification, although he already knew, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda as if he did not know, for the purpose of initiating a conversation:
"Ānanda, why is it that the Saṅgha of bhikkhus seems so diminished?
Previously, Ānanda, many bhikkhus used to come together to attend upon me, receive the recitation and the interrogation, and engage in study."

The monastery appeared like a single lamp. But now, after the lapse of about half a month, the community of monks has become as if thinned out—sparse, weak, few, and scattered. What could be the reason for this? Have the monks departed in all directions?
Then the Venerable Ānanda, failing to perceive through the ripening of karma their impending death, [reflected] on account of his practice of the meditation subject of foulness (asubha-kammaṭṭhāna).

But observing [the situation], and having said, "Indeed so, Bhante, Blessed One," and so forth, he requested another meditation subject for the bhikkhus to attain arahantship, saying, "It would be well, Bhante, Blessed One," and so on. Its meaning is this:
"It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would explain another method by which the Saṅgha of bhikkhus might be established in arahantship. [He spoke thus regarding] the great ocean...

Just as there are descent-places (tīrtha), so too there are many meditation subjects for ascending to Nibbāna, such as the ten recollections (dasānussati), the ten kasinas, the analysis of the four elements (catudhātuvavatthāna), the divine abidings (brahmavihāra), and the various types of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānassati).
The intention [of the questioner] is: "May the Blessed One, having comforted the bhikkhus, explain one of these meditation subjects."
Then the Blessed One, desiring to act in such a manner, spoke the words beginning with "Therefore, Ānanda," in order to dispatch the Elder.
Therein, "depending on Vesālī" means: summon all those who dwell within a *gāvuta* or half a *yojana* surrounding Vesālī;
this is the meaning. "Having assembled them all in the assembly hall" refers to [the Elder] going himself...
Having gone himself to the appropriate place and sent young bhikkhus elsewhere, he gathered the entire assembly of bhikkhus in the assembly hall in just a moment.
Regarding the words, "Venerable sir, it is time for the Blessed One to do as he sees fit," this is the intended meaning:
the Blessed One, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, has assembled; this is the time for a discourse on the Dhamma for the bhikkhus.
"To perform [this], to give instruction; now, whatever you deem the right time for, that should be done.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, this too...

Having thus addressed them, and wishing to explain another method for the attainment of arahantship by the bhikkhus than the previously taught meditation subject on foulness (asubha), he said: "The concentration of mindfulness of breathing," and so forth.
In this context, *ānāpānassatisamādhi* means concentration associated with mindfulness that apprehends inhalation and exhalation;
or, it is concentration in mindfulness of breathing, hence *ānāpānassatisamādhi*. *Bhāvito* means generated or increased.
*Bahulīkato* means practiced repeatedly. *Santo ceva paṇīto ca* means both peaceful and sublime. In both cases...
By the word "only" (eva), a restriction is to be understood. What is meant?

For just as this meditation subject on foulness is both peaceful and sublime solely by way of penetration, yet is neither peaceful nor sublime by way of its object because its object is gross and repulsive, it is not in any manner whatsoever non-peaceful or unsublime.
Furthermore, it is peaceful and tranquil because of the continuity of its object (*ārammaṇa*), and because of the continuity of its factors (*aṅga*) known as penetration;
it is sublime because of the sublimity of its object, and because of the sublimity of its factors. Therefore it is said: "It is both peaceful and sublime.

Regarding the phrase "an unsatiating and pleasant abiding": here, "unsatiating" (*asecanaka*) means that there is no "pouring out" (*secanam*) of it; it is not something to be poured upon, but is unsurpassed.
It is distinct and unique; here there is no state of being "peaceful" through preparatory work (*parikamma*) or access concentration (*upacāra*).
From the very moment of initial attention (*ādi-samanāhāra*), it is peaceful and sublime by its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*)—this is the meaning.

Some say that "unfailing" (*asecanaka*) means not needing to be sprinkled with anything else, but being full of essence (*ojavanta*) and sweet by its own nature. Thus, this [jhāna] is unfailing at every moment of absorption (*appita*).
It should be understood as "a pleasant abiding" because it conduces to the attainment of bodily and mental happiness.
"As they arise" means when they have not been suppressed. "Evil" means base. "Unwholesome states" means states produced by lack of skill.
"He makes them disappear on the spot" means he makes them disappear and suppresses them in that very moment. "He allays them" means...

It thoroughly pacifies; because it partakes of penetration (*nibbedhabhāgiya*), it gradually reaches the growth of the Noble Path and utterly cuts off—what is meant is that it causes [defilements] to subside.

"In the last month of summer" means in the month of Āsāḷha. "Dust and dirt have been swept away" means that for eight months the dust and dirt were blown upward from the earth, which had been dried by wind and sun and broken up by the trampling of the feet of cattle, buffaloes, and other animals.

"The dust and the pollen stirred up and raised in the air. A "great unseasonable cloud" is a rain-cloud that arises having overspread the entire sky, raining for a full half-month during the bright fortnight of the month of Āsāḷha.
For it is intended here as an "unseasonable cloud" because it arises before the proper rainy season has arrived. "He makes it vanish on the spot; he calms it" means he does so in an instant.

He leads him to invisibility and causes him to settle down within the earth. "In the same way" is a demonstration by means of a simile. What follows thereafter is exactly according to the method already stated.
10. Commentary on the Kimila Sutta.
986. "In the city named Kimilā. The Elder said this, it is said, after reflecting:
"This teaching has not been arranged according to its proper sequence; I shall lead it to its proper sequence.

Thus, joining the sequence of the teaching, he spoke this. "'One or another of the bodies': among the bodies such as earth and so forth, I speak of one or another; I speak of the air-body (vāyokāya)."
The meaning is as follows. Alternatively, the twenty-five material components—namely, the eye-base … [and so on] … up to physical nutriment—are called the "material body" (*rūpakāya*).

Among these, because mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) is included within the tangible-object base (*phoṭṭhabbāyatana*), it is one of the constituents of the body; therefore, he spoke thus. "Therefore, then" (*tasmātihā*):
because, among the four bodies, it is either the air-body (*vāyokāya*) or, among the twenty-five components, it is part of the material body.
He contemplates one or another of the breaths; therefore, the meaning is "contemplating the body in the body. The meaning should be understood in this way in all instances.
"One or another feeling" means one among the three feelings; this was said with reference to pleasant feeling.
"Careful attention" means the excellent attention that has arisen by way of experiencing rapture and so forth. What?

But is attention itself pleasant feeling? It is not; rather, this is a heading for the teaching. For just as in the passage "devoted to the practice of the development of the perception of impermanence," wisdom is stated by way of the term "perception," so too here it should be understood that the feeling of jhāna is stated by way of the term "attention.
For in this tetrad, in the first phrase, feeling is stated under the heading of "rapture" (pīti), while in the second phrase, it is stated by its own specific name as "pleasure" (sukha).
It has been stated. Regarding the pair of terms *cittasaṅkhāra* (mental formations), because of the statement: "Perception and feeling—these mental states are bound to the mind;

they are mental formations," and because of the statement: "With the exception of applied thought and sustained thought, all factors associated with the mind are included under mental formations," feeling is spoken of by the name *cittasaṅkhāra*. All that...
Having included it under the name "attention," it is here called "careful attention.
Even so, one might argue that since this feeling is not itself the object [of observation], the contemplation of feelings (vedanānupassanā) is not tenable.
This is not the case; for even in the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta and other texts, by taking various bases of pleasure and so forth as objects, [the contemplation is established].
Feeling feels; however, based on that occurrence of feeling, there is the mere conventional expression, “I feel.
With reference to this, it was said: “When feeling a pleasant feeling, one knows: ‘I am feeling a pleasant feeling,’” and so forth.
Furthermore, the resolution of this point has already been stated in the commentary on the meaning of such passages as “experiencing rapture. For this has indeed been stated in the *Visuddhimagga*:
“Rapture is experienced in two ways: by way of the object and by way of non-delusion. How is rapture experienced by way of the object?

One enters the two jhānas accompanied by rapture; at the moment of attainment, through the acquisition of the jhāna, rapture is experienced by way of the object because the object is experienced. How [is it experienced] by way of non-delusion?”
How is rapture experienced? Having entered and emerged from two jhānas accompanied by rapture, one contemplates the rapture associated with those jhānas as subject to destruction and vanishing.
At the moment of insight, because of non-delusion through penetration of the characteristics [of phenomena], rapture is experienced.
For this is said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "By means of long inhalation, one-pointedness of mind..."
"For one who understands non-distraction, mindfulness becomes established; through that mindfulness and that knowledge, that rapture is clearly experienced.
In this same manner, the remaining terms should also be understood according to their meaning.
Thus, just as by the attainment of jhāna, rapture, pleasure, and mental formations are clearly experienced with respect to the object, so too...
Thus, by this attainment of attention consisting of feeling associated with jhāna, feeling is clearly understood from the perspective of its object.
Therefore, it is well said: "On that occasion, the bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings.

Regarding the statement, "Ānanda, I do not say this of one who is unmindful and lacking clear comprehension," the intended meaning here is this: because [the practitioner] is "clearly comprehending the mind..."
Although a bhikkhu who proceeds according to the method beginning with “I shall breathe in” takes the sign of the breath— inhalation and exhalation—
as his object, he is nevertheless called a “contemplator of mind” because he proceeds by establishing mindfulness and clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) upon that mental object.
For the development of concentration through mindfulness of breathing is not possible for one who is muddled in mindfulness or lacking clear comprehension.
Because it exists, therefore, "on account of the object, by way of the mind's full awareness, on that occasion a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the mind in the mind.
Regarding the statement, "Having seen with wisdom that which is the abandoning of covetousness and dejection, he becomes thoroughly equanimous":
here, covetousness is simply the hindrance of sensual desire, and the hindrance of ill will is shown by way of dejection.
This tetrad is indeed stated by way of insight alone. And the contemplation of phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) is fivefold, beginning with the section on the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*);
of that, the section on the hindrances is the first; and of that too, these two hindrances are the first.

Thus, in order to show the beginning of the contemplation of phenomena, he said: "covetousness and grief. "Abandoning" means [the abandoning] of the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence.

"He abandons" means that the knowledge of abandoning is intended in this way. "Having seen that with wisdom" refers to that knowledge of abandoning—consisting of the knowledge of impermanence, fading away, cessation, and relinquishment—by means of another wisdom of insight;
and that [other] by yet another, thus he shows a succession of insights.
"He becomes one who looks on with equanimity" means that he looks on with equanimity both toward that which has entered the path and toward its unified manifestation.
"He looks on with equanimity" (ajjhupekkhati) means that there are two ways of looking on with equanimity:
looking on with equanimity toward co-nascent states and looking on with equanimity toward the object. Here, looking on with equanimity toward the object is intended.

Therefore, "In this way, Ānanda"—because [the practice] proceeds according to the method beginning with "I shall breathe in contemplating impermanence," it does not apply only to phenomena such as the hindrances.

Furthermore, having seen with wisdom the knowledge that effects the abandoning of those states spoken of under the heading of covetousness and dejection, he dwells as one who looks on with equanimity;
therefore, it should be understood that at that time the bhikkhu dwells contemplating mind-objects as mind-objects.
"In this very way" (evameva kho): here, the six sense bases should be regarded as being like the crossroads, and the heap of dust upon it...
The defilements are like carts and chariots coming from the six directions; the four foundations of mindfulness are like the four carts and chariots proceeding toward the four objects.
Just as a mound of dust is crushed by a single cart or chariot, so too should the crushing of evil, unwholesome states through the practice of body-contemplation and the others be understood.
The First Chapter on a Single Dhamma.
2. The Second Chapter: 1–2.
Commentary on the Icchānaṅgala Sutta and others.
987–988. In the first [sutta] of the second chapter, why does he declare his own dwelling in attainment (*vihārasamāpatti*) with the words, "you should explain it thus"?
It is for the purpose of clearing away reproach. For if they were to say, "We do not know," then the heretics (*titthiya*) would ask them:
"If you do not even know that 'our Teacher dwelt for three months in such-and-such an attainment,' then why..."
If others were to raise an objection, saying, "Dwell attending upon that [breath]," he spoke thus for the sake of releasing them from that charge.
Now, why is it that the word *eva* (just/exactly) is used elsewhere—as in "mindful he breathes in, or breathing in long"—but is not used here?
Because of its absolute tranquility. For in other cases, either the inhalation or the exhalation is manifest.
Since both of these are clearly evident to the Blessed One due to his constant state of established mindfulness, they were not mentioned because they are entirely peaceful.
Now, why was it said only “I shall breathe,” without saying “I am training”? It is because there is no longer anything to be trained in.

For the seven trainees (*sekha*) are called “trainees” because they have something to train in, whereas those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) are called “non-trainees” (*asekha*) because there is nothing further to train in.
The Tathāgatas are not called "those beyond training" (asekha) because there is no task for them to train in; it is not so stated because of the absence of anything further to be trained in.
The second [sutta] is self-evident.
3–10. Commentary on the First Ānanda Sutta and others.
989–996. "In the third [jhāna], he investigates" means he investigates by way of impermanence and so forth.
The other two phrases are synonyms for this very term. "Unworldly" (nirāmisā) means free from defilements; through the subsiding of physical and mental distress, both body and mind become tranquil.
"He becomes concentrated" (samādhiyati) means he is properly established; it becomes like the mind in absorption (appanā). "He dwells with equanimity" (ajjhupekkhitā)—
"He is one who looks on with equanimity" means he is one who looks on with equanimity by means of co-nascent equanimity.
Thus, for a bhikkhu who comprehends the body in these fourteen ways, mindfulness regarding that body is the mindfulness enlightenment factor;

the knowledge associated with that mindfulness is the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor; and the bodily and mental energy associated with those very factors is [the energy enlightenment factor].

The enlightenment factor of energy; the enlightenment factors of rapture, tranquility, and one-pointedness of mind—these are the enlightenment factors of rapture, tranquility, and concentration respectively;
and the enlightenment factor of equanimity is the mode of neutrality consisting in neither falling short of nor overreaching these six enlightenment factors.
For just as when horses are proceeding evenly, a charioteer does not prick them thinking, "This one is lagging," nor [slacken] thinking, "This one is overrunning."
There is no drawing [the mind] toward [one side], but for one who sees thus, there is simply the mode of remaining;
in the same way, the neutral mode of these six enlightenment factors—consisting in neither falling short nor overreaching—is called the enlightenment factor of equanimity (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*).

What has been stated up to this point? It has been stated that the insight-enlightenment factors (*vipassanā-bojjhaṅga*) exist within a single moment of consciousness and possess various flavors and characteristics.

The phrases beginning with "based on seclusion" (*vivekanissita*) have already been explained in their respective places. Here, however, the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*) is spoken of as mixed;
the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) rooted in breathing are the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*), and the mindfulness of breathing which is their root is also the preliminary stage.

The foundations of mindfulness rooted in the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are the preliminary stage, and those factors of enlightenment themselves are likewise the preliminary stage. [This leads to] the fulfillment of clear knowledge and liberation (*vijjā-vimutti*).
However, the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are supramundane (lokuttara), while clear knowledge (vijjā) and liberation (vimutti) are associated with the noble fruits (ariyaphala).
Alternatively, clear knowledge is associated with the fourth path, and liberation is associated with the fruit. The fourth, fifth, and sixth [chapters] have the same divisions as this one.
The rest is entirely obvious throughout.
The commentary on the Connected Discourses on Mindfulness of Breathing is finished.
11. The Connected Discourses on Stream-Entry.
1. The Chapter on Bamboo Gate.
1. Commentary on the Cakkavatti-rāja-sutta. 997.
In the first sutta of the Saṃyutta on Stream-entry, the phrase "kiñcāpi" is a particle used in the senses of favoring and censuring.
For while he favors sovereignty, lordship, and kingship over the four great continents, he censures the fact that the four states of deprivation have not been abandoned.
Reproaching them, the Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, although a wheel-turning monarch... and so forth.
In that context, “of the four continents” means of the four great continents, each surrounded by two thousand smaller islands.

“Sovereignty and lordship”: sovereignty (*issariya*) is the state of being a lord; lordship (*ādhipacca*) is the state of being a ruler. [The phrase] “in this kingdom, not through cutting or breaking” refers to sovereignty and lordship.

"Sovereignty and lordship. "Having exercised" means having caused such a kingdom to be administered. Regarding the phrase, "Even though, monks, he may be a noble disciple," the particle *kiñcāpi* is used here in the sense of favor and praise.

For, favoring his subsistence by means of alms-food and praising the fact that the four states of misery have been abandoned, the Teacher said, "Even though, monks, he may be a noble disciple," and so forth. In this context:
"Endless pieces" means infinite fragments. For even a cloth or garment measuring thirteen cubits is reckoned as "endless pieces" from the point where it has been cut into ten strips.
"With verified confidence" means with unshakable confidence. But is this confidence single or manifold? It is indeed single; it is the confidence that has arrived by way of the Path.
However, in accordance with those factors in which it arises simultaneously and without sequence, it is expressed as "with verified confidence in the Buddha," and so forth.
It is stated in three ways according to the method. And because it is one, it is therefore without differentiation.
For a noble disciple, great confidence, affection, and reverence are not directed toward the Buddha alone and not toward the Dhamma or the Saṅgha;

nor are they directed toward the Dhamma alone and not toward the Buddha or the Saṅgha; nor toward the Saṅgha alone and not toward the Buddha or the Dhamma; nor toward the Buddha or the Dhamma and not toward the Saṅgha. This does not exist.
The phrases beginning with "Thus indeed is the Blessed One" have already been explained in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Beloved by the Noble Ones" means dear and pleasing to the Noble Ones (*ariya*). For the Noble Ones do not violate the five precepts even when they have passed into other existences;
thus, these are dear to them. It is with reference to these that this was said. The terms "unbroken," and so forth, are used in the sense of being faultless.

It has been said: for just as a vessel with a portion of its rim broken is called "broken," one split in the middle is called "perforated," a cow with a patch of dissimilar color in one place is called "spotted," and one variegated with various spots is called "speckled"—in the same way, virtue (sīla) that is broken at the beginning or at the end in succession is called "broken" (khaṇḍa);
that which is broken in the middle is "perforated" (chidda); and [that which is broken] anywhere...
Because two or three [factors] are broken in succession, it is "with flaws" (*sabala*); because they are broken with a single interval, it is "defective" (*kammāsa*).

Their state of being "unbroken" and so forth should be understood through the absence of those faults. "By means of those who are free" (*bhujissehi*) means by means of those things that produce the state of being free.

"Praised by the wise" (*viññuppasatthehi*) means praised by the wise, such as the Buddha and others. "Unadulterated" (*aparāmaṭṭhehi*) means [not thinking], "This was done by you; this was transgressed."

"By those things that are impossible to misapprehend. "Conducive to concentration" means capable of leading to either absorption concentration (*appanā-samādhi*) or access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*).
2. Commentary on the *Brahmacariyogadha Sutta* (The Discourse on the Foundation of the Holy Life)

998. In the second [verse], by the phrase "in whom there is faith," confidence in the Buddha is included; by the word "virtue" (sīla), the virtues dear to the Noble Ones (ariyakanta-sīla) are included;
by the word "confidence" (pasāda), confidence in the Saṅgha is included;

and by the phrase "vision of the Dhamma," confidence in the Dhamma is included—thus the four factors of stream-entry (sotāpattiyaṅga) are stated. "They arrive at the right time" means they reach it at the proper time.
"The bliss of plunging into the holy life" refers to the bliss associated with the three higher paths, which stands having plunged into the holy life.
As for this "confidence" mentioned in the verse, what kind of confidence is it? First, the Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷa-Abhaya said, "It is the confidence of the path.
The Elder Tipiṭaka-Cūḷa-Nāga said, "It is the confidence of reviewing the path that has been attained."
Both elders are wise and learned; the well-spoken words of both are excellent.
This is a mixed praise. 3. Commentary on the Dīghāvu Upāsaka Sutta 999.

In the third [verse], "therefore" (*tasmā*) means because you are seen to possess the four factors of stream-entry (*sotāpatti-aṅga*); therefore, [you are praised] as one who partakes in true knowledge (*vijjābhāgiya*).
"Those who possess the factors of true knowledge. "In all conditioned phenomena" means in all conditioned phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence.
Thus, the insight for the three higher paths has been explained for him. "Affliction" means suffering.
4–5. Commentary on the First Sāriputta Sutta, etc.
1000–1001. The fourth [section] is self-evident. In the fifth, "factor of stream-entry" (*sotāpattiyaṅga*) refers to the factor of acquisition belonging to the preliminary stage of stream-entry.

Furthermore, the qualities already acquired—such as unwavering confidence in the Buddha and so forth—are called the factors of one who has entered the stream; these too are included under the heading of "factors of stream-entry.
Herein, the meaning of both terms is as follows: while serving, associating with, and attending upon true persons, [one hears] the Dhamma...
One who hears [the Dhamma], attends to it properly, and practices the preliminary path in accordance with the Dhamma attains stream-entry (*sotāpatti*).

Thus, association with superior persons (*sappurisa-saṃseva*) and the other factors are "limbs for the sake of stream-entry" (*sotāpatti-attha-aṅga*), and are therefore called "limbs of stream-entry" (*sotāpatti-aṅga*);
alternatively, they are also "limbs of stream-entry" because they are limbs of the stream-entry that is designated as the first path. For one who has penetrated the path of stream-entry...
The path of stream-entry is also a factor of stream-entry because it is a constituent part of it.
6. Commentary on the Thapati Sutta (1002).
"They dwell in Sādhuka" means they live in their own village of property named Sādhuka. Among them...
Isidatta was a once-returner (*sakadāgāmī*), and Purāṇa was a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*) content with his own wife.

They stationed a man on the road because, it is said, the Blessed One’s path of travel passed through their village gate. Therefore, thinking, "The Blessed One might pass by at any time—whether at the right time or not, or while we are asleep or negligent—and then we would not get to see him," they stationed a man in the middle of the road.
"Followed closely behind" means they did not follow from a distance;
rather, while the Blessed One proceeded by way of the footpath in the middle of the cart-track, the others followed along both sides. "Having descended from the road":
for when Buddhas travel with anyone at all, it is proper to offer them a formal welcome.
[They were] standing, having sat for a portion of the day with someone. Therefore, the Blessed One thought:
"It is not appropriate for me to exchange greetings while walking along with these; nor is it appropriate to do so while standing.
For these [monks] have already attained the fruits of mastery in my teaching. It is only by sitting together with them for a portion of the day that one can exchange greetings."
Thinking, “I shall do so,” he descended from the path and approached the foot of a certain tree.

He sat down on the prepared seat. It is said that they went along having had him take a sunshade and sandals, a walking staff, oil for anointing his feet and other such things, the eight kinds of beverages, and a couch with legs; and they brought the couch as well.
Having prepared them, they gave them; the Teacher sat upon that [seat].

"They sat down to one side" means that after saying, "Give the remaining items, such as the sunshade and sandals, to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," they too paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
The entire passage beginning with "He set out on a wandering tour among the Kosalans from Sāvatthī" is spoken with reference to the Middle Country.
Why? Because of its fixed nature. For the Blessed One’s wandering on tour and his causing dawn to break are both fixed:
he wanders only within the Middle Country and causes dawn to break only in the Middle Country. It is because of this fixed nature that it is stated "by way of the Middle Country.
As for the phrase "The Blessed One will be near to us," their joy arises not merely from his mere proximity; [it arises from the certainty of his presence].
Then, thinking, "Now we shall be able to give gifts, perform worship with perfumes, garlands, and the like, listen to the Dhamma, and ask questions," they were filled with joy.
Therefore, householder-stewards, because the household life is a confinement, and because I have now become distant from you— householder-stewards, [the household life is a confinement].
There is no small measure of mental distress, yet nearby there is no small measure of mental joy;
therefore, this too should be understood: "The household life is a confinement. For it is through the fault of the household life that such things happen to you.
But if you were to renounce the household life and go forth, then even as you go with me and come back again, such things would not happen to you.
Explaining this point, he spoke thus. In that context, "confinement" (sambādhatā) should be understood in the sense of being possessed of possessions and possessed of impediments.
For even for one living in a large dwelling, the household life is indeed a confinement by virtue of being possessed of possessions and possessed of impediments.

"The path of dust" (rajāpatho) means the path of the dust of lust, hatred, and delusion; the meaning is the place where they come from. "The open air is the going forth" (abbhokāso pabbajjā) means that the going forth...
Furthermore, it is "open space" in the sense of being without possessions and without impediments.

For even in a four-cubit room, when two monks sit with their cross-legged postures joined together, their renunciation is indeed called "open space" in the sense of being without possessions and without impediments.
And it is sufficient for you, masters of the household, for the sake of diligence—even while dwelling in the cramped life of a householder.
The meaning is that it is appropriate for you to practice only heedfulness.
"Let them sit one in front and one behind"— it is said that those two women were made to sit thus upon two elephants adorned with all ornaments,
with the king’s elephant placed in the middle and the two on either side.
They go [to such places], therefore they spoke thus. "The nāga also must be protected" means he must be protected in such a way that he does not perform any improper act.
"Those sisters also" means they must be protected in such a way that they do not fall into negligence.
"One's own self also" means one's own self must be protected by those who refrain from smiling, laughing, talking, gazing, and so forth.
"By acting in that way, even one's own self cannot be protected. For by acting thus, one must be restrained as 'this man is a traitor.

Therefore, O chamberlains, because the King constantly has you handle royal property, for that reason too the household life is a crowded place, a path of dust. But because he has you handle even a monk who wears rag-robes..."
"There is none; therefore, the life of a renunciant is like the open air. Thus, in all respects, he shows: "Enough, O householders!
You should practice heedfulness; indeed, practice only heedfulness.

"One who has relinquished" (*muttacāga*) means one who has abandoned attachment. "Pure-handed" (*payatapāṇi*) means one whose hands are washed for the purpose of giving to those who come. "Delighting in relinquishment" (*vossaggarata*)...
"Delighting in relinquishment characterized by serenity": one who delights in giving. "Devoted to being asked" means one who is intent on what should be requested.
"Delighting in giving and sharing" means one who delights both in giving and in sharing even the slightest thing that has been obtained.
"Not partitioned" means not having made a division such as, "This shall be ours; this shall be for the bhikkhus"; the meaning is that everything remains simply as something to be given.
7. Commentary on the Veḷudvāra Sutta 1003.
Regarding the seventh [sutta]: "Veḷudvāra" is the name of a village so called because of the presence of a bamboo grove that has come down by tradition at its village gate.
"Attupanāyikaṃ" means that which should be applied to oneself. "Samphappalāpabhāsena" means by speaking frivolous talk. "Samphappalāpabhāsena" [is explained as] by speaking idle chatter.
The meaning is: by means of idle chatter, which is purposeless speech characterized by ignorance.
8–9. Commentary on the First Giñjakāvasatha Sutta, etc., 1004–5. In the eighth [sutta], regarding the phrase "among kinsmen":
there were two sons of a younger uncle and an elder uncle who lived in dependence upon a single pond.
*Gāmā*: in one of those villages. *Giñjakāvasathe*: in a dwelling made of brick. *Orambhāgiyānaṃ*: of those belonging to the lower part;
the meaning is "those which cause the taking of rebirth-linking specifically within the realm of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*).

Alternatively, they are called *orambhāgiya* because they are to be abandoned by the three paths that have received their respective names. Among them, sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) and ill-will (*byāpāda*)—these...

When not suppressed by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) or severed by the Path (*magga*), these two do not allow one to go to the higher realms—the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*) or the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*)—by way of rebirth.
As for the three beginning with personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*), even though they lead to rebirth there, they cause one to be reborn here again;
thus, all of them are indeed "lower-fettering" (*orambhāgiya*). One who is "of a nature not to return" (*anāvattidhamma*)...
The nature of not returning by way of rebirth-linking.

Regarding the phrase "the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion," the state of being attenuated should be understood in two ways: both as their occasional arising and as the mildness of their manifest obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*).
For in the case of a once-returner, lust and the other defilements do not arise as frequently as they do in the case of worldlings (*puthujjana*).
They arise only at certain times. And when they do arise, they do not arise in thick layers as they do for worldlings;
rather, they arise thinly, like the film on a fly's eye. However, the Elder Mahāsīva, the Great Reciter of the Dīgha Nikāya and master of the Tipiṭaka, said:
"Since once-returners have sons and daughters, and even female attendants, their defilements must therefore be thick. This..."

"But it was spoken by way of the attenuation of existence (*bhavatanuka*). Regarding that, the Commentary states: "For a stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*), there is no attenuation of existence beyond seven existences;
for a once-returner (*sakadāgāmin*), there is no attenuation of existence beyond five existences, excluding two;
and for a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), there is no attenuation of existence within the sense-sphere realm (*kāmabhava*), excluding the fine-material and immaterial realms."
Because it has been stated, "For one whose taints are destroyed, there is no thinning of existence (*bhavatanuka*) in any state of becoming," this [position] is rejected.
"This world" refers to this sense-sphere world (*kāmāvacara-loka*). This is the intended meaning here:
for if one who has attained the fruit of a once-returner (*sakadāgāmi-phala*) among humans is reborn among the devas and realizes *arahantship*, then this— [...is so.]
It is well. But if one is unable [to attain it there], one must necessarily return to the human world and realize it.
Even if one has attained the fruit of a once-returner among the devas, if one is reborn among humans and realizes arhatship, that is well.
But if one is unable [to do so], one must necessarily go to the deva-world and realize it.

*Vinipāta* means falling into ruin; one whose nature is not subject to such ruin is *avinipātadhamma*. The meaning is: one whose inherent nature is not to fall into the four states of misery (*apāya*).

*Niyata* means fixed by the fixedness of the Dhamma. *Sambodhiparāyaṇa* means that enlightenment—consisting of the three higher paths—is his supreme goal (*paraṃ ayanaṃ*), his destination, refuge, and what is inevitably to be attained; thus he is *sambodhiparāyaṇa*.

"Vihesāvesā" means: Ānanda, this is merely physical fatigue for the Tathāgata as he surveys the various destinations of knowledge, the various rebirths through knowledge, and the various future destinies through knowledge; it indicates that Buddhas have no mental distress.

"Dhammādāsaṃ" means a mirror made of Dhamma. "Yena" means by which mirror of Dhamma he is endowed. "Khīṇāpāyaduggativinipāto" means the states of deprivation, miserable rebirths, and the fallen realms have been exhausted.

This is stated solely by way of synonyms for hell and the other realms. For hell and the rest are called *apāya* because they are states from which there is no escape (*aya*) once one has fallen away from prosperity;
they are the destination and refuge of suffering. They are called *duggati* (bad destination).
They are called *vinipāta* (ruinous fall) because those who have committed evil deeds fall into them helplessly (*vivasā*). The ninth [verse] is self-evident.
10. Commentary on the Third Giñjakāvasatha Sutta 1006.
In the tenth [sutta], "more than fifty" (*paropaññāsa*) means exceeding fifty. "More than ninety" (*sādhikanavuti*) means exceeding ninety.
"Six in excess" (*chātirekāni*) means six more. It is said that although that village was not very large, there were many noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*) residing there. Regarding that:
Therein, by the disease of snake-bite, two million four hundred thousand living beings died all at once;
among them, there were such-and-such numbers of noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*). The rest is clear throughout.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Bamboo Gate Chapter (*Veḷudvāravagga*).
2. The Chapter on the Royal Monastery (Rājakārāmavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Saṅgha of One Thousand Bhikkhunīs (Sahassabhikkhunisaṅghasuttavaṇṇanā) 1007.

In the first [discourse] of the second [chapter], "in the royal monastery" (rājakārāme) means in that monastery which had received its name because it was caused to be built by a king; it was [built] by the king.
It was performed by Pasenadi of Kosala. It is said that during the First Enlightenment, upon seeing the Teacher who had attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of fame, the sectarians thought:
"The ascetic Gotama has attained the pinnacle of gain and the summit of fame;
yet he has not attained this pinnacle of gain and summit of fame by relying on any particular virtue or concentration. Rather, he has seized the very head of the earth."
“If we too could have a monastery built near Jetavana, we would have attained the highest gain and the highest fame.
Having thus exhorted their respective attendants, they obtained one hundred thousand kahāpaṇas and, taking them with them, went into the presence of the king.
The king asked, “What is this? They replied, “We wish to establish a monastery for the non-Buddhist sects near Jetavana.”
They gave bribes, saying, "Let us do it; if the ascetic Gotama or the disciples of the ascetic Gotama come, do not allow them to stop us.
Having accepted the bribes, the king said, "Go and have it built.
They went and, having had their own attendants bring the building materials, they proceeded with the erection of the pillars and other work.
They made a great clamor, a loud noise, a single tumultuous uproar. The Teacher emerged from the Fragrant Chamber, stood at the entrance, and asked:
"Ānanda, who are those making such a loud noise, such a great noise? They sound like fishermen hauling in their catch!
"Venerable Sir, it is the heretics who are building a monastery for the heretics near the Jeta Grove. "Ānanda, these people are opposed to the Teaching."
“They will cause discomfort for the community of monks; having informed the king, have them removed.
The Elder went with the community of monks and stood at the king’s gate. They announced to the king, “Your Majesty, the Elders have arrived.
Because he had accepted a bribe, the king did not come out. The Elders went and reported this to the Teacher.
The Teacher dispatched Sāriputta and Moggallāna. The king did not grant them an audience either.
They returned and reported to the Teacher, "Venerable Sir, the king has not gone out.
At that very moment, the Teacher declared, "He shall not be permitted to pass away while remaining in his own kingdom."
On the second day, he himself went forth accompanied by the community of monks and stood at the king’s gate.
Hearing that the Teacher had arrived, the king came out, led him into his residence, and having seated him upon a couch of precious materials, offered him rice gruel and solid food.
After the Teacher had consumed the gruel and the hard food, [the king said: "Until the meal is finished, remain in the presence of the Teacher."
Thinking, “I shall sit down,” he approached and sat beside the king.

Without saying, “Great King, you have done such-and-such a thing,” [the Elder thought], “I shall persuade him by means of a reason,” and related this past event: “Great King, it is not fitting for those who have gone forth to cause one another to fight.
In the past as well, sages, having caused one another to fight, [were destroyed] along with their kingdoms.”
"The king has entered the ocean. "When was that, Blessed One?
"In the past, Great King, in the kingdom of Bharu, a king named Bharu reigned.
Two groups of seers, each consisting of five hundred, went from the foot of a mountain to the city of Bharu for the purpose of consuming salt and sour gruel; they arrived not far from the city."
There were two trees; the group of seers who arrived first sat down at the foot of one tree, and those who arrived later sat down at the foot of the other.
Having dwelt there as long as they pleased, they departed for the foothills of the mountain.
When they returned again, they sat down at the very same roots of their respective trees. As time passed, one of the trees withered; when it had withered—
The ascetics who arrived later thought, "This tree is large; it will suffice for both us and them," and they sat down on one portion of the root of the other tree.
When those coming after them did not enter the base of the tree but remained outside, they asked, "Why are you sitting here?
The teachers replied, "Our tree is dry; this tree is large."
"You too must enter; it will suffice for both you and us. They replied, "We will not enter; you yourselves come out!
Having thus increased their dispute, [the monks] seized them by the hands and other limbs, saying, "You shall not go out by your own will!
and dragged them out. Thinking, "Very well, we shall train them," they used their supernormal power (*iddhi*) to create two golden wheels.
Having fashioned a silver axle and rolling it along, they went to the king’s gate.
They announced to the king, "Your Majesty, ascetics stand here bearing such a gift. The king was delighted and said, "Summon them!
Having summoned them, he said, "A great deed has been performed by you; is there anything we can do for you? "Yes, Great King," [they replied].
“There is a place for sitting at the foot of a single tree; it has been taken by other seers. Grant that to us.
The king sent men and had the ascetics driven out.
Standing outside, they looked on, wondering, “What indeed did they give to receive this? and seeing what it was, they thought, “We too—”
Thinking, "We shall take it back after giving a bribe," they used their supernormal power (*iddhi*) to create a golden chariot-fender, took it with them, and departed.
When the king saw this, he was delighted and asked, "Venerable sirs, what must be done?
They replied, "Great King, another group of seers is sitting at the foot of our tree; have that tree granted to us. The king sent men and had them driven out.
Having quarreled with one another, the ascetics, feeling remorseful and thinking, "We have acted improperly," returned to the foot of the mountain.
Then a deity, becoming angry and thinking, "This king, having taken bribes from the hands of two groups of seers,
caused them to quarrel with each other," caused the great ocean to overflow and [submerge] that king.
They turned the conquered territory, measuring a thousand yojanas, into nothing but ocean.
"Having placed the seers in between, King Bharu—so I have heard—was destroyed along with his kingdom; that king passed away from existence."

When the Blessed One had thus shown this past event, the king—since the mere mention of the Buddhas inspires deep conviction—reflected upon his own actions and thought, "Without due consideration, I committed an act that should not have been done.
Having caused the heretics to be driven out with the words, "Go, men! Drive them out!", he reflected: "I have caused [this to be done]..."

"There is no monastery; we shall have a monastery built right there. Having said this, he had the monastery built without even giving them the building materials. It was with reference to this that it was said.
2–3. Commentary on the Brāhmaṇa Sutta, etc.

1008–9. In the second verse, "leading to rising" means leading to one’s own prosperity. "One should await death" means one should desire death, or one should long for it. The third verse is self-evident. 4.
Commentary on the *Duggatibhayasutta* (The Discourse on the Fear of an Evil Destiny). 1010.
In the fourth verse, "one who has transcended the fear of all evil destinies" implies that human misfortune is rejected.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on the Fear of the Lower Realms and Ruin (Duggativinipātabhayasutta) 1011.
In the fifth [discourse], by the phrase "one who has transcended all fear of the lower realms and ruin," the four states of misery, together with the wretchedness of human existence, are excluded.
6. Commentary on the First Discourse on Friends and Enemies (Paṭhamamittāmaccasutta)
1012. Sixth: "Friends" refers to transactional friends who share material goods in each other's homes.

"Ministers" refers to those whose functions operate together in matters such as consultation, deliberation, and bodily postures. "Relatives" refers to those on the side of one's father and mother-in-law.
"Kinsmen" refers to those sharing the same blood, such as brothers, sisters, maternal uncles, and so forth.
7. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Friends and Relatives (Mittāmaccasutta) 1013.
In the seventh [verse], "change" (*aññathatta*) is of many kinds: change of clarity, change of state, change of destiny, change of characteristic, and change through transformation.
Among these, it is the change of state (*bhāva-ññathatta*) regarding the great elements that is intended here.
For when the earth element, which exists in a solid state as gold and so forth, melts and enters into the state of water, its prior state disappears and a change in its state becomes apparent;
yet its characteristic does not disappear, for it remains characterized by hardness.
And when the water element, which exists in the form of a liquid consistency as sugarcane juice and so forth, dries up...
When it reaches the state of a dense mass of earth, its prior state disappears and a change in its nature becomes apparent.
However, its characteristic does not disappear; it still possesses the characteristic of cohesion.

In this context, "change" refers specifically to a change in destination (*gati-aññathatta*), for that does not exist for a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*). There is also a change in clarity (*pasāda-ññathatta*).

There is indeed no [other] non-existence; however, here, in order to manifest the fruit of serene confidence (*pasāda*), only the alteration of destiny (*gati-aññathatta*) has been shown. The rest is clear in every respect.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Chapter on the Royal Monastery (*Rājakārāmavagga*). 3. The Chapter on Saranāni (*Saraṇānivagga*).
1–2. Commentary on the First Mahānāma Sutta, etc. 1017–18.

Regarding the first [sutta] of the third [chapter]: "Prosperous" (*iddha*) means abundant with oil, honey, molasses, and so forth. "Flourishing" (*phīta*) means beautifully blossomed through ornaments such as those for the hands, head, and neck.
"Crowded with people" (*ākiṇṇamanussa*) means filled with people without any gaps. "With congested thoroughfares" (*sambādhabyūha*): here, "thoroughfares" (*byūha*) are so called...
"Sambādhabyūha" means that because the streets are not separated [by crossroads], those who exit by the very path they entered find themselves in many congested enclosures (*byūha*);
this also illustrates the dense population of the city.
"By one who is wandering" means by one who roams here and there with agitated conduct. The second [verse] is self-evident.
3. Commentary on the Godha Sutta (Sakka) 1019.
Regarding the third [sutta], the Blessed One himself would know whether one is endowed with these qualities or not.
This refers to Sakka’s recognition of the state of stream-entry (*sotāpatti*) for a person endowed with three qualities, and with four...
He spoke with the intention that only the Blessed One knows the state of stream-entry (sotāpanna) for one endowed with such qualities.
"Some occurrence of phenomena might arise" means that some cause whatsoever might arise.
"The Blessed One would be on one side and the Saṅgha of bhikkhus on the other" refers to that cause having arisen whereby the Blessed One [differs] from the Saṅgha of bhikkhus in their various views.
"Having made one statement, he should speak as one"; the meaning is that the Saṅgha of monks, speaking one thing, would be "one.
For this very reason it is said: "Whatever statement you make, I would accept that very same one. But surely, for a noble disciple, there is no diversity in his confidence toward the Triple Gem;
so why did he speak thus? [The answer is: Because of the Blessed One’s omniscience.
Thus it occurs to him: "The Saṅgha of bhikkhus might speak even without knowing due to their own lack of omniscience, but for the Teacher, there is no such thing as ignorance.
Therefore he spoke thus. "Apart from what is lovely, apart from what is wholesome" means: I speak only of what is lovely and only of what is wholesome;
I do not speak of anything other than the lovely and the wholesome. Furthermore, this is free from the fault of being blameless.
4. Commentary on the First Saraṇāni-Sakkasutta 1020.

In this fourth [sutta], the phrase "here, Mahānāma, a certain person" is introduced to show that not only Saraṇāni himself was liberated from the states of misery, but these persons as well were liberated. "They find satisfaction through mere reflection" means by way of measure.
And they endure the looking upon [the world]. By this, he shows the person standing on the path who follows by the Dhamma (dhammānusāri).

For it is not appropriate to say of the person standing on the path that "he has gone to no hell" in the sense that he is already liberated from the states of misery (apāya), or that he will be liberated;
however, it is appropriate to say that "he is being liberated. And because he is being liberated, therefore he is not called one who "has gone."

When he is called "one who does not come," the meaning is that he does not go. By the phrases "mere faith" and "mere affection," he indicates the person standing on the path of the follower by faith (*saddhānusāri*).
By saying "great sal trees," he speaks while pointing out four great *sāra* trees standing nearby.
"He undertook the training at the time of death" shows that at the moment of death, he was one who fulfilled the three trainings (*sikkhā*).
5. Commentary on the Second Saraṇāni Sutta 1021.
In the fifth [verse], "bad field" (*dukkhetta*) means an uneven field. "Bad soil" (*dubbhūma*) means saline ground, afflicted by salt. "Broken" (*khaṇḍāni*) means shattered.
"Rotting" (*pūtīni*) means having become putrid through being soaked with water. "Struck by wind and heat" (*vātātapahatāni*) means [struck] by wind and heat.
Because they have been worn out, they have become free from impurities. "Without their core taken" means their core has not been extracted; their core has not been seized.
"Not well-stored" means they were not placed securely by being put into storehouses and such. "Well-stored" means they did not move from their place of storage for four months.
6. Commentary on the First Anāthapiṇḍika Sutta.
1022. In the sixth instance, "feeling would be allayed at once" means that feeling would be allayed in an instant.
"By wrong knowledge" means by wrong reflection; "by wrong liberation" means by a liberation that does not lead out [from suffering].
Therefore, the verse beginning with "Faith and virtue... has already been explained. "Yatra hi nāma" means "one who indeed."
7. Commentary on the Second Anāthapiṇḍika Sutta 1023.

In the seventh [sutta], "the fear of death pertaining to the future life" means the fear of death caused by the future life. "Suitable for householders" means appropriate for laypeople. The rest is clear in every respect.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Saraṇāni Chapter.
4. The Chapter on the Floods of Merit (Puññābhisandavagga) 1. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Floods of Merit (Paṭhamapuññābhisandasuttavaṇṇanā) 1027.

In the first [discourse] of the fourth [chapter], "floods of merit" (*puññābhisandā*) and "floods of the wholesome" (*kusalābhisandā*) refer to rivers of merit and rivers of the wholesome. "Nutriments of happiness" (*sukhassāhārā*) means conditions for happiness.
4. Commentary on the First Devapada Sutta 1030.
In the fourth [verse], "devapadāni" means the footprints traversed by the knowledge of the devas, or by the knowledge of a deva.
"Visuddhiyā" means for the purpose of purification. "Pariyodapanāya" means for the purpose of cleansing thoroughly, that is, for the purpose of making radiant. In this sutta...
Even the four persons who have attained the fruits [of the path] are called "gods" in the sense of being purified.
8. Commentary on the Vassa Sutta 1034.
In the eighth [verse], "having gone to the further shore": the "further shore" (pāra) is said to be Nibbāna; the meaning is, "having reached that. For the destruction of the taints (āsava).
"They lead toward" does not mean that they lead toward [Nibbāna] after first going to Nibbāna; rather, they lead toward it while they are themselves proceeding.
However, the teaching was formulated in this manner.
10. Commentary on the Nandiyasakkasutta.
1036. “For seclusion by day and for retirement by night”: this means for the sake of seclusion during the day and for the sake of retirement at night.
“The states do not become manifest” means that the states of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) do not arise. The rest is clear in all respects.
The fourth chapter, on the Floods of Merit, is concluded.
5. Sagāthakapuññābhisandavagga 1.
Commentary on the First Abhisanda Sutta 1037.
In the first [sutta] of the fifth [chapter], "incalculable" (*asaṅkhyeyya*) means incalculable by the measure of an *āḷhaka*; however, in terms of *yojanas*, its—
There is a number. "Many terrors" (*bahubherava*) means it is full of many terrors by way of terrifying objects, both conscious and unconscious.
"Diverse" (*puthu*) means many. "Flowing" (*savantī*) means streaming forth. "Approaching" (*upayantī*) means coming near. 2.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on Abundances (*Abhisanda-sutta*).
1038. In the second [sutta], "where these great rivers flow together and meet" means that in which these great rivers converge and become one;
the meaning is that they become continuous. 1039.
In the third, "one desiring merit" means one who seeks merit. "Established in the wholesome" means established in the wholesome path.
"He develops the path for the attainment of the Deathless" means he develops the path of Arahatship for the purpose of reaching Nibbāna.

"Attainment of the essence of the Dhamma": the essence of the Dhamma is called the Noble Fruit (ariyaphala); one who has that attainment of the essence of the Dhamma is "one who has attained the essence of the Dhamma," meaning one who has attained the fruit.
"Delighting in destruction" means delighting in the destruction of the defilements (kilesa).
4. Commentary on the First Discourse on Great Wealth (Paṭhamamahaddhanasutta-vaṇṇanā) 1040.

In the fourth [discourse], "wealthy and of great wealth" means that he is both wealthy and of great wealth by means of the sevenfold noble wealth (*ariyadhana*). By that very same possession, he is "of great enjoyment. The rest is clear in every respect.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Flowing Forth of Merit with Verses (Sagāthakapuññābhisandavagga).
6. The Chapter on the Wise (Sappaññavagga) 2. Commentary on the Discourse on Having Spent the Rains (Vassaṃvuttasutta-vaṇṇanā) 1048.
In the second sutta of the sixth chapter, this is the intended meaning: a monk who is a stream-enterer, not falling into complacency because of just that much, [should continue striving].
Having integrated those very same faculties, powers, and factors of enlightenment, and having increased insight, one will reach the path of the once-returner;
the once-returner [will reach] the path of the non-returner; and the non-returner [will reach] the path of arahantship.
It is with reference to this meaning that the Blessed One has declared this sequence and tradition in the teaching within this sutta.
3. Commentary on the Dhammadinna Sutta 1049.
Regarding the third [sutta], "Dhammadinna" is one among seven persons.

During the time of the Buddha, there were the lay follower Dhammadinna, the lay follower Visākha, the householder Ugga, the householder Citta, Hatthaka of Āḷavī, Cūḷa-Anāthapiṇḍika, and... [the seventh].
Mahānāthapiṇḍika—these seven persons were accompanied by a retinue of five hundred lay followers (*upāsaka*). Among them, he was one of these.
"Profound" means profound in Dhamma, such as the *Salla-sutta* and others. "Profound in meaning" means profound in sense, such as the *Cetanā-suttanta* and others.

"Supramundane" means those that illuminate supramundane matters, such as the *Asaṅkhata-saṃyutta* and others. "Connected with emptiness" means those that illustrate the emptiness of sentient beings and so forth.
The *Khajjanika-sutta* and others. "Having attained, we shall dwell" means: having acquired it, we shall dwell.

"In this way, Dhammadinna, you should train yourselves"—thus, while fulfilling the moon-like practice, the chariot-yoked practice, the practice of the noble silence (*moneyya*), and the practice of the great noble lineage, you should train yourselves. Thus the Teacher [spoke] to these...
He placed an unbearable burden upon the lay followers. Why? It is said that these men did not request instruction while standing on their own ground;
rather, as if they were capable of lifting every burden without distinction, they requested, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One exhort us.
Therefore, placing an unbearable burden upon them, the Teacher spoke thus: "Indeed, not for them..."
This is not so; rather, it should be understood that the letter *na* here is merely for the purpose of euphonic junction (*byañjanasandhi*).
"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means: because you are now requesting instruction while standing on your own ground.
4. Commentary on the Gilāna Sutta (The Sick Monk)

1050. Regarding the fourth [phrase], "But this is not indeed [so]": "na kho amhehi etaṃ" means "this is certainly not [the case] for us. "A wise lay follower" (sappañño upāsako) refers specifically to one who has attained the stream-entry (sotāpanna).
"By means of the qualities that provide consolation" (assāsanīyehi dhammehi) means by means of those qualities that produce consolation.

"May the venerable one console himself" (assāsatāyasmā) means "may the venerable one find comfort. "Mārisa" refers to one who is subject to death. "Subject to death" (maraṇadhammo) means having the nature of death. "Direct your resolve" (adhimocehi) means "place [your mind]."
"Adhimocitaṃ" means established. "Of one whose mind is thus liberated" means of one whose mind is liberated by the liberation of the fruit of Arahantship.
"That which is called 'liberated by liberation'"—whatever distinction regarding liberation might need to be stated concerning this liberation, that I do not speak of.
For, in the case of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, regarding the duties for the shrine courtyard, the Bodhi-tree courtyard, and the eighty rules of conduct...
Thus, there is no measure for the qualities to be acquired; however, once the path or the fruit has been realized, there is no difference between lay followers and monks.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on the Attainment of Wisdom.

1055. Regarding the phrase "in the ninth [chapter], they lead to the acquisition of wisdom": here it should be understood that the seven trainees (sekkha) are said to "acquire wisdom," while the one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is said to have "already acquired wisdom. The same principle applies to the subsequent sections beginning with "for the increase of wisdom" and so forth.
The rest is entirely plain in every respect.
The Sixth Chapter: On Wisdom (Sappaññavagga).
7. The Great Wisdom Chapter (Mahāpaññavagga). 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Great Wisdom (Mahāpaññāsuttavaṇṇanā).

1058. Regarding the passage beginning with "In the seventh [chapter], they lead to great wisdom," the meaning of all terms in every instance is to be understood exactly according to the method stated in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga*: "Great wisdom is so called because it grasps great meanings," and so forth. The rest is clear throughout.
The commentary on the *Sotāpatti-saṃyutta* is finished.
12. Connected Discourses on Truth (Saccasaṃyutta) 1.
The Chapter on Concentration (Samādhivagga) 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Concentration (Samādhisuttavaṇṇanā)

1071. In the first discourse of the Saṃyutta on Truths, the Teacher—thinking that those monks were falling away from one-pointedness of mind (*citt’ekaggatā*)—began this teaching with the words, “Therefore, monks, ‘This is suffering,’ [‘This is the origin of suffering,’ ‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering’], so that they might attain one-pointedness of mind, develop their meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*), and reach distinction. Thus he spoke. Therefore, monks, “This is suffering.”
Regarding the phrase "yoga is to be practiced," here the cutting off of causes should be understood by way of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*), and so forth. For this is what is meant:

"Monks, because a concentrated monk understands the four truths as they truly are, therefore, you too, being concentrated, for the sake of understanding the four truths as they truly are, [should practice] yoga [with the thought]: 'This is suffering.'"
It is to be practiced. Likewise, because the four truths become manifest only through the appearance of a Tathāgata,
because they have been well-analyzed by the Tathāgata, because they possess immeasurable synonyms and immeasurable words and phrases,
and because the cycle of existence increases as long as they have not been penetrated— yet from the moment they are penetrated, it no longer does so.
It increases; therefore, thinking "in this way the round will not increase for us," you must apply yourselves to the practice: "This is suffering.
2. Commentary on the *Paṭisallāna Sutta* 1072.
The second [sutta] was spoken for the purpose of those who lack physical seclusion attaining physical seclusion.
3. Commentary on the First Discourse on the Son of Good Family, etc.
(1073–75). In the third [discourse], "for the sake of realization" (*abhisamayāya*) means for the purpose of clear comprehension (*abhisamaya*).

And here, by "ascetics and brahmins," those who follow the Dispensation (*sāsana*) are intended. Likewise in the fourth and fifth [discourses]; however, these were spoken according to the inclinations of those who would understand through various modes of expression.
6. Commentary on the Second Discourse on Ascetics and Brahmins (Dutiyasamaṇabrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā) 1076.

"They proclaimed him as one who has attained full enlightenment" means they proclaimed themselves, saying, "I have attained full enlightenment. For in this discourse, both omniscient Buddhas and [other] ascetics are included under the term "ascetics" (samaṇa).
10. Commentary on the Discourse on Animal Talk (Tiracchānakathā-sutta-vaṇṇanā)
1080. In the tenth [section], *anekavihitam* means "of many kinds. *Tiracchānakatham* refers to talk that is "animal-like" because it does not lead to the paths of heaven or liberation.

Regarding *rājakatham* and the others: talk concerning kings—such as "Mahāsammata, Mandhātā, Dhammāsoka were so majestic"—is *rājakatham*. The same method applies to talk concerning thieves and so forth.
Among these, talk concerning householders in the manner of "Such-and-such a king was handsome and beautiful to behold," and so forth, constitutes frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).
However, talk that occurs in the form of "Even he, who possessed such great power, has come to destruction," remains within the state of a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
Regarding thieves as well, [talk such as] "Mūladeva was so powerful" or "Meghamāla was so powerful"—of these...
Discourse based on worldly attachments such as, “Oh, what heroes! regarding kamma, is frivolous talk (*tiracchānakathā*).

Even regarding battles such as the Mahābhārata war, discourse that proceeds by way of attachment to sensual pleasure—such as, “So-and-so was killed by so-and-so in this way; he was pierced in that way”—is frivolous talk.
However, when it occurs in the form, “Even they have indeed come to destruction,” it becomes a subject of meditation (*kammaṭṭhāna*) in every respect. Furthermore:

Regarding food and so forth, it is not permissible to speak by way of sensual gratification (*kāmasāda*), saying, "Thus we ate, consumed, drank, and enjoyed that which was endowed with such color, fragrance, flavor, and texture.
However, having made it purposeful (*sātthaka*), one may say:
"Formerly, there was food, drink, clothing, bedding, garlands, scents, and ointments endowed with such color and other qualities..."
It is permissible to say, "We gave to those who were virtuous; we made offerings at the cetiya.

However, even in conversations regarding relatives and the like, it is not permissible to speak out of a sense of attachment, saying, "Our relatives are brave and capable," or "In the past, we traveled about in such diverse vehicles. But if one speaks for a purposeful reason, [saying] "They too..."
One should not say, "Our relatives have perished," or "In the past we gave such sandals to the Saṅgha.

Even in talk about villages and the like, it is not permissible to speak with a sense of gratification—such as by way of whether they are well-settled or ill-settled, or whether there is plenty of food or scarcity—nor to say, "The inhabitants of that village are brave and capable.
However, if it serves a purpose, one may say, "They are faithful..."
It is permissible to say, “she was confident,” or “she has reached destruction. The same principle applies to talk concerning cities, royal capitals, and provinces.

Regarding talk about women, it is not permissible to speak in terms of gratification based on their complexion, shape, and so forth; however, it is permissible to say, “she was faithful, confident, and has reached destruction.
The same applies to talk about heroes, such as saying, “the warrior named Nandamitta was a hero.”
