It is not permissible to speak in terms of gratification (*assāda*); it is only permissible to say, "He was faithful and confident; [that state] has come to an end.
There is also a reading *surākathā*. Even regarding that talk about liquor, it is not permissible to speak in terms of gratification, such as, "Liquor of such a kind, when drunk, produces delight";
rather, it must be spoken in terms of its disadvantage (*ādīnava*), according to the method beginning with, "[It is] conducive to madness," and so forth.

It is permissible. Regarding talk about streets (*visikhākathā*), it is not permissible to speak out of a sense of gratification (*assādavasena*) such as, “That street is well-situated,” “That street is poorly-situated,” or “The inhabitants of that street are brave and capable”;
however, it is permissible to say, “They are faithful, confident, and have reached destruction [of the taints].
Talk about a water-pot stand (*kumbhaṭṭhānakathā*) refers to talk about a watering place; it also refers to talk about a slave-girl carrying a water-pot (*kumbhadāsī*).

Or: even she [is not permitted] by way of enjoyment on the grounds that "she is attractive, skilled in dancing and singing"; it is only permissible in the manner of "she is faithful, confident," and so forth.
"Talk about the departed" (pubbapetakathā) is talk concerning deceased relatives; the determination (vinicchaya) therein is the same as for talk concerning living relatives.
"Diverse talk" (nānattakathā) is talk of various kinds, devoid of meaning, distinct from the preceding and succeeding types of talk. "Worldly gossip" (lokakkhāyikā)—
“This world was created by whom? It was created by one named So-and-so; the crow is white because its bones are white;
the crane is red because its blood is red”—such are the discursive arguments and frivolous debates of the Lokāyatikas.

The so-called “Exposition of the Ocean” [begins]: “Why is the ocean called *sāgara*? It is *sāgara* because it was dug by the god Sāgara; ‘It was dug by me,’ [he said], making the gesture with his hand.”
"Because it was reported, the ocean [exists]"—such is talk that merely reports on the ocean to no purpose. Thus, "existence" (*bhava*) and "non-existence" (*abhava*):
whatever talk is engaged in after stating some such meaningless cause is "talk about existence and non-existence" (*itibhavābhavakathā*).
And herein, "existence" means eternalism; "non-existence" means annihilationism. "Existence" means increase; "non-existence" means decrease. "Existence" means sensual pleasure...
"Non-existence" refers to self-mortification. Thus, together with these six kinds of talk concerning existence and non-existence, there are what are called the thirty-two types of "animal talk.
The remainder is clear in meaning throughout.
This concludes the first section.

2. The Chapter on the Setting in Motion of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattanavagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on the Setting in Motion of the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakkappavattanasuttavaṇṇanā) 1081.
In the first [discourse] of the second [chapter], "At Bārāṇasī" means in the city of that name. "In the Deer Park at Isipatana" means in the [park] of the seers (isīnaṃ).
In the monastery known as Migadāya (the Deer Park), so called because it was given as a gift of safety to the deer that had acquired that name through their constant coming and going;
for here all the Omniscient Ones who have arisen fall [upon it], meaning they sit down for the purpose of setting the Wheel of Dhamma in motion.
Having emerged from the attainment of cessation after seven days had passed from the Nandamūla mountain cave, he went to Lake Anotatta.
Having performed their duties such as washing their faces, they come through the air and descend here in order to alight at the dwelling place of the Paccekabuddhas;
they also assemble here for the purpose of the Uposatha and on non-Uposatha days, and when returning to Gandhamādana, they likewise take flight from this very spot.
Because of this coming and going of the seers (isīnaṃ), it is called "Isipatana" (the Seers' Descent).
"Addressed": beginning from the time he made his resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha, while fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs), he eventually went forth in his final existence,
reached the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), and sitting there upon the invincible throne (aparājita-pallaṅka),
having shattered the army of Māra, he recollected his past lives during the first watch of the night and attained the divine eye (dibbacakkhu) during the middle watch.
Having purified himself, at the conclusion of the final watch of the night, he attained omniscience while making the ten-thousandfold world system resound;
after spending seven weeks at the seat of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), requested by Mahābrahmā to teach the Dhamma,
he surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and, out of compassion for the world, went to Bārāṇasī and instructed the group of five monks, turning the Wheel of Dhamma.
Desiring to set it forth, he addressed them:
"Bhikkhus, these two extremes. These two, bhikkhus, are two divisions.
Now, with the utterance of this phrase, the sound of the utterance reached down to the Avīci hell and up to the peak of existence (bhavagga), spreading throughout the ten-thousandfold world system.
He stood there. At that very moment, eighteen koṭis of Brahmās assembled;
while the sun was setting in the western direction, the full moon, conjoined with the Āsāḷha constellation, was rising in the eastern direction.
At that time, the Blessed One, beginning this Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, said: "Bhikkhus, these two extremes... and so forth.
In this context, "by one who has gone forth" means by one who has entered the homeless life after cutting the fetters of a householder.

"Should not be cultivated" means should not be indulged in. "And that devotion to the pleasure of sensual desires among sensual pleasures" refers to the pursuit of defiled sensual pleasure regarding objective sensual objects.
"Low" means base. "Vulgar" means belonging to those who dwell in villages. "Common to the ordinary person" means [belonging to] blind, foolish people.
*Āciṇṇo*. "Un-Aryan" (*anariyo*) means not an Aryan, not pure, not supreme, or not belonging to the Aryans.
"Connected with what is harmful" (*anatthasaṃhito*) means not connected with what is beneficial; the meaning is that it does not provide the cause for welfare and happiness.

"Devotion to self-mortification" (*attakilamathānuyogo*) means devotion to one's own mortification; the meaning is the infliction of suffering upon oneself. "Suffering" (*dukkho*) [refers] to such things as lying on a bed of thorns.
It brings suffering through the killing of oneself.

It is "vision-producing" (*cakkhukaraṇī*) because it produces the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*). The second term is a synonym for that very same thing. "For the sake of peace" (*upasamāya*) means for the sake of the pacification of the defilements (*kilesa*).
"For direct knowledge" (*abhiññāya*) means for the sake of directly knowing the four truths. "For full enlightenment" (*sambodhāya*) means for the sake of fully awakening to those very same truths.
"For the sake of Nibbāna" means for the realization of Nibbāna. Whatever else might need to be said here has already been stated below in various places.
The discourse on the Truths (*sacca-kathā*) has also been explained in detail in every aspect in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Three turnings" (*tiparivaṭṭa*) refers to the three turnings consisting of the knowledge of the Truths, the knowledge of the task, and the knowledge of what has been done.
For herein, the knowledge that knows the four truths as they truly are—namely, “This is the noble truth of suffering;

this is the origin of suffering”—is called *sacca-ñāṇa* (knowledge of the truths). The knowledge that knows the task to be performed regarding those very truths—namely, “It is to be fully understood; it is to be abandoned”—is called *kicca-ñāṇa* (knowledge of what is to be done).
The knowledge that knows the state of having completed each respective task—namely, “It has been fully understood; it has been abandoned”—is [called *kata-ñāṇa*].

"Knowledge of what has been done" (katañāṇa) means this. "Twelve aspects" (dvādasākāra) refers to those same [three turnings] having twelve aspects by way of three aspects for each of the [four] truths.
"Vision of knowledge" (ñāṇadassana) is the vision consisting of the knowledge arisen by way of these twelve aspects of the three turnings.
"The eye of Dhamma" (dhammacakkhu): elsewhere, the three paths and the three fruits are called the eye of Dhamma.
Here, it is the first path itself.
Regarding the "Wheel of Dhamma," this refers both to the knowledge of penetration (*paṭivedha-ñāṇa*) and the knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*).

For indeed, there is the twelvefold knowledge of penetration that arose regarding the Four Truths while he was seated at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhipallaṅka*), as well as [the twelvefold knowledge] while he was seated at Isipatana.

The knowledge of teaching (*desanā-ñāṇa*) set in motion by the teaching of truth is also called the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). For both of these are indeed the very knowledge that proceeds from the breast of the One Possessing Ten Powers (*dasabala*).
By the Blessed One revealing [the truth] through this teaching, it is said that the Wheel of Dhamma was set in motion.
Furthermore, this Wheel of Dhamma [was turned] until the Elder Aññā Koṇḍañña [and the others], together with eighteen koṭis of Brahmās...

As long as he establishes himself together with the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala), the Blessed One is said to be "setting it in motion"; and once established, it is said to have been "set in motion.
With reference to this, it was said: "When the Wheel of Dhamma had been set in motion by the Blessed One, the earth-dwelling deities raised a cry," and so forth.
Therein, "earth-dwellers" refers to the deities who inhabit the earth.

"They made their voices heard" means that they uttered the words beginning with "This has been understood by the Blessed One," having given a simultaneous shout of approval. "The radiance" refers to the radiance of the knowledge of omniscience;
for it then shone forth, surpassing the natural splendor of the gods. "Koṇḍañña has indeed understood!"—thus [they spoke].
The sound of the utterance of this *udāna* also pervaded the ten-thousandfold world system and remained there.
9. Commentary on the Saṅkāsana Sutta: 1089.
In the ninth [verse], "immeasurable qualities" means immeasurable syllables (*akkhara*). "Phrases" (*byañjana*) is a synonym for those very same things.
Or, "parts of the phonemes" refers to what are called consonants (*byañjana*). "Clarification" (*saṅkāsanā*) refers to the case-endings (*vibhatti*).
For when each truth is being explained in its entirety in every aspect, there is no end to the phonemes and so forth. Therefore, he spoke thus.
10. Commentary on the *Tathasutta* (Discourse on Suchness)
1090. In the tenth [meaning], it is "such" (*tatha*) in the sense of not abandoning its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). For suffering is indeed stated to be suffering;

because its intrinsic nature is unfailing, it is "not otherwise" (*avitatha*), for suffering never becomes non-suffering. Because it does not undergo change into another state, it is "not otherwise" (*anaññatha*);
for suffering never attains the state of the origin (*samudaya*) and so forth. This same method applies to the origin and the other [truths] as well.
The second chapter: The Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma.
3. The Chapter on Koṭigāma. 1.
Commentary on the Koṭigāma Sutta.
1091. In the first [alternative] of the third [tetrad], "non-comprehension" (*ananubodha*) means by way of not comprehending; "non-penetration" (*appaṭivedha*) means by way of not penetrating.
2. Commentary on the Second Koṭigāma Sutta 1092.

In the second [sutta], "liberation of mind" (*cetovimutti*) and "liberation by wisdom" (*paññāvimutti*) are names for the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) and the wisdom of fruition (*phalapaññā*).
7. Commentary on the *Tathasutta* (1097).

Regarding the seventh [verse], "therefore they are the Noble Truths": because they are suchness (*tathā*), non-falsehood (*avitatha*), and non-otherwise-ness (*anaññathā*), they are called the truths of the Noble Ones (*ariyasaccāni*). For the Noble Ones do not penetrate what is false as a Noble Truth.
8. Commentary on the *Lokasutta*.

1098. Regarding the eighth [discourse], they are called "Noble Truths" (*ariyasaccāni*) because they were penetrated and taught by the Noble One, the Tathāgata. Since they belong to the Noble One due to having been realized and taught by him, the meaning is that they are "Noble Truths" because they are the truths of the Noble One.

1100. In the tenth [discourse], *Sahañcanika*, [the phrase] means "in the city of Sahañcaniya. The passage beginning, "O monks, he who sees suffering also sees the origin of suffering," and so forth, is stated by way of a single penetration; for in this sutta, only a single penetration is discussed.
The Third Chapter: The Chapter on Koṭigāma.
4. The Chapter on the Sīsapā Grove. 1.
Commentary on the Sīsapāvana Sutta.
1101. Regarding the first part of the fourth [sutta], "namely, 'above'": these refer to those things mentioned above. "In the Sīsapā Grove" means in the grove of *Sīsapā* trees. 2.
Commentary on the *Khadirapatta-sutta* (The Khadira-Leaf Sutta) 1102.
In the second [sutta], "without having fully realized" (*anabhisamecca*) means not having attained through knowledge; the meaning is "not having penetrated."
3. Commentary on the Daṇḍa Sutta 1103.

Regarding the third [verse], "from this world to the next world": from this human world, they go to the next world—whether to hell, the animal realm, the sphere of hungry ghosts, the human world, or the deva world—repeatedly within the cycle of existence itself.
The meaning is "they are being produced. 5.
Commentary on the Sutta of the Hundred Spears (Sattisatasutta) 1105.

Regarding the fifth: "If it were thus, bhikkhus," means: "Bhikkhus, if this were to be so—that for one being struck incessantly by a hundred spears, the realization of the Truths would occur together with that very pain and mental distress. This is the meaning.
9. Commentary on the Indakhīla Sutta 1109.
Regarding the ninth [sutta], "looking at the face": they look at the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*). Here, "face" is intended to mean the underlying intention.
10. Commentary on the Vādatthika Sutta
1110. *Silāyūpa*: a stone pillar. *Soḷasakukkuka*: sixteen cubits (or *hattha*) in height. There is also a reading as *soḷasakukkū*.
*Heṭṭhā nemaṅgamā*: having entered into a pit at the bottom. *Aṭṭha kukku uparinemassa*:
eight cubits would stand rising above the rim of the pit. *Bhusā*: powerful. Everywhere else, the rest is self-evident.
The Fourth Chapter: The Sīsapā Grove.
5. The Chapter on the Precipice. 1.
Commentary on the Discourse on Worldly Reflections.
1111. "In the first [watch] of the fifth [night], at the lotus pond named Sumāgadhā": at the lotus pond bearing that name.
"Musing on worldly thoughts" means he sat down reflecting on such worldly concerns as: "By whom were the moon and sun made? By whom was the great earth made? By whom was the great ocean made?
By whom were sentient beings produced? By whom were the mountains, mangoes, palm trees, coconut trees, and so forth, created? Thus he sat musing on worldly thoughts.
"Viceto" means one whose mind has departed or whose mind is distracted. "He saw what was truly real" (bhūtaṃyeva addasa):

it is said that those asuras, having turned the Sambari-māyā around, resolved that he should see them just as that man saw them when they were mounting the elephants and horses, and entering through the openings of the lotus roots and stalks.
It is with reference to this that the Teacher said, "He saw what was truly real."
He said: "Deceiving even the gods" means causing the minds of the gods to be deluded. "Therefore" means because one who ponders worldly concerns becomes like a madman; therefore [it is said].
2–3. Commentary on the *Papāta-sutta* and others.

1112–13. In the second [simile], “a peak of eloquence” (*paṭibhānakūṭa*) refers to a single large boundary-stone resembling a mountain. In the third, “unpleasant form” (*aniṭṭharūpa*) means having an unpleasant nature.
4. Commentary on the *Kūṭāgāra-sutta* (Discourse on the Gabled House), 1114.
“Without having built the lower part of the house” means without having constructed the lower portion of the house by means of erecting pillars, building walls, laying foundations, and so forth.
5. Commentary on the Vālasutta 1115.
In the fifth [verse], "in the assembly hall" (*santhāgāre*) means in the hall for learning crafts. "Practicing archery" (*upāsanaṃ karonto*) means practicing the craft of shooting arrows.
"Missing the mark" (*asanaṃ atipātentī*) means letting the arrow pass beyond the target. "Arrow after arrow" (*poṅkhānupoṅkhaṃ*) means having shot one arrow...

Just as one arrow would pierce the notch of a first arrow, and another, called "following the notch," would pierce the notch of that second arrow, and yet another would pierce the notch of that [third], so did he see him shooting them.
"Yatra hi nāma" means "that it should indeed be so. "Durabhisambhavataṃ" means more difficult to achieve.
"One should pierce the tip with the tip of a hair split sevenfold" refers to a single hair.

The meaning is: having split [the arrow] into seven parts, taking one part, binding it to the middle of a wood-apple fruit (*vātiṅgaṇa*), and binding another part to the tip of the arrow, while standing at a distance of a bull’s length, one would pierce that tip bound to the wood-apple with the tip bound to the arrow.
"Therefore" means: because the Four Truths are thus difficult to penetrate, therefore.
7. Commentary on the First Sutta on the Hole and the Yoke (Paṭhamachiggaḷayugasuttavaṇṇanā) 1117.

Regarding the seventh [sutta], "mutual devouring" (aññamaññakhādikā) means eating one another. "Devouring the weak" (dubbalakhādikā) means the devouring of weak fish and other creatures by stronger fish and other creatures.
8. Commentary on the Second Sutta on the Hole and the Yoke (Dutiyachiggaḷayugasuttavaṇṇanā)

1118. "The great earth" (mahāpathavī) refers to the great earth within the interior of the world-system (cakkavāḷagabbha). "'This is a rare occurrence, venerable sir' (adhiccamidaṃ, bhante)" means that this is something arising by chance;
it implies: "If that yoke were not to rot, if the water in the ocean were not to dry up, and if that turtle were not to die—would it ever happen by mere chance? This is the meaning.
"In this way, monks, this is a matter of great chance": here, the Elder Mahāsīva demonstrates four "yokes.

For the acquisition of human birth is a matter of great chance, like the insertion of the neck of that blind turtle through the hole of a yoke cast by a man standing at the eastern rim of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*). [Likewise,] of a yoke cast by one standing at the southern rim of the world-system...
However, for one who has been whirled around and has reached the first yoke, the appearance of a Tathāgata—
like the insertion of a neck through a hole after having ascended from one hole to another— is an occurrence of extreme rarity.
But for one who has been whirled around and placed at the rim of the western world-system, reaching the second yoke and ascending from one hole to another through a hole...
The illumination of the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata is as difficult to achieve as threading a needle with a string that has climbed up its eye;
for it is like a string cast from the rim of the northern Cakkavāḷa, which, while revolving,
reaches the first three ages and then passes through the eye of a needle that has likewise climbed up the eye of a second needle positioned at the rim of the southern Cakkavāḷa.

The penetration of the Four Noble Truths should be understood as being exceedingly difficult to bring about. The ninth and subsequent [discourses] are exactly as described in the *Abhisamaya-saṃyutta*.
The fifth chapter, the "Chapter on the Precipice," is concluded.
6. Commentary on the "Chapter on Realization" (*Abhisamaya-vagga*).
1121. The Chapter on Realization (*Abhisamayavagga*) has already been explained in detail within the *Nidānavagga* in the *Abhisamayasaṃyutta*.
7. The First Sub-Chapter on Raw Grain (*Paṭhama-āmaka-dhañña-peyyālavagga*). 3. Commentary on the Fifty Discourses (*Paññāsutta-vaṇṇanā*).
1133. In the section on raw grain (*āmaka-dhañña-peyyāla*), "with the noble eye of wisdom" means with the eye of knowledge—both mundane and supramundane—beginning with insight (*vipassanā*).
4. Commentary on the Sutta on Liquor and Intoxicants (Surāmeraya-sutta) 1134.

Regarding the phrase "abstaining from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence": here, "fermented liquor" (*surā*) refers to flour-based liquor (*piṭṭhasurā*) and rice-based liquor (*odanasurā*).

There are five kinds [of intoxicants]: *pūvasurā* (fermented flour), *kiṇṇapakkhittā* (fermented grain), *sambhārasaṃyuttā* (compounded liquor), *merayaṃ* (distilled spirits), and *āsava* (spirituous liquor).
*Merayaṃ* refers to any kind of fermented liquor, such as flower-liquor or fruit-liquor. They become intoxicated by both of these, or by any other intoxicant apart from *surā* and *āsava*.
The volition (*cetanā*) by which they drink them is a basis for negligence (*pamādaṭṭhāna*), because it is a cause of negligence.
The meaning is: "named," that is, "abstaining from that. 6–7.
Commentary on the *Matteyyasutta* and others. 1136–37. *Matteyyā*:
meaning "beneficial to one's mother," that is, "properly behaved toward one's mother. Regarding *petteyyā* and the others: those who are beneficial to their father are *petteyyā*.
8–9. Commentary on the *Sāmañña-sutta* and others (1138–39).

*Sāmañña* means that which is beneficial for recluses (*samaṇa*). *Brahmañña* means that which is beneficial for brahmins (*brāhmaṇa*). These are designations specifically for those who have correctly entered upon the respective paths.
10. Commentary on the *Pacāyika-sutta*.
1140. "Honoring those who are senior in the family" (*kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino*) means honoring those who are senior in the family; the meaning is that they live in a humble manner.
8. The Second Subsection on Raw Grain. 8. Commentary on the Sutta on Seed-Fields (*Bījagāmasutta*).

1148. *Bījagāmabhūtagāmasamārambho*: This means abstaining from the destruction—by way of cutting, cooking, and so forth—of both the fivefold class of seeds, namely root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, crown-seeds, and seed-seeds, as well as any class of living beings (*bhūtagāma*) such as green grasses, trees, and the like.
It means refraining from their disturbance.
9. Commentary on the Discourse on Eating at Improper Times (Vikālabhojana-sutta-vaṇṇanā) 1149.
"Eating at improper times" means eating beyond the proper time; the meaning is the consumption of what is to be eaten during the day starting from the passing of midday.
10. Commentary on the Discourse on Perfumes and Ointments (Gandhavilepana-sutta-vaṇṇanā)
1150. Regarding "garlands" and so forth: "garland" refers to any kind of flower; "perfume" refers to any kind of fragrant substance; "ointment" refers to that which colors the skin.
In this context, those who wear them are said to "bear" them; those who fill out deficient parts are said to "adorn" them;
and those who take pleasure in them by way of their fragrance and their coloring of the skin are said to "beautify" themselves. "Occasion" (ṭhāna) means a cause.
Therefore, the meaning is: one abstains from that unwholesome volition (*dussīlya-cetanā*) by which the great multitude performs such acts as wearing garlands and so forth.
9. The Third Sub-chapter on Crude Grain (Āmaka-dhañña-peyyāla-vagga) 1. Commentary on the Discourse on Dancing and Singing (*Nacca-gīta-sutta-vaṇṇanā*)
1151. Because it is contrary to the Dispensation (*sāsana*), it is a sight that acts as an obstacle and a hindrance;

thus, it is called "the sight of frivolous displays" (*visūkadassana*). Furthermore, because there is the seeing of dances, songs, and instrumental music—whether performed by oneself through dancing, causing others to dance, and so forth, or even those occurring through the dancing of peacocks and the like—it is called "the sight of frivolous displays consisting of dancing, singing, and instrumental music. [The term] *naccādīni* refers to dancing and the rest.
Indeed, it is not permissible for either monks or nuns to use [such items] themselves, to have others use them, or even to witness their use.
2. Commentary on the Discourse on High Beds and Seats.
1152. "High bed" (*uccāsayana*) refers to that which exceeds the [prescribed] measure. "Large bed" (*mahāsayana*) refers to an unsuitable covering; the meaning is: abstaining from those. 3.
Commentary on the Discourse on Gold and Silver (Jātarūpasutta) 1153.
"Gold" (*jātarūpa*) means gold. "Silver" (*rajata*) means a *kahāpaṇa*—namely, a copper coin, a wax coin, or a wooden coin.

Those who engage in worldly commerce refrain from accepting both of these. The meaning is that they neither take it themselves nor cause others to take it, nor do they approve of what has been set aside for them.
4. Commentary on the Sutta on Raw Grain (*Āmakadhaññasutta*)
1154. “Accepting raw grain” means the acceptance of the seven kinds of raw grain, namely:
rice (*sāli*), paddy (*vīhi*), barley (*yava*), wheat (*godhuma*), millet (*kaṅgu*), panic seed (*varaka*), and kudrūsa grass.
Not only is the acceptance of these forbidden for monks, but even touching them is not permitted.
5. Commentary on the Discourse on Raw Meat (Āmakamaṃsasutta) 1155.

Regarding "the acceptance of raw meat": here, for monks, the acceptance of raw meat and fish—except when specifically authorized—is not permitted; however, the mere touching of them is not prohibited. 6.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Maiden (Kumārikasutta)

1156. Regarding "accepting women and girls": here, a "woman" refers to one who has gone over to another man; the other is called a "girl. Accepting them as well as touching them is indeed not allowable.
7. Commentary on the Discourse on Slaves (Dāsidāsasutta): 1157. Regarding "accepting female and male slaves":

here, accepting them specifically as slaves is not permitted; however, if it is said, "I give [her] as a servant for the purpose of providing what is allowable," or "I give [him] as a monastery attendant," then it is permitted.
10. The Fourth Subsection on the Summary of Raw Grain (Catuttha-āmaka-dhañña-peyyāla-vagga) 1.

Commentary on the Discourse on Fields and Land (Khettavatthu-sutta-vaṇṇanā) 1161. Regarding goats, sheep, and so forth, ending with fields and land, the method for what is allowable and what is unallowable is to be examined according to the Vinaya.
In this context, "field" (*khetta*) refers to that in which grain crops grow; "site" (*vatthu*) refers to that in which other crops grow.
Alternatively, that in which both grow is a field, while a plot of ground not yet cultivated for that purpose is a site.
Furthermore, by the terms "field" and "site," reservoirs and similar structures where crops are sown are also included.
2–3. Commentary on the Suttas on Buying and Selling, etc. (1162–63).
"Buying and selling" (*kayavikkaya*) means both buying (*kaya*) and selling (*vikkaya*). "Messengership" (*dūteyya*) refers to the work of a messenger;
it means going here and there after receiving a letter or a message from householders. "Going as an errand" (*pahiṇagamana*) refers to one who has been sent from one house to another.
"Going on a minor errand. "Engagement" means performing both of those tasks. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as "engaging in going on errands as a messenger.
4. Commentary on the Sutta on False Scales (Tulākūṭasutta)
1164. Regarding "fraud" (*kūṭa*) in the context of fraud with scales (*tulākūṭa*) and so forth, it means deception. Therein, fraud with scales is fourfold:

fraud regarding the form (*rūpakūṭa*), fraud regarding the parts (*aṅgakūṭa*), fraud regarding the grasping (*gahaṇakūṭa*), and concealed fraud (*paṭicchannakūṭa*). Among these, "fraud regarding the form" refers to making two scales appear identical in appearance;
when taking [goods], one uses the larger scale, but when giving, one uses the smaller. "Fraud regarding the parts" refers to...
When taking [the weight], one steps on the scale with the hand at the rear; when giving, one does so at the front.
"Deceit by taking" means that while taking, one grasps the rope at the base, whereas when giving, one grasps it at the tip.
"Concealed deceit" means making the scale hollow and filling the interior with iron filings; then, when taking, one places it at the rear, and when giving, at the front.
*Kaṃsa* means a golden bowl; cheating by means of that is *kaṃsakūṭa*. How so? Having made one golden bowl, they make two or three other bowls of bronze with a golden color.
Then, having gone to the countryside and entered some wealthy family, they say, "Buy golden vessels," and when asked the price, they offer them at a lower price [than the true gold].

When they wish to give [the bowls] away, and those [people] ask, "How is it to be known whether these are gold?", they say, "Take them after testing them," and having struck the golden bowl against a stone, they give all the bowls and depart.
Fraudulent measuring (mānakūṭa) is of three kinds: by breaking the heart, by breaking the crest, and by breaking the cord. Among these, breaking the heart—
The "measuring by dripping" (*sappitelādi-minana*) occurs at the time of measuring ghee, oil, and the like.

For one who takes these, having said "pour slowly," measures by means of a vessel with a hole at the bottom, causing much to flow out into the container; whereas one who gives them closes the hole and gives quickly so as to fill it.
The "breaking of the peak" (*sikhābheda*) occurs at the time of measuring sesame, rice, and the like. For one who takes these [measures] the peak slowly...
He takes it after having raised it up; when giving, he gives with such haste that he breaks the crest [of the boundary].
The breaking of the cord occurs at the time of measuring out fields and lands. For those who do not receive a bribe measure out a small field as being large.
5. Commentary on the Sutta on Reopening.
1165. Regarding "bribery" (*ukkoṭana*) and so forth: "bribery" is the taking of a bribe to turn an owner into a non-owner.
"Deceit" (*vañcana*) is the cheating of others by various means. Here is one story: It seems a certain hunter was coming along carrying both a deer and a fawn.
A certain rogue asked him, "Sir, what is the price of the deer? What is the price of the fawn? He replied.

When it was said, "The deer is worth two kahāpaṇas, and the fawn is worth one," he paid a kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, and after walking a short distance, turned back and said, "Sir, I have no need for the fawn; give me the deer.
"In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas. "But sir, did I not already give you one kahāpaṇa? "Yes, it was given."
"Take this young deer as well; thus there will be two kahāpaṇas—the kahāpaṇa itself and this young deer worth a kahāpaṇa.
Perceiving that "he is stating a reason," he took the young deer and gave it for the deer.
A "deceiver" (nikatī) is one who, by means of trickery or deceit, calls a non-girdle a girdle, a non-jewel a jewel, or what is not gold [gold].
“Making gold” refers to deception by means of a counterfeit. “Crooked practice” (*sāciyoga*) means crooked application;
this is a name for those very things such as reopening settled cases (*ukkoṭana*) and so forth. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows:

crooked practice through reopening cases, crooked practice through deception, and crooked practice through guile (*nikati*). Some say that “crooked practice” is the exchange of one thing for another while showing something else; however, that is already included within deception itself.
6–11. Commentary on the *Chedana-sutta* and others (1166–71).

Regarding "cutting" (*chedana*) and the following terms: "cutting" refers to the amputation of hands and so forth. "Slaying" (*vadha*) means death. "Binding" (*bandha*) refers to confinement by means of ropes and the like.
"Robbery" (*viparāmosa*) is of two kinds: robbery by snow and robbery by thickets. That which occurs during the time of a snowfall...
When they deceive people traveling on a road by concealing themselves with snow, this is "deception by snow" (*himaviparāmoso*).
When they deceive them by concealing themselves in thickets and the like, this is "deception by a thicket" (*gumbaviparāmoso*).
"Looting" (*ālopa*) refers to the act of plundering villages, market towns, and so forth. "Violence" (*sahasākāra*) means a rash or forceful act; [for example], having entered a house...
Placing a weapon upon the chests of human beings and taking desired goods [constitute theft]. Thus, they abstain from cutting, killing, binding, robbing, plundering, and acts of violence.
The rest is clear in meaning throughout.
The commentary on raw grain, fermented liquor, and salt is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the Mahāvagga of the Saṃyutta Nikāya Aṭṭhakathā, titled the Sāratthappakāsinī.
The Concluding Discourse.
To this extent:

"In order to compose a commentary on the meaning of the excellent *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, for those ascetics who are of great service and possess intelligence skilled in the practice of insight (*vipassanā*)."
“Desiring that the True Dhamma endure for a long time,
I have composed this subtle commentary named the *Sāratthappakāsinī*.
For it has been completed by extracting the essence from the Great Commentary (*Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*).”
By way of recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*), there are seventy-eight [sections] for the Pāḷi.
Furthermore, since the *Visuddhimagga* consists of fifty-nine recitation sections,
it was composed for the purpose of elucidating the meaning of the scriptures.
“Therefore, including that companion commentary, by counting the recitation sections (*bhāṇavāra*),
there are one hundred and thirty-seven, not yet complete. Thus,
the measure is one hundred and thirty-seven recitation sections.”
To those who dwell in the Mahāvihāra, who proclaim the *samaya*: "By me,
in composing this work having extracted the essence of the *Mūlaṭṭhakathā*,
whatever merit has been accumulated— by that, may the entire world be happy."
For the purpose of composing this work, the Elder Bhadanta Jotipāla—
possessing pure virtue and manifesting wisdom through well-spoken words— requested me,
who desires the prosperity of the Dispensation and is endowed with auspicious qualities.
"May all people become happy by whatever merit has been attained [thereby].
[This was written] by one adorned with supreme purity of faith, wisdom, and energy; endowed with a multitude of virtues such as virtue, conduct, speed, and gentleness;
capable of plunging into the depths of both his own and other systems; possessed of analytical discernment; and [versed] in the various divisions of the scriptural tradition of the Tipiṭaka.

In the Teacher’s Dispensation together with its commentaries, there were the Elders dwelling at the Mahāvihāra—lamps of the lineage of elders whose intellects were firmly established in the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) adorned with various qualities such as the six direct knowledges (chaḷabhiññā) and surrounded by the analytical knowledges (patisambhidā);
who were pre-eminent among speakers, great poets, and masters of exposition; who possessed the splendor of unimpeded wisdom;
and who were endowed with the grace of sweet, noble, and eloquent speech arising from the perfection of their literary skill.
This commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya, titled the *Sāratthappakāsinī*, was composed by the Elder named Buddhaghosa—
so called by his teachers— who was an ornament to the lineage and possessed vast, purified intelligence.
“May it remain as long as there exist in the world those seeking to cross over the world...”
Showing the way for sons of noble family toward the purification of virtue:
"As long as even the mere name 'Buddha'— belonging to the Pure-Minded One,
the Tathāgata, the World-Chief, the Great Sage— is current in the world."
The commentary on the Saṃyutta Nikāya,
entitled the Sāratthappakāsinī, is thus completed in every respect.
